questions.q: Your report subagent writes correct reports, yet every run makes exactly 40 API calls, its guard limit. In the trace, the first 6 responses have `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and their tools run. From response 7 on, each one has `stop_reason: "end_turn"`, no tool calls and the same report text. The debug log prints `continue=True` on all 40 passes. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The system prompt never says that the subagent should stop working once its report has been written.
The guard is set far too high, so a run has room to continue long after the useful work has ended.
The continue check tests a value saved earlier, not the signal on the newest response received.
The tool results are not reaching the model, so it keeps repeating its report and cannot move past it.
questions.explain: The model signalled `end_turn` at response 7, but the code still reports `continue=True`, so the check is not reading each new `stop_reason`. A blames the model, which had already stopped. B only limits the waste and leaves the guard as the real stop. D does not fit, since the report is correct and the model finished.
bullets: The loop lifecycle: send a request, read stop_reason, run the requested tools, return the results, repeat
Control flow that continues on stop_reason tool_use and ends on end_turn
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: The document analysis subagent gained a third tool last week. Since then about 30% of runs fail with a 400: `tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after`. The failing traces all show a response with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and three `tool_use` blocks, followed by a user message with one `tool_result`. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The loop handles a single block per response, but every `tool_use` block needs its own `tool_result`.
Each of the three results has to travel in its own user message, and the loop merged them into just one.
The tool definitions now exceed what one request can hold, so the API drops the later `tool_use` blocks.
The text block ahead of the tool calls has to be removed from the assistant turn before the next request.
questions.explain: One response can carry several `tool_use` blocks, and each one needs a matching `tool_result` in the next user message; the trace shows three calls and one result. B is backwards, since all results belong together in a single user message. C invents a limit, and the trace shows all three blocks arriving. D is wrong because the assistant turn goes back as it came, and text ahead of a tool call is normal.
bullets: The loop lifecycle: send a request, read stop_reason, run the requested tools, return the results, repeat
Adding tool results to the context between iterations so new information reaches the model

questions.q: A new developer adds an `issue_replacement` tool to a manual support loop and tests it. Claude responds with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and a block holding the right order number, the code logs the response, and the script exits. No replacement ever appears in the order system. What is the actual problem?
opts: The tool description is too short, so Claude is unsure the replacement is really meant to be issued.
`tool_choice` is left on `auto`, and it must be set to `any` before Claude is able to execute a tool.
Claude's service account lacks write access to the order system, so its update was rejected silently.
Claude only asks for the call; the application must run the tool and send a `tool_result` back.
questions.explain: Tool use is a contract: the model emits a structured request and your code runs the operation, then returns the result on the next request. A is wrong because Claude picked the tool with correct arguments. B misreads `tool_choice`, which affects whether a tool is called, not who runs it. C assumes Claude touches the backend itself, which it never does.
bullets: The loop lifecycle: send a request, read stop_reason, run the requested tools, return the results, repeat
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: To cut latency on your support agent, an engineer proposes a shortcut: when Claude requests `lookup_order`, the code runs it and shows the order record straight to the customer, skipping the next model call. Logs show that after a lookup, about 40% of conversations go on to `process_refund` or `escalate_to_human`. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Accept it: records from the backend are authoritative, so the model adds nothing after a lookup.
Reject it: Claude has to receive that output in order to work out what the case needs next.
Reject it: raw records read poorly in chat, so a model should always rewrite them for customers.
Accept it for plain status questions, using a keyword check on each message to pick those out.
questions.explain: The loop is not finished when a tool runs: the output goes back so the model can reason about the next action, and here 40% of cases need one. A confuses accurate data with a decision about what to do next. C reaches the right verdict for a minor reason; a formatting template would answer it, and the next action would still be lost. D replaces the model's reasoning with a keyword rule.
bullets: The loop lifecycle: send a request, read stop_reason, run the requested tools, return the results, repeat
Tool results are added to the conversation history so the model can reason about its next action
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: A test-fixing agent runs the suite through `Bash`. To keep history small, a helper replaces each test output with just `exit code 1` before adding it as the tool result. Since then the agent edits unrelated files in 35% of runs and often re-runs the suite with no change. Its reasoning says it cannot tell which test failed. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: `Bash` is an unreliable way to run tests, and a dedicated test tool would give the agent steadier results.
The model can only reason from what reaches its history, and the helper removed the failure details.
The model is too weak for debugging work, and a higher-tier model would work out which test had failed.
The system prompt lacks an instruction to read the test output with care before it edits any of the files.
questions.explain: Tool results are how new information reaches the next decision, and the failing test's name never arrived; the agent even says so. A blames a tool that ran correctly. C expects a better model to recover facts it was never given. D tells the model to read carefully, but the output is no longer there to read.
bullets: Tool results are added to the conversation history so the model can reason about its next action
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your web search subagent must `search`, then `fetch_source` using URLs from the search results. To shrink requests, the loop keeps only the latest `tool_use` and `tool_result` pair in history. The agent now searches again before nearly every fetch, tripling its calls, and its citations sometimes point at the wrong URL. Which change is most effective?
opts: Hard-code each run in code to alternate one search with one fetch, so that the order can never drift.
Instruct the agent, through its prompt, to memorise each URL and avoid searching one topic twice.
Switch this subagent to a higher-capacity model, so that URLs from past searches are recalled reliably.
Keep earlier tool results in history, and trim their verbose fields instead of dropping whole results.
questions.explain: Each iteration should build on all earlier results, and dropping them removes the URLs the next step needs. Trimming unneeded fields still meets the goal of smaller requests. A swaps model-driven reasoning for a fixed order and still loses the URLs. B asks the model to remember what is no longer in its context. C does not help, because the loop is deleting the data, whatever the window size.

questions.q: Customers often hold several orders, and your support agent calls `get_customer`, reads the returned order list, then calls `lookup_order` for the one that matches the complaint. To save a round trip, an engineer proposes making the agent request both tools together in its first response. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Keep two iterations: the second call's input depends on what the first one returns.
Adopt it: the model can infer a likely order number from what the customer has said.
Adopt it: code can fill in the order number on the second call once the first returns.
Adopt it: parallel calls run faster, and a wrong order can be corrected in a later turn.
questions.explain: Choosing the order requires reasoning over the list, and that list exists only once the first result is in the history. B has the model guess an identifier before it has the data. C moves the choice into code, which cannot match a complaint to an order the way the model can. D accepts lookups on wrong orders as a cost of speed, and the saving is lost to correction turns.
bullets: Tool results are added to the conversation history so the model can reason about its next action

questions.q: Your web research subagent always runs search, then fetches the top three hits, then summarises. On niche topics only 2 of 10 hits are relevant, so one fetch in three is noise; on simple topics the first search already answers the question, yet three pages are fetched anyway. Which redesign best addresses both problems?
opts: Add branches keyed on hit count and topic type, so the code picks the right number of fetches per run.
Have Claude write its complete tool plan at the start, and then execute that plan without any revisions.
Give Claude the goal and tools in a loop, so each next call is chosen from what the last result showed.
Raise the fixed fetch count to ten, so that a relevant page is nearly always among those that are read.
questions.explain: The right next step depends on what the last result contained, so the choice belongs with the model inside the loop. A grows a decision tree that still cannot read the results. B is still a fixed sequence, only written earlier, and it is set before any result exists. D makes the noise and the waste on simple topics worse.
bullets: Model-driven decisions (Claude picks the next tool from context) versus fixed decision trees or tool sequences
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: A legacy-system assistant classifies each ticket as build, test or runtime, then follows that category's fixed tool order: for example `Grep`, then `Read`, then `Bash`. Results reach the model correctly. In a review of 300 runs, 28% reached a wrong conclusion, and in most of those the first `Read` had pointed at a generated config that the fixed order never opened. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The next step was fixed before the results existed, so what `Read` revealed could not change the route.
Three categories are too few, and a larger trained classifier would have sent these tickets to better paths.
`Grep` returned too few matches for the agent to find the config, so a better search tool is needed first.
The model lost the `Read` output between iterations, because the tool results were not reaching its history.
questions.explain: The failing runs found the lead and could not follow it, because the order was set in advance. B adds more fixed paths, and new categories still cannot react to a result. C blames `Grep`, yet the first `Read` had already reached the lead. D contradicts the stem, which says results reached the model.
bullets: Model-driven decisions (Claude picks the next tool from context) versus fixed decision trees or tool sequences

questions.q: Each new microservice needs the same four steps: render the service template, add the standard config, add the CI file, run the linter. Over 400 past runs, the steps never changed and the order never mattered to any result; lint failures simply stop the job for an engineer. Which design fits this task best?
opts: A model-driven loop with every tool available, because letting Claude choose is always more reliable.
A coordinator with four subagents, one per step, so that each step gets its own focused context.
A model-driven loop with an extra instruction listing the four steps that it should always follow.
A fixed sequence of the four steps, because nothing here depends on judging an earlier result.
questions.explain: Model-driven choice earns its place when the next step depends on what was just learned; here the path is known in advance, so a fixed sequence is simpler and repeatable. A overrates autonomy, since there is nothing to decide. B adds orchestration to four predictable steps. C pays for reasoning and then tells the model what to do anyway, with only a prompt holding the order.
bullets: Model-driven decisions (Claude picks the next tool from context) versus fixed decision trees or tool sequences

questions.q: A monthly dependency-upgrade agent must update the lockfile, run the tests, repair anything that broke, then open a pull request. The first, second and last steps never vary. Repairs vary widely: some need one import changed, others need several files read and a changelog checked. Which design is most effective?
opts: Let Claude choose every step in one open loop, so the whole job adapts to each repository.
Fix the outer stages in code, and run a model-driven loop for the repair stage alone.
Fix all stages in code, and give the repair stage three scripted retries of one prompt.
Fix all stages in code, and map each known test error message to a stored repair recipe.
questions.explain: Each part gets the control it needs: the stages are known in advance, and only the repair depends on what each result reveals. A gives up a repeatable order for steps that hold no decision. C repeats the same attempt without letting the model investigate. D is a decision tree, which fails on any error it has not seen.
bullets: Model-driven decisions (Claude picks the next tool from context) versus fixed decision trees or tool sequences
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: Your report subagent's loop is written `while response.stop_reason != "end_turn"`. In 6% of runs it reaches its 25-call guard. The traces show `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` from about the fourth call on, with no `tool_use` blocks, so the loop finds nothing to run and sends the request again. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Raise the guard from 25 calls to 100, so that long reports have more chances of reaching `end_turn`.
Raise `max_tokens` for this subagent and leave the loop condition just as it is written today.
Loop only while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`, then branch on whichever other value ended the loop.
Exit the loop as soon as a response contains any text, and treat that text as the finished report.
questions.explain: Looping until `end_turn` retries every other stop reason, including ones with no tool to run. The loop should continue only on `tool_use`, and any other value exits and gets handled. A lets the same request repeat for longer. B helps this one stop reason, but a refusal would spin the same way. D is the text-as-completion anti-pattern and would also accept the truncated output.
bullets: Control flow that continues on stop_reason tool_use and ends on end_turn
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: A legacy-code explainer answers one-file questions well. On questions that span several modules, about 30% of answers end with "Next I will read the billing module", and nothing follows. In those runs the second response has `stop_reason: "tool_use"`, its `Read` call never executes, and the code returns that response's text. What is the most effective change?
opts: Raise `max_tokens`, so that the second response has enough room to finish the whole explanation.
Instruct the agent, through its prompt, to collect all it needs within its opening response.
Set `tool_choice` to `any` on every request, so that the agent always carries on working to the end.
Replace the single tool pass with a loop that repeats until a response stops asking for tools.
questions.explain: The model asked for another tool and the code did not honour it, so tool handling has to repeat for as long as `stop_reason` is `tool_use`. A treats this as truncation, which would show `max_tokens`. B asks for a fixed amount of work up front, although each read decides the next. C misreads the setting: forcing a tool on every request means the model can never give its final text answer.
bullets: Control flow that continues on stop_reason tool_use and ends on end_turn
The loop lifecycle: send a request, read stop_reason, run the requested tools, return the results, repeat

questions.q: A repository summariser has five tools, but small repositories need only two of them. An engineer proposes that after `stop_reason: "end_turn"` the code should check whether every tool was used and, if not, send another request asking for the rest. Runs currently finish with good summaries. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Reject it: `end_turn` means Claude has finished, and which tools it needs is its own decision.
Accept it, because a run cannot be complete until each registered tool has been called at least once.
Accept it, but limit it to three extra requests so that the additional tool calls stay under control.
Reject it, and instead hard-code the five tools in a fixed order so that each run uses all of them.
questions.explain: The loop ends on `end_turn`, and Claude chooses tools from the task, so unused tools are not a defect. B treats the tool list as a checklist. C keeps the same mistake with a limit on it. D also ignores what each repository needs, by forcing a fixed sequence.
bullets: Control flow that continues on stop_reason tool_use and ends on end_turn
Model-driven decisions (Claude picks the next tool from context) versus fixed decision trees or tool sequences

questions.q: Your document analysis subagent has 30 seconds per round and runs four `fetch_paper` calls concurrently, each taking about 20 seconds. As each finishes, its output is appended to a list, and the list is zipped with the response's `tool_use` blocks to build the `tool_result` blocks. No errors appear, but 7% of reports credit findings to the wrong paper. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Run the fetches one at a time, so outputs always come back in the order the blocks appear in.
Add a step where the synthesis agent checks each citation against the source papers before it writes.
Record each call's `id` when it starts, and set that value as the `tool_use_id` on its own result.
Instruct the model through the system prompt to fetch one paper per response, which avoids any mix-ups.
questions.explain: The results are paired by finish order, so a fast paper can land on another call's id, and the model then reasons from mislabelled evidence. The id is what ties a result to its call. A would take about 80 seconds, well over the 30-second budget. B blames a later agent, which has to catch errors the loop created. D relies on a prompt and also gives up parallel calls.

questions.q: A scaffolding agent's migration step fails in 12% of runs with `column already exists`. Today the code ends the run on any failed tool call and pages an engineer. In 50 paged runs, 34 needed only a small next step, such as checking the schema and skipping that migration. Which change is most effective?
opts: Have the code retry the failed command three times before it pages an engineer about the run.
Send the failure text back as an error result, so the agent can decide on its own next step.
Report the step to the agent as a success with empty output, so that the run can carry on.
Add a table in code that maps each known database error to the fix that should be applied.
questions.explain: A failure is new information too: once it reaches the history, the model can check the schema and adapt, and the instructive error text tells it what happened. A repeats a command that will fail the same way. C hides the failure, so the model builds on a step that did not work. D is a fixed decision table that takes the reasoning away from the model and covers only known errors.
bullets: Adding tool results to the context between iterations so new information reaches the model
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A research subagent repeats each `search_archive` call up to five times, then reports that the archive had no usable data. The archive's own logs show every query returning 20 or more matching records. In the conversation history, each of those calls has the same tool result: `status: ok`. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Expand the tool description, so the agent understands what kind of data the archive gives back.
Cap `search_archive` at one call per run, so that the agent moves on to its other sources sooner.
Tell the model in the prompt to trust the archive and to stop searching after the first attempt.
Return the matched records themselves as the tool result, in place of the bare status line.
questions.explain: The search worked, but only a status line reached the history, so the model had no new information to reason from. A explains the tool better while the records stay missing. B stops the repeats and still gives the model nothing. C asks the model to trust data it never received.
bullets: Adding tool results to the context between iterations so new information reaches the model
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your support agent is told to write `ROUTE: human` when a case needs a person, and a regex in the loop hands the conversation over when it sees that string. In 3% of cases the reply says something like "no need to ROUTE: human yet" and the case is handed over wrongly. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Have the agent call `escalate_to_human`, so the handover is a tool call and not a string in prose.
Tighten the regex so that the marker only counts when it sits alone on the last line of the reply.
Add a system prompt rule that forbids mentioning the marker unless a handover is truly intended.
Run a second model call that reads each reply and judges whether it truly means to hand the case over.
questions.explain: A control decision hidden in free text is a sign that it belongs in a tool call, which is structured and unambiguous. B keeps parsing language and only moves the failure to new wordings. C asks a prompt to protect a parser, which reduces the misses without ending them. D adds a second model and more cost to paper over a signal that should have been structured.

questions.q: A nightly boilerplate job on the Agent SDK sets `max_turns=12`, and its script catches all exceptions and keeps the last assistant text as the finished work. About 11% of repositories are left half-generated, yet the dashboard shows every run as done. Most repositories need 6 to 10 turns, and a few need 20 or more. Your lead wants the limit raised. How should you evaluate that?
opts: Raise `max_turns` to 200 for all repositories, so that no run can reach the limit in the first place.
Require the agent to end with the word COMPLETE, and have the script search the final text for that word.
Check the result `subtype`, and resume `error_max_turns` runs with a higher limit; 12 is only a guard.
Lower `max_turns` to 8 and split each repository into several jobs, so every job stays within the cap.

A removes the guard and the script would still trust any last text. B goes back to parsing language for completion. D treats the cap as the design driver and still cannot tell finished work from cut-off work.

questions.q: An engineer ran your Agent SDK assistant on "improve test coverage across this repo", and it worked for hours and ran up a large bill. Your manager proposes `max_turns=10` on every run as the way to stop this. Normal bug-fix tasks need 30 to 50 turns. How should you evaluate the proposal?

Reject it: let runs end when Claude finishes, with a `max_budget_usd` guard whose error you handle.
Reject it: have code stop the run as soon as any tool call repeats, since repeats show lost progress.
Accept it, and have Claude state its progress each turn, so code can extend the cap when work remains.

A looks reasonable but keeps a cap as the main stop, and open-ended runs would still end cut off. C stops valid work, since re-running tests is a repeated call. D keeps the cap too low and parses language to decide whether to go on.

questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: To remove a step, your document analysis subagents now save findings to a shared folder, and the synthesis subagent reads whatever is there when a 10-minute timer ends. Since the change, 9% of reports silently lack one document. Synthesis is told how many documents to expect and logs the shortfall, but nothing acts on it. In each case an analysis subagent crashed, and its error appears in that subagent's own log only. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Analysis subagents have no local retry, so one crash ends the work with no second attempt.
Exchanges skip the coordinator, so nothing able to recover ever hears about a failure.
Synthesis is not told how many documents to expect, so a short set looks complete to it.
The 10-minute timer is too short, so synthesis starts before slower analysis runs finish.
questions.explain: Crashes stay in one log because the exchange goes around the coordinator, the agent meant to see failures and decide on recovery. A could help with brief faults, but a lasting failure would still go unseen. C is ruled out because synthesis already knows the count and logs the shortfall, yet it cannot re-delegate. D is ruled out because these subagents crashed and would never have delivered.

Add a step that compares each new reply with earlier ones and holds any that appears to contradict them.
Return outcomes and errors to the coordinator, and let it compose the one reply that is sent.

questions.q: In a chat with your research coordinator, a user says: "only use sources from 2022 onward." What is the most likely root cause?

Subagents do read the chat, but they give more weight to the prompt than to old turns.
The spawn prompt omitted the rule; the subagent sees none of the parent's chat or prompt.
The search tool ranks by relevance alone, so older pages keep appearing whatever the request says.

questions.q: Your support coordinator verifies the customer and finds the order, then spawns a returns subagent with the prompt "handle this return." In 22% of cases the subagent asks the customer for an order number they already gave, and the customers complain. What is the most effective fix?

Tell the returns subagent in its definition not to ask customers to repeat any detail.
Have the subagent call `lookup_order` first, before it asks the customer for anything.
Copy the coordinator's system prompt into the returns subagent's own system prompt.

C cannot work without the order number or customer ID, which is what the subagent lacks. D copies standing instructions and none of this customer's facts.

questions.q: Your coordinator's gap check tells it to "list the pages each search subagent opened" before deciding what to do next. The subagents' final reports contain only a findings summary. Audits show 15% of the listed URLs were never opened by anyone, though each subagent's own transcript looks correct. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The search subagents log opened pages under the wrong URL in their own transcripts.
The coordinator's context filled up, so older tool results were dropped before the check.
The coordinator received the tool results, but parallel runs got their URLs mixed up.
Each report is all it receives from a subagent, so it filled the list in by itself.
questions.explain: A subagent's tool calls stay inside its own context, so the coordinator had no URLs to list and supplied some itself. The fix is to require the URLs in each final report. A is ruled out, as the transcripts look correct. B assumes the results reached the coordinator, which they never did. C would give real URLs against the wrong subagent, not URLs nobody opened.
bullets: Subagents run with isolated context and do not automatically receive the coordinator's conversation history
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A legacy audit tool has security, performance and dependency subagents, and the engineer receives their three final reports joined end to end. Reviewers find the same slow query flagged three times, with two conflicting recommendations and no overall priority. Each report is accurate for its own area. Which change is most effective?
opts: Define one severity scale in all three subagents' prompts, so that the reports rank alike.
Have the coordinator merge the three outputs and settle any conflicts before delivery.
Run the subagents in sequence, so each one sees earlier findings and skips any repeats.
Replace the specialists with one general audit subagent that writes one combined report.
questions.explain: Combining results is part of the coordinator's job, and here it is skipped while each specialist does its part. A makes rankings comparable but leaves the duplicates and the conflicting advice. C adds delay to independent work and still leaves nobody to settle a conflict. D gives up the specialisation that made each report accurate.
bullets: The coordinator's job: break the task down, delegate, combine results, and pick subagents according to query complexity
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Customers often write messages like "refund order 118 and change the address on order 204." Logs for such chats show your support coordinator spawning one subagent with the customer's message as its prompt. In 18% of them the refund is done, the address is unchanged, and the case closes as resolved. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Spawn every subagent with the full message, so that each one can act on its own part.
Broaden the billing subagent's tools, so that it can also make any account changes.
Have the coordinator break out each ask, delegate them, then combine the outcomes.
Check with the customer before closing, so that any open request is caught at that point.
questions.explain: Breaking a message into parts, delegating each and combining the outcomes is the coordinator's role, and the logs show one subagent handed everything. A brings back the full pipeline and risks two subagents acting on one request. B over-provisions a specialist. D relies on the customer to find the gap and works against first-contact resolution.
bullets: The coordinator's job: break the task down, delegate, combine results, and pick subagents according to query complexity
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your research coordinator has the Task tool and also `web_search`, added for quick checks. Its prompt already tells it to delegate searches, yet in 45% of runs it does the searching itself. Its context then fills with raw pages, and it ends up giving subagents shorter briefs and losing details from earlier results. Which change best restores its role?
opts: Strengthen the prompt's delegation wording, and add examples of searches that go to subagents.
Have the coordinator summarise each raw page as soon as its own search returns.
Switch the coordinator to a bigger context window, so that raw pages fit more easily.
Remove `web_search` from the coordinator, so findings come via subagents only.
questions.explain: The coordinator should decompose, delegate and combine, and removing the tool makes delegation the only route while keeping raw pages out of its context. A adds more prompt guidance to a rule that already fails 45% of the time, while removing the tool guarantees the route (guidance would be the first step only if no rule existed yet). B spends the coordinator's context on a specialist's work. C leaves it doing that work too, with more room.
bullets: The coordinator's job: break the task down, delegate, combine results, and pick subagents according to query complexity
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: An engineer asks your code exploration agent to "find everywhere we store customer email addresses." The coordinator's log shows three assignments: the users service, the orders service and the billing service. All three subagents report accurately. A compliance review later finds the addresses also sit in nightly export jobs and in a support tool. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Those places appear in none of the assignments, so nobody was sent to search them.
The explorer subagents' `Grep` patterns were too strict to match the address fields in other code.
The summary step discarded the matches found in the export jobs before it reached the engineer.
The explorer subagents use too small a model to follow references out of their assigned services.
questions.explain: The log shows the gap in the assignments: nobody was asked to look outside three services, while each subagent did its own job well. B blames patterns that were never run on that code. C assumes matches existed, but no agent searched there. D expects a subagent to go beyond its brief, which is the wrong place for scope to be set.
bullets: Decomposition that is too narrow leaves parts of a broad research topic uncovered
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Reports on "how cities adapt to extreme heat" cover tree canopy and cool roofs but not health, housing or water. Your lead proposes doubling search subagents from 3 to 6. In a trial, sources rose from 40 to 85, and the coordinator's log listed subtasks such as street trees, roof coatings and canopy surveys; 2 of 8 expected areas were covered, as before. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Accept it, and add a gap check in synthesis to flag areas that remain missing.
Accept it, and let synthesis fill any remaining gaps from general knowledge.
Reject it: extra agents do not help while the assigned subtasks stay this narrow.
Reject it: widen each search subagent's queries so that each covers all eight areas.
questions.explain: Doubling the agents doubled the sources and left coverage at 2 of 8, and the log shows why: every subtask sits in the same two areas. A only reports the gap after paying for six agents. B fills it with unsourced text. D makes subagents stray beyond their assignments and leaves the decomposition as it was.
bullets: Decomposition that is too narrow leaves parts of a broad research topic uncovered
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your research system's dashboard shows 99% subtask success, yet readers rate 30% of reports as incomplete. A sample shows those reports omit whole areas that the request named. Your manager wants to know whether the system is healthy. How should you evaluate it?
opts: Review a sample of subagent outputs for accuracy, and treat it as healthy if they hold up.
Score each report against its request's areas; subtask success does not measure scope.
Have each subagent rate its own completeness, then average that into a coverage figure.
Track sources per report, as a high count would suggest that coverage is sufficient.
questions.explain: Subtasks can all succeed while the set of subtasks misses part of the request, so coverage must be measured against the request itself. A checks the quality of assigned work, which may be fine. C uses self-assessment, and a subagent cannot see what it was never assigned. D counts volume, which can pile up in one narrow area.
bullets: Decomposition that is too narrow leaves parts of a broad research topic uncovered
Refinement loops: evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries, re-run synthesis until coverage is enough
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your support coordinator's prompt lists the billing, returns and account subagents as the standard handling for a ticket. Finance finds that 2% of billing-only tickets led to return labels nobody asked for. The traces show the returns subagent locating the order and starting a return, as its own instructions say. What is the root cause?
opts: Billing did not tell the returns subagent that no return was needed for this ticket.
The returns subagent's `description` is too vague for it to recognise its own tickets.
The coordinator invokes returns without checking that the request involves one.
The returns subagent's model misjudges these tickets, so a stronger model is needed.
questions.explain: The returns subagent acted correctly on a ticket it should not have received, so the coordinator needs to choose by what each ticket requires. A adds a link between subagents to patch the routing. B is wrong because a `description` guides the coordinator's choice, and this coordinator follows a standing list. D blames a model that did what it was told.
bullets: Coordinators that analyse each query and choose which subagents to invoke, instead of always running the full pipeline
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: A classifier labels each query simple or complex before your coordinator starts, and the label fixes the subagent list for that run. In 12% of simple runs, the search results reveal conflicting figures, but analysis is not on the list, so the report just states one figure. Which design best addresses this?
opts: Retrain the classifier on more examples, so that fewer of these queries are labelled as simple.
Add a third, medium label to the classifier with its own fixed list of subagents for the run.
Run all four subagents on every query, so that analysis is never left out when it is needed.
Let the coordinator pick each next subagent from what the latest result actually showed.
questions.explain: The need for analysis only became visible in the search results, so the choice has to be made as results arrive. A and B still decide before any result exists. C brings back the full pipeline, with its cost on every simple query.
bullets: Coordinators that analyse each query and choose which subagents to invoke, instead of always running the full pipeline
The coordinator's job: break the task down, delegate, combine results, and pick subagents according to query complexity
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: Since a model upgrade, your developer agent's coordinator spawns two subagents for single-file edits that one tool call could finish, and those tasks now take four times as long. It still does well on wide multi-service investigations, where delegation clearly helps. What should you configure first?
opts: Add guidance to the coordinator on when to delegate and when to work directly.
Remove the Task tool from `allowedTools`, so that the coordinator can never spawn.
Set a low `maxTurns` on each subagent definition, so that the spawned runs end sooner.
Build a router in code that counts files in each request and picks a path from that.
questions.explain: Telling the coordinator when subagents are and are not warranted keeps wide investigations and stops small ones being delegated, and it is the smallest change. B removes the delegation you want to keep. C cuts subagents short but they still spawn. D adds a layer of infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.
bullets: Coordinators that analyse each query and choose which subagents to invoke, instead of always running the full pipeline
The coordinator's job: break the task down, delegate, combine results, and pick subagents according to query complexity
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A user asks what one new port-fee regulation means for shippers. The question is too narrow to split into subtopics, so your three search subagents get the same brief, and 75% of the pages they return are shared. Primary filings are barely represented. What is the best way to divide this work?
opts: Give each subagent a differently worded version of the same question, so that their results differ.
Assign each subagent a source type, such as official filings, academic papers and trade press.
Raise each subagent's results limit, so that the shared pages form a smaller share of the total.
Remove duplicate pages after the search step, and pass the unique pages on to the analysis agent.
questions.explain: When a topic has no natural subtopics, source type is another way to give each agent distinct ground, and it brings in the missing filings. A still lands on the same top pages. C adds volume without separating the work. D cleans up after the wasted effort and does nothing about the missing primary sources.
bullets: Dividing research scope across subagents, by distinct subtopic or source type, so that they duplicate less work
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: To document how services handle retries, your coordinator spawns four explorer subagents with the same brief: "survey retry logic in this monorepo." All four start at the top of the repository, and 65% of the files they read are read by more than one. Two services at the edge of the tree are never reached. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Have subagents note each file in a shared list, so that the others can skip it as they go along.
Raise `maxTurns` on the four subagents, so that each one can work its way out to the edge of the tree.
Tell every subagent in its prompt to avoid any files the others have probably already read.
Have the coordinator list the services and assign each subagent its own distinct group.
questions.explain: Dividing the repository up front removes the overlap and gives every service an owner. A adds a channel outside the coordinator, and all four still start from the same brief. B lets the agents keep duplicating each other for longer. C asks a subagent to guess at work it cannot see, since subagents share no context.
bullets: Dividing research scope across subagents, by distinct subtopic or source type, so that they duplicate less work
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your three search subagents overlap by about 50%. An engineer proposes running them one after another and pasting each one's results into the next one's prompt, with "don't repeat these." Overlap would fall, but each search takes about 50 seconds, and the three areas of the topic are independent. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Accept it, because seeing earlier results is the only way a subagent can avoid repeating them.
Accept it, since 150 seconds is a fair price for cleaner input to synthesis.
Reject it: dividing the scope up front removes the overlap and lets the three run in parallel.
Reject it, and instead let the subagents run as now and remove all duplicates after they finish.
questions.explain: The areas are independent, so distinct assignments remove the overlap and keep the phase at about 50 seconds, not 150. A is wrong because a good partition prevents repeats with no sharing at all. B accepts a threefold delay that distinct assignments make unnecessary. D still pays for the duplicated searches.
bullets: Dividing research scope across subagents, by distinct subtopic or source type, so that they duplicate less work
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: Your coordinator repeats search and synthesis until the synthesis subagent ends its draft with `COVERAGE: COMPLETE`. Runs stop after one round about 90% of the time, yet an audit finds that 30% of final reports miss an area named in the request. What is the most effective change?
opts: Have the coordinator judge each draft against the request, looping until all is covered.
Require the synthesis subagent to justify its `COVERAGE: COMPLETE` line in a few sentences.
Run exactly three rounds on every request, whatever the state of the draft after each round.
Tighten the parser so that the marker counts only when it stands alone on the final line.
questions.explain: The coordinator should judge the draft against the request instead of accepting a self-report in free text, and the criteria then decide when to stop. B improves the wording of the same self-assessment. C replaces the signal with a fixed count, which wastes rounds on easy topics and can stop early on hard ones. D polishes the parsing of a signal that is wrong in the first place.
bullets: Refinement loops: evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries, re-run synthesis until coverage is enough
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your coordinator is writing a guide to a legacy payments module. It notices that the draft says nothing on retry handling, so it respawns the explorer with "look deeper and find more." The second pass reads 80% of the same files and adds nothing, and this happens on most gaps. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Raise the explorer's turn limit, so that a deeper pass can reach more of the module's files.
State the specific gap and the files already covered in the new prompt to the explorer.
Spawn three explorers with the same "look deeper" prompt, to widen what the pass can find.
Have the writing subagent fill in the retry section from what it knows of payment systems.
questions.explain: A re-delegation should be a targeted query, and a new explorer knows only its prompt, so the prompt must name the gap and what was already read. A gives more turns to an aimless brief. C runs the same vague brief three times. D writes unsourced content into the guide instead of closing the gap.
bullets: Refinement loops: evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries, re-run synthesis until coverage is enough
Subagents run with isolated context and do not automatically receive the coordinator's conversation history
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your refinement loop finds strong new material on a missing area in round two, and the coordinator spawns synthesis again, passing the new findings. The new draft covers the gap well, but 60% of the round-one citations are gone and two earlier sections have vanished. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The round-two sources were so strong that synthesis chose to discount all earlier ones.
The synthesis subagent's `max_tokens` is too low, so its output stopped before the rest.
The new run knows only its prompt, which held none of the first round's material.
The coordinator's context overflowed, so its copy of the first draft had been removed.
questions.explain: Each spawned subagent knows only its prompt, so a re-run of synthesis needs all the findings, old and new. A has no support in the stem, and synthesis had no earlier sources in front of it to discount. B would cut off the end of a draft, not remove citations throughout. D does not explain it, because the stem shows only the new findings being passed.
bullets: Refinement loops: evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries, re-run synthesis until coverage is enough
Subagents run with isolated context and do not automatically receive the coordinator's conversation history
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your support coordinator uses the fraud subagent's internal risk score to decide on escalation, and the reply-drafting subagent reads the same results feed. A reviewer finds that 1 in 300 customer replies quotes the score. A prompt rule against mentioning it cut the rate by half, but not to zero. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Strengthen the prompt rule with few-shot examples of replies that do not mention the score at all.
Scan each reply for the word "score" in code, and send any matching reply back to be drafted again.
Remove the score from the fraud subagent's results, so that no agent has it to quote.
Send fraud results to the coordinator, which gives the drafter only what a reply needs.
questions.explain: Routing through the coordinator controls what each subagent receives, so the drafter cannot quote a score it never gets. A adds more of a prompt approach that has already fallen short. B catches one word, not the many ways to express a score. C also takes the score away from the coordinator, which needs it to decide on escalation.
bullets: Sending all subagent communication through the coordinator for observability, consistent errors and controlled flow
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: Over time your research system gained three direct subagent-to-subagent calls, each with its own failure logic. In one incident, analysis retried a dead search endpoint 40 times while synthesis gave up after one failure on the same endpoint, and neither event reached the coordinator's logs. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Remove the direct calls, so that failures reach the coordinator and it applies one policy.
Copy the same retry settings into all three direct calls, and keep the calls where they are.
Add a shared retry library for the subagents, and have it send an alert after 40 failed tries.
Tell each subagent, in its prompt, to give up after a sensible number of failed attempts.
questions.explain: Failure policy differs because three places own it, and the coordinator cannot see any of them; sending the traffic through the hub fixes both. B aligns the numbers today, but the calls stay invisible and will drift apart. C makes the retries uniform and still leaves the coordinator unable to decide on recovery. D swaps code for a vague prompt rule.
bullets: Sending all subagent communication through the coordinator for observability, consistent errors and controlled flow
Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator manages all communication between subagents, plus error handling and information routing
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your developer assistant's subagents communicate only through the coordinator. Support engineers now need a trace for each run showing which subagents ran, what each was asked and what came back. Which approach is simplest and most reliable?
opts: Ask each subagent to end its final message with a summary of what it was asked and what it did.
Record each Task call and its returned result at the coordinator, as all of them pass through it.
Turn on a log inside each subagent, and join the files afterwards using a run ID.
Parse the coordinator's final answer afterwards to work out which subagents must have contributed.
questions.explain: Because all communication passes through the coordinator, one logging point there captures every prompt and result in code. A depends on what each subagent chooses to report. C works, but needs a log and a join for every subagent when one point already sees everything. D infers events from prose and will miss subagents whose work was not quoted.
bullets: Sending all subagent communication through the coordinator for observability, consistent errors and controlled flow
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A research coordinator on the Agent SDK has so far worked alone with `allowedTools: ["WebSearch", "Read"]`. You are adding two specialists, `web-search` and `doc-analysis`, and the coordinator should decide for itself when to use them. Which configuration is correct?
opts: Define both under `agents`, and put "Task" in the `tools` list of each of those two definitions.
Define both under `agents`, and add "Task" to the coordinator's `allowedTools` list.
Define both under `agents`, and add `web-search` and `doc-analysis` to the `allowedTools` list.
Describe both specialists in the coordinator's system prompt, and leave the current options as they are.
questions.explain: A definition makes a subagent available, and the coordinator starts it through the spawning tool. The guide expects that tool, Task, in the coordinator's `allowedTools`, and the docs list it there to auto-approve it; the docs call the tool `Agent`. A puts the spawning tool on the specialists, not on the agent that delegates. C lists agent names, but `allowedTools` holds tool names. D has no definitions, so the coordinator has nothing to spawn by name.
bullets: The Task tool is how subagents are spawned, and a coordinator's allowedTools has to include it
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: The acceptance test for a code-migration agent passes when its final message names the `security-reviewer` subagent. A spot check of 40 passing runs finds 9 where that message says the reviewer approved the change, yet no output from any reviewer exists in the run. How should the test change?
opts: Require the final message to quote the reviewer's verdict word for word before the test will pass.
Have the reviewer end its reply with a fixed token, and check the final message for that token.
Add a second model call that judges whether the final message sounds like real delegation took place.
Check the message stream for a spawn tool call with that `subagent_type`, not the wording.
questions.explain: A subagent only runs when the agent makes the spawn call, so that structured event is the evidence; the docs say to match both names, `Agent` and `Task`. A and B still read text the main agent writes, and an agent that can claim an approval can also write a quote or a token. C has one model grade another's wording, and the run's record already holds the fact.
bullets: The Task tool is how subagents are spawned, and a coordinator's allowedTools has to include it
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: While debugging, a developer added "Task" to the `tools` list of all five subagents in a research system. Before the change a run made about 6 spawns. Now it makes about 30, run trees go three levels deep, and the coordinator's own log accounts for only 6 of them, so failures deeper down are invisible to it. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Take the spawning tool off the five definitions, so that only the coordinator holds it.
Keep the lists, and set `max_budget_usd` so that a run stops before the tree can grow very large.
Keep the lists, and tell every subagent through its system prompt to finish tasks without delegating.
Keep the lists, and add a hook that copies each nested spawn into the coordinator's log for review.
questions.explain: Giving a subagent the spawning tool lets it delegate on its own, so work leaves the coordinator's view; removing the tool restores one hub and takes away a capability the subagents never needed. B caps the bill and leaves the nesting. C asks a prompt to hold back a capability the agent still has. D improves the log, but the coordinator still does not control or handle that work.
bullets: The Task tool is how subagents are spawned, and a coordinator's allowedTools has to include it
Coordinator prompts that set goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures, so subagents can adapt
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A support coordinator spawns `policy-check`, which reports that a warranty exception applies to the customer. Minutes later it spawns `policy-check` again with the prompt "Given the exception you found, work out the replacement option." The second run repeats the policy lookups and says it has no record of any exception. Which change is best?
opts: Add the exception to the coordinator's system prompt, where each later spawn is able to read it.
Add the exception to the `description` in the `policy-check` definition before spawning it again.
Write out the exception and its details in the text of the second spawn request.
Extend the prompt with an instruction to recall earlier results before starting any new lookups.
questions.explain: A new invocation shares no memory with the last one, so what it needs has to travel in its own prompt. A fails because a subagent does not receive the parent's system prompt. B changes what the coordinator reads when choosing an agent, not the subagent's working context. D asks it to recall something it never had.
bullets: Subagents get context only through their prompt: nothing is inherited from the parent or kept between invocations
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: In a 200-package monorepo, a developer and the main agent spend ten minutes narrowing a flaky test down to one race. The agent then delegates with "Fix the race we found." The subagent runs for 18 minutes, reads 60 files and patches a different lock in another package. Which change is most effective?
opts: Write the file, failing test and agreed diagnosis into the delegation message itself.
Record each bug under investigation in the project CLAUDE.md, so that every subagent loads it.
Run the subagent on a more capable model, so that it can trace the same race on its own.
Limit the subagent's `tools` to `Read` and `Edit`, so that it has fewer ways of wandering off.
questions.explain: The subagent saw none of that ten-minute discussion, and the delegation message is the only way to hand it over. B misuses a file for standing project rules to carry one task's state. C asks a better model to rediscover what is already known. D narrows what the subagent can do, and it still does not know where the race is.
bullets: Subagents get context only through their prompt: nothing is inherited from the parent or kept between invocations
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your migration subagent obeys every naming rule in the project CLAUDE.md. Earlier in the session an engineer told the main agent to target only the v2 payments client, and the main agent agreed. Given the prompt "Migrate the checkout module", the subagent used v1 in 5 of 12 files. What best explains this mix of behaviour?
opts: CLAUDE.md outranks instructions given in conversation whenever the subagent finds that the two of them disagree.
The instruction was dropped when the main conversation compacted, so it never reached any later agent.
The subagent did inherit the session history, and it gave that history less weight than its system prompt.
Project memory loads at subagent start, while chat decisions travel only inside the spawn prompt.
questions.explain: A non-fork subagent starts with its own prompt, tool definitions and project CLAUDE.md, but not the parent's conversation, and this spawn prompt never mentioned v2. A invents a conflict, since CLAUDE.md says nothing on the client version. B blames compaction, which nothing in the stem shows. C is the common misreading: no history was inherited to weigh.
bullets: Subagents get context only through their prompt: nothing is inherited from the parent or kept between invocations
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A support system defines `billing-specialist` and `account-specialist`, and both have the description "Helps customers with their account issues." Their system prompts are detailed and accurate. In 22% of spawns the coordinator picks the wrong one: a duplicate charge goes to `account-specialist`, for example. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Add routing examples to each specialist's system prompt, showing which requests belong to it.
Rewrite each description to say which requests it takes and which it leaves to the other.
Add a keyword table to the coordinator's prompt that maps common phrases to a specialist.
Add a small classifier in code that chooses the specialist before the coordinator ever runs.
questions.explain: The coordinator chooses from the descriptions, and these two are identical, so distinct ones are the direct fix. A is the near miss: a system prompt is read only after the specialist has been spawned, too late to affect the choice. C keeps the vague descriptions and adds a phrase list that fails on new wordings. D is extra machinery before the simple fix has been tried.
bullets: AgentDefinition settings per subagent type: description, system prompt and tool restrictions
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your `doc-auditor` subagent's definition has a description and a system prompt only. The prompt says "Report problems; never change files." Across 500 runs, 11 contain an `Edit` call. A new policy says this agent must be unable to alter a file. Which change meets the policy?
opts: Add few-shot examples to the prompt that show the auditor reporting a problem and leaving the file alone.
Take `Edit` off the coordinator's `allowedTools` list, so that the call is no longer approved.
Set the definition's `tools` field to `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`.
Repeat the rule in the `description`, so that it is stated in both parts of the definition.
questions.explain: With `tools` omitted, a subagent gets every tool available to subagents, while a tool left off the list is not in its session at all. A is still a prompt, and the policy says unable. B misreads `allowedTools`, which approves calls and does not remove tools. D only restates the rule in text that does not bind it.
bullets: AgentDefinition settings per subagent type: description, system prompt and tool restrictions
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A developer moves a 60-line review checklist into the `description` of `contract-analyzer`, leaving its `prompt` as "You review documents." The coordinator now selects this agent reliably, but its reviews cover a few items in no consistent order. The coordinator's spawn prompts do not mention the checklist. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Long descriptions are cut off at a fixed length, so only the first few checklist items are kept.
The coordinator's system prompt is inherited by the subagent and overrides what the checklist asks for.
Definitions are ignored once a subagent is running, so the checklist belongs in each spawn request.
`description` serves the choice of agent, while the agent's working instructions come from `prompt`.
questions.explain: The description tells the coordinator when to use the agent, and the `prompt` field is the agent's system prompt, which here is one vague line. A invents a cut-off; the selection improved, and the docs state no such rule. B is false, since the parent's system prompt is not passed down. C is false, because the definition's `prompt` does reach the subagent.
bullets: AgentDefinition settings per subagent type: description, system prompt and tool restrictions
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: After a 40-minute analysis of 30 supplier filings in one SDK session, a script produces two report drafts, one on cost risk and one on legal risk. It passes `resume` with the analysis session ID for the cost draft, then does the same for the legal draft. The legal draft keeps referring to conclusions from the cost draft. What should the script do on next month's run?
opts: Use `continue` for the legal draft, so that it picks up from the latest session in the directory.
Set `fork_session` on both draft runs, so that each one branches from the analysis.
Spawn two fresh subagents for the drafts, and include the analysis session ID in their prompts.
Keep `resume`, and add a line to the legal request telling it to ignore the cost draft.
questions.explain: Resume adds to the same session, so the second draft inherits the first, while a fork starts from a copy and leaves the original unchanged. A also adds to that same session. C gives the subagents an ID and no analysis, since a session ID in a prompt loads nothing. D asks the model to set aside text that is still in its history.
bullets: Forking a session to explore different approaches from one shared analysis baseline
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Mid-way through a long session, an engineer has mapped how a reporting service works and is building a nightly export. She wants to find out whether event-driven exports are workable. That trial may take days, and the current line of work must carry on meanwhile, with both keeping everything learned so far. Which approach fits?
opts: Open a second terminal, and resume the same session ID there for the event-driven trial.
Delegate the trial to a subagent, and give it a one-page summary of the service in its prompt.
Fork the session, then work each line under its own session ID.
Finish the export first in this session, then use it for the trial once that work is done.
questions.explain: A fork gives two independent sessions that hold the same history and can each be picked up separately. A adds both lines to one session, so they would mix. B starts from a summary, not from everything learned, and a subagent does not fit days of back-and-forth. D breaks the requirement that both go on at once.
bullets: Forking a session to explore different approaches from one shared analysis baseline
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A nightly script forks an analysed session twice to trial two dependency upgrades in one checkout, the second trial running after the first. Each fork has its own session ID, and the agent changes `package.json` with `Edit`. The second trial's build keeps failing with version conflicts on a package it never touched. What should you change?
opts: Enable file checkpointing, and rewind to the pre-fork checkpoint before each trial.
Fork the second trial from the first fork's session ID, so that the two histories line up.
Instruct the second fork to disregard any changes it finds that it did not make itself.
Resume the original session between the trials, so that its unchanged history resets the files.
questions.explain: A fork copies conversation history, not files, so the first trial's edits are still in the checkout. Checkpointing is the feature that reverts them. B stacks the trials and makes the overlap worse. C asks the model to ignore real files that the build still reads. D assumes history controls the disk, and resuming a session restores nothing there.
bullets: Forking a session to explore different approaches from one shared analysis baseline
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Reports from your research system cite news sites well but rarely use the PDFs. The document analysis subagent returns about 14 findings per run. The synthesis prompt has a full "Web findings" section, then one line: "Document analysis has also been completed." What is the best fix?
opts: Grant synthesis the `Read` tool, so that it can open the PDFs and study them for itself.
Paste those 14 findings in full into the synthesis prompt beside the web section.
Let the document analysis subagent send its results straight to synthesis.
Add a rule to the synthesis system prompt saying that both kinds of source carry equal weight.
questions.explain: Synthesis sees only its prompt, and the prompt holds none of the analysis. A repeats finished work and gives synthesis a tool outside its role. C bypasses the coordinator, which should route all communication between subagents. D sets a weighting for material that never arrives.
bullets: Putting the complete findings of earlier agents directly into the next subagent's prompt
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: An audit of research reports finds that 40% of figures are vague or a year out when compared with what the search subagents returned. Yet every one of those figures matches the synthesis subagent's spawn prompt, wording included. The search subagents' outputs check out against their sources. Where is the most likely fault?
opts: In the search subagents, whose final messages were too short to hold the figures in the first place.
In the synthesis subagent, which reworded precise figures while it was writing the final report.
In the coordinator's handover, which restated the results and lost precision on the way.
In the coordinator's context window, which cut off the results as they came back from search.
questions.explain: The figures are right on leaving search and already wrong on entering synthesis, so the loss sits in the handover, which should carry findings complete. A is ruled out because the search outputs hold the exact figures. B blames an agent that reproduced its input faithfully. D would cause missing results, and nothing in the stem shows truncation; these figures are present but altered.
bullets: Putting the complete findings of earlier agents directly into the next subagent's prompt
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A coordinator spawns `code-explorer`, which returns a 300-line report of 19 call sites, then spawns `test-writer` with "Write tests for the call sites the explorer found." `test-writer` spends 25 minutes rediscovering them and misses 4. Which design is best?
opts: Let `test-writer` message `code-explorer` directly and ask it for each call site it needs.
Give `test-writer` the spawning tool, so that it can run its own explorer before it writes tests.
Tell `test-writer` in its system prompt to search more thoroughly before it writes any test.
Have the coordinator carry the report over, in full, inside the next spawn prompt.
questions.explain: The coordinator already holds the report, and passing it on avoids both the delay and the misses. A routes work around the coordinator and loses its view of what passed between them. B repeats the exploration one level down. C pushes for a better rediscovery of facts that already exist.
bullets: Putting the complete findings of earlier agents directly into the next subagent's prompt
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Each analysis subagent returns a paragraph of findings on one filing, ending with the filing's name. Compliance now needs every figure in a report traced to its document and page. In a sample of 200 figures, reviewers could place only 55%, because one paragraph blends figures from many pages. What is the most effective change?
opts: Return each finding as a record with separate claim, document and page fields.
Tell the synthesis subagent to give a page number for every figure that it reports.
Add a later step that searches the filings for each figure and fills in its page number.
Pass the full text of each filing to synthesis, so that the pages are there if needed.
questions.explain: The page is lost at the source, so the analysis output has to carry it as its own field through every handover. B asks synthesis for data it never received. C rebuilds the link afterwards and can match the wrong page when a figure repeats. D floods the prompt, and synthesis still has to work out which page backs which claim.
bullets: Structured formats that keep content apart from metadata such as URLs, document names and pages, so attribution survives
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A synthesis subagent's prompt holds 15 sources pasted one after another, each opening with a line such as `From: annual-report.pdf, p.12`. About a quarter of the report's claims credit the wrong source, usually a neighbour in the list. You decide to change how the prompt lays the sources out. Which layout is best?
opts: Give each source a header block with its name and page, then a rule of equals signs, then its text.
List all 15 names and pages in a numbered index at the top, with the texts below carrying only their numbers.
Wrap each in a `<document>` tag with `<document_content>` and `<source>` subtags.
Wrap each text in a `<document>` tag, and keep its name and page as the first line of the content.
questions.explain: Tags give every source a clear boundary and hold its metadata in its own subtag beside the content, the form the docs recommend. A is a header and a divider in plain text, which is close to the layout that already fails. B moves the metadata far from the text it describes and relies on the model matching numbers across the prompt. D wraps the text but leaves the metadata inside the content, so nothing separates the two.
bullets: Structured formats that keep content apart from metadata such as URLs, document names and pages, so attribution survives
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A bug-tracing subagent reports: "The config loader lacks a guard for empty values, close to where retries happen." The coordinator passes that sentence on, complete, to a fix subagent. The repository has three `config.py` files, and in 6 of 20 runs the fix lands in a file that was never faulty. What is the most effective change?
opts: Add a human confirmation step, in which someone approves the target file before each fix is made.
Have the tracer return separate fields for file path, line number and its finding.
Ask the tracer in its prompt to write fuller sentences that describe where the code is.
Give the fix subagent `Grep`, so that it can search for the loader before it edits anything.
questions.explain: The tracer knew the location, but it travelled as loose words, and fields keep it exact through the handover. A adds a person to carry a detail the system already has. C keeps location inside prose, so its exactness still depends on the wording. D makes the fix agent guess again among three matching files.
bullets: Structured formats that keep content apart from metadata such as URLs, document names and pages, so attribution survives
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A coordinator runs academic, news, patent and filings searches one per turn, which makes the research phase take four minutes. No search depends on another. A platform engineer proposes a Python thread pool outside the agent that makes four separate `query()` calls and pastes the results into the coordinator's first prompt. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Prefer one coordinator response holding all four spawns, keeping the work in its hands.
Prefer the pool, since a coordinator can only run its subagents one at a time.
Prefer the pool, provided that all four `query()` calls share a session ID to keep them linked.
Prefer one broad search subagent covering all four source types in a single spawn.
questions.explain: Several spawn calls in one response give the speed-up, and the coordinator still decides what runs and handles what returns. B is false, because subagents can run concurrently. C keeps code deciding in advance what the coordinator should decide. D drops the parallelism and the division of the work into separate source types.
bullets: Parallel subagents: several Task calls in one coordinator response, not one per turn
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: To speed things up, a coordinator's prompt now says "Make all your Task calls in your first response." Each run then emits three search spawns and one synthesis spawn together. All four complete without errors, yet in every run the synthesis output says no findings were supplied. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Subagents spawned in one response cannot return their results to the same coordinator.
Synthesis has no tool for reading the outputs of the search subagents running beside it.
Four spawns went past the concurrency limit, so the search results were discarded.
Its spawn prompt was written before any search had returned anything to include.
questions.explain: Parallel spawning suits independent work, and synthesis depends on the searches, so its prompt had nothing to carry at the moment it was written. A is false, since parallel results do return to the coordinator. B is the near miss, but subagents should not read each other's output; the coordinator passes it. C is wrong because the default limit is 20 and a refused spawn returns an error.
bullets: Parallel subagents: several Task calls in one coordinator response, not one per turn
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A customer writes about a late parcel, a double charge and a warranty claim. The support coordinator spawns a specialist for each, one per turn, and the reply takes 100 seconds. No specialist needs another's output, and all three need the customer ID from the original message. Which change is best?
opts: Spawn the first specialist, and let it start the other two so that they can share what it has found.
Spawn one general specialist with all the tools, so that a single call covers all three issues.
Emit all three spawns in a single response, with the ID written into each prompt.
Emit all three spawns in a single response, and let them read the ID from the conversation history.
