questions.explain: Independent work belongs in one response, and each subagent needs the ID in its own prompt. A moves the spawning away from the coordinator and still delays two of the issues. B removes the specialisation and over-provisions one agent. D is the near miss: the timing is right, but subagents do not see the conversation, so they would not have the ID.
bullets: Parallel subagents: several Task calls in one coordinator response, not one per turn
Subagents get context only through their prompt: nothing is inherited from the parent or kept between invocations
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A coordinator's prompt to its explorer reads: "Grep for chargeCard, open the first three hits, list their callers." Last sprint the payments team renamed that function, and since then the explorer returns "no callers found" and the coordinator reports nothing to change, though about 30 call sites exist. Which change to the prompt is best?
opts: Add the new function name, and keep a list of renames in the prompt as further changes land.
Ask for every path that reaches card payment, and say what a complete answer must contain.
Add a fallback step: if the grep finds nothing, search for the word `charge` and read five hits.
Keep the steps as they are, and run the explorer on a stronger model that can spot the rename.
questions.explain: A goal with a completeness bar lets the explorer adapt when a step comes back empty. A fixes this rename and needs editing after the next one. C adds another scripted step that fails in its own way. D leaves the agent bound to steps that end in an empty result.
bullets: Coordinator prompts that set goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures, so subagents can adapt
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: After a review called your prompts too procedural, the coordinator now tells search subagents only: "Research the impact of heat pumps on grid demand." The subagents do vary their approach, but 45% of their returns rest on two or three blog posts, and synthesis has little to weigh. Nothing in any prompt says what counts as a sufficient return. What is the best next change?
opts: Bring back numbered search steps that name the sites to use, now that the weakness has been measured.
Have synthesis reject thin returns, so that the coordinator can send those topics back for more searching.
Raise the subagents' turn limit, so that they have the room to keep on searching for longer.
Say what an acceptable return looks like: source types, recency, and a source for each claim.
questions.explain: The prompt gained freedom and lost its standard, and the fix is quality criteria that leave the method open. A undoes the adaptability. B is the near miss: synthesis has nothing to reject against, since no criteria exist, and every thin return is paid for first. C gives more time and no reason to search differently.
bullets: Coordinator prompts that set goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures, so subagents can adapt
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A coordinator's prompt to its returns subagent says: "Call get_customer, then lookup_order, then offer a 10% credit." This suits late deliveries, but damaged goods and subscription issues are now 35% of cases, and those often get the wrong remedy. An engineer proposes adding if/else steps for each case type. What should you do?
opts: State the outcome wanted and the conditions a sound resolution has to meet.
Move the if/else steps into a code router that picks one script for each case.
Add a worked example of each case type's exact tool sequence to the prompt.
Create one subagent per case type, each with a fixed script of its own to follow.
questions.explain: An outcome and its conditions let the subagent choose tools and remedy from what it finds. B keeps the scripts and moves them into code, so each new case type needs another branch. C still teaches fixed sequences. D multiplies the scripts, and a case that spans two types has no home.
bullets: Coordinator prompts that set goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures, so subagents can adapt
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: Your boilerplate agent has two team rules. A database snapshot must exist before `db_migrate` runs, because one unprotected migration last quarter cost a day of data. Separately, the team likes named exports over default exports, with some exceptions for framework files. Both rules sit in CLAUDE.md today. Where should each one live?
opts: Put the snapshot steps in a skill the agent invokes before migrating, and leave exports in CLAUDE.md.
Use a hook that denies the call until a snapshot exists, and leave exports as a CLAUDE.md line.
Use one hook for each rule, so that both are applied the same way on every matching tool call.
Move the snapshot rule to the top of CLAUDE.md, and put exports in a path-specific rules file.
questions.explain: A rule that must hold every time belongs in code, while a preference with exceptions can stay as guidance. A looks structured, but the model still chooses whether to invoke the skill. C blocks the legitimate framework exceptions. D only moves the costly rule to another place the model reads.
bullets: Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) versus prompt-based guidance for workflow ordering
Prompt instructions alone keep a non-zero failure rate where compliance must be deterministic
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A new `transfer_balance` tool must run only after identity is verified. The team registers a `PostToolUse` hook on it that checks for a verified ID and, when none exists, writes an alert to the security channel. Alerts arrive for every unverified transfer, yet the unverified rate stays at 9 per 1,000 and each alerted transfer had already moved money. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The hook's matcher is too broad, so alerts for other tools bury the ones that concern transfers.
The alert should be returned to the model as added context, so that the agent can react to it.
The hook should run asynchronously, so that checking identity does not slow the transfer down.
The check runs after the tool has executed, so it can report a breach and cannot prevent one.
questions.explain: `PostToolUse` fires once the tool has run, so it works for auditing and not for prerequisites; a check that must block belongs before the call. A is ruled out, since every unverified transfer did raise an alert. B gives the model information about a transfer that already happened. C would make the check even less able to affect the call.
bullets: Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) versus prompt-based guidance for workflow ordering
Programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until earlier steps have completed
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your support prompt says the agent should usually call `search_faq` before asking the customer a clarifying question. It does so in about 90% of chats, and a miss costs one extra question. An engineer proposes a gate that blocks every reply until `search_faq` has run. Many order-status chats never need the FAQ, but a keyword check to spot them misfiled about one chat in five when tried. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Reject it: a miss costs little and many chats rightly skip the step, so guidance suits this order.
Adopt it: the 10% of misses show a non-zero failure rate, and that is what calls for a gate in code.
Adopt it with an exemption for order-status chats, detected by a keyword check on the first message.
Reject it, and add few-shot examples until the prompt reaches full compliance on this ordering rule.
questions.explain: A non-zero failure rate matters when compliance must be deterministic; here a miss is cheap and the model should be free to skip the step. B applies that test without asking what a miss costs. C keeps the needless gate and adds a brittle keyword rule. D chases full compliance on a rule that does not need it, and many chats should skip the step anyway.
bullets: Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) versus prompt-based guidance for workflow ordering
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A Claude Code agent on your platform team must run `terraform validate` before any `terraform apply`, and CLAUDE.md says so. Auditing 300 long sessions, you find the rule was followed on every apply in the first 30 turns, but on only 88% of applies after turn 120. The rule is still in context at that point. Which change best meets a requirement of 100%?
opts: Move the rule into a skill that the agent loads before it runs any apply command.
Send the rule again as added context every 20 turns, using a `UserPromptSubmit` hook.
Add a `PreToolUse` command hook that denies `terraform apply` until validate has passed.
End each session at 100 turns with `/clear`, so that the rule is always fresh in context.
questions.explain: A requirement of 100% needs a gate in code, which does not depend on how far into a session the model is. A moves the rule to another place the model has to choose to follow. B repeats guidance, which raises the rate and leaves the choice with the model. D shortens the exposure and keeps a non-zero failure rate.
bullets: Prompt instructions alone keep a non-zero failure rate where compliance must be deterministic
Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) versus prompt-based guidance for workflow ordering
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Before launching account closures, your team tests a prompt rule that the agent must verify identity before calling `close_account`. In 2,000 scripted test chats it verified every time, so an engineer says a code gate is now unnecessary. A wrongful closure cannot be undone. How should you evaluate the claim?
opts: It holds, because 2,000 chats with no failures is strong evidence the rule will last in production.
It holds if a daily audit of closures is added, so any miss is noticed and raised within a day.
It fails: no failures in a sample is not a guarantee, and this action needs one before it runs.
It needs more data: run 20,000 varied chats, and drop the gate if there are still no failures.
questions.explain: A prompt leaves the decision to the model each time, so a clean sample lowers the estimated rate and does not make it zero; an irreversible action needs a guarantee. A treats a test as a proof. B finds a wrongful closure after it can no longer be undone. D gives a tighter estimate with the same limit.
bullets: Prompt instructions alone keep a non-zero failure rate where compliance must be deterministic
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: After an agent deployed without the smoke test, your team rewrote the CLAUDE.md line in capitals with the word IMPORTANT. Two weeks later it happened again. The session log shows the file was loaded and the line was in context, and no other instruction conflicted with it. Your manager asks why the rewrite failed. What is the best explanation?
opts: Capitals are ignored by the model, so a numbered checklist at the top of the file would have held.
A line in that file is read and weighed, so strong wording improves the odds and no more.
The line sits at the wrong level of the hierarchy, and a project-level copy would have applied.
The line gave no reason, so adding the cost of skipping the test would have made the model follow it.
questions.explain: CLAUDE.md is guidance the model weighs, so any wording improves the odds and gives no guarantee; a must-happen step needs a hook. A and D only swap one wording for another, which can lower the miss rate and still leaves the decision with the model. C is ruled out because the line was in context.
bullets: Prompt instructions alone keep a non-zero failure rate where compliance must be deterministic
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your agent's handoffs carry four set fields: customer ID, order number, refund amount and recommended action. Human agents still reopen the investigation on 64% of tickets, repeating the same lookups before approving anything. When reviewers check, the recommendation was right in 91% of cases. A trial that added the chat transcript to tickets changed nothing. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The recommended action is too loose, and it should name the exact tool call the human must make.
The ticket shows no confidence score, so human agents cannot tell which recommendations to accept.
The tickets reach human agents too late, after the details have already gone stale in the backend.
Nothing in the ticket says what went wrong, so the advice cannot be judged without rework.
questions.explain: The four fields leave out the analysis behind the recommendation, so a human has to rebuild it to trust it. A tightens a recommendation that is already right in 91% of cases. B adds a self-reported number and no reason. C has no support in the stem, since the lookups repeat what the agent already found.
bullets: Structured handoff protocols for mid-process escalation: customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A customer's two-item return is escalated partway through: `process_refund` has already succeeded for the kettle, and the lamp needs a policy exception. The handoff gives the customer ID, the root cause and a recommended lamp refund, and human agents cannot see the chat. Last month, 4 such tickets ended with the first item refunded twice. What is the most effective fix?
opts: State each action already taken and its result in a required section of the handoff.
Open one ticket per item, so that each human agent deals with a single item of the return.
Escalate as soon as any exception appears, before the agent has refunded any other item.
Have human agents ask the customer which refunds have arrived before they approve another.
questions.explain: A mid-process handoff has to say what has already happened, or the human may repeat it. B splits the return but the kettle ticket still does not say it was refunded. C holds up the routine item, and any step taken before the escalation still goes unreported. D relies on the customer for a fact the agent already holds.
bullets: Structured handoff protocols for mid-process escalation: customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions
Structured handoff summaries for human agents who cannot see the conversation transcript
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A migration agent working for an internal team stops at step 3 of 5 on a conflict, and pages the on-call engineer with "Migration failed, check logs". The engineer cannot open the agent's session, and twice this month re-ran the early steps, which damaged data. Which change most improves this handoff?
opts: Link the raw 9,000-line session log from the page, with the final error line copied into the alert.
Have a stronger model retry the conflict first, so that it pages the engineer far less often overall.
Send requester, repository, work done, cause and suggested next step as fixed fields.
Add a runbook section that shows engineers how to work out which steps ran from the database state.
questions.explain: The engineer needs what a support handoff carries: who it is for, what was done, why it stopped and what to do next. A gives the engineer a pile to search and still does not state those conclusions. B changes how often the handoff happens, not what it carries. D makes the engineer reconstruct what the agent already knows.
bullets: Structured handoff protocols for mid-process escalation: customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your gate blocks `process_refund` until `get_customer` has appeared in the session's tool log. A monthly audit still finds refunds on unverified accounts. In each case `get_customer` had returned zero matches or two matches and the agent carried on. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Require a `customer_id` argument in the `process_refund` schema, so a refund cannot name no account.
Open the gate only on a stored result holding exactly one confirmed account ID for the session.
Add a `verified: true` argument the agent must set on `process_refund`, and have the gate test it.
Extend the prompt so the agent halts whenever a `get_customer` lookup looks unusual or incomplete.
questions.explain: The prerequisite is a verified ID, so the gate must test the tool's outcome and not the fact that it ran. A makes the model supply an ID, but nothing checks that it was verified. C turns the gate into a check of the model's own claim. D hands the decision back to a prompt in the exact case the gate exists for.
bullets: Programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until earlier steps have completed
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your gate blocks `process_refund` until a verified customer ID is stored for the session. An audit finds 7 refunds that passed it. In each, a real customer verified correctly, then gave an order number they had seen on someone else's parcel, and the refund posted to that order. Which change closes this gap?
opts: Run `get_customer` again just before each refund, so that the stored ID is fresh when the gate is checked.
Add a system prompt rule that customers may only ever request a refund on an order placed on their account.
Clear the stored ID after each refund, so that every later refund in the chat must pass verification again.
Have the gate look up the order named in the call, and refuse it unless its owner is the stored ID.
questions.explain: The gate proves that someone is verified, not that this refund belongs to them, so it must compare the call's order with the stored ID. A and C repeat a check that this customer passes honestly each time. B moves a must-hold rule back into a prompt.
bullets: Programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) versus prompt-based guidance for workflow ordering
Programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until earlier steps have completed
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your new gate stops unverified refunds by raising a bare `Error 500`. Since launch, the agent retries the blocked call four times in about 15% of chats, then tells customers the refund system is down. The refund service has had no outage, and in those chats the agent never calls `get_customer`. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The rejection says nothing of what is missing, so the model has no way to see its next step.
The error is not marked as non-retryable, so the agent's retries are what leads it to give up.
The prompt no longer tells the agent to call `get_customer`, since that rule moved into code.
The block comes at call time, when it is too late in the chat for the agent to change its plan.
questions.explain: A block helps only if it says what is missing, because Claude reads the rejection and decides what to do next. B would stop the retries, but the agent would still never learn that it must verify first. C is not the cause, since the agent reads each result and could adapt to a clear reason. D is wrong because a rejected call simply returns to the model, which can take another step.
bullets: Programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until earlier steps have completed
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your research coordinator's `publish_report` is blocked until `verify_citations` passes, and a flag records the pass. An audit finds that 5% of published reports hold claims with no checked source, though the gate logged a valid pass for each. In those runs, the last `Edit` timestamp is later than the pass. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Tell the coordinator through its prompt to run `verify_citations` again after any change to a draft.
Let the gate accept only a pass recorded within the last ten minutes, so that old passes expire.
Save the pass against a hash of that draft, and refuse the call unless the hash still matches.
Run `verify_citations` over published reports each night, and retract any report that fails the check.
questions.explain: The prerequisite is a verified version of this report, so the pass must be tied to the exact content being published. A puts a must-hold step back in a prompt. B narrows the window, yet an edit made inside ten minutes still opens the gate. D catches the problem after the report is out.
bullets: Programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until earlier steps have completed
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your coordinator verifies the customer, splits a message into three concerns and starts three parallel subagents through the Task tool. Each subagent then calls `get_customer` and asks the customer for an identifier, so customers are asked three times in one chat. Satisfaction on these chats fell 18 points. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Parallel subagents cannot share one session, so the concerns have to be worked through in sequence.
The subagents need a shared datastore, because a coordinator has no direct way to hand them any data.
The subagents do see the coordinator's history, but they are told to treat every step as unverified.
A subagent knows only what its spawn prompt holds, and the record was not put in those prompts.
questions.explain: Subagents start without the parent's conversation, so the verified record has to travel in each prompt. A gives up the parallel work without supplying the record. B builds infrastructure when the prompt is already a direct channel. C has it backwards, since history is not inherited.
bullets: Splitting multi-concern requests into items, investigating them in parallel with shared context, then one unified resolution
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A customer writes that order 512 arrived late and was also overcharged. Two parallel subagents, one per concern, each have `process_refund` access, and each issues £30. The ledger shows both payments trace to one duplicate shipping fee. About 5% of multi-concern chats pay twice for one fault, and a trial that ran the two one after the other changed nothing, since the second subagent never sees what the first did. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Give both subagents a `get_refunds` tool, so that each can check what has been paid before it pays.
Limit them to read-only tools, and have the coordinator combine findings before any money moves.
Extend each subagent's prompt with a rule against paying for any fault its sibling already settled.
Run the subagents one after the other, and keep the `process_refund` access each one has today.
questions.explain: Investigation can run in parallel, but action comes after the findings are combined, which is where the shared cause shows up. A leaves a race, since parallel subagents can both check before either pays. C asks each subagent to respect work it cannot see. D has no step that compares the findings, and gives up the parallel work.
bullets: Splitting multi-concern requests into items, investigating them in parallel with shared context, then one unified resolution
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A single-label intent classifier sends each support message to one workflow. Reviewing 1,000 chats, you find that 27% of messages raise two or more concerns, and everything after the labelled one goes unanswered. Label accuracy is 96%. Which redesign best addresses this?
opts: Retrain the classifier on more multi-topic data, so that it finds the customer's main request more often.
Add combined labels such as refund-and-address, so that the most common pairs have their own workflows.
Have the agent break each message into a list of separate issues, and work every item.
Finish the labelled workflow, then ask the customer if anything else is needed before the chat closes.
questions.explain: One label cannot describe a message with several issues, so the message has to become a list of items. A improves a score that is already fine. B grows a fixed set of pairs that can never cover every mix. D makes the customer repeat what they already wrote.
bullets: Splitting multi-concern requests into items, investigating them in parallel with shared context, then one unified resolution
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: Your support agent splits a message into three concerns and starts a subagent for each, in parallel, with the customer record in every prompt. Each subagent posts its own reply as it finishes. In 21% of these chats the customer sends a confused follow-up, usually because one reply promises a refund to the card while another says the same order was cancelled for store credit. Which redesign is best?
opts: Have subagents return findings to the coordinator, which settles overlaps and sends one reply.
Run the subagents one at a time, so that each reply can refer to what the earlier ones said.
Hold every subagent's reply for a short delay, so that the three replies land together in the chat.
Put all three concerns in each subagent's prompt, so that each can mention the related outcomes.
questions.explain: Investigating in parallel is fine, but the outcomes must be reconciled in one place before the customer sees anything. B still posts separate replies, and each only sees the earlier ones. C changes when the replies arrive, not whether they agree. D has three subagents decide on the same outcomes independently, so they can still disagree.
bullets: Splitting multi-concern requests into items, investigating them in parallel with shared context, then one unified resolution
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: `escalate_to_human` takes one free-text `notes` string. The system prompt lists what a note must contain, yet 18% of tickets lack the refund amount, and human agents cannot see the transcript to find it. You want every ticket to carry each item. Which change is most effective?
opts: Lengthen the tool description, and repeat there the full list of items that each note has to contain.
Ask the agent to write `notes` as a JSON object, with one key for each item that a ticket must carry.
Run a regex over each note after the call, and flag tickets with no amount for a human to fill in.
Replace `notes` with separate required properties, and set `strict: true` on the definition.
questions.explain: Required properties under strict mode make the content part of the tool's contract, not a request. A adds more instructions to a rule that is already missed. B looks structured, but it is still a free string the schema does not check. C notices the gap afterwards and leaves the human without the amount.
bullets: Structured handoff summaries for human agents who cannot see the conversation transcript
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: In 6% of escalated tickets, the refund amount differs from the order record: for example, £200 on a £120 order. The chat logs show that the customer typed the higher figure in each case. Human agents cannot see those chats and approve what the ticket says. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Take the figure from the `lookup_order` result, and show the claim as a separate item.
Remove the amount from the handoff, so that a human looks it up afresh for each new ticket.
Have the agent ask the customer to confirm the amount once more before creating the ticket.
Tell the agent through its prompt to add a remark whenever a figure came from the customer.
questions.explain: The handoff should carry the verified value and keep the customer's claim visible as a claim, so the human sees the gap. B throws away a fact the agent already holds and adds work. C confirms the same unverified figure. D leaves the wrong number in the amount and depends on the agent remembering a remark.
bullets: Structured handoff summaries for human agents who cannot see the conversation transcript
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your `escalate_to_human` schema requires `root_cause`. When a customer demands a person in the first message, the agent escalates at once, as it should, with no investigation done. Audits show that 30% of those tickets state a cause no tool result supports, and human agents waste time chasing it. How should you resolve this?
opts: Hold the escalation until the agent has investigated enough to fill `root_cause` with a real finding.
Let the field take an explicit `unknown` value, and say in the prompt that this is acceptable.
Remove `root_cause` from the schema, since a part of the tickets cannot be trusted on this field.
Add a self-reported confidence score beside `root_cause`, so that humans can decide how far to trust it.
questions.explain: A required field with no honest way to say "not known" pushes the model to make something up, so it needs a stated way out. A delays a customer who asked for a person. C loses the field for the many tickets where the cause is real. D adds a self-reported number to a guess, and the invented text stays on the ticket.
bullets: Structured handoff summaries for human agents who cannot see the conversation transcript
Structured handoff protocols for mid-process escalation: customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your web search subagent reads pages through an MCP tool that returns the full page. In a sample of 200 results, about 70% of the text was menus, cookie notices and adverts, and long topics now run out of context before the synthesis step. Each result carries a URL and publication date, which the citations need. What is the most effective fix?
opts: A PostToolUse hook that returns `additionalContext` marking which sections of each page are noise.
A PreToolUse hook that rewrites each URL to the site's print view, which usually has less page furniture.
A PostToolUse hook that replaces each result with the body text plus its source fields.
Automatic compaction, which will summarise the older pages whenever the context comes close to full.
questions.explain: Replacing the result means the noise never enters context, and the citation fields are kept. A adds text beside the original output, so the context grows. B depends on every site offering a print view. D lets the noise in first, and its summaries can lose the URLs and dates the citations need.
bullets: Hooks such as PostToolUse catch tool results and transform them before the model reads them
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Tax identifiers must never reach your support agent's context. A synchronous PostToolUse hook on `get_tax_record` detects them and returns `decision: "block"` with the reason "tax ID redacted". Your logs show the hook firing and returning on every call, yet the agent still quoted a tax ID in 2% of its replies. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: `block` leaves the original output in place, so the identifier still reaches the model.
`block` is not valid here; a result is only withheld when the hook returns `permissionDecision: "deny"`.
The result had already been added to the conversation, because a PostToolUse hook can only observe it.
The reason names the field without its value, so the model cannot tell what should be left out of replies.
questions.explain: On PostToolUse, `block` adds the reason next to the result and the original stays; replacing it takes `updatedToolOutput`. B borrows a PreToolUse field that does not withhold a result. C is wrong because this hook can replace the output before the model sees it. D treats it as a wording problem, when the value is still in the model's context.
bullets: Hooks such as PostToolUse catch tool results and transform them before the model reads them
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A repository clean-up agent has a `delete_stale_branches` tool. To protect release branches, a PostToolUse hook checks the branch list in each result and, on a match, replaces the output with "blocked: protected branch". The agent then reports that nothing was deleted. Last week `release/9.2` vanished from the remote during such a run. What is the root cause?
opts: The hook returned a replacement; it should have returned `decision: "block"` to cancel the running call.
The match ran on the text of the result, which lists branches only after the remote has been updated.
Replacing output works only for MCP tools, so the agent's report came from the unchanged result.
The check runs once the tool has finished, so the rewrite changed only the model's view of it.
questions.explain: PostToolUse fires after the tool has run, so rewriting the result changes what the model sees and nothing else; a check that must stop an action belongs on the outgoing call. A is wrong because `block` on this event only adds a reason. B describes the ordering but keeps the check in the same too-late place. C is false, since the replacement works for any tool, and the agent's report shows it applied.
bullets: Hooks such as PostToolUse catch tool results and transform them before the model reads them
Hooks catch outgoing tool calls so that a compliance rule is applied before the call runs
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Goodwill credits are limited to 200 pounds per case, and a case may receive several. A hook on `issue_credit` denies any call above 200, and single large credits have stopped. This month's audit found 31 cases with three or four credits of about 90 pounds each. Which change best enforces the rule as written?
opts: Have the hook deny any second credit in a case, so that one call can never be followed by another.
Have the hook add the case's earlier credits to the requested amount before it decides.
Add a PostToolUse hook that returns the case total as `additionalContext`, so the model stops at the limit.
Have the hook deny any credit issued within 24 hours of an earlier one on the same case.
questions.explain: The limit applies to the case but the check looks at one call, so the decision needs the case total. A forbids repeat credits that the policy allows. C gives the model better information but leaves the decision with the model. D only spreads the same credits over more days.
bullets: Hooks catch outgoing tool calls so that a compliance rule is applied before the call runs
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Files under `infra/prod/` sync to production on write. Your platform assistant has a PreToolUse hook with a `Write|Edit` matcher whose callback denies those paths by reading `file_path`. The assistant also runs tests through `Bash`. Over 900 sessions the hook logged no denials, yet 6 production files changed, and each of those sessions contains a `sed -i` step. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Widen the matcher to match every tool, and keep the callback's `file_path` check just as it is.
Remove `Bash` from the assistant, so that every file change has to pass through `Write` or `Edit`.
Add a PostToolUse hook on `Bash` that restores any production file changed by a shell command.
Also intercept `Bash`, with a callback that checks `tool_input.command` for that folder.
questions.explain: A shell write never reaches a `Write|Edit` matcher, so interception must cover that route and read the argument that tool has. A runs on `Bash` but looks for a `file_path` that its input does not contain. B breaks the test runs the assistant needs. C restores the file after it has already synced to production.
bullets: Hooks catch outgoing tool calls so that a compliance rule is applied before the call runs
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Legal has listed 40 publisher domains that your research subagents must never request, because of a licence dispute. The subagents use `WebFetch` on many other sites, and the list changes monthly. A prompt rule was missed in 11 of 5,000 fetches. How should you configure the control?
opts: A PreToolUse hook matching `WebFetch`, whose callback reads the URL and denies listed domains.
A PreToolUse hook whose matcher is a regex of the 40 domains, so that it fires for those fetches only.
A PostToolUse hook on `WebFetch` that replaces the page with a notice when the URL is on the list.
A PreToolUse hook on every tool that returns the 40 domains as `additionalContext` before each call.
questions.explain: The block must come before the request, and the domain is an argument, so the callback has to inspect it. B misreads matchers, which test the tool name and would never see a domain. C hides the page but the prohibited request has already gone out. D only gives the model a stronger reminder, so it is still the model's choice.
bullets: Hooks catch outgoing tool calls so that a compliance rule is applied before the call runs
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Accounts with an open dispute must never be closed by your support agent. The agent calls `close_account` about 150 times a day, and the dispute flag can be read from the billing system. Closure takes effect at once and cannot be reversed. Where should the check go?
opts: In a PostToolUse hook on `get_account` that adds a dispute warning as context for the next decision.
In the `close_account` tool description, as a condition that the agent has to confirm before calling it.
In a PreToolUse hook on `close_account` that reads the flag and denies the call if needed.
In a first step that forces a call to `get_dispute_status` through `tool_choice` at the start of each chat.
questions.explain: The rule must hold on every closure, so code has to decide on the outgoing call. A informs the model and leaves the choice with it. B is a prompt instruction in another place. D makes the status call happen but nothing ties the later closure to its answer.
bullets: Hooks catch outgoing tool calls so that a compliance rule is applied before the call runs
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Law forbids shipping replacement goods to embargoed regions, and any breach must be reported to a regulator. Your team tuned the support agent's prompt until an evaluation of 3,000 conversations showed no embargoed shipments. The manager now wants to release as it is, since "the data proves the prompt works". How should you evaluate this?
opts: Release it: 3,000 clean conversations are enough evidence that this rule holds in production.
Hold it for a check in code on the shipping call, as a clean sample describes past runs.
Release it, and make the evaluation a gate that must pass again on every change to the prompt.
Hold it until adversarial test conversations also come back with zero embargoed shipments.
questions.explain: Whether the model follows a prompt is decided again on each turn, so a clean score does not rule out a breach, and this rule allows none. A treats a test result as a guarantee. C catches regressions in testing but enforces nothing in production. D produces a better estimate of the same kind.
bullets: Hooks give deterministic guarantees, while prompt instructions give only probable compliance
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A PreToolUse command hook denies `release_hold` calls above 400 units, and policy says the limit is a guarantee. Before launch the team plans to run 5,000 simulated customer chats, including pushy ones, and require zero breaches. Each run takes three days, and the hook's decision depends only on the call it receives. Which verification is most effective?
opts: Run the 5,000 chats nightly for a month, and release only if no breach appears in any run.
Send scripted calls straight to the hook at 399, 400 and 401 units, and assert each decision.
Have a second model read the hook script and rate how likely it is to block every large call.
Run the chats once with a prompt-only agent, and release if the hook cuts the breaches tenfold.
questions.explain: The hook returns the same decision for the same call whatever the model says, so scripted inputs test it directly, quickly and at the edges. A samples conversations, which only reach the edge cases by luck and cost three days a run. C asks a model for a probability about code that can simply be run. D measures a reduction in a rate, which suits a prompt and is not the proof a guarantee needs.
bullets: Hooks give deterministic guarantees, while prompt instructions give only probable compliance
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Reviewers want your research synthesis agent to favour peer-reviewed papers when they conflict with blog posts, and blogs are often the only source on recent events. Runs are unattended. After a hook fixed a compliance issue elsewhere, an engineer proposes one that denies fetches from any site outside a list of 200 journals. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Keep it in the prompt with clear criteria, since weighing two sources takes judgment.
Use the proposed hook, since a preference that reviewers rely on should not depend on the model.
Use the hook with an `ask` decision, so that a reviewer approves each fetch outside the journal list.
Use a PostToolUse hook that removes a blog result whenever a journal result covers the same topic.
questions.explain: Hooks suit rules that hold the same way every time, while deciding which source to trust in a conflict needs the model to think. B cuts off the blogs that recent events depend on. C needs a reviewer, and the runs are unattended. D makes the same judgment in code, and code cannot tell when two sources really conflict.
bullets: Hooks give deterministic guarantees, while prompt instructions give only probable compliance
Choosing a hook over a prompt rule when the business needs guaranteed compliance
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: Your support agent calls three MCP tools that report money differently: billing sends integer pence, shipping sends a decimal string, and returns sends text with a currency sign. In 9% of partial-refund cases the agent adds these up wrongly. The servers belong to other teams and will not change this year. Which approach is best?
opts: A `calculate_total` tool, and a prompt rule telling the model to send every sum through it.
A PostToolUse hook that returns `additionalContext` stating the unit of each money field.
A PostToolUse hook that rewrites every money field into a single format.
A format table in the system prompt, so that the model can convert each value on its own.
questions.explain: The mismatch sits in the results, so code should settle it once, before the model reads them. A moves the arithmetic, but the model must still read each format correctly to fill in the inputs. B labels the units and leaves the conversion with the model. D has the same weakness, and it is where the 9% comes from.
bullets: Writing PostToolUse hooks that bring mixed data formats from different MCP tools into one form
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your research agent builds timelines from a US news archive and a UK court register, both MCP servers. Both return dates like `03/04/2025`, each in its own country's usual order. A value such as `25/04/2025` is clear, but most are not, and 12% of timelines misorder events. How should the PostToolUse normaliser work?
opts: Try day first on every value, then fall back to month first when that fails to parse.
Pick the date order for each result from `tool_name`, then rewrite the values in ISO 8601.
Call a small model inside the hook to infer each date's order from the text around it.
Keep each raw date and return `additionalContext` warning the model that it may be ambiguous.
questions.explain: The same string can mean two dates, so the value alone cannot settle it, but the hook knows which tool produced it and each source has one order. A silently reads most US dates wrongly. C replaces a fact the code has with a guess. D passes the same ambiguity back to the model, which has no better way to resolve it.
bullets: Writing PostToolUse hooks that bring mixed data formats from different MCP tools into one form
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: An incident-review agent combines deployment records in Unix seconds with error logs in ISO 8601 with offsets. A PostToolUse hook now rewrites both as `YYYY-MM-DD`, which ended the format mix-ups. But in 15 of 60 reviews the agent says it cannot tell whether a deployment came before an error on the same day. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The shared format holds no time of day, so same-date events have no order.
The hook applied offsets unevenly, so events from the two tools no longer line up within a day.
A PostToolUse hook sees one tool's result at a time, so it cannot align values across two tools.
The model needs each tool's original strings, because it cannot compare values that a hook rewrote.
questions.explain: Normalising should unify the format and keep the meaning, and this format dropped the detail the question depends on, so full UTC timestamps are needed. B would give wrong orders, not an agent unable to tell. C is wrong because each value can be converted alone to one shared format. D is ruled out by the stem, where the rewrite ended the mix-ups.
bullets: Writing PostToolUse hooks that bring mixed data formats from different MCP tools into one form
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Four research subagents read three archive MCP servers whose results use numeric status codes for items such as preprint, published and retracted. Each subagent's prompt holds a paragraph decoding them. When one archive redefined code 7, one paragraph was updated, and retracted papers were cited in 5% of reports for a month. Which design best prevents a repeat? Even the subagent with the updated paragraph misread about 2% of codes.
opts: One shared prompt fragment, imported by all four subagents, that holds the decoding table.
A `decode_status` tool that each subagent is told to call whenever a result contains a code.
A table in the coordinator's prompt, which it copies into each Task prompt that it sends.
One PostToolUse hook that turns each code into its meaning before any subagent reads it.
questions.explain: Code turns every code into a word before any model reads it, so nothing is decoded by a model and a change is made once; the 2% shows that decoding by the model is itself unreliable. A fixes the duplication but still leaves the decoding with each model. B depends on the model choosing to call the tool. C leaves the decoding with the model too, and adds a copying step.
bullets: Writing PostToolUse hooks that bring mixed data formats from different MCP tools into one form
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A hook denies `export_customer_data` when a request lacks a signed consent form. To redirect those cases, it puts "Do not retry. Call `escalate_to_human`" in `systemMessage` and leaves `permissionDecisionReason` empty. The agent keeps retrying the export, and customers see the message on screen. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: `systemMessage` is delivered on the next turn, so it arrives after the agent has already retried.
A denied call removes the other tools for that turn, so the agent has only the export left to call.
The model never received the redirect, because it was written to a field meant for the user.
The deny needs `continue: false` as well, or the model treats the denial as a temporary failure.
questions.explain: `systemMessage` is shown to the user, which the stem confirms, while the deny reason is what the model reads, and here it is empty. A invents a delay, and the text would not reach the model at any time. B invents a rule, since a denial leaves the other tools available. D would stop the agent, which is the opposite of redirecting it.
bullets: Writing interception hooks that block a policy-violating action and redirect to another workflow
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A hook denies your citation subagent's fetches from paywalled journals, and its reason says to use `request_licensed_copy` instead. That tool works when the coordinator calls it. The subagent is defined with `tools: ["WebSearch", "WebFetch"]`. After each denial it makes no further call for that source and writes "source unavailable", which now affects 18% of citations. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The reason is worded as advice, so the subagent is free to treat the redirect as optional.
The redirect names a tool that this subagent's definition does not give it.
A deny ends a subagent's work on that source, so that only the coordinator can act on it.
The coordinator is not told of each denial, and it must approve the next step for the subagent.
questions.explain: A redirect only works if the alternative is reachable, and the definition lists two tools that do not include it. A would call for firmer wording, but no wording makes a missing tool callable. C is wrong because a denial reaches the model as a reason and the subagent can carry on. D invents an approval step between denial and the next call.
bullets: Writing interception hooks that block a policy-violating action and redirect to another workflow
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A hook denies `reverse_chargeback` for flagged accounts and opens a ticket itself from the call's arguments, an account ID and an amount. The fraud team works from its ticket queue and cannot open agent sessions. In 60% of these tickets the analyst must ask the customer to explain everything again. The agent's only other route to a person is `escalate_to_human`. What is the most effective change?
opts: Have the deny reason direct the model to call `escalate_to_human` with a structured summary.
Add the session ID to each ticket, so that the analyst can look up what the customer has said.
Have the hook read the transcript file and paste the whole conversation into each ticket.
Have the hook copy every field of `tool_input` to the ticket, so the analyst has all the arguments.
questions.explain: The hook sees only the call, while the model holds the cause and the customer's account of it, so the redirect should send it to a handoff that carries those; with the call denied, that route is the only one left, so the model has little choice but to take it. B points to sessions the team cannot open. C gives a raw transcript with no root cause or recommended action. D copies the same two fields again.

opts: Set `strict: true` on the tool, so that arguments are guaranteed to match the schema.
Set `tool_choice` to `create_ticket`, so that the call is always made with every field filled in.
Add `input_examples` that show calls with `components` filled in for typical tickets.
Expand the `components` description with three paragraphs on how to choose between queues.
questions.explain: Examples show the model when an optional parameter is worth including and how a nested object looks. A guarantees valid arguments, and these already validate. B forces the call, which does not fill an optional field. D adds to a description that already explains the field, when concrete patterns are what is missing.
bullets: Descriptions should carry input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries against other tools
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: After a merger, your support agent has `lookup_shipment` from the retail team and `track_package` from the logistics team. Both are described as "Gets the delivery status of a shipment", call the same backend and return identical fields. The agent picks `lookup_shipment` 58% of the time and `track_package` 42% for the same kinds of request. Both tools sit in the lists of five other agents with different prompts. What is the best change?
opts: Write a longer description for each tool, to bring out how it differs from the other.
Keep one of the two tools and retire the other, since there is no difference to describe.
Add a system prompt line telling the agent to prefer `lookup_shipment` for delivery questions.
Force `track_package` with `tool_choice` whenever a message contains a tracking number.
questions.explain: The split between the tools follows their identical descriptions, and there is nothing true to say that would tell them apart, so one should go. A would have to invent a difference. C patches one agent's prompt while five others keep the duplicate. D forces a tool on one kind of message and leaves the overlap in place.
bullets: Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting between near-identical tools
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: Your research agent has `search_internal_wiki`, described in detail as searching Acme's engineering wiki. You add a third-party MCP server whose only search tool is `search`, described as "Search for information." Afterwards the share of internal-wiki questions answered with `search_internal_wiki` falls from 82% to 19%, and answers cite public pages that contradict internal standards. The wiki tool and its description are unchanged, and its remaining calls succeed. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The model favours whichever tool was added most recently, whatever its description says.
The wiki tool's calls now fail validation, so the model gives up on it after the first error.
The new tool's broad description fits nearly any request, so it competes with the wiki tool.
The longer tool list went over a size limit, so the wiki tool is no longer sent to the model.
questions.explain: A description as broad as "Search for information" fits every question the wiki tool should get, and the drop followed the addition. A describes a preference for recency that is not how selection works. B is ruled out by the stem, which says its remaining calls succeed. D is ruled out because the agent still uses the wiki tool in 19% of cases.
bullets: Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting between near-identical tools
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your coding agent has `run_linter` ("Checks code for problems and style issues") and `run_type_check` ("Checks code for type problems"). Of 120 sampled requests that clearly need a type check, 46 went to `run_linter`; of 150 that clearly need a lint pass, 4 went to `run_type_check`. Linter output never contains type errors. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: `run_linter` is described broadly enough to include type problems, so it absorbs the other tool's requests.
The two names are too alike, which would send requests to either tool about equally often, both ways.
`run_type_check` is registered after `run_linter`, and the model leans toward tools that are listed earlier.
`run_type_check` returns too much output, so the model avoids calling it whenever it can find another route.
questions.explain: The misroutes run almost one way: requests for the narrow tool go to the broad one, which says its job includes "problems" in general. B would produce errors in both directions. C and D invent behaviours that the numbers do not call for; the same agent calls `run_type_check` correctly for 62% of requests that need it.
bullets: Ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting between near-identical tools
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your support agent's system prompt contains the line "Customers who mention cancellation want their subscription cancelled: call `cancel_subscription`." The tool descriptions are detailed and correct. Of 120 sampled conversations that contain the word "cancellation", 14 triggered `cancel_subscription` although the customer had only asked what the cancellation policy was; among 120 conversations without the word, none did. Which explanation fits the evidence best?
opts: `cancel_subscription` is listed before `get_policy_text`, and the model favours tools listed first.
The prompt line ties a word to a tool, and the model acts on it even for a question about policy.
The conversations were long enough that the model lost track of what each tool does.
Sampling randomness makes tool choice drift whenever a request mentions a change to an account.
questions.explain: Every wrong call sits in conversations that contain the trigger word, which points at the instruction and not at the descriptions. A and D name causes that would not follow the word. C would show up in long conversations generally, and the sample is defined by the word.
bullets: System prompt wording can create unintended tool associations through keyword-sensitive instructions
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: After a move to a newer model, your support agent calls `search_kb` on 93% of turns, including "thanks" and "ok", which adds about two seconds of latency each time. The system prompt, unchanged from the older model, includes "CRITICAL: You MUST call search_kb before answering ANY message." The tool descriptions are fine. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Set `tool_choice` to `none` on any turn where the customer message is shorter than 20 characters.
Add a classifier that detects pleasantries and strips the tools from those requests before the call.
Lower the sampling temperature so that the model makes tool calls less often overall.
Replace the line with plain wording: "Use search_kb when a question needs policy details."
questions.explain: Models that follow the system prompt more closely act on forceful wording, so softening it restores the model's own judgment about when a call is useful. A uses message length as a stand-in for intent and will cut off short questions that need the knowledge base. B builds a separate component for what a wording change fixes. C misreads temperature, which does not decide whether a tool is needed.
bullets: System prompt wording can create unintended tool associations through keyword-sensitive instructions
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A research agent is given `query_filings_db`, whose description says it holds filings for single companies and no industry data, plus `web_search`. The system prompt says: "Anything about market size goes to query_filings_db." Of 90 sampled questions about industry market size, all 90 called the database first, 64 got an empty result, and the agent then wrote an answer from memory with no search at all. Industry questions that do not use the phrase went to `web_search`. Which explanation best accounts for the database calls?
opts: The prompt line pairs a phrase with a tool that the description rules out, and the model follows the line.
The questions read like company questions, so the database description looks as if it covers them.
The `web_search` description lacks the words "market size", so the model cannot match it to these questions.
The model weighs a tool description and a prompt instruction equally, so it picks between them at random.
questions.explain: All 90 calls went to one tool, which a random choice would not do, and the only thing tying these questions to that tool is the prompt line. B describes how the failure was handled afterwards, and does not explain why the database was called. C adds a cause that would send some questions elsewhere, and none went. D is contradicted by 90 of 90.
bullets: System prompt wording can create unintended tool associations through keyword-sensitive instructions
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your coding agent's prompt says "For anything about a build, use the `ci_status` tool." It was added because, before it, the agent sometimes skipped CI checks when asked about failing pipelines. Now about 1 in 5 requests like "build a pagination helper for the orders list" make the agent poll `ci_status` for the main branch before writing any code. The tool descriptions are accurate. What is the best fix?
opts: Delete the line, since the tool descriptions already say when to check CI.
Repeat the line in capitals, so that the agent sees it as the rule that governs CI questions.
Reword it around the intent: use `ci_status` when asked whether a pipeline run passed or failed.
Add a second line telling the agent to skip `ci_status` for any request that starts with the verb "build".
questions.explain: The word "build" means two things and the instruction keys on the word, so naming the intent keeps the behaviour the line was added for. A brings back the skipped checks. B makes the keyword rule stronger. D patches one phrasing and leaves "compile the project" or "building a feature" to find their own way in.
bullets: Reviewing system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that override good descriptions
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: You are adding `search_invoices` next to the existing `get_invoice`. `get_invoice` takes an invoice ID and returns line items and a PDF link. `search_invoices` takes a customer ID and an optional date range, and returns up to 20 summaries (ID, date, total) without line items. Which description for `search_invoices` best prevents mix-ups?
opts: "Finds invoices. Useful when customers ask about their invoices, or want to know what they were charged for in a given month."
"Lists up to 20 invoice summaries (ID, date, total) for a customer ID and optional dates. No line items: use get_invoice."
"Returns invoice data from the billing system, including identifiers, dates and totals, as JSON with a stable field order."
"Searches invoices by customer. Prefer get_invoice whenever an invoice ID is known, and call this only as a last resort."
questions.explain: It states the input, the output, the limit, and which tool to use for the missing detail. A says only that it finds invoices, which is also what the other tool does. C describes formatting and is silent on when to use it. D gives a preference order and leaves the model unsure what the tool returns or accepts.
bullets: Writing descriptions that differentiate purpose, inputs, outputs and when to use a tool versus alternatives
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your SRE assistant has `get_metrics` ("Returns metrics for a service") and `get_slo_report` ("Returns SLO data for a service"). For questions such as "is checkout within its latency SLO this week?" the agent calls `get_metrics`, then computes the burn rate itself, and is wrong in 30% of 200 sampled answers. `get_slo_report` returns pass or fail per window with the burn rate already computed. The agent also needs `get_metrics` for graph and trend questions. What change is most effective?
opts: Write the burn-rate formula into the system prompt and let the agent work it out from raw metrics.
Remove `get_metrics` from the agent, so that the only route to an SLO answer is the report tool.
Rewrite both: the report tool gives pass or fail and burn rate; the metrics tool gives raw points.
Give the agent a `calculate` tool, so that its arithmetic on the raw data points is exact every time.
questions.explain: The descriptions say what both tools return in the same loose terms, so the model takes the raw data and does its own sums. Stating the output and when to use each sends SLO questions to the tool that already has the answer. A keeps the wrong path and tries to make it work. B takes away a tool the agent needs for trends. D makes the arithmetic exact but leaves the wrong inputs.
bullets: Writing descriptions that differentiate purpose, inputs, outputs and when to use a tool versus alternatives
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: You added `apply_promo_code`, which lowers the total of an open order, next to `issue_credit`, which gives store credit after payment. Since launch, 21% of promo-code requests from unpaid orders have gone to `issue_credit`, and some customers received credit they did not ask for. Which description for `apply_promo_code` best fixes the mix-up?
opts: "Applies a promo code to an unpaid order and returns the new total. Takes the code as typed, such as SPRING25. After payment, use issue_credit."
"Applies a promo code to an order. Returns the new total and a list of the discounts applied, each with its code, amount and expiry date, as JSON."
"Reduces what a customer pays. Takes the code the customer typed, exactly as typed, and applies it. Customers often ask about this at checkout."
"Applies a promo code to an order. The code goes in the `code` field; see the schema for details. Do not use it for refunds or returned goods."
questions.explain: It gives the input, the output and the boundary against `issue_credit`, which is the tool that took the requests. B says what comes back and nothing about when to use it instead of the credit tool. C describes the customer's goal and gives no boundary. D draws its boundary against refunds, which are not the confusion in the logs.
bullets: Writing descriptions that differentiate purpose, inputs, outputs and when to use a tool versus alternatives
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your research agent has `get_data`, which queries the internal metrics warehouse, and `get_info`, which fetches public web pages. Each description already says accurately what it returns and what it does not. Even so, the agent picks the wrong one in 25% of 200 sampled runs, and its stated reasoning shows it choosing from the names ("get info about the market"). What is the best change?
opts: Add a third tool, `route_query`, that decides which of the two the agent should call each time.
Lengthen both descriptions with five further example questions for each one of the two tools in use.
Force `get_data` with `tool_choice` whenever the question contains a figure or a number.
Rename them `query_internal_metrics` and `fetch_public_web_page`, keeping descriptions in line.
questions.explain: The agent reads the names, which say almost the same thing, so the names must carry the difference as well as the descriptions. A adds a layer to fix what a rename fixes. B adds text to descriptions that are already accurate, while the names keep misleading. C forces a tool on a keyword and ignores the questions that contain no figure.
bullets: Renaming tools and updating descriptions to remove functional overlap
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: After a merger your agent has `update_address`, which changes the billing address on the account, and `change_address`, which changes the delivery address on an open order. Both are described as "Changes the customer's address", and 19% of address requests change the wrong one. What should you do?
opts: Rename them `update_billing_address` and `update_delivery_address`, saying which address each changes.
Merge them into one `manage_address` tool with a `kind` parameter, and keep the shared description as it is.
Add a system prompt table that maps each kind of address request to one of the two tools by name.
Keep the names and add "Do not use for delivery addresses" to one of the two descriptions only.
questions.explain: The two tools do different things but are named and described as if they were the same, so names and descriptions both need to say which address changes. B can be fine when actions share a contract, but here it keeps the shared description and moves the confusion into a parameter. C relies on a table in the prompt for what the tools should say about themselves. D corrects one side and leaves the other still ambiguous.
bullets: Renaming tools and updating descriptions to remove functional overlap
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: To remove an overlap, your team renamed `run_checks` to `run_unit_tests` and rewrote its description. Right afterwards 22% of sessions log "unknown tool: run_checks", and the agent then skips testing and commits. The new description is accurate and `run_unit_tests` is in the tool list of every affected agent. Where should you look first for the cause?
opts: At how tool definitions from earlier sessions are stored and served to the model.
At the system prompt and instructions, for text that still names `run_checks`.
At the new name, which may be so specific that the model hesitates to call it.
At the new description, which should mention the old name so that the model can map it.
questions.explain: The model is asking for a name that the tool list no longer holds, so it is reading it from text written before the rename, and instruction text is where such text sits. A has the tool list sent fresh on each request. C would not produce calls to a name that is gone. D treats a stale reference as a missing alias and keeps the old name alive.
bullets: Renaming tools and updating descriptions to remove functional overlap
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your support agent has one `manage_subscription(action, ...)` tool, where `action` is "pause", "cancel", "change_plan" or "refund_remaining". Each action needs different fields and returns a different shape, and in a sample of 300 conversations 8% of customers who asked to pause were cancelled. What is the most effective redesign?
opts: Keep one tool and add a `confirmed` boolean that the model must set before it cancels anything at all.
Keep one tool and put a table of each action's fields and results into its description text.
Split it into `pause_subscription`, `cancel_subscription`, `change_plan` and `refund_balance`.
Keep one tool and add a PostToolUse hook that restores any subscription cancelled by mistake.
questions.explain: Four jobs with different fields and results are hidden behind one entry point, so the model picks the job through a string value; one tool with an action parameter is fine when the actions share a contract, and these do not. Separate tools put each job's name, inputs and output in its own definition. A adds a flag the model can set wrongly as easily. B documents the differing contracts without removing them. D repairs the mistake after the customer has been affected.
bullets: Splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your database assistant has one tool, `run_sql(statement)`, used for SELECT reports and also for UPDATE and DELETE maintenance. Security wants every write to need a developer's approval in the IDE, while reads must stay unattended, and approvals are set per tool. A hook that searches the statement text for UPDATE or DELETE was tried and let through a `WITH ... DELETE` statement. What should you do?
opts: Add "never write without approval" to the `run_sql` description, and repeat it in the system prompt.
Require approval on every `run_sql` call, so that reads and writes share one safe rule.
Keep one tool and extend the text-matching hook to cover `WITH ... DELETE` and other forms.
Split it into `query_readonly` and `modify_data`, so approval can apply to the write tool alone.
questions.explain: Two different jobs, with different risk, share one entry point, so no rule on the tool can tell them apart; splitting gives each job its own contract and its own approval. A is an instruction, and the requirement is a guarantee. B ends the unattended reads. C keeps guessing at intent from text, which the missed statement already showed to be fragile.
bullets: Splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: Your `analyze_document` tool takes a `document_id` and returns the same summary-and-key-figures structure for PDFs, Word files and web pages. 3% of calls time out on files over 200 pages. An engineer proposes splitting it into `analyze_pdf`, `analyze_docx` and `analyze_webpage` to fix this. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Reject it: the split is by file type with one contract, so it adds near-duplicates and leaves timeouts.
Accept it: narrower tools with narrower descriptions are selected more reliably than one general tool is.
Accept it, and keep `analyze_document` as a general fallback for any other file format that comes up.
Reject it, and add a `format` parameter that tells the tool what the file is, so timeouts get set per format.
questions.explain: A split is for jobs with different purposes and contracts, while one tool is fine when the contract is shared; these three jobs are the same, and the failure is about length. B ignores that three near-identical descriptions create the overlap a split is meant to remove. C does the same and keeps a fourth tool. D relocates the same distinction into a parameter and does not touch the cause of the timeouts.
bullets: Splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A support agent's system prompt has 14 rules written by four teams. Six name a tool next to a trigger phrase, for example "when the customer mentions a chargeback, use `open_dispute`", and some of them were added to fix real routing failures. Overall tool-selection accuracy is 93% on your standard request set. Before launch you want to find unintended tool associations. Which review is most effective?
opts: Ask the model to list the prompt rules that might conflict with a tool description, and then fix what it reports.
Write requests with each rule's phrase that need another tool, and compare results with and without the rule.
Raise the launch bar for overall accuracy from 93% to 97% on the standard request set used so far.
Remove every rule that names a tool, and rely on the tool descriptions alone.
questions.explain: A misrouting caused by a phrase shows up only on requests that contain the phrase and belong elsewhere, and a with-and-without comparison shows which rule does it. A relies on the model's own opinion of its prompt. C raises a bar on a set that does not contain such requests. D discards rules that fixed real failures.
bullets: Reviewing system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that override good descriptions
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A support prompt says "Answer simple questions directly, without looking anything up." The agent now answers "how long do I have to return an electronics item?" from its own wording of the policy and is wrong in 17% of 300 such questions. The `search_kb` description already says it holds the current return and warranty policy. What is the best fix?
opts: Add "ALWAYS call a tool first" to the prompt, so that nothing at all is answered from memory.
Set `tool_choice` to `any`, so that every single turn of the conversation must call a tool.
Add three more sentences to the `search_kb` description saying that it holds the return policy text.
Name what may be answered directly, such as greetings, and send policy questions to the tool.
