questions.explain: The word "simple" lets the model decide that a short policy question is simple, and the instruction is the thing overriding a good description. Stating what counts as answerable without tools removes that reading. A swings to the opposite extreme. B also forces calls on greetings. C repeats what the description already says.
bullets: Reviewing system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that override good descriptions
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A research platform's usage report counts failed tool calls by scanning each result's text for the word "error". One archive server answers in German with "Zugriff verweigert" when it refuses a request. The dashboard shows 99% of calls succeeding, yet 22% of the failed calls were never counted, and several reports have gaps. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Add the German phrases, and those of the other archives, to the keyword list the report scans for.
Ask each subagent to end its summary with the line FAILED whenever a tool call did not work.
Count calls by the `isError` flag in each tool result, and have every server set it on a failure.
Run a small model over every tool result to label it as a success or a failure.
questions.explain: The flag is the agreed signal for a failed call, so counting it needs no reading of text in any language. A chases wording one language at a time and will miss the next phrasing. B relies on a model remembering to add a line, which is the kind of probabilistic step the report is trying to avoid. D adds a model call per result to recover what the server could state outright.
bullets: The MCP isError flag is how a tool tells the agent that a call failed
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A coordinator's harness ends a research run as soon as any MCP tool result carries `isError: true`, on the view that a flagged call cannot be recovered. 14% of runs now end this way. In a replay of 10 sampled runs, nine of the failed tools had said which argument was out of range, and a corrected call would have worked. How should you evaluate the harness rule?
opts: It discards what the flag is for: the model should see the error text, adjust and retry.
It is sound, because a flagged result means the run is unsafe to continue, so keep it and restart the run.
It is sound for tools the team owns, and should be relaxed only for tools from third-party servers.
It needs a threshold, so that the run ends after three flagged results in a row instead of the first one.
questions.explain: The flag reports that the call failed and the text says why, which lets the model correct itself; ending the run throws that away. B treats a failed call as a failed run. C separates tools by owner, but the cause of the failure and not its owner decides whether a retry can work. D still ends runs that a single corrected call would have saved.
bullets: The MCP isError flag is how a tool tells the agent that a call failed
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: A developer assistant has an in-process `query_metrics` tool whose handler lets exceptions escape. When the metrics service throttles it, Claude reads the raw message `HTTPStatusError: Client error '429 Too Many Requests' for url ...` and tells developers that "the metrics service is broken" in 25% of such cases, although the throttle clears in 30 seconds. What change fits best?
opts: Add a prompt rule that explains how to read raw HTTP exception messages from the tools.
Catch the error and return empty content, so that the assistant moves on to its next task.
Raise the handler's timeout so that fewer calls reach the point of failing in the first place.
Catch it in the handler and return `isError: true` with the cause and the wait.
questions.explain: An uncaught exception still reaches Claude as an error, but with the raw message; catching it lets the handler write what failed and what to do next. A asks the model to decode internals that the tool could simply state. B hides the failure and so invites a wrong conclusion. C targets timeouts, while this failure is a throttle.
bullets: The MCP isError flag is how a tool tells the agent that a call failed
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A subscription server labels a failure "transient" for any 5xx status and "validation" for any other 4xx. A customer asks to downgrade in month four of a 12-month contract, the backend answers 409 "contract term active", and the tool reports a validation error. The agent asks the customer to re-enter the plan code up to three times, in about 38 conversations a week. What is the most effective change?
opts: Report 409 as transient, so that the agent waits and tries again once the backend is ready.
Add a "business" category for contract and policy refusals, set by cause.
Tell the agent in its prompt to stop after two validation errors in a row and apologise.
Return the backend's 409 text as the whole error and drop the category from the response.
questions.explain: A refusal under a contract is a business error, which neither a retry nor a corrected plan code can change, so it needs its own kind, decided by what went wrong rather than by status code. A mislabels it and invites waiting for something that will not happen. C caps the repeats but still tells the customer nothing true. D removes the category that lets the agent choose a response.
bullets: Transient, validation, business and permission errors are different kinds that call for different responses
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: An engineer proposes that your assistant's tools report failures with only `isRetryable`, calling categories "overkill since the agent just needs retry or not". A week of logs holds 500 failures: 180 timeouts, 140 calls with bad arguments, 90 refusals for missing access and 90 breaches of a business rule. A routing script sends missing-access failures to an access-request queue. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Adopt it, because a yes or no flag covers every case and fewer fields leave fewer places for a tool to be wrong.
Adopt it, and describe the kind of failure in the message text so the model can read it there.
Keep the category: the 320 non-retryable failures need different responses, and the script reads it.
Reject it, but only to add a retry-after field for timeouts and leave the other failures with the flag.
questions.explain: Not retrying is one outcome, but the next step differs: fix the arguments, request access, or explain the rule. A flag cannot say which, and the script cannot read prose reliably. A treats one bit as enough for four kinds of failure. B leaves the kind in text that code cannot route on. D improves timeouts only and keeps the other three kinds indistinct.
bullets: Transient, validation, business and permission errors are different kinds that call for different responses
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: The developer assistant's `get_payroll_report` tool returns an error with category "permission" and `isRetryable: false`, because its service account has no payroll scope. A developer asked for the report to plan a team budget. The analytics export tool, which the assistant can call, is not meant to expose payroll data. Which behaviour should the assistant show?
opts: Stop trying to read that report, tell the developer which access is missing, and let them request it.
Retry after a pause, in case the permission change that was approved earlier has not yet taken effect.
Retry with a narrower date range, since smaller requests sometimes pass the access check.
Read the same figures through the analytics export tool, which the assistant is able to call.
questions.explain: A permission failure needs someone with authority to grant access, so the assistant should report it and stop at that resource. B retries what the flag says cannot succeed. C changes the arguments, which do not decide access. D gets around the control through another route to the same data.
bullets: Transient, validation, business and permission errors are different kinds that call for different responses
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: An `exchange_item` tool returns "Request could not be completed" for every failure. In 300 reviewed chats the agent apologised and offered a phone number, and in 55% of them the server log reads "size M out of stock; size L available". The customers had not asked for the phone line. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The agent is too ready to give up, and its prompt should tell it to try other sizes.
The response carries no cause, so the agent cannot tell a stock gap from a fault.
The failures are temporary, and the agent should retry the exchange before it apologises.
The agent has too many tools, so it picks the wrong exchange route and cannot complete it.
questions.explain: The cause is in the log and not in the response, so the agent has nothing to act on. A asks for initiative with no information to use it on. C assumes a temporary fault, but the log shows a stock position that a retry will not change. D blames tool choice, when the tool that ran was the right one.
bullets: A uniform 'Operation failed' response leaves the agent unable to choose a recovery
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A `charge_saved_card` tool returns "Operation failed" for declines, expired cards and gateway outages alike. In 11 of 80 reviewed chats the agent told the customer "your card was declined" while the gateway log shows an outage at that moment, and several customers then cancelled their orders. Which change is most effective?
opts: Add a prompt rule that forbids the agent to name a reason for a failure.
Switch to a larger model, which gives fewer unsupported explanations when a tool says little.
Retry the charge once inside the agent loop before the customer is told anything.
Return a category and a plain description of the cause, so the agent can report it.
questions.explain: A tool that gives no cause leaves the model to fill the gap with a guess, and the fix is to supply the cause. A would stop the guess but leave the agent unable to say anything useful. B treats the symptom with a bigger model and still gives it no facts. C retries a decline that cannot succeed and does nothing for the wrong message.
bullets: A uniform 'Operation failed' response leaves the agent unable to choose a recovery
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A platform team returns the same "Internal error" for every tool failure, "so we never leak internals", and the developer assistant on top of the tools retries blindly and wastes minutes. Security's real concern is hostnames and stack traces reaching the model. How should you evaluate the design?
opts: Keep it: any extra detail in an error is a leak, so one fixed message is the safe design.
Keep the message, and let the assistant read the server logs to learn what went wrong.
Return a category, a retry flag and a description; keep traces and hostnames in server logs.
Return the full exception with its stack trace, since the assistant runs inside the company network.
questions.explain: The concern is leaking internals, not giving the agent a cause, and a short description can carry the cause without any hostname or trace. A gives up recovery to avoid a risk that has a narrower answer. B opens more of the internals than the description would. D sends exactly what security wanted kept out.
bullets: A uniform 'Operation failed' response leaves the agent unable to choose a recovery
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A `run_linter` server returns `isRetryable: true` on every error. The harness retries a flagged call up to three times with a 5-second pause. Of 400 failing calls in a week, 310 were "file not found" for a path the agent had mistyped, and only 15 retried calls ever succeeded. What is the root cause of the wasted time?
opts: The server flags every failure as retryable, so the flag tells the harness nothing.
The harness allows three retries per call, which is more than most tool calls need to succeed.
The pause between retries is too short for the linter to recover from its own failures.
The agent has no tool for checking that a path exists before it calls the linter tool.
questions.explain: The harness is doing what the flag asks, so the flag has to be right: mistyped paths cannot succeed on a retry and should be reported as not retryable. B changes the number of wasted attempts without removing them. C assumes recovery that cannot happen for a missing file. D adds a prevention step, but the waste comes from retrying.
bullets: Retryable and non-retryable errors differ, and structured metadata prevents wasted retries
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A carrier API answers your `track_parcel` tool with HTTP 429 and a `Retry-After` of 30 seconds. Which error should the tool return to the support agent?
opts: Category "business", `isRetryable: false`, and the message "Tracking limit applies to this account."
Category "transient", `isRetryable: true`, and the message "Carrier is limiting requests; retry after 30 seconds."
Category "transient", `isRetryable: false`, and the message "Too many requests; try again later."
Category "permission", `isRetryable: true`, and the message "Carrier refused this request; retry after 30 seconds."
questions.explain: A 429 throttle is temporary, the same call will work after the wait, and the description tells the agent how long. A calls a temporary throttle a rule about the account and stops the agent. C contradicts itself, since it calls the failure transient yet forbids the retry. D files a throttle under access and so points the agent at the wrong response.
bullets: Retryable and non-retryable errors differ, and structured metadata prevents wasted retries
Return errorCategory, isRetryable and a human-readable description
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A `build_preview` tool returns `isError: true`, category "validation" and `isRetryable: false` for an unknown branch name. The harness log shows the identical call three times, two seconds apart, while the model request log shows a single assistant turn. What is the root cause?
opts: The model ignores the structured fields and needs a prompt telling it not to repeat a failed call.
The flag is honoured only when its value is repeated in the description text of the error as well.
The retry logic can act on the error only when it is raised as a JSON-RPC protocol error by the server.
The retry logic around the call treats any flagged result as retryable, whatever `isRetryable` says.
questions.explain: The repeats happen inside the harness within one model turn, in code that retries whatever is flagged. Metadata helps only if the code that retries reads it. A blames the model, but only one assistant turn occurred. B and C describe behaviour that the stem gives no sign of.
bullets: Retryable and non-retryable errors differ, and structured metadata prevents wasted retries
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: An `apply_coupon` tool returns an error with category "validation", `isRetryable: true` and the description "ERR_CPN_114". In 40 chats the agent told the customer "the system reported error 114", and none of them got a usable next step. Which fix is best?
opts: Put a table that explains the ERR codes in the system prompt, and keep the code in the description.
Map every ERR code to an HTTP status and return that status as the description.
Replace the code with a plain statement of what is wrong and what to supply.
Set `isRetryable` to false so that the agent stops mentioning the code to the customer.
questions.explain: A description is written for a reader who has to act on it, and a code that only the server team understands is not that. A pushes decoding into a prompt table that drifts from the codes. B swaps one opaque value for another. D misreads the flag: it controls retries, not what the agent says.
bullets: Return errorCategory, isRetryable and a human-readable description
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Four teams own twelve internal MCP tools. Failures that clear on their own are labelled "temp", "transient", "retry_later" and "TRANSIENT_ERR" depending on the team, and the agent retries some and not others. All four teams can change their servers. What is the best way to fix this?
opts: Define one shared set of categories and the retry flag in a helper every server imports.
Add a table of the four spellings to the agent's system prompt and say they mean the same thing.
Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each spelling into one before the agent reads the result.
Let each team keep its own labels, and publish a style guide that explains how to name them.
questions.explain: The servers are all owned, so the definition belongs at the source, where one shared list makes a mismatch impossible. B depends on a model matching spellings every time. C patches downstream what the owners could fix once. D leaves four vocabularies in place and only documents them.
bullets: Return errorCategory, isRetryable and a human-readable description
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A `search_trials` tool takes six parameters and rejects a bad call with category "validation" and the description "Invalid argument." The agent repeats the same call twice and then drops the registry from its report in 20% of runs. Which change is most effective?
opts: Allow the harness three more attempts per call, so the agent has room to find the right arguments.
Say which argument failed, why, and which values are accepted, beside the category and flag.
Return the tool's complete input schema with every validation error and let the model compare.
Make the system prompt list the legal value of each parameter for all of the tools the agent has.
questions.explain: The description should point to the argument that failed and how to correct it, so the next call can differ from the last. A adds attempts of the same failing call. C sends the whole schema when one parameter is wrong, which buries the answer. D copies tool details into a prompt that goes stale, and still does not say which argument failed.
bullets: Return errorCategory, isRetryable and a human-readable description
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A `buy_gift_card` tool refuses an order that contains a promotion code and returns "Declined: rule GC-9". About 25 customers a week are told "your payment was declined" and re-enter their cards. Which response from the tool is best?
opts: The same text with category "transient", so the agent suggests trying again later.
A "transient" error that says gift cards cannot be bought with a promotion code, so try later.
A success reply stating that no gift card was issued for this order.
A "business" error, `isRetryable: false`: no gift cards with a promotion code.
questions.explain: A rule breach is a business error: the agent should stop retrying and be able to tell the customer the real reason. A suggests a wait and gives no reason. B gives the reason but files it as transient, so the agent invites a retry that cannot succeed. C reports a refusal as a success, so nothing marks the call as failed.
bullets: For business-rule violations return isRetryable: false and a customer-friendly explanation
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A support agent's tools enforce 40 policy rules and fail with "Blocked: rule R-17, `isRetryable: false`". The team plans to keep the customer-facing wording in a system-prompt table keyed by rule number. Policy text changes about once a month, and the prompt table has already drifted from it twice. How should you evaluate the plan?
opts: Adopt it: one table in one place is easier to update than 40 strings spread across the tools.
Adopt it, and load the table through a CLAUDE.md file so that every deployment picks it up.
Have each enforcing tool return its own customer wording, so rule and text change together.
Adopt it, and add a nightly test that checks every rule number has a row in the table.
questions.explain: The explanation belongs with the code that enforces the rule, so an edit to the rule cannot leave stale wording behind. A moves the wording away from the rule it describes. B changes where the table is stored and keeps the split. D detects a missing row but not a row whose wording has gone out of date.
bullets: For business-rule violations return isRetryable: false and a customer-friendly explanation
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your developer assistant has a `purge_logs` tool, and company policy keeps audit logs for seven years. When asked to clean up a 3-year-old log set, the tool must refuse. How should the refusal be configured so the assistant handles it well?
opts: A "business" error with `isRetryable: false`, explaining that logs under retention cannot be purged.
An error with category "transient" and `isRetryable: true`, so the assistant tries again at a quieter time.
An error with category "validation", so the assistant supplies a different date range and asks again.
A success result that reports 0 logs purged, so the assistant carries on with the rest of its cleanup.
questions.explain: The refusal is a policy rule, so the assistant must stop and tell the developer why. B turns a rule into a wait. C implies the request was malformed, so the assistant would hunt for dates that pass. D reports a refusal as a success and hides that the cleanup did not happen.
bullets: For business-rule violations return isRetryable: false and a customer-friendly explanation
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A fetch subagent, which can fetch any URL it is given, reads six PDFs from one mirror, times out on two of them, and tells the coordinator "2 sources unavailable". The coordinator hands the two to a fresh subagent, which tries the same mirror and fails, and the loop repeats three times in 31% of runs, although the publisher's own site would serve both files. What is the root cause?
opts: The coordinator's timeout is too short for the mirror to answer.
The coordinator should resume the original subagent and not create a new one for the retry.
The subagent lacks a web fetch tool and so cannot reach the publisher's site.
The report says what failed but not what was tried, so the same route is repeated.
questions.explain: The coordinator can choose another route only if it knows which routes have been used, and the report does not tell it. A and B change the attempt that repeats and not the information the next attempt lacks. C is ruled out because the subagent can fetch any URL it is given.
bullets: Recover from transient failures inside the subagent; pass up only unresolved errors with partial results and attempts
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: One run of a research subagent hit four problems: an archive 503 that cleared on the second attempt, a throttle that cleared after a 20-second wait, a licensed database that refused access to six papers, and a scanned PDF with no extractable text for which it has no OCR tool. Which should it send up to the coordinator?
opts: All four, so that the coordinator has the complete picture of the run.
The refused papers and the scanned PDF, with the results so far and what was tried.
Only the refused papers, because the scanned PDF is a content problem and not an access one.
The 503 and the throttle, because the coordinator owns the timing of any retries.
questions.explain: The subagent can settle the two transient failures itself, and only what it cannot resolve needs a decision from above, together with the partial results and the attempts made. A moves problems that were already solved. C keeps back a failure the subagent cannot fix either. D sends up the problems that were resolved and keeps back those that were not.
bullets: Recover from transient failures inside the subagent; pass up only unresolved errors with partial results and attempts
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A test-running subagent retries a flaky test-database connection with no limit. One run held for 25 minutes on the same failure and kept the coordinator, and four sibling subagents waiting on its result, from finishing. Which design is best?
opts: Cap local retries with backoff, then return the failure plus results of the tests that ran.
Remove local retries so the first connection failure goes straight to the coordinator.
Let the coordinator cancel any subagent after 10 minutes and discard whatever it produced.
Raise the database connection timeout so that each attempt waits longer before it counts as failed.
questions.explain: Local retry fits a transient failure, but it needs a limit, after which the failure goes up with partial results and the attempts made. B sends up failures that one retry would have fixed. C throws away work and ends the subagent without a report of what it tried. D makes each attempt slower and still has no end.
bullets: Recover from transient failures inside the subagent; pass up only unresolved errors with partial results and attempts
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A `find_usages` tool returns `references: []` both when no code uses a function and when the repository's index is still building. The assistant was told that `legacy_total()` had no usages in `billing-v2`, deleted it, and three modules stopped compiling. The index build for that repository had not finished. Which change is most effective?
opts: Tell the assistant in its prompt to confirm every empty result with Grep before deleting any code.
Return `references: []` together with the time of the last index build, and let the model judge it.
Return an error that the index is still building; keep an empty list for real no-hit searches.
Give new repositories a higher priority in the index queue, so that builds finish sooner.
questions.explain: A search that could not run says nothing about usages, so it must not look like a search that found none. A relies on the model remembering a check for each deletion. B leaves the ambiguity in place and makes the model reason about a timestamp. D shortens the window in which the failure happens but does not remove the confusion.
bullets: Tell an access failure (a retry decision) apart from a valid empty result (a successful query)
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A support agent's `order_history` tool returns a successful empty list for a customer with no orders in the past 90 days. A proposal says the tool should return an error in that case, "so the agent definitely notices". Logs show the current agent already tells such customers that nothing was found. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Adopt it: an error is noticed more reliably than an empty list, which an agent may skip.
Keep it a success with an empty list, and name the period searched.
Adopt it, and set `isRetryable: true` so that the agent checks again before it answers.
Keep it as a success, but return the customer's older orders so that the list is never empty.
questions.explain: A lookup that ran and found nothing has given a true answer, and flagging it as an error would send the agent into retries or escalation for no reason. A treats a correct answer as a fault. C adds retries for a lookup that worked. D changes the answer by returning orders outside the period that was asked for.
bullets: Tell an access failure (a retry decision) apart from a valid empty result (a successful query)
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A systematic-review agent calls a `search_all` tool that queries four sources and merges whatever comes back. In 9% of runs the report says "no registered trials found", although a manual check finds some. In those runs the clinical trials registry logged a timeout, and the tool still returned the other three sources' results without any note. What is the root cause?
opts: The synthesis agent should have cross-checked the registry through a separate web search.
The registry's timeout is set too short for its busiest hours.
The synthesis prompt does not tell the agent to confirm that trials are absent before reporting.
The merge step drops a failed source, so a source never searched looks like no matches.
questions.explain: The tool turned an access failure into an empty contribution, so the agent could not tell 'searched, nothing' from 'could not search'. A and C ask the agent to compensate for a signal the tool should have given. B concerns how often the failure happens and not why it goes unnoticed when it does.
bullets: Tell an access failure (a retry decision) apart from a valid empty result (a successful query)
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A developer assistant is connected to five MCP servers (git, tickets, CI, docs, database) and now exposes 27 tools. A typical task uses at most five of them. In a 300-task sample it called a wrong but similar tool in 11% of tasks, against 2% when it had 6 tools. Which change most effectively lowers the error rate?
opts: Move to a stronger model tier, which can tell 27 similar tools apart.
Give each kind of task an agent holding only the few tools it uses.
Place a table of all 27 tools and when to use each in the system prompt.
Require the model to say which tool it will call, and why, before each call.
questions.explain: Selection gets harder as the number of options per decision grows, so splitting the work into agents with small, role-specific tool sets attacks the cause. A leaves the same 27 options in front of the model. C adds more text about the same list without reducing the choices. D asks for reasoning over the same 27 options.
bullets: Giving an agent too many tools (18 instead of 4 or 5) makes tool selection less reliable
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A support agent holds 14 tools for orders, shipping and refunds, and wrong-tool calls have risen from 3% at 6 tools to 9%. Product wants to add three gift-card tools (issue, check balance, void). They are needed in about 4% of chats and have nothing to do with the existing work. What is the best way to add them?
opts: Add them to the agent and rewrite the refund tool descriptions so the gift-card tools are not confused with them.
Add them and let a keyword router switch on only the 8 tools that look relevant to each message.
Give them to a separate gift-card agent, and have the coordinator hand it those requests.
Add them and drop the three least-used existing tools so that the total stays at 14.
questions.explain: A separate agent keeps the main agent's choice set from growing and gives the new tools a small set of their own. A leaves the agent with 17 tools to choose between. B adds a brittle routing layer in front of the model. D removes working capability to make room.
bullets: Giving an agent too many tools (18 instead of 4 or 5) makes tool selection less reliable
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A research team measured tool-selection accuracy for one agent as it was given more tools, keeping every description accurate and distinct: 98% with 4 tools, 94% with 9, 86% with 17 and 71% with 30. A teammate says the descriptions must be failing. Which reading of the data is best supported?
opts: Every added tool is one more option to tell apart, so accuracy falls; split the tools by role.
The descriptions are failing, so rewrite the 26 that were added after the first four.
Definitions fill the context, so cutting every description in half should restore the accuracy.
Tools late in the list get skipped, so ordering the list by how often each tool is used should restore it.
questions.explain: The decline tracks the number of tools while the descriptions stay accurate, which points to decision complexity, and the lever is a smaller tool set per agent. B contradicts the stem's description that they are accurate and distinct. C shortens the very descriptions the model relies on. D assumes a position effect that the data does not show.
bullets: Giving an agent too many tools (18 instead of 4 or 5) makes tool selection less reliable
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A citation-checking subagent should only compare quoted passages with source texts supplied in its prompt. Its definition has a description and a prompt but no tools field. In 6% of runs the report file was rewritten, and in others the agent searched the web for new quotes. The spawn prompt always contains the passages and the sources. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The subagent cannot see the coordinator's conversation, so it fills the gaps by acting on its own.
Its description is too short for the coordinator to understand what the subagent is for.
The definition grants every available tool, and an agent with spare tools tends to use them.
The sources arrive as text, so it goes looking for the original documents.
questions.explain: With the tools field left out the subagent inherits everything, and tools beyond its job get used. A is ruled out because the prompt carries the passages and sources. B concerns when the coordinator delegates, not what the subagent does once running. D does not explain the rewritten report file.
bullets: Agents holding tools outside their specialty tend to misuse them
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A code-review subagent was tested in two configurations over 400 reviews each. Configuration 1 had Read, Grep and Glob. Configuration 2 added Bash "to run the linter". Configuration 2 ran the full test suite in 23 reviews, ran git commands unrelated to the diff in 9, and modified a file in 3; configuration 1 showed none of this. Review quality scores were the same. What does the result best support?
opts: Bash is unreliable inside subagents, so shell access should be removed from every agent.
The reviewer prompt needs a longer checklist, because the extra actions show it misunderstood its task.
The gap is probably noise, because review quality scores were the same in both configurations.
The extra tool opened actions outside the job and they were used; supply lint output another way.
questions.explain: Capability beyond the role was used, so the cause is the tool set, and the linter need can be met with a narrower route. A overgeneralises from one extra tool. B treats a tool-set problem as a prompt problem. C ignores that 35 unrequested actions appeared in one arm and none in the other; equal quality scores do not make them harmless.
bullets: Agents holding tools outside their specialty tend to misuse them
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A refund-policy subagent holds `process_refund` as well as its lookup tools, because the team wanted to avoid a second hand-off. A prompt line "Answer policy questions only; never issue refunds" cut unintended refunds from 12 per 1,000 chats to 5 per 1,000, and three rewordings have not improved on that. What is the best next step?
opts: Move the sentence to the top of the prompt and put the key word in capitals, to stress it.
Remove `process_refund` from this subagent; another agent is meant to issue refunds.
Add ten examples of correct refusals to the prompt, since the rule alone is not enough.
Have it state its intended action in text before each call, so mistakes can be caught.
questions.explain: An instruction lowers the odds of misuse but cannot remove it while the tool is available; taking the tool away does. A and C keep trying to persuade a model that still has the capability. D relies on the model reporting its own errors correctly before they happen.
bullets: Agents holding tools outside their specialty tend to misuse them
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: In a support system the billing, shipping and returns subagents each hold only their own tools. The returns subagent needs the carrier's delivery date in 70% of its cases. It is one read-only field available through the shipping subagent's tracking tool, so each time returns asks the coordinator and waits for a shipping subagent to run. Operations also want every cross-agent request to stay visible in the coordinator's log. Which design keeps the roles and removes most of the delay?
opts: Give returns the shipping subagent's full toolset so it can look up anything it wants about a parcel.
Give returns a read-only `get_delivery_date(order_id)` tool; the rest goes via the coordinator.
Paste the delivery date of every open order into the returns subagent's prompt at each spawn.
Let returns message the shipping subagent directly whenever it needs a delivery date.
questions.explain: A single narrow, read-only tool covers the frequent need while the role boundaries and the coordinator's visibility stay. A hands over a whole role's capability. C ships data nobody asked for and goes stale. D bypasses the coordinator, which the stem says must see cross-agent requests.
bullets: Scoped tool access: only the tools a role needs, plus a few limited cross-role tools for frequent needs
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: Over a week a coordinator logged what its test-writer subagent requested from the code-explorer subagent: 58% single-symbol signature lookups, 25% "find all callers of this function across modules" (needing several rounds of judgment about indirect calls), and 17% other. Each relay costs about 30 seconds. The test-writer holds only Read and Write. Which addition best fits scoped cross-role access?
opts: A narrow `get_signature(symbol)` tool for the test-writer; the explorer keeps caller tracing.
A general `search_repo` tool that lets the test-writer run Grep across the whole repository.
A `trace_callers(function)` tool for the test-writer, since it removes the slowest requests.
No new tool; the coordinator pre-loads the explorer's entire index into the test-writer's prompt.
questions.explain: The frequent, simple need gets a narrow tool, and the complex multi-round work stays where judgment is available. B covers all three request types and so erases the role boundary. C moves a task needing repeated judgment into a single-call tool. D loads far more than any task uses.
bullets: Scoped tool access: only the tools a role needs, plus a few limited cross-role tools for frequent needs
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: In a five-subagent research system every subagent is limited to its own tools and sends all other needs to the coordinator. By the middle of a typical run the coordinator's context is 80% full, and most of it is relay traffic: "convert this amount to USD" and "what weekday was this date" requests and answers, repeated dozens of times. Report quality drops after that point. What is the most effective change?
opts: Give each subagent the complete toolset of whichever agent usually answers, so nothing is relayed.
Have the coordinator summarise its own context whenever it passes 70% full, to free up room.
Start a second coordinator to take over once the first reaches 80% of its context window.
Give subagents two small tools for those two lookups, keeping the rest on the coordinator.
questions.explain: The two frequent needs are simple, so narrow tools remove most of the traffic while the roles stay intact. A erases the role boundaries. B copes with the symptom and still sends the relays through. C adds a second coordinator to carry the same traffic.
bullets: Scoped tool access: only the tools a role needs, plus a few limited cross-role tools for frequent needs
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A support chat agent has five tools and runs with `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}`. When customers send "hello" or "thanks, that's all" (about 15% of chats), it calls `get_customer` with an empty identifier, gets an error, and then apologises for a system problem. What is the best fix?
opts: Switch to `auto`, so the model can reply in text when no tool fits the message.
Keep `any` and make `get_customer` return a friendlier error for an empty identifier.
Force `get_customer` by name, so there is no doubt which tool is called.
Keep `any` and add a prompt rule that greetings need no lookup.
questions.explain: `any` requires a tool call on every turn, so a message with no tool need still produces one; `auto` lets the model answer in text. B softens the error but the pointless call remains. C makes the call certain rather than optional. D asks the prompt to override a setting that requires a call.
bullets: The tool_choice options: auto, any, and forced selection of a named tool
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A research pipeline makes one request per step. Step 1 offers four tools and must begin with `plan_subtopics`. Step 2 offers the same four tools; the model may call any of them or reply with a plain-text status. Step 3 lists only `submit_summary` and `submit_full`; one of them must be called and the model decides which. Which `tool_choice` values for steps 1, 2 and 3 meet this?
opts: `any`, `auto`, forced `submit_full` by name
`auto`, `auto`, `any` on all three steps
forced `plan_subtopics`, `auto`, `any`
forced `plan_subtopics`, `any`, `auto`
questions.explain: Step 1 needs one named tool, so forced selection; step 2 allows free choice including text, so `auto`; step 3 needs some tool without naming it, so `any`. A uses `any` where a named tool is required and forces the choice step 3 leaves to the model. B cannot guarantee step 1. D stops step 2 from replying in text and lets step 3 skip the call.
bullets: The tool_choice options: auto, any, and forced selection of a named tool
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A reviewer is checking the `tool_choice` plan for a developer-productivity agent. Which line would not behave as its author expects?
opts: Open questions about the repository use `auto`, so the model can answer in plain text when no tool is needed.
The first request of a session forces `load_config` by name, because it has to run before anything else.
The verdict step lists `approve_change` and `reject_change` and uses `any`, so a verdict is always recorded.
The lint step uses `any`, because `lint_report` has to run and that setting selects that tool.
questions.explain: `any` guarantees that some tool is called but leaves the choice to the model; running a particular tool takes forced selection by name. A, B and C each match the setting to what it does: free text with `auto`, a named first call with forced selection, and one of two listed tools with `any`.
bullets: The tool_choice options: auto, any, and forced selection of a named tool
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: You are defining a `document-reader` subagent that must read and search files but never write them or run commands. Which definition does that?
opts: Leave the `tools` field out and give it the description "Read-only document reader".
`tools: Read, Grep, Glob`
`disallowedTools: Read, Grep, Glob`
`tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash`, with Bash used only for `cat` and `ls`.
questions.explain: An explicit allowlist gives the subagent exactly those tools. A omits the field, which means it inherits every tool whatever the description says. C removes the very tools it needs. D includes a shell that can write files, with the limit stated only in words.
bullets: Restricting each subagent's tool set to its role to prevent cross-specialty misuse
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A documentation-lookup subagent needs two tools, `search_docs` and `fetch_page`. It runs in a project where five MCP servers expose 25 tools, and a new server is added about once a week. Its tools field is currently omitted, and it picks a wrong tool in 8% of lookups. Which change keeps its tool set right over the coming months?
opts: Set its `tools` field to `search_docs` and `fetch_page`.
Leave `tools` out and list the 23 other tools in `disallowedTools`.
Leave `tools` out and add a prompt paragraph naming the two tools it should prefer.
Move the five servers to user scope so that subagents no longer see them.
questions.explain: An allowlist stays correct as servers are added, because anything not listed is not available. B works today but each new server's tools are inherited until someone lists them. C leaves every tool available and relies on the prompt. D changes where the servers are configured, not which tools a subagent inherits.
bullets: Restricting each subagent's tool set to its role to prevent cross-specialty misuse
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A research system has three subagents: search, analysis and synthesis. The available tools are `web_search`, `fetch_page`, `read_document`, `compute_stats` and `write_report`. Which assignment follows the principle of restricting each subagent to its role?
opts: All three get all five tools, and each prompt names the tools that particular agent should use.
Search gets all five tools since it runs first, while analysis and synthesis keep only their own.
Search: `web_search`, `fetch_page`. Analysis: `read_document`, `compute_stats`. Synthesis: `write_report`.
Search and analysis keep their own tools; synthesis also gets `web_search` to fill gaps found while writing.
questions.explain: Each agent holds exactly the tools its job needs. A puts the restriction in the prompt only. B gives the broadest toolset to the agent most likely to wander. D lets synthesis do search work, which is the cross-role misuse the split is meant to prevent.
bullets: Restricting each subagent's tool set to its role to prevent cross-specialty misuse
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A deployment assistant has one generic `run_shell(command)` tool. Its real duties are restarting three named services and reading the last N log lines of each. Over 1,200 sessions it also installed packages in 14 and deleted a temp directory in 2, none requested. The team has already seen `curl | sh` and `apt` get past command deny lists. Which change best addresses this?
opts: Add a PreToolUse hook that denies any command containing `rm`, `pip` or `npm`, and logs the attempt.
Add a prompt section that lists the only shell commands the assistant may use during a session, with examples.
Log every command and have an engineer review the whole log each morning.
Replace it with `restart_service(name)` and `tail_log(name, lines)` for the three service names.
questions.explain: Tools that can do only the two duties, and validate their input, remove the unwanted actions at the source. A covers only the commands someone thought of; other installers and delete forms pass. B relies on the model following the list. C finds problems after they have happened.
bullets: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained one that validates its input
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A support agent uses a generic `send_email(to, subject, body)` tool. An audit of 2,000 chats found 17 replies sent to an address the customer had typed into the chat instead of the account's address, once exposing order details to a third party. Which change best fixes the tool design?
opts: Keep `send_email` and ask the agent to read the address back to the customer before sending.
Replace it with `send_order_update(order_id, template)`, recipient taken from the account.
Keep `send_email` and list the permitted recipient domains in the system prompt.
Add a PostToolUse hook that records each sent message for weekly compliance review.
questions.explain: A constrained tool that fixes the recipient and the content type makes the unsafe send impossible. A has the customer confirm an address that may be a third party's. C asks the prompt to police a tool that accepts any recipient. D records the leak after the message has gone.
bullets: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained one that validates its input
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: To stop research subagents fetching login pages and images, a team added a validated `load_document(url)` tool that rejects anything but supported document types. They left the generic `fetch_url` in the tools list "as a fallback". Two weeks later 8% of calls still go to non-document pages, almost unchanged, and the logs show every one of them is a `fetch_url` call. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The generic tool is still listed, so the agent can pick it and the unsafe path stays open.
`load_document` needs more worked examples in its description to compete with the simpler tool.
Subagents ignore their tool list unless the prompt repeats the names of the permitted tools.
The unsupported pages arrive through redirects that `load_document` follows without checking.
questions.explain: A constrained tool only helps when the generic one is gone; while both exist the agent can still take the open route. B tries to win the choice by persuasion rather than removing it. C describes behaviour that does not match an explicit tool list. D is ruled out because every bad call is `fetch_url`.
bullets: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained one that validates its input
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A docs-writer subagent has a narrow read-only `get_package_version` tool that covers most of its needs. While updating examples it must find out whether a breaking change in version 3 affects any of three modules that each use a different part of the library. What should it do?
opts: Call `get_package_version` for each module and infer the impact from the version numbers.
Ask for the build subagent's manifest-editing tool so that it can read the changelogs itself.
Hand the question back so the coordinator can route it to the code-explorer subagent.
Write the examples for version 3 and mark the three modules as unverified in a footnote.
questions.explain: The narrow tool answers the frequent simple question; an impact analysis across modules is a complex case, and those go through the coordinator. A treats a version string as evidence of impact. B asks for a tool that can edit manifests. D completes the task while leaving the question unanswered.
bullets: Giving a scoped cross-role tool for a frequent need while routing complex cases through the coordinator
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: In a support system, 90% of the billing subagent's cases need only to know whether the customer's identity was verified earlier in the chat. The identity subagent holds `get_customer` (the full record, including payment details), `send_verification_code` and `update_contact`. Which option best serves billing?
opts: Give billing `get_customer`, since the tool only reads data.
Give billing `send_verification_code`, so it can verify the customer itself when unsure.
Run every billing case through the identity subagent, to leave billing's tools unchanged.
Give billing an `is_verified(customer_id)` tool that returns only true or false.
questions.explain: The frequent need is a yes or no answer, so a tool that returns exactly that serves it with no more access than required. A exposes payment details billing does not need. B hands over an action that contacts the customer. C sends 90% of cases through a relay.
bullets: Giving a scoped cross-role tool for a frequent need while routing complex cases through the coordinator
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A synthesis subagent was given `check_figure(claim_id)`, which returns the source's value for one figure, and it worked well for single figures. Logs now show it calling the tool up to 15 times on a claim where two sources disagree, getting a different value each time, and then writing the average into the report. What is the best change?
opts: Add a prompt rule not to call `check_figure` more than twice per claim.
Make the tool flag conflicting sources and return no value, so the claim goes to the coordinator.
Give the subagent the full source-comparison toolset that the analysis subagent uses to compare them.
Cache the first value returned so every repeat call gives the same figure.
questions.explain: The cross-role tool should stay narrow and signal when a case is beyond it, so that the complex disagreement is routed through the coordinator. A caps the calls but the average still gets written. C turns a limited tool into a second analysis agent. D hides the disagreement behind a stable but arbitrary number.
bullets: Giving a scoped cross-role tool for a frequent need while routing complex cases through the coordinator
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A repository assistant edits files for tickets. When a ticket touches the `migrations/` folder it must call `check_schema_lock(migration_path)` before any edit; the tool needs a path that only migration tickets have. With a prompt rule alone, 5 of the last 40 migration tickets skipped the check. What is the most effective setup?
opts: Force `check_schema_lock` first when code sees a `migrations/` path, then use `auto`.
Force `check_schema_lock` on the first request of every ticket, so the rule cannot be missed.
Use `any` on the first request of every ticket, so some tool is called before editing.
Run `check_schema_lock` after the edits and revert them if the schema turns out to be locked.
questions.explain: The application knows from the ticket whether the check applies, so it forces the tool only then and returns to `auto` for later steps. B forces a call that needs a migration path on tickets that have none. C guarantees some tool, not this one. D checks after the damage is done.
bullets: Forcing a specific tool first, then handling later steps in follow-up turns
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: In a research pipeline `plan_subtopics` must run first, so the first request forces it. What happens next depends on what the searches return, which cannot be predicted from the plan: sometimes `read_page` is needed on known sources, sometimes another `web_search`. A developer proposes forcing each later call in code from the plan's `breadth` field, giving a fixed script of forced calls. Which approach is better?
opts: Force each later call from the plan's `breadth` field, producing a fixed script.
Start a new conversation for each step, pasting the plan into the prompt.
Send its result back with the history and let the model choose the next tool.
Use `any` on the follow-up requests so that a tool is called at every step.
questions.explain: Only the first step needs a guarantee; later steps go in follow-up turns where the model, which sees the results so far, picks the tool. A hard-codes a sequence that the stem says depends on unpredictable results. B drops the history the model needs. D rules out ending the loop with a plain-text answer.
bullets: Forcing a specific tool first, then handling later steps in follow-up turns
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: A support chat agent must begin each conversation by calling `lookup_customer`, and the team enforced that with a forced `tool_choice`. Median reply time has risen from 2 s to 7 s, and the logs show lookup calls on messages such as "what are your opening hours?". What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Customer lookups are not cached, so each forced call repeats the full lookup.
`any` was set in place of a forced tool, so the model repeats a lookup it has already made.
The prompt does not say the customer should be looked up once per conversation.
The forced setting is applied to every request, not only the first of the conversation.
questions.explain: Forcing is for the step that must come first; if the same setting goes on every later request, every message triggers the call. A would make repeated calls cheaper but would not explain why they occur. B names a different setting than the one used. C asks the prompt to override a forced choice.
bullets: Forcing a specific tool first, then handling later steps in follow-up turns
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A support platform needs every chat to end with a recorded disposition, through the tools `resolve_ticket`, `escalate_ticket` or `request_callback`. With `tool_choice: auto`, 6% of chats close with a sympathetic sentence and no tool call. Operations added a regex over the reply to guess the disposition, and it misreads 1 in 5 of those chats. The disposition is requested in a closing request of its own that lists only these three tools. What is the best fix?
opts: Add more patterns to the regex until it reads the sympathetic sentences correctly.
Set `tool_choice` to `any` on that closing request, so a disposition tool is called.
Force `resolve_ticket` by name, since most chats end that way in practice.
Ask the model to end each message with a bracketed disposition keyword and match that.
questions.explain: `any` guarantees a tool call and lets the model choose which disposition fits, so no text needs parsing. A keeps guessing from free text. C records the wrong disposition for every chat that is not a resolution. D is a prompt request, which can be skipped like the original rule.
bullets: Using tool_choice any to guarantee the model calls a tool instead of replying in text
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A research coordinator's routing step has the tools `route_to_search`, `route_to_analysis` and `finish`, and the model decides which fits the state. To stop 4% of text-only replies a developer forced `route_to_search` by name. The text-only replies vanished, but now every run goes to search and the budget is spent before any analysis starts. What is the right configuration?
opts: Use `any`, so a tool is called at each step and the model still picks which.
Keep the forced tool and add a prompt rule to route to analysis once enough sources exist.
Use `auto` and resend the request whenever the reply is text only.
Force `route_to_search` on odd steps and `route_to_analysis` on even steps.
questions.explain: `any` removes the text-only replies without choosing the route for the model. B asks the prompt to override a forced choice. C goes back to a setting that allowed the text-only replies and pays for the resends. D replaces the model's routing judgment with a fixed alternation.
bullets: Using tool_choice any to guarantee the model calls a tool instead of replying in text
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: Compliance says no pull request may be left without a recorded outcome, so the review step must end in a tool call (`approve`, `request_changes` or `comment_only`). A team tried three setups on 1,000 requests each: a prompt line "call a tool" gave a tool call in 94%; `auto` with up to three resends on a text-only reply gave 99.4%; `tool_choice: any` gave 100%. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: Resending is the best option, because 99.4% is close enough to 100% for compliance purposes.
The prompt line works best once it is moved to the top of the system prompt, ahead of the rest.
Of the three setups, only `any` guarantees a call; the others make text-only replies rarer.
`any` is unsuitable here, because it stops the model from choosing among the three tools.
questions.explain: A requirement that no request goes unrecorded needs a guarantee, and `any` provides one while leaving the choice of tool to the model. A accepts 6 unrecorded pull requests per 1,000. B is a guess the data does not test. D is wrong because `any` still lets the model pick any of the three.
bullets: Using tool_choice any to guarantee the model calls a tool instead of replying in text
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your 14-engineer platform team onboards people with a wiki page of six `claude mcp add --scope user` commands for the shared Sentry, GitHub and deploy-status servers. After the Sentry URL changed, 5 of the 14 laptops still point at the old one and fail, and two engineers added a different seventh server by hand. The team lead proposes a nightly script, pushed to every laptop, that re-runs the six commands. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Adopt it: the script keeps every user-scoped entry identical, so the six servers stay consistent on all 14 laptops.
Reject it: define the six servers once in a committed `.mcp.json`, and keep user scope for personal servers.
Adopt it, and add a CI job that fails whenever a laptop's server list differs from the list on the wiki page.
Reject it: keep the wiki, put the new Sentry URL at the top, and ask each engineer to re-run that one command.
questions.explain: Shared servers belong in the one place the team already shares and reviews: a committed `.mcp.json` arrives with every pull, so there is nothing to push to laptops. A keeps copying per-machine configuration and still depends on the script reaching each laptop. C only detects drift afterwards, and a CI job cannot read laptops anyway. D leaves the update to people remembering, which is how the 5 stale laptops happened.
bullets: Project scope (.mcp.json) for shared team servers versus user scope (~/.claude.json) for personal or experimental ones
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A research team of nine shares one repository. Everyone needs the citations-index server and the news-archive server. One researcher also runs a bookmarks-search server over her own exported browser data, in every project she opens, and nobody else wants it. Which placement fits?
opts: Citations and archive in a committed `.mcp.json`; bookmarks in her user-scoped `~/.claude.json`.
All three in the committed `.mcp.json`, with a README line saying that the bookmarks entry is hers alone.
All three at user scope, with each of the nine researchers adding the two shared servers on their own laptop.
Citations and archive in each researcher's own `.mcp.json` kept out of git; bookmarks at user scope.
questions.explain: Servers the whole team needs go in the committed project file, and a server that belongs to one person across all her projects goes in her user scope. B puts a personal server in front of eight people who will then be asked about it. C and D both leave the shared servers as nine separate copies that drift apart.
bullets: Project scope (.mcp.json) for shared team servers versus user scope (~/.claude.json) for personal or experimental ones
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A freelance engineer works in two clients' repositories on one laptop. Client A's internal wiki server must be available to every engineer on Client A's team through that repository. It must not load in Client B's repository, where its tools could pull Client A's pages into Client B's work. Where should the server be configured?
opts: In her user-scoped `~/.claude.json`, because the server is hers to use on this laptop across projects.
In both repositories' `.mcp.json` files, with a note in Client B's repository saying that it is switched off.
In Client A's CLAUDE.md, which tells Claude Code which servers to start for that project.
In Client A's committed `.mcp.json`, so that it loads in that project and travels with it.
questions.explain: Project scope is tied to the repository, so the server loads there for the whole team and nowhere else. A loads it in every project on her machine, including Client B's. B ships Client A's server into Client B's repository. C describes a file that holds instructions, not server definitions.
bullets: Project scope (.mcp.json) for shared team servers versus user scope (~/.claude.json) for personal or experimental ones
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: Your research team's committed `.mcp.json` points the archive server at the production archive. Engineers who test against the staging archive keep editing the file and have committed the staging URL 7 times this quarter. Everyone else must still get a working server with no setup, and testers should switch targets by setting one shell variable. Which `url` value does this?
opts: `"https://archive.example.com/mcp"`, with testers told to run `git update-index --assume-unchanged .mcp.json` first.
`"${ARCHIVE_BASE}/mcp"`, with every engineer told to export `ARCHIVE_BASE` once.
`"${ARCHIVE_BASE:-https://archive.example.com}/mcp"`
`"${ARCHIVE_BASE:=https://archive.example.com}/mcp"`, which assigns the default for later use.
questions.explain: `${VAR:-default}` uses the variable when it is set and the default when it is not, so most people need nothing and testers set one variable. B has no default, so for anyone who has not exported the variable the unexpanded text is kept and the URL is broken. A still has testers editing a tracked file. D uses a shell form that Claude Code does not list; it supports `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}`.
bullets: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json keeps credentials out of version control
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A support team's committed `.mcp.json` launches a local ticket-export server as a stdio command. The server takes its database connection string, which contains a password, only as a `--dsn` argument and ignores its environment. The file must hold no password, no wrapper script may be added, and each engineer keeps their own credentials in their shell. How should the entry be written?
opts: Put `"--dsn", "${EXPORT_DSN}"` in the `args` list, and have each engineer export `EXPORT_DSN`.
Add `"env": {"EXPORT_DSN": "${EXPORT_DSN}"}` and leave `--dsn` out, because variables expand only in `env`.
Write the shared test-database connection string into `args`, and let engineers override it locally when needed.
Put `"--dsn", "EXPORT_DSN"` in `args`, because Claude Code swaps a bare variable name for its value.
questions.explain: Claude Code expands `${VAR}` in `command`, `args`, `env`, `url` and `headers`, so the argument can reference the variable and the file holds no secret. B assumes expansion is limited to `env`, and the server never reads its environment. C commits a password. D relies on a substitution that Claude Code does not perform, so the server would receive the literal name.
bullets: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json keeps credentials out of version control
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A new `.mcp.json` entry sends `"Authorization": "Bearer ${DEPLOY_API_TOKEN}"`. To make onboarding "work out of the box", an engineer proposes committing a `.env` file that holds the team's real token, which a setup script loads into each shell. The repository is private. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Accept: a private repository gives the token the same exposure as the rest of the source code.
Reject: commit a `.env.example` with a placeholder, and have each engineer use their own token.
Accept, and add `.env` to `.gitignore` in a later commit so that the file stops being tracked.
Reject: store the token base64-encoded in `.mcp.json` instead, so it cannot be read at a glance.
questions.explain: The reason to use `${VAR}` is that values stay out of the committed file, and a committed `.env` puts the same secret straight back into git. A treats a private repository as a safe place for a shared secret. C leaves the token in history after the first commit. D is encoding, not protection, and it moves the secret into the config file.
bullets: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json keeps credentials out of version control
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: Your support agent in Claude Code uses four MCP servers (billing, shipping, returns and CRM) with about 35 tools in all. A staff engineer proposes a gateway server that wraps the four, "so that the agent can combine data from several systems in one request". The four servers belong to other teams and rarely change. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Build it: tools from separate servers can be used together only if one server exposes them.
Build it for billing and shipping only, the pair that the agent needs together most often.
Skip it: the agent already has the tools of all four servers at once.
Skip it, and run one subagent per server so that each system's data is gathered separately.
questions.explain: Claude Code connects to every configured server, and the agent can discover and call tools from all four servers, so a request can use billing and then shipping with nothing in between. A states a limit that does not exist. B builds the same unneeded layer for a smaller set. D splits work that one agent can already do and adds a merging step.
bullets: Tools from every configured MCP server are discovered at connection time and available to the agent together
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A developer asks the agent when a service was last deployed, and it answers from `git log`, which only shows merges. Teammates' sessions answer the same question from the `deploys` server's tools. In this developer's session, none of the `deploys` tools appear in the tool list, while the other three servers' tools do. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The `deploys` tool descriptions are too short, so the agent chooses its built-in tools instead.
Claude Code offers tools from only three servers at a time, and `deploys` was connected last.
The agent needs a CLAUDE.md line that names the `deploys` tools before it will consider them.
The server never connected, so its tools were never discovered or offered.
questions.explain: Tools are discovered when a server connects, and this one apparently never connected, so the agent had nothing to call. A is ruled out because the same descriptions work in teammates' sessions. B invents a limit on servers. C asks for a prompt workaround for a server that is not running.
bullets: Tools from every configured MCP server are discovered at connection time and available to the agent together
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A research agent in Claude Code has two servers connected. The `literature` server has a tool `search` described as "Search for relevant information." The `notes` server, which holds the team's meeting notes, also has a `search` tool with the same description. In 28 of 80 logged runs the agent sent a question about published papers to the `notes` server's `search` and reported no results. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Both are offered together, and identical descriptions give the agent no way to tell them apart.
The two tools share a name, so one overwrites the other and only the later server's `search` is offered.
Claude Code lets only one tool called `search` run per session, and the `notes` server connected first.
The agent tries servers in alphabetical order, so the `notes` tool is always tried before `literature`.
questions.explain: Every connected server's tools sit in the same pool, and the agent picks between them from the descriptions, so two that read alike get mixed up; each should say what it searches and what it returns. B is wrong because a tool's full name includes its server, so the two do not collide. C and D describe selection rules that Claude Code does not have.
bullets: Tools from every configured MCP server are discovered at connection time and available to the agent together
Writing detailed MCP tool descriptions so the agent does not prefer built-in tools such as Grep
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your coding agent's `search_docs` tool queries a 600-page internal handbook. Traces show 4 to 6 searches per session just to learn which sections exist before the right page turns up. The server can publish its section tree: titles, paths and a one-line purpose for each. Engineers want the tree in view from the start of a session, without relying on the model deciding to look for it. What should the server do?
opts: Add a `list_sections` tool, and tell the model in the prompt to call it before any search.
Publish the section tree as an MCP resource that engineers attach with an @ reference.
Raise `search_docs` from 5 to 25 results per call so that the right page appears sooner.
Paste the section tree into the `search_docs` description so it is seen with every call.
questions.explain: A resource is content the application attaches as context, so the model sees what exists without spending calls to find out. A still depends on the model choosing to call the tool. C returns more of the same results and does not show the structure. D puts a large tree into a description, where long text is cut off.
bullets: MCP resources expose content catalogues (issue summaries, documentation trees, schemas) to cut exploratory tool calls
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Your warehouse server publishes a `warehouse://schema` resource that engineers attach to sessions. Since it went live, discovery calls fell from 6 to 1 per session, but "table not found" errors rose to 22 a week, clustered in the days after schema migrations. The server is redeployed only at release time. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Claude Code cuts attached resources off after 50 entries, so later tables never reach the agent.
The agent ignores an attached resource whenever the question names a specific table.
The catalogue is a snapshot from the last release, so it describes tables as they were then.
The client fetches resources once a day, so changes appear only after the next daily refresh.
questions.explain: A catalogue exists to be trusted instead of explored, so it must be built from the live schema when it is read; content fixed at release time goes stale between releases, which fits errors after migrations. A and B would hit tables at random, not those just changed. D invents a daily fetch cycle.
bullets: MCP resources expose content catalogues (issue summaries, documentation trees, schemas) to cut exploratory tool calls
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: The `run_query` tool of your analytics server has a 40-table schema, about 30,000 characters, pasted into its description so that the agent knows the tables. The agent often invents column names that appear only in the second half of the schema. Which change fixes this?
opts: Cut the description down to table names only, so it stays within what Claude Code keeps.
Repeat the column lists at the end of the description, where they are read last.
Replace `run_query` with 40 per-table tools, each carrying its own columns in its description.
Move the schema to an MCP resource, and keep the description to what `run_query` does.
questions.explain: Claude Code cuts a long description and the agent sees only the text before the cut, which is why the later columns are guessed. A catalogue belongs in a resource that is attached when needed, leaving the description short and useful. A removes the columns the agent needs. B puts them at the end, which is the part that gets cut. C swaps one tool for 40 and loads the same schema text, spread across 40 descriptions.
