bullets: MCP resources expose content catalogues (issue summaries, documentation trees, schemas) to cut exploratory tool calls
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Which entry in the committed `.mcp.json` gives every engineer the same remote Sentry server, each using a personal token, with no secret in git?
opts: `"sentry": {"type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.sentry.example.com/mcp", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${SENTRY_TOKEN}"}}`
The same entry with `"Authorization": "Bearer ${SENTRY_TOKEN:-team-shared-token}"`, so the server works before anyone sets a token.
The same entry with `"Authorization": "Bearer <your-token>"`, which each engineer edits locally before starting a session.
The same entry with an empty `headers` object, and each engineer adds their own header to a user-scoped `sentry` entry.
questions.explain: The variable reference keeps the secret out of the file, and each engineer's shell supplies their own value. B puts a shared token in git as the default. C has everyone edit a tracked file and risk committing the edit. D fails because when one name is defined in two scopes, the project entry is used whole and the user entry is ignored.
bullets: Configuring shared servers in a project-scoped .mcp.json with variable expansion for auth tokens
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A pull request adds a community-built Kafka-inspection server to the repository's `.mcp.json`, with its token written as `${KAFKA_TOKEN}`. Engineers get an approval prompt for project servers in interactive sessions, and a reviewer wants to merge because "each engineer will vet it when prompted". The repository also runs `claude -p` in CI on every pull request. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Merge: the approval prompt gives each engineer a chance to vet it, and CI is covered by the same prompt.
Review it before merging: non-interactive runs load project servers without asking.
Merge: a token passed as a variable means the server cannot reach anything beyond what that token allows.
Reject: community-built servers may not be committed to `.mcp.json`; only custom servers belong there.
questions.explain: A committed project server reaches every engineer and every CI run, and where Claude Code cannot show the prompt it loads the server without asking, so the review has to happen at merge time. A assumes a prompt that CI never sees. C mixes up the token's reach with the server's, which runs its own code. D contradicts the guidance to prefer existing servers for standard integrations.
bullets: Project scope (.mcp.json) for shared team servers versus user scope (~/.claude.json) for personal or experimental ones
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: A researcher adds this to the repository's `.mcp.json`: an `archive` entry with `"url": "https://archive.example.com/mcp"` and `"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${ARCHIVE_TOKEN}"}`. Everyone has exported `ARCHIVE_TOKEN`, yet nobody sees any archive tools, and a configuration warning about the entry appears at startup. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: A header value cannot contain a variable reference, because only `env` values expand.
A root-level `.mcp.json` is read only for stdio servers; remote ones need `.claude/mcp.json`.
The entry has no `type`, so Claude Code reads it as a stdio server and skips it.
The token must first be listed in a committed `.env`, or the entry is rejected at startup.
questions.explain: A remote entry needs `"type": "http"`; without it Claude Code treats the entry as a local command, finds none, and skips it with a warning. A is wrong because `headers` is one of the places that expand. B and D invent file locations and a `.env` requirement that Claude Code does not have.
bullets: Configuring shared servers in a project-scoped .mcp.json with variable expansion for auth tokens
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A staff engineer wants to trial a new code-search server for two weeks. It starts in about 20 seconds and exposes 3 tools. To make it easy for the 11 engineers who want to try it, she proposes adding it to the committed `.mcp.json` and "removing it if it doesn't work out". The other 12 engineers have not asked for it. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Accept: removing the entry later is one more commit, so nobody is harmed in the meantime.
Accept it on a long-lived branch that only the interested engineers check out and keep up to date.
Accept it, with a README note that the server is experimental and optional for everyone.
Reject it: interested engineers add it at user scope, and promote it if the trial succeeds.
questions.explain: A trial server is personal and experimental, so it belongs at user scope, and only a server the team has decided to adopt belongs in the shared file. A and C put the approval prompt and the server in front of all 23 engineers. B turns the trial into a branch to be kept in step with the main one.
bullets: Configuring personal or experimental servers in user-scoped ~/.claude.json
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A researcher wrote a stdio script, `/home/maya/tools/notes_mcp.py`, that searches her own markdown notes. She wants it available in every project she opens, and no teammate has that file. Which command sets it up?
opts: `claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope user notes -- python /home/maya/tools/notes_mcp.py`
`claude mcp add --transport stdio notes -- python /home/maya/tools/notes_mcp.py`, run once in each project that she opens
`claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope project --env NOTES_DIR=/home/maya/notes notes -- python /home/maya/tools/notes_mcp.py`
`claude mcp add --transport http --scope user --env NOTES_DIR=/home/maya/notes notes /home/maya/tools/notes_mcp.py`
questions.explain: `--scope user` stores the server in her `~/.claude.json` for all her projects, and everything after `--` is the command that starts the script. B leaves out the scope, so the default local scope applies and each project needs its own command. C writes her home path into a file the team shares. D treats a local script as an HTTP endpoint.
bullets: Configuring personal or experimental servers in user-scoped ~/.claude.json
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: An engineer adds an `analytics` server at user scope, pointing at her sandbox URL, to try a new endpoint in all her repositories. In the team repository, whose committed `.mcp.json` also defines `analytics` with the shared URL, her sessions still reach the shared server and she sees only its tools. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Claude Code merges the two entries field by field, and the URL from the file loaded first wins.
The project entry outranks the user entry, and is used whole while her sandbox entry is ignored.
User-scoped servers apply only in repositories that have no `.mcp.json` file of their own.
Entries in `~/.claude.json` load only once she approves them with `claude mcp reset-project-choices`.
questions.explain: When a name is defined in more than one scope, Claude Code connects once, using the whole entry from the highest-precedence scope, and project scope ranks above user scope. A is wrong because fields are not merged. C invents a restriction on user scope. D mixes up the reset command, which concerns approvals for project servers.
bullets: Configuring personal or experimental servers in user-scoped ~/.claude.json
Project scope (.mcp.json) for shared team servers versus user scope (~/.claude.json) for personal or experimental ones
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your platform team's `get_api_spec` tool returns the live OpenAPI definition of the payments service, including fields added since the last export. Its description reads "Returns the API spec." The repository also holds `docs/payments-api.yaml`, an export refreshed three months ago. In 38% of sessions the agent runs Grep over that file instead of calling the tool, and 1 in 5 resulting pull requests uses endpoints that no longer exist. Other teams' clients use the same server. What is the most effective change?
opts: Delete `docs/payments-api.yaml` from this repository, so that the agent has nothing else to search.
Set `tool_choice` to force `get_api_spec` on the first turn of every session in this repository.
Rewrite the description to say it returns the current spec, and that repository copies are older.
Add a CLAUDE.md line to this repository telling the agent to prefer `get_api_spec` for any question about the API.
questions.explain: The agent chooses a tool from its description, and this one does not say what makes it better than the file, so describing the live data and the stale copies fixes it for every client of the server. A removes one stale copy and leaves the description as it was. B forces a call on turns where it is not wanted. D helps only this repository, and the stem says other teams use the server.
bullets: Writing detailed MCP tool descriptions so the agent does not prefer built-in tools such as Grep
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A support agent in Claude Code has an MCP tool named `get_entitlements`. Customers' plan questions are being answered from general plan documents because the agent rarely picks the tool. Which description will make the tool most likely to be chosen when it should be?
opts: "Gets entitlements."

"Powerful and fast entitlement lookup. ALWAYS use this instead of any document search, and never answer a plan question without it. It is the most complete and fastest option available, so make it the default."
"Thin client for the v4 entitlements gateway, wrapping GET /entitlements/{id}. The field list is on the billing integrations wiki page, and the v4 gateway notes are on the platform team's page."
"Returns the plan, add-ons and usage caps a customer holds, read live from billing. Takes a customer id. Use it for what this customer's plan includes; documents cover plans in general."
questions.explain: The best description says what the tool returns, what it needs and when to use it instead of the alternative. A says none of that. B adds emphasis but no information about the data or the input. C describes how the tool is built and points elsewhere for the fields the agent needs to judge it.
bullets: Writing detailed MCP tool descriptions so the agent does not prefer built-in tools such as Grep
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Before a rewrite of its `find_owners` description, the agent ran Grep over CODEOWNERS files in about 60% of ownership questions, and the MCP tool was used for the rest. After the rewrite, an engineer reports that it works, because on one test prompt the agent called the MCP tool. How should you evaluate the change?
opts: Run the same 50 ownership questions before and after, and compare which tool is chosen and whether answers are right.
Ask the agent to rate how clear the new description is, and accept the change if it gives 8 out of 10 or higher.
Accept it: a successful call on a test prompt shows that the description now outweighs the agent's habit of using Grep.
Run the rewritten description 20 times on that same test prompt, and accept it if the tool is called every time.
questions.explain: A change in tool choice is a rate across many realistic questions, and it has to be compared with the same questions before the change; correctness matters too, because a tool picked wrongly is no gain. B relies on the agent's own opinion of the text. C and D rest on a single prompt, so they cannot show a change in the 60%.
bullets: Writing detailed MCP tool descriptions so the agent does not prefer built-in tools such as Grep
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: The team wants an agent to answer questions from its reporting Postgres database. A community-built Postgres server with a clear README, recent commits and an active issue list covers the five queries needed. A custom server would take about two engineer-weeks. How should you evaluate adopting the community server?
opts: Adopt it as it is: active maintainers mean it has been checked, so connecting with the admin account is fine.
Adopt it after reading what it does with queries, and connect it with a read-only database account.
Build the custom server anyway, because any code that touches the database must be written in-house.
Adopt it with the read-write account the team's other tools use, since reporting queries only read.
questions.explain: A standard integration should come from an existing server, with a check on what it does and the least access it needs, here a read-only account. A treats maintenance as a security review and hands over full rights. C spends two weeks on something that exists. D gives a server that can run any statement more access than reporting needs.
bullets: Choosing an existing community server for standard integrations and a custom server only for team-specific workflows
questions.principle: Give each agent and tool only what its role needs; extra capability gets misused.

questions.q: Your support team uses a well-maintained community ticketing server that covers searching, reading, commenting and updating tickets. The agent also needs an `sla_breach_risk` tool that applies your own contract-specific rules to a ticket's history. One engineer has part of a week each month for this. What is the best plan?
opts: Fork the community server, add the SLA logic to it, and merge its upstream releases by hand.
Replace the community server with a custom one covering all five operations, so that everything follows one design.
Keep the community server for standard operations, and add a small custom one for `sla_breach_risk` only.
Ask the community server's maintainers to add the SLA rules, and enable the agent after their next release.
questions.explain: Standard operations should come from the existing server, and only the logic unique to your contracts needs code you own, so a small custom server with one tool keeps the upkeep tiny. A makes a part-time engineer carry the whole community server through every upstream change. B rebuilds four tools that already work. D asks outsiders to implement rules that are specific to your company.
bullets: Choosing an existing community server for standard integrations and a custom server only for team-specific workflows
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: The team needs its agent to search a Confluence space, fetch pages and browse the page tree, read-only, and finds three community servers. One has the most GitHub stars and runs read-only, but only fetches a page by id. One has 40 tools and was last updated 18 months ago. The third covers search, page fetch and listing a space's page tree, was updated last month, and can be run read-only. Which should the team choose?
opts: The one with the most stars: it is widely used and already runs read-only.
The one with 40 tools, because the broadest server will cover whatever the agent needs later.
None of them: write a custom server so that the tools match the team's own naming.
The one covering search, fetch and page-tree listing, recently updated and read-only.
questions.explain: Pick the existing server that covers the operations needed, is still maintained, and can be limited to reading. A is popular and read-only, but cannot search or browse. B takes breadth and age over fit, and a stale server is an upkeep risk. C builds a custom server for a standard integration and gains only naming.
bullets: Choosing an existing community server for standard integrations and a custom server only for team-specific workflows
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A research agent reads papers through a `fetch_paper(id)` tool on an internal server. The ids are opaque strings, and in 41% of sessions the agent spends 3 to 5 calls searching and guessing before it finds an id that exists. The server can list its 3,000 papers with id, title and year. Which change most directly removes the guessing?
opts: Expose the paper list (id, title, year) as a resource, readable before any fetch call.
Make `fetch_paper` return the five closest ids whenever an id is not found.
Add an instruction telling the agent to try ids in ascending order until one resolves.
Raise the agent's turn limit so that the guessing has room to finish before an answer is due.
questions.explain: The agent guesses because it cannot see what exists, and a catalogue resource shows it before the first call. B still makes the agent fail, then try again, and C turns guessing into a procedure. D accepts the wasted calls and gives them more room.
bullets: Exposing content catalogues as MCP resources so agents can see what data exists without exploratory calls
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your support agent's server holds 2,400 open cases. The agent opens full case records one by one, about 6 `get_case` calls per new complaint, to find duplicates, and each full record averages 8,000 characters. Case titles are often generic, such as "Billing problem". The server owner wants to expose a case catalogue as a resource. What should it contain?
opts: Every open case in full, so that the agent never needs `get_case` again.
One line per case: id, title, status and a short summary.
One line per case with its id and title only, to keep the list short.
The 50 most recent cases in full, since duplicates are usually recent.
questions.explain: A catalogue should be short enough to attach and rich enough to choose from, so the agent can spot a likely duplicate and open only that case. A is about 19 million characters. C leaves generic titles with nothing to tell cases apart. D drops older cases that may be the duplicate and still carries 400,000 characters.
bullets: Exposing content catalogues as MCP resources so agents can see what data exists without exploratory calls
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Your warehouse schema changes most days. About one session in five touches the warehouse, mostly analytics questions rather than edits to warehouse files, and those sessions waste 5 or 6 calls discovering tables. Someone proposes a nightly job that writes the schema into a section of the repository's CLAUDE.md. Which approach is best?
opts: Do the nightly CLAUDE.md job, since memory files are always in context and cannot be missed.
Write the nightly job's output to a path-scoped rules file, so that it loads when warehouse files are open.
Expose the schema as an MCP resource that the server builds from the live database when it is read.
Add a `describe_schema` tool and a prompt rule telling the agent to call it at the start of every session.
questions.explain: A resource is read when wanted and generated from the live database, so it is current and costs nothing in the four sessions in five that never touch the warehouse. A loads a day-old schema into every session. B loads only when warehouse files are open, which these sessions do not do. D makes all sessions spend a call at the start.
bullets: Exposing content catalogues as MCP resources so agents can see what data exists without exploratory calls
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Your team is dropping the `legacy_pdf` package from a 1,800-file monorepo. Before the dependency is removed, the agent must list every source file that uses the package, and nobody has a record of which services import it. Which approach gives that list most directly?
opts: Read the dependency manifests and take the modules listed beside the package as the ones that use it.
Glob for `**/*pdf*` and treat each file that matches as one that depends on the package.
Grep for import lines that mention `legacy_pdf` across the source tree.
Glob every `.py` file and read the top of each one, since imports sit at the start of a file.
questions.explain: Finding which files import a package is a search of file contents, which is what Grep does. A manifest says that the dependency exists, not which files use it (A). Glob matches names, and a file can import the package without having pdf in its name (B). D would open thousands of files to read a few lines of each.
bullets: Grep searches file contents for patterns such as function names, error messages and import statements
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A research agent has a folder of 600 saved earnings-call transcripts named `call_0001.txt` to `call_0600.txt`. Asked which calls discuss a covenant waiver, it ran Glob with `**/*covenant*`, got no results and reported that none do. An analyst opens three of the files and finds the phrase in each. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The file names are sequence numbers, so a name pattern cannot tell which files hold a phrase.
Glob returns only files changed recently, and the transcripts were saved too long ago to show up.
Glob skips files that `.gitignore` lists, and the transcripts folder is one of the ignored paths.
The pattern needed the extension, as in `**/*covenant*.txt`, because Glob ignores names without one.
questions.explain: Glob compares a pattern with file names only, and these names hold a number and nothing else, so an empty result says nothing about the text; a content search with Grep is the tool for this job. B invents a recency filter: Glob sorts by modification time, it does not drop older files. C has it backwards, since Glob does not apply `.gitignore` by default. D invents an extension rule.
bullets: Grep searches file contents for patterns such as function names, error messages and import statements
Glob matches file paths by name or extension patterns
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: In a 5,000-file monorepo the agent greps for `TIMEOUT_MS` to see where a service reads the setting. The search returns 900 lines, most of them from a vendored `third_party/` folder, and the next two turns spend most of the context window on them. The agent needs to see the lines that read the setting, and the service's own code is all under `services/`. What is the most effective change?
opts: Switch to Glob over `**/*.py` and read the files whose names look related to the service.
Search again for `TIMEOUT_MS`, but ask Grep to return only the number of matches in each file.
Read the largest of the matching files first, since the setting is most likely read where it is mentioned most.
Run the same Grep limited to `services/`, using the `glob` or `type` option for the service's language.
questions.explain: Narrowing the search to first-party code keeps the useful lines and leaves the vendored matches out; Grep can be scoped by path, by a `glob` pattern or by a language `type`. A swaps a content search for a name search, which cannot show where a setting is read. B drops the lines the agent needs and still lists every vendored file. C guesses from file size and pays for whole files.
bullets: Grep searches file contents for patterns such as function names, error messages and import statements
Choosing Grep to search code content, for example for all callers of a function or for an error message
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A platform engineer has 60 repositories checked out under one workspace folder and asks the agent to list every `CODEOWNERS` file, wherever it sits, so that ownership can be audited. Which approach finds them?
opts: Grep the workspace for the word `CODEOWNERS` and list the files that contain it.
Glob with `**/CODEOWNERS`, which matches that file name at any depth.
Read the `.github` folder of the first repository and assume the others are laid out the same way.
Read the workspace folder to get its listing, then open the root of each repository in turn.
questions.explain: Locating a file by its name is a pattern match on paths, which is Glob, and `**` reaches every depth. Grep searches contents, so it returns files that mention the word and misses an ownership file that never contains it (A). C assumes a layout nobody has confirmed. Read opens files, not directories (D).
bullets: Glob matches file paths by name or extension patterns
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A research pipeline keeps its inputs as CSV files under `data/`. Asked how many there are, the agent runs Glob with `data/**/*.csv` and answers 100. The data engineer's own `find` count is about 1,400, and a second run of the agent's Glob again gives 100. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Glob keeps only files modified in the last 100 days, so older CSV files drop out.
Glob respects `.gitignore`, and most of the CSV files in `data/` are ignored by git.
The `**` in the pattern reaches only the first two levels below the `data/` folder.
The list is capped at 100 files, and the agent counted it as if it were complete.
questions.explain: Glob returns at most 100 files and sets a truncation flag, so a count of exactly 100 means the list was cut short; the agent should narrow the pattern, for example by subfolder, and count each part. Results are sorted by modification time, not filtered by it, so A is wrong. B is backwards, because Glob does not apply `.gitignore` by default. C is wrong because `**` matches at any depth.
bullets: Glob matches file paths by name or extension patterns
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Support exports each ticket as one JSON file named like `2025-03-14_T88231.json`. The date exists only in the file name, because the body stores the time as epoch seconds. A manager wants the agent to pull every March 2025 ticket for a quality review. The export holds 3,000 tickets, about 60 of them from March. Which approach is best?
opts: Glob with `**/2025-03-*.json`, which selects the files by the date in their names.
Grep for `2025-03` in the file contents, since each ticket records when it was created.
Grep for `March 2025` in the ticket text, which customers often write when they describe an issue.
Read the export folder and pick out the March files from the listing it returns.
questions.explain: The date is a property of the file name, so a name pattern selects exactly the right files without opening any of them. B searches the contents for a date format the body does not use. C finds tickets that happen to mention the month, which is a different set. D fails because Read opens files, not directories.
bullets: Glob matches file paths by name or extension patterns
Choosing Glob to find files by a naming pattern such as a test-file suffix
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: In a 600-line `settings.py`, the agent must change the default `MAX_RETRIES = 3` to 5. That line appears once, and nothing else in the file should change. Which operation makes the change with the least risk to the rest of the file?
opts: Read the file, then Write the whole file back with the single value changed.
Write a new file that holds only the changed line and let the loader merge it.
Edit the line, replacing `MAX_RETRIES = 3` with `MAX_RETRIES = 5`.
Grep for the line, then Write the matching line over the file at that position.
questions.explain: Changing text that appears once is what Edit is for, and every other line stays as it was. Read plus Write would retype 600 lines to change one, which is where accidental changes creep in (A). Write does not merge, so B relies on a feature it lacks. D assumes Write can place text at a position, but Write replaces the whole file.
bullets: Read and Write handle whole files, while Edit changes a file through unique matching text
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: The support team's agent project keeps its dependencies in `pyproject.toml`. To add a `[tool.pytest]` section, the agent called Write with just the three new lines and reported success. The next build fails because the project name and every dependency are missing from the file. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Write replaces a file with the content it is given, and it was given only the new section.
Write merges by section header, and it matched `[tool.pytest]` against the wrong table.
The agent did not Read first, so the tool threw away the copy of the file that it had stored.
Write appended the section, and the TOML parser then dropped the keys above the new one.
questions.explain: Write creates or overwrites a file with the full content provided, so a three-line call leaves a three-line file. Adding a section needs Edit, or Read plus a Write of the complete file. B and D credit Write with merge or append behaviour it does not have. C blames a missing Read, which is not why content disappears.
bullets: Read and Write handle whole files, while Edit changes a file through unique matching text
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: After two failed Edit calls on a config file, a teammate proposes a convention for the developer productivity agent: make every change with Read followed by Write, since that never fails to find the text. Over a month the agent makes about 300 small changes, mostly single-line fixes to text that appears once, and reviewers have started to see unrelated lines changed in the diffs. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Adopt it: a complete rewrite is more reliable than text matching, and the diffs will settle as the agent adapts.
Reject it: Edit suits targeted changes, and Read plus Write is the fallback when no unique text exists.
Adopt it, and add a check that reverts unrelated line changes after every Write.
Reject it, and move every change to Edit with `replace_all` so that no anchor text is ever ambiguous.
questions.explain: Edit changes only the text it matches, so the rest of the file stays as written; a whole-file rewrite is the fallback for when no unique anchor exists, and it means the agent regenerates every line, so unrelated lines can change. A treats the symptom as a habit that will pass. C patches the output of the wrong tool choice. D would change every occurrence of the text, not the one that was meant.

questions.q: The agent edits a Makefile and tries to replace the line `    $(CC) -o app main.o`, typed with four spaces, with a new link line. Edit returns an error saying the text was not found. The agent assumes the line is too common to match, and starts a Read plus Write of the 400-line file. What is the right response to the error?
opts: Switch to `replace_all`, because an Edit error means the line occurs more than once.
Look at the line as the file holds it, copy its exact indentation, and retry Edit.
Carry on with Read plus Write, which copes with any Edit error at no extra cost.
Retry Edit with extra lines around the target, since more context makes a match more likely.
questions.explain: Edit needs the text exactly as written, to the character of whitespace, and a Makefile indents recipe lines with tabs, so the text really was absent. Fixing the call fixes the problem. A mistakes a missing match for several matches. C rewrites 400 lines to avoid a one-character fix. D adds context around the same wrong indentation.
bullets: Read and Write handle whole files, while Edit changes a file through unique matching text

questions.q: A support knowledge-base export, `kb_export.json`, is 9,000 lines and has the same `"status": "draft"` line in 200 entries whose surrounding lines are byte-identical, so no unique context exists. Edit rejects the change, so the agent reads the file in three pages with `offset` and `limit`, assembles the content and writes it back with the one entry fixed. The next day the file holds 6,000 lines, the entries from the last third are missing, and the export job fails. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Write keeps at most two thirds of any file, so the tail was dropped when the file was saved.
The failed Edit left the file locked, so the later write kept only the part that had been flushed.
The pages were stitched together for Write, and the last page was left out of the content.
Write merged the new text into the file by line number and removed the entries after the changed line.
questions.explain: Write overwrites the file with exactly the content it is given, so anything the agent left out of that content is gone. The Read plus Write fallback works only when the complete file is written back, and when the file is paged that includes every page. A and D invent a size limit and a merge, and B invents a lock.

questions.q: A service is moving from `old-api.internal` to `new-api.internal`. In the 800-line `client.ts`, the host name appears in 12 places and every one of them must change. Edit rejects the first attempt because the text appears more than once, and the agent starts planning to read the file and write it back in full. What is the most proportionate way to finish?
opts: Edit each of the 12 places separately, adding surrounding lines so that every call has a unique anchor.
Read the file and Write it back in full, because Read plus Write is the fallback for repeated text.
Grep for the host name and ask the developer to change the 12 lines by hand.
Edit again with `replace_all` set, which replaces every occurrence in one call.
questions.explain: When every occurrence should change, `replace_all` does it in one call. Read plus Write is for text that cannot be pinned to the one place that should change, and nothing here needs pinning (B). A does the same job in twelve calls, where one call is the fewest. C gives up on a change the tools can make.
bullets: Read and Write handle whole files, while Edit changes a file through unique matching text
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A production log shows `InvoiceRounding: negative remainder -0.03 on line 4`. The agent must find where the service raises this error. The amount and the line number change on every occurrence, and the message is built in several modules. Which search is best?
opts: Grep for the full logged line, including `-0.03` and `line 4`, so that the match is exact.
Grep for the fixed text `InvoiceRounding: negative remainder`, then read the matches.
Glob for `**/*rounding*` and read each file whose name matches.
Grep for `negative`, which is the most distinctive word in the message.
questions.explain: Grep matches text in the source, and the source holds only the constant part of the message; the amount and line are filled in at run time. A searches for values that never appear in code. C finds files named like the error, not the code that raises it. D matches a common word all over the codebase.

questions.q: A research agent audits 300 tracked documentation pages to find every page that cites Smith 2021. Its Grep for `Smith 2021` returns 4 pages, but the author knows the paper is cited on roughly 30. Opening three of the missed pages shows the citation on a single line in each, for example `Smith (2021)` and `Smith et al., 2021`. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Grep respects `.gitignore`, and most of the missing pages are ignored by git.
Patterns match within one line, and the citation is split across a line break on the missed pages.
The literal pattern fits one way of writing the citation, and other pages write it differently.
Grep returns only the first file in each folder unless the output mode is changed to show content.
questions.explain: A literal string matches one spelling. Grep takes a regular expression, so a single pattern that allows an optional comma, parentheses or `et al.` covers the variants. The pages are tracked, which rules out A. Each citation sits on one line, which rules out B. D is wrong because the default mode lists every file that matches.

questions.q: Before deleting `format_legacy_ticket` from a Python service, the agent greps for the name with the `type` option set to `py` and finds no callers. After the deletion, the nightly export job fails with a missing-function error that comes from `ops/nightly.yml`, which names the function as a string. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Grep ignores files that have not changed recently, and the YAML file had been stable for a year.
Grep patterns cannot match inside quote marks, so a function named in a string is invisible.
The agent used the wrong output mode, so matches in the YAML file were counted but never listed.
The search covered Python files only, so the YAML reference was never looked at.
questions.explain: The `type` option restricts a search to one language, which suits finding Python callers and hides every other kind of file. Before deleting something, search all file types, or add each type that can hold a reference. A invents a recency rule, B invents a limit on strings, and C is wrong because every output mode reports the files that match.

questions.q: Four services each keep a `db/migrations/` folder with several hundred files named like `0098_add_index.sql`, `0150_drop_old_table.sql` and `0231_backfill.sql`. The agent must list the migrations numbered 0100 to 0199 in all four, about 40 files in total. Which call returns them?

Glob with `**/db/migrations/*.sql`, then keep the files whose numbers fall in the range by reading each name.
Glob with `**/db/migrations/01*.sql`, which selects by the number at the start of each name.
Read each `db/migrations` folder and note the files in the range from the listing.
questions.explain: The range is written into the file names, so a name pattern selects it directly. B returns every migration in the four folders, and Glob caps its list at 100 files, so the range could be cut off before the filtering even starts. questions.q: A developer asks the agent to list the TypeScript source files of a web app, to plan a new lint rule. `src/*.ts`, which matches every `.ts` file inside `src/`.

questions.q: In a long session, the agent read `deploy.yaml` 40 turns ago. Meanwhile a teammate has pulled two commits that changed that file. What should the agent do?

Retry Edit with `replace_all`, then restore the other two services' values from the summary.
Write now, then compare the result with the repository using Grep and repair the differences.
Read the file again now, then Write it back in full with only the replicas line changed.

questions.q: A research pipeline's `config.toml` has 80 lines and needs nine scattered changes to move it to a new schema. Which approach is most reliable?

Run the nine Edit calls again in a different order until all of them are accepted.
Set `replace_all` on the failing Edit calls, then correct any lines that changed by mistake.
Make nine temporary copies of the file with Write, edit one in each, and merge them.

questions.q: A config-maintenance subagent is defined with `tools: ["Read", "Grep", "Edit"]`. About 4% of its runs end with "could not apply change", always where the line to change is repeated in the file, and each failure is an Edit error saying the text appears more than once, in blocks that are byte-identical around the target so no unique context exists. Add `Write`, so it can read the file and write the whole file back.
Replace `Edit` with `Write`, since rewriting whole files avoids matching problems.
Add `Glob`, so that it can find a second copy of each file to edit instead.

questions.q: A new developer asks the agent where invoice PDFs are produced in a 2,000-file Django project and how the data reaches the renderer. The agent's first plan is to read every file under `billing/` and `documents/`, about 300 files. Which plan is the most effective?

Read `billing/models.py` in full, since the data for an invoice comes from the models.
Read the settings file and the README, then describe the flow from the module names.
Grep for the rendering call, then Read its callers and follow their imports.

The trace shows that the function is defined in 90 lines of the second module and called from two places. What is the most likely root cause?

Prefer X, because reading every file means that no file was missed.
Prefer X, and move it to a model with a bigger window so the follow-up questions have room.

questions.q: A support platform's `gateway.submit_charge(order, amount)` is wrapped by a `PaymentsClient` class whose public methods `charge()` and `charge_async()` call it, and application code uses only the client. The team will change the signature of `submit_charge` and wants every affected call site. A Grep for `submit_charge` returns 2 hits, both inside `PaymentsClient`. What should the agent do next?

Grep for `PaymentsClient` and count every file that imports the class as an affected site.
Read `PaymentsClient` for the methods that call `submit_charge`, then Grep for each method name.
Grep for `submit` and `charge` separately, which will surface any caller that spells the name differently.

Grep for `open_corpus`, the name at the top of the chain and the one researchers import.
Read only `pkg/__init__.py`, take its exported names, and Grep for those.
Read each re-exporting module to list the helper's names, then Grep for all of them.
questions.explain: Researchers can import the helper under either public name, so the plan has to follow the chain through each module and search for every name it carries: `load_corpus` and `open_corpus`. A finds only the definition and the re-export lines. B misses everyone who imports `load_corpus` from `pkg.compat`. C gets only `open_corpus` from the package file and misses `load_corpus`.

questions.q: The team keeps its testing standards in `docs/testing.md`, read by humans and by CI. You want Claude to have that exact text in context from the start of every session in this repository, without a second copy. Which line in the root CLAUDE.md does that?
