bullets: Choosing plan mode for architectural work: restructuring, large library migrations, integration approaches with different infrastructure
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A direct-execution run moved 58 files from an old date library to a new one. Review found two conventions for the start of the week: a global setting in 21 files and a per-call option in 37. Weekly report totals now differ by module, in about 3% of reports. Which change to the process would best prevent this next time?
opts: Plan the migration first, so one convention is chosen and then applied to every file.
Give each directory its own direct request with an identical prompt, so every run follows the same instructions.
Add the preferred convention to CLAUDE.md after the migration, so later work follows it.
Add a lint rule that rejects whichever of the two conventions is less common.
questions.explain: Where one change spans many files, the approach has to be decided once and then applied everywhere, which a reviewed plan does. B repeats the decision independently in every run. C arrives after the migration and cannot fix it. D picks the winner by popularity instead of by correctness and acts only after the inconsistency exists.
bullets: Choosing plan mode for architectural work: restructuring, large library migrations, integration approaches with different infrastructure
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A ticket asks for `order_shipped` events to reach a logistics partner. The partner accepts either a webhook push, which needs a public endpoint, a retry queue and signing keys, or a nightly file drop that runs on the existing job runner. Either would touch about six files, and operations must provision whatever infrastructure is chosen. What is the best way to start with Claude Code?
opts: Build the file drop directly, since it needs the least infrastructure, and revisit it if the partner objects.
Use plan mode to lay out both designs with their infrastructure needs, and decide before any edits.
Build the webhook directly behind a feature flag, so it can be switched off if operations cannot provision it.
Ask an Explore subagent to build both versions in parallel, and keep the one that passes the tests.
questions.explain: Two valid integrations with different infrastructure needs are an architectural choice, and plan mode lets Claude lay out both before anything is built. A and C commit to one design before operations has agreed to its infrastructure. D cannot work, because Explore is a read-only subagent that does not edit files.
bullets: Choosing plan mode for architectural work: restructuring, large library migrations, integration approaches with different infrastructure
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A CI helper runs Claude Code on a failing build while no one is watching. The log shows one failed test, `test_parse_duration`, with the assertion and the line in `parse_duration()` that returns 3600 for the input `1h30`. The job now starts with an Explore subagent that surveys the repository, and runs average 9 minutes against about 2 minutes for jobs without that step. What is the most effective change?
opts: Run it in plan mode, so the cause is confirmed in a plan before the function is edited.
Keep the survey but move it to a smaller model, since the cost comes from the reading.
Replace the survey with a two-step job that proposes the fix and then waits for approval.
Pass the failure output to Claude to fix the function directly, then rerun the test.
questions.explain: The log already names the function and the failing behaviour, so there is nothing to discover or design, and a fix with a rerun of the test is enough. A adds a plan to a change with one obvious location. B keeps the survey and only makes it cheaper. C adds an approval step to an unattended job, where nobody is there to give it.
bullets: Choosing direct execution for well-understood changes with clear scope, such as a single-file fix with a clear stack trace
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A CI job runs `claude -p --permission-mode plan` when a snapshot test fails, to update one snapshot file. The log shows the failing test and its diff, Claude reads the file and prints a sensible change, and the run ends green. Over two weeks none of the 40 runs committed a change, and the snapshot still fails on the next build. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The prompt omits the failing test's name, so Claude cannot find the snapshot file.
Claude cannot edit snapshot files in non-interactive runs.
The effort level is too low for Claude to commit to an edit on a single-file fix.
The run is in plan mode, so it proposes the change and waits for an approval.
questions.explain: Plan mode researches and proposes but makes no edits until a plan is approved, and an unattended job has nobody to approve it, so a one-file fix that suits direct execution never lands. A is contradicted by the stem, where Claude printed a sensible change to the file. B and C invent limits that the stem gives no sign of.
bullets: Choosing direct execution for well-understood changes with clear scope, such as a single-file fix with a clear stack trace
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A lead is considering a rule that every change under `billing/` must start in plan mode, because billing code is sensitive. Meanwhile a developer needs to correct one misspelled label, "Invoce date", in a single template under `billing/templates/`. Tests and code review already cover that folder. How should you evaluate the rule when applied to this change?
opts: Adopt the rule: the sensitivity of the folder, not the size of the change, decides the mode.
Reject the rule here: the scope is clear, and tests and review guard the folder.
Adopt the rule, but approve the plan automatically since it will contain a single step.
Use an Explore subagent over `billing/` first, then correct the label in plan mode.
questions.explain: The mode should follow the task's scope and open decisions, and a one-word fix in one file has neither, while the existing tests and review already protect the folder. A chooses the mode by location, not by scope. C keeps the ceremony and removes the review it exists for. D adds a survey of a folder to a one-word fix.
bullets: Choosing direct execution for well-understood changes with clear scope, such as a single-file fix with a clear stack trace
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A migration has four phases: find the usages of a deprecated API, design the replacement, edit, and test. In the main conversation the discovery phase read 310 call sites across 190 files. A `/compact` before the edit phase dropped 40 of the sites from its summary, and the edits missed them. The raw file contents were needed only to build the list of sites, which itself is under 2,000 tokens. Which fix is most effective?
opts: Run discovery in an Explore subagent that returns the sites grouped by pattern.
Start a new session for each phase and paste the previous phase's full output into the next one.
Run `/compact` with a focus on the call sites after discovery, so the summary keeps all 310.
Switch to a model whose window is larger, to hold discovery and editing together.
questions.explain: The file reads are the bulk and only the list matters, so a subagent can read them in its own context and return the list, which keeps the main context free for the later phases. B pastes the whole output into each new session, which refills the context. C still loads every file first and depends on a lossy summary that has already failed once. D delays the squeeze without removing the unneeded reads.
bullets: Using the Explore subagent for verbose discovery phases so multi-phase tasks do not exhaust the context window
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A developer needs to add a shared retry adapter to a new service. First they must learn how three existing services implement retries, which means reading about 120 files of client code, and then they will write the adapter with Claude Code. Which approach best protects the main conversation's context?
opts: Switch to plan mode for the reading, because plan mode makes Claude read fewer files in the first place.
Search for `retry` and read only the matching files, one service at a time, in the main conversation.
Have Explore read the code and summarise each service, then write the adapter in the main chat.
Choose a model with more room in its window, so all 120 files fit next to the adapter work.
questions.explain: The reading is verbose discovery, and Explore reads in its own context and returns only a summary, leaving the main conversation free for the adapter. A misreads plan mode, which limits edits and does not reduce how much Claude reads, so the same files still fill the context. B still brings every matching file into it and can miss retry code that is named differently. D delays the problem and keeps the unneeded file contents.
bullets: Using the Explore subagent for verbose discovery phases so multi-phase tasks do not exhaust the context window
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Explore has summarised how three services handle retries, and the main conversation now holds that summary. The developer must edit the loop in `client_b/retry.py` and needs its exact current code. What is the most effective next step?
opts: Resume the Explore subagent and ask it to paste the whole file into its summary.
Read that one file in the main conversation, since it is now the target of the edit.
Repeat the discovery in the main conversation so that every source file is available for editing.
Ask Explore for a very thorough pass, which includes the full text of each file.
questions.explain: Once the work narrows to one file that will be edited, reading it directly costs little context and gives Claude the exact text. A cannot work, because the built-in Explore agent is one-shot and cannot be resumed. C undoes the isolation that protected the context. D expects the very thorough level, which the docs describe as comprehensive analysis, to return whole files, and Explore returns a summary.
bullets: Using the Explore subagent for verbose discovery phases so multi-phase tasks do not exhaust the context window
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A developer has spent 40 minutes in a default-mode session on a flaky integration test that spans three services. Claude now knows the test setup, but the cause is still unknown and several fixes are possible. The developer wants the cause found without any edits and then wants the chosen fix applied in the same session. What is the best way to do this?
opts: Prefix the investigation with `/plan`, approve the chosen plan, then let the session make the fix.
Open a second session for the fix, and copy the findings across by hand when the first one is done.
Stay in default mode and tell Claude not to edit anything until the developer says so.
Restart Claude with `--permission-mode plan` so the investigation starts from a clean session.
questions.explain: Plan mode for the investigation and approval for the implementation keeps the session's context and blocks edits while the cause is unknown. B copies findings by hand and loses what the session knows. C relies on an instruction where the mode gives a guarantee. D throws away the 40 minutes of context that the investigation needs.
bullets: Combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation of the planned approach
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A planned change to a shared type and its 50 call sites across four packages is half done when the session compacts. The developer fears the plan is lost and proposes pasting it into CLAUDE.md and also ending the session at 70% context to restart with the whole plan pasted. The plan was written in plan mode. How should you evaluate those precautions?
opts: Both are needed: a plan lives only in the conversation, and compaction replaces it with a summary.
Only the restart is needed, because a compacted session cannot follow a plan made before compaction.
Only CLAUDE.md is needed, because that file is reloaded in every session while plan files are not.
Neither: Claude wrote the plan to a file, and Claude Code re-injects it after each compaction.
questions.explain: In a long cross-package session the plan file is re-injected after each compaction, so the plan survives where conversation history may not and the planned approach can be carried out in the same session. A wrongly assumes the plan lives only in the conversation. B has no basis, since the plan is back in context after compaction. C is wrong because the plan file is exactly what is re-injected.
bullets: Combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation of the planned approach
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A plan to change 52 files to a new date library was approved and execution has finished two groups cleanly. In group 3, Claude finds six call sites that use a custom subclass of the old date type, which the plan does not mention and which can be handled in two different ways. What is the best way to continue?
opts: Continue executing and let Claude pick a way for the six sites, since the plan fixes the general approach.
Discard the plan and restart the migration from plan mode, because the plan has proved wrong.
Return to plan mode for those six sites, update the plan, then resume executing it.
Ask an Explore subagent to rewrite the six sites in its own context and return the diffs.
questions.explain: The plan holds for the groups already done, but the six sites carry a new design choice, so planning is needed for them and direct execution can resume afterwards. A makes that choice unreviewed, and it may differ from other uses of the subclass. B throws away two groups of valid work. D fails because Explore is read-only.
bullets: Combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation of the planned approach
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A data-team engineer asks Claude Code to "standardise the phone numbers in customers.csv" for an import tool. Run on the same 500-row sample five times, the output differs: some runs write `+44 7700 900123`, others `07700900123`, others `+447700900123`. The instruction has been reworded twice with more detail about spacing and prefixes, and the variation continues. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Put a rule in CLAUDE.md that phone numbers get one standard form, and ask Claude to apply it strictly.
Show a few rows as raw value and exact output, including one number with no country code.
Run the task three times and keep the format that appears most often in the results of those runs.
Ask Claude to announce the format it has chosen at the start of each run and to hold to it for the whole file.
questions.explain: Pairs of raw input and exact output pin down the transformation, including the case the prose left open. A moves the same wording to another file. C picks the most popular output, which need not be the required one. D has Claude report a choice it makes anew in each run, so the formats still differ between runs.
bullets: Concrete input/output examples communicate a transformation best when prose is read inconsistently
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A finance engineer wants Claude Code to rewrite expense lines like `Taxi 12.50 USD` into the ledger form `TRAVEL|1250|USD`. She supplies three examples: a taxi, a train and a bus fare, each with a decimal amount in USD. On a test batch, `Hotel 140 EUR` comes out as `TRAVEL|140|EUR` in some runs and `LODGING|14000|EUR` in others. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Three examples are too few; a format cannot be generalised until a dozen or so have been shown.
A transformation cannot be applied to lines whose currency differs from the one shown in the examples.
The examples differ only in item and amount, so the whole-number and non-USD lines were never shown.
The target form must first be given as a template with placeholders before any examples can be used.
questions.explain: Examples teach only what they cover, and these three share the same shape, so Claude guesses at the cases the batch contains and guesses differently each time. A invents a threshold, since a few varied examples can be enough. B describes a limit that does not exist. D adds a step that would not change what is missing, which is cases showing whole numbers and another currency.
bullets: Concrete input/output examples communicate a transformation best when prose is read inconsistently
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A platform team has Claude Code tidy changelog entries "into our house style" before each release. The written style guide is already pasted into the prompt. Reviewers see that about a third of runs capitalise the word after the colon, a third do not, and the order of entries varies. The team lead suggests running the job three times and keeping the version that appears most often. What is the better fix?
opts: Run it five times instead of three, and keep the version that appears most often among them.
Move the style guide to the end of the prompt, where the last instructions are read first.
Rewrite the style guide as a numbered list of ten formatting rules, one sentence each.
Add a few entries as before and after text, covering capitalisation and order.
questions.explain: Before-and-after entries show the style where the written guide is read in different ways. A and the lead's plan only choose among outputs and do not define the right one. B changes where the same text sits. C is more prose, from which the same variation would come.
bullets: Concrete input/output examples communicate a transformation best when prose is read inconsistently
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: You are adding a `shipping_fee()` function to a checkout service. The fee has weight tiers (up to 1 kg, over 1 to 5 kg, over 5 kg), free shipping above an order-value threshold, and an error for zero or negative weights. You want Claude Code to deliver a correct implementation with the least back-and-forth. Which approach is most effective?
opts: Write tests for tier boundaries, the threshold and bad weights first, then let Claude iterate to green.
Describe the rules in a detailed prompt, then compare the finished function against the list by reading it.
Have Claude implement the function first, then write tests from its code to confirm the behaviour it built.
Have Claude implement the function in two separate sessions, then compare the two versions for differences.
questions.explain: Tests written first define done independently of the code, and each failure tells Claude what to change. B leaves the checking to a manual read. C writes the tests from the implementation, so they confirm whatever was built. D compares two guesses with each other, and does not check either against the rules.
bullets: Test-driven iteration: write the tests first, then iterate by sharing the failures
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A developer asks Claude Code to fix a failing `test_prorate_refund` suite that runs only on the team's CI server. After each attempt, the developer replies with a summary such as "the refund amounts are still slightly off". Six rounds in, Claude has changed rounding, date arithmetic and the currency lookup, and 3 of 9 cases still fail. What is the most likely reason progress is slow?
opts: The suite is too large for Claude to read in one pass, so it works from the first few cases.
Claude is told how the result looks, not which cases fail or what each one expected and got.
Claude Code cannot repair tests that run on a CI server, only those that run on the developer's machine.
The test names do not describe the checks well enough for Claude to infer what each case covers.
questions.explain: A loop only converges when Claude sees the specific failures, so the failing assertions with expected and actual values should be pasted. A is unsupported by the stem, which says it touched three areas. C describes a limit that does not exist. D concerns naming, while the missing information is the actual output of the failing cases.
bullets: Test-driven iteration: write the tests first, then iterate by sharing the failures
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A developer has written 12 tests for a discount engine before any code exists. Claude Code is asked to make them pass. Each round the developer pastes only the output of the one test being targeted. After three rounds, five tests are failing every time, but a different five each round, and the developer is losing track of what each change breaks. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Claude cannot work on more than one failing test at a time, so regressions are expected.
Each round runs in a fresh context, which discards what the earlier rounds established.
Only one test's result is shared, so what each change breaks elsewhere stays hidden.
A suite of 12 tests is too large to converge, and it should be split into smaller suites.
questions.explain: Iteration works when the failures Claude sees show the effect of its last change on the whole suite, so the full result of each run should be shared. A invents a one-test limit. B contradicts the stem, which describes a continuing series of rounds. D treats a small suite as too big.
bullets: Test-driven iteration: write the tests first, then iterate by sharing the failures
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: You asked Claude Code to interview you about a retry policy for an outbound email service you had never designed. After 14 questions about per-recipient limits, bounce handling and provider outages, it says it has enough to write the spec. You want the build to begin from a clean context and a written definition of done. What should you do next?
opts: Ask Claude to start coding in the same session, so that the interview's wording stays in context.
Ask Claude to record the interview answers in CLAUDE.md so that every later session loads them.
Run /compact and let the build start from the compacted interview in the same session.
Have Claude write the spec to a file, then start a fresh session and build from that file.
questions.explain: A spec file captures the answers and gives the build a written target, and a fresh session starts without the interview's back-and-forth. A keeps the long interview in context. B puts a one-off design into a file that loads on every task. C leaves a summary of the conversation in place of a spec.
bullets: The interview pattern: Claude asks questions to surface considerations the developer has not anticipated
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A developer asked Claude Code to "add retries to the job queue worker and handle every failure mode". Claude added exponential backoff. In review, the team found that the jobs charge cards, so a duplicate run after a timeout is a serious risk, and failed jobs also need a dead-letter record. The developer has not worked on payment queues before and does not know which failure modes matter. They want to catch needs like these before coding next time. Which approach would best have surfaced them?
opts: Ask Claude to interview the developer about failures and duplicate runs before implementing.
Use plan mode, so that Claude proposes a design and the developer approves it if it looks sound.
Add "consider duplicate runs and dead letters" to the prompt of every future queue task.
Ask Claude to list the failure modes it can think of and then implement every one of them.
questions.explain: Questions to the developer bring out requirements that only the developer knows, such as card charges. B shows what Claude assumed, and the developer can approve a plan without noticing what is missing. C is a fix for these two cases and does not help with the next unknown. D relies on Claude's guesses about a system it cannot see.
bullets: The interview pattern: Claude asks questions to surface considerations the developer has not anticipated
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A team runs Claude Code headless in CI each night to fix lint violations flagged by a fixed ruleset, then opens a PR. A colleague proposes adding the interview pattern, so that Claude asks questions about each violation before editing. The ruleset and its fixes are well understood, and nobody is present when the job runs. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Adopt it: questions before every edit remove the risk of a wrong fix.
Decline it: nobody is there to answer, and nothing here is new enough to need it.
Adopt it, with Claude answering its own questions from the repository before it edits.
Decline it: the interview pattern only works in plan mode and does not run headless.
questions.explain: The pattern pays off when a developer is present and the domain is new to them; neither holds here. A adds waiting for answers that no one can give. C removes what makes an interview useful, which is the developer's own knowledge. D states a restriction that is not part of the pattern.
bullets: The interview pattern: Claude asks questions to surface considerations the developer has not anticipated
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A dashboard has two open bugs: sessions go stale, and some users stay signed in after logout. The developer first asks Claude Code about the stale sessions, and it adds a cache TTL. The logout bug is raised next, Claude clears the cookie, and the stale sessions return. After three rounds of alternating, both symptoms still appear. Which next step is best to take?
opts: Keep alternating, but ask Claude to run the whole suite after each fix so a regression shows at once.
Run /clear and report each bug again in its own message, in the original order.
Describe both bugs in one message, with how each fix affects the other and what must hold.
Fix the logout bug first, since a security problem should be settled before a stale cache.
questions.explain: The two fixes touch the same session handling, so Claude needs both problems and their dependency at once to design them together. A catches the regression but repeats the same one-at-a-time cycle. B restarts the sequence that produced the flip-flop. D chooses an order, but any order has the same effect on the other bug.
bullets: When to put all issues in one message (they interact) and when to fix them one by one (they are independent)
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Four items are open on an internal tools repo: a missing database index slowing the audit-log page, a mobile layout overflow on the settings screen, a misspelt label in the billing form, and an out-of-date base image in the Dockerfile. Each was reported by a different team and sits in a different part of the repo. How should you raise them with Claude Code?
opts: All four in one detailed message, so that Claude can plan the changes together.
Two messages: the two user-facing items together, and the two infrastructure items together.
Group by size: the two quick fixes in one message and each larger item in a message of its own.
One at a time, checking each result before raising the next.
questions.explain: Independent problems are best handled sequentially, so each change gets Claude's full attention and its result can be checked on its own. A bundles unrelated work without any dependency to justify it. B and C group items by theme or size, which has no bearing on whether the fixes affect each other.
bullets: When to put all issues in one message (they interact) and when to fix them one by one (they are independent)
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: After a dependency upgrade, a CI run fails in three places: a type error in `OrderMapper`, a runtime error in a checkout API test and a snapshot mismatch in the invoice report. All three stack traces pass through the upgraded `fetchCustomer` helper. The engineer pastes the three failures into one message with the request "fix these". Claude adds a cast in `OrderMapper`, and the other two failures change shape but remain. What is the most likely reason?
opts: The message does not say the failures share a cause, so each is fixed on its own.
Three failures are too many for one message, and each should have been sent on its own.
Type errors have to be fixed before runtime errors, and the message did not give that order.
Snapshot mismatches cannot be repaired from a CI log and have to be regenerated by hand.
questions.explain: Interacting problems need one detailed message that says how they relate; here that is the library's new nullable return type, which the three fixes must handle consistently. B pushes toward the sequential approach that suits independent problems. C invents an ordering rule. D is false, as a snapshot can be corrected from its diff.
bullets: When to put all issues in one message (they interact) and when to fix them one by one (they are independent)
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Claude Code is generating TypeScript models from a database schema. The prompt says "convert column names to our camelCase convention". Across runs, `user_id` becomes `userId` or `userID`, and `address_line_2` becomes `addressLine2` or `addressLine_2`. Which change to the prompt is most effective?
opts: Add a second sentence describing the convention in more detail, covering acronyms and trailing digits.
Add three input and output pairs: a plain column, one with an acronym and one with a number suffix.
Point Claude to the team's style guide file and ask it to follow that file closely.
Have Claude convert the first ten columns, then tell it to continue in the same style for the rest.
questions.explain: A few pairs that cover the awkward cases show the exact output, which prose keeps leaving open. A is more of the wording that is already read in two ways. C adds another piece of prose to interpret. D uses Claude's own first ten outputs as the pattern, so whichever way it chose becomes the rule.
bullets: Giving 2-3 concrete input/output examples when a prose description produces inconsistent results
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A team has 60 recorded before-and-after pairs from a past manual conversion of release-note drafts into a fixed customer-facing form. An engineer prompts Claude Code to convert the next batch. A prose-only attempt gave inconsistent output, and the choices on the table are to paste all 60 pairs or to keep the prose. How should you evaluate them?
opts: Paste all 60 pairs, since each extra pair narrows the variation a little further.
Keep the prose and add more rules, since 60 pairs would take up too much of the context.
Use neither as they stand: pick a few varied pairs, awkward ones included.
Paste the first 10 pairs in file order, as those came from the most recent conversion.
questions.explain: A handful of relevant and varied pairs is what guides the transformation, and the awkward ones carry the most information. A treats volume as the goal and buries the unusual cases. B returns to the prose that already produced inconsistent results. D chooses by position in the file, which says nothing about coverage.
bullets: Giving 2-3 concrete input/output examples when a prose description produces inconsistent results
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A CI step asks Claude Code to normalise product codes in a data file and gives three examples. `ab-12 ` becomes `AB-12`, `cd-07` becomes `CD-07`, and `ef-3 ` becomes `EF-3 `. Across runs, about half of the codes with a trailing space come out trimmed and half do not. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Claude reads only the first example, and the third is ignored whenever a trailing space is present.
Three examples are too few, and a larger set would settle the behaviour for trailing spaces.
The file reader removes trailing spaces before Claude sees them in about half of the runs.
The examples disagree about trailing spaces, so the output follows one of two valid readings.
questions.explain: The first example trims the space and the third keeps it, so Claude has two consistent readings to follow. Examples must agree with each other as well as cover the cases. A invents a rule about which example is read. B suggests more examples, which would not help while they conflict. C assumes a reader fault that the stem gives no sign of.
bullets: Giving 2-3 concrete input/output examples when a prose description produces inconsistent results
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: You are about to ask Claude Code to write `dedupe_contacts()`, which merges duplicate rows in a contact list that can reach 2 million rows and must finish within 60 seconds. You decide to write the tests first. Which test plan is best?
opts: Ordinary duplicates, an empty list and mixed-case near-duplicates, plus a 2-million-row timing test.
Ordinary duplicates, an empty list and mixed-case near-duplicates; the 60-second limit is checked once the logic passes.
Ordinary duplicates and a 2-million-row timing test; edge cases will appear as failures once real data runs through it.
Ordinary duplicates at several sizes up to 2 million rows, with empty and mixed-case inputs left to code review.
questions.explain: Only the first plan puts expected behaviour, edge cases and the performance requirement into the suite before any code exists. B defers speed, so a slow solution can pass as complete. C leaves edge cases to be found in use. D covers size but relies on review to catch the edge inputs.
bullets: Writing tests for expected behaviour, edge cases and performance before implementing, then sharing failures
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A CI job for a nightly export runs Claude Code's generated `build_report()`. All 38 tests pass, yet the job takes 14 minutes against a 2-minute budget, and an engineer who reads the code finds nested loops over the full row set. The tests were written before the implementation and check output values only. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The CI runners are slower than the developer's machine on which Claude iterated.
Speed was never expressed as a test, so a correct but slow solution counted as done.
Claude Code prefers short code by default and writes loops in place of library calls.
The 38 tests are too few; with 100 tests the slow code would have failed some of them.
questions.explain: Claude stops when its checks pass, and none of them measured time. A would not account for the nested loops that the engineer found. C is a guess about habits, not something the stem shows. D confuses count with coverage, since more value checks would still pass on slow code.
bullets: Writing tests for expected behaviour, edge cases and performance before implementing, then sharing failures
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Before any implementation exists, you ask Claude Code to draft tests for a new rate-card importer from the ticket. It returns 24 tests. You disagree with six of the expected values, which you think come from a misreading of the ticket. What is the best next step?
opts: Start the implementation, and correct the six values later if they still fail.
Delete the six disputed tests, and let the remaining 18 drive the implementation.
Correct the six expectations with Claude now, then implement against the agreed suite.
Implement against all 24, then ask Claude to explain which failures it thinks are test errors.
questions.explain: The suite is the definition of done, so it should be right before it is used as a target. A builds code toward values you believe are wrong. B removes cases and leaves their behaviour undefined. D asks Claude to decide which expectations to trust, after it has already adjusted the code toward them.
bullets: Writing tests for expected behaviour, edge cases and performance before implementing, then sharing failures
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: You asked Claude Code to interview you before it builds your first payment-provider webhook receiver. Its open questions, such as "How should duplicate deliveries be handled?", get the answer "not sure" nine times out of twelve, and the interview is stalling. What is the most effective change?
opts: End the interview and have Claude implement with its own defaults, then review the code.
Tell Claude to ask fewer questions, limited to the three it considers most important.
Answer each question with a best guess, and correct the guesses that prove wrong in review.
Ask for each question as a few options, with what each option would mean for the receiver.
questions.explain: Questions that offer concrete options let a newcomer choose without already knowing the answer, and the interview keeps surfacing considerations. A returns to unexamined defaults. B trims the number of considerations surfaced. C feeds guesses into the spec as if they were decisions.
bullets: Using the interview pattern in unfamiliar domains to surface design considerations such as failure modes
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Before adding a job scheduler, a developer wrote: "If anything is unclear, ask me before you start." Claude Code replied that nothing was unclear and wrote a scheduler with an in-process lock. In staging, with four instances running, jobs ran four times. The developer has never built distributed scheduling. What change to the request is most effective?
opts: Ask for an interview about scheduling and failure behaviour, run until a spec could be written.
Replace the sentence with "ask me anything you might need to know", to make the trigger broader.
Add "the scheduler will run on several instances" to the prompt, and ask for the same implementation.
Switch to plan mode, so that Claude describes its approach before it changes any files.
questions.explain: Making the interview the task means Claude must put its questions about the unfamiliar parts to the developer, whatever it thinks it already knows. B is the same optional wording with a wider trigger. C fixes the one fact the developer now knows, while the other unknowns stay hidden. D shows an approach built on the same assumptions.
bullets: Using the interview pattern in unfamiliar domains to surface design considerations such as failure modes
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A team has never run zero-downtime database migrations and wants Claude Code to add a migration step to its CI pipeline. The repository has no earlier migration scripts, and nobody can say which risks apply to them, such as locks on large tables or the rollback of a half-applied change. Which opening is best?
opts: Ask Claude to search the repository for how migrations are normally done here, and copy that.
Ask Claude to interview the team about risks and constraints before it writes the step.
Ask Claude for the standard migration step that most teams use, and adjust it in review.
Ask Claude to write the step, plus a runbook of every risk it can think of, for reading later.
questions.explain: In an unfamiliar domain, questions put to the team bring out the design considerations, such as locking and rollback, before code exists. A looks for a pattern the repository does not contain. C imports another team's assumptions. D produces the risks only after the step has been written around them.
bullets: Using the interview pattern in unfamiliar domains to surface design considerations such as failure modes
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A migration script copies `orders` into a new table. Rows where `shipped_at` is NULL (about 8% of 1.2 million) end up with `shipped_at` set to 1970-01-01, and legacy rows holding `0000-00-00` crash the run. The developer's last message said "handle bad dates properly" and made things worse. Which next message is most effective?
opts: Say the script must be careful with dates, and ask Claude to check every date column again.
Say that the 1970 values are wrong, and ask Claude to wrap each date conversion in a try/except.
Give three cases: NULL gives NULL, `0000-00-00` gives NULL, a valid date is copied as it is.
Paste the stack trace from the crash, and ask Claude to make the script stop failing.
questions.explain: Specific inputs with the exact expected outputs define what "properly" means for each edge case. A repeats the vague request. B stops the crash but leaves open what the new value should be, and could hide bad rows. D shows where it failed, and not what the result should have been.
bullets: Giving specific test cases with example input and expected output to fix edge-case handling
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Finance reports that invoice totals are off by one cent on about 1 in 300 invoices. Claude Code's rounding fix passed the developer's check on three sample invoices, and the discrepancies continued. The developer wants to pin the behaviour down before another attempt. Which input is most effective?
opts: Export 500 recent invoices with the totals the current code produces as the expected values.
A written description of the rounding rule, with an instruction to apply it to every line item.
The number of one failing production invoice, with a request to make that invoice's total correct.
A few cases on half-cent amounts, a zero line and a credit, each with its exact total.
questions.explain: Specific inputs at the boundaries, each with the exact expected output, define the edge-case behaviour and give Claude something to run. A treats the buggy code's own output as the answer. B is prose, which is where the ambiguity began. C fixes one invoice and leaves the cases around it unspecified.
bullets: Giving specific test cases with example input and expected output to fix edge-case handling
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Claude Code fixed an off-by-one error in `days_in_range(start, end)` after the developer gave it three cases: 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-31 returns 31, a one-day range returns 1, and a reversed range raises an error. Over the next two weeks, other changes broke the function twice before anyone noticed. How should the three cases have been kept so that the next breakage is caught when it happens?
opts: As tests in the repository's suite, so that they run on every later change.
As comments above the function, so that later editors can see the intended results.
As a rule in CLAUDE.md, so that Claude remembers the cases in later sessions.
As a message re-sent to Claude Code each time somebody touches the function.
questions.explain: Cases with example input and expected output become a check that runs without anyone remembering it. B and C are text that still depends on someone reading it, and C reaches only sessions that involve Claude. D needs a person to recall the step each time, which is how the two breakages went unnoticed.
bullets: Test-driven iteration: write the tests first, then iterate by sharing the failures
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A list API sorts by `created_at` and returns an opaque cursor that encodes the last row's `created_at`. Claude Code changes the ORDER BY to `updated_at`, and the second page of results then repeats and skips rows, because the cursor still encodes `created_at`. The sort and the cursor must agree with each other. How should the developer raise the follow-up?
opts: Revert the sort change, ask for the cursor change, then ask again for the sort change.
Describe the sort change, the cursor encoding and their dependency in one message.
Ask only for the cursor fix, then see whether the sort order is also wrong afterwards.
Open a new session for the cursor and keep the sort change in the current session.
questions.explain: The two changes are coupled, so one detailed message lets Claude design them to agree. A and C handle them in turn and invite a mismatch between the two. D separates them across sessions that cannot see each other's work.
bullets: Describing interacting issues together in one detailed message, independent issues sequentially
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A schema change renamed `customer.region` to `customer.sales_region` and made it nullable. The next CI run fails in four places: an ORM mapping, a report query, a fixture loader and an API serializer. Each log line cites the old name or a null error. An engineer plans to give Claude Code the failures one at a time, in the order CI printed them, re-running CI between each. How should you evaluate this plan?
opts: Sound: each failure is small, and focused messages give Claude the clearest view of each.
Sound, provided CI is re-run after each message so that any new failure is caught early.
Weak: all four stem from one schema change, so one message should carry all of them.
Weak: the order should follow the dependency graph, so the ORM mapping is fixed first.
questions.explain: The four failures come from one change and the fixes must be consistent with each other, so they interact and are best described together. A and B treat the failures as independent, and the re-runs only find a mismatch after the fact. D keeps the one-at-a-time sequence and changes only which item is first.
bullets: Describing interacting issues together in one detailed message, independent issues sequentially
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A developer has two tickets: report exports time out at 30 seconds, and duplicate invoices appear when clients retry. Logs show duplicates also follow 503 responses that arrive within 2 seconds, and last month a change to one HTTP client setting doubled the duplicates. Her plan is two separate requests to Claude Code: raise `client.timeout` for the first ticket, then change `client.retries` for the second. How should you evaluate this plan?
opts: Sound: these are separate tickets, and separate requests keep each change small enough to review.
Sound: raising the timeout first removes the timeouts that trigger retries, and the retries can be handled after.
Weak: both tickets come down to one problem, so a single change to the retry count and timeout would be enough.
Weak: the two settings affect each other, so both fixes should be described together.
questions.explain: The timeout and the retry count act on the same behaviour, as last month's change showed, so the fixes must be designed together. A judges by ticket boundaries, not by whether the fixes interact. B overlooks the duplicates that follow 503s, which a longer timeout does not touch. C merges two different causes into one change and still leaves the duplicates unaddressed.
bullets: Describing interacting issues together in one detailed message, independent issues sequentially
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A merge gate on a CI runner with a clean checkout starts `claude --bare "Check this branch for hard-coded internal hostnames"` to get a fast, repeatable start. The step prints nothing and is cancelled at the 30-minute job limit; the runner has no terminal attached. What is the most effective change?
opts: Add `--max-turns 3` so that the run is forced to stop early.
Keep `--bare` and set a shorter job timeout, so a stuck step fails sooner.
Add `-p` so the prompt runs non-interactively and the answer is printed.
Replace `--bare` with `--continue`, so the run picks up an earlier session.
questions.explain: `--bare` only skips auto-discovery of hooks, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md for a repeatable start; it does not make the session non-interactive, and `-p` is what prints the answer and returns control. A caps agentic turns but does not change how the session starts. B turns a hang into a quicker failure with the same empty output. D reopens an older conversation, and a clean checkout on a fresh runner holds none.
bullets: The -p (--print) flag runs Claude Code non-interactively inside automated pipelines
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A nightly job runs `claude -p "Fix the lint errors in src/"` on a runner. It exits 0 in under a minute, but the commit step finds no changed files on any night. The run's log shows Claude reading the files and proposing edits. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Pass `--allowedTools "Read,Edit"` so edits are not denied for lack of approval.
Remove `-p`, so that Claude can ask for permission before it makes each edit.
Say in the prompt that Claude has permission to edit files and should apply every change.
Raise the turn limit with `--max-turns 20` so Claude has enough turns to finish the edits.
questions.explain: In a `-p` run nobody can answer an approval prompt, so a call that needs approval is denied and the run carries on; naming the tools in `--allowedTools` lets the edits happen. B brings back the interactive session that hangs a pipeline. C is a prompt instruction, and permission is decided by the tool settings, not by what the model is told. D fixes a limit that was never reached, since a run that hits it exits with an error.
bullets: The -p (--print) flag runs Claude Code non-interactively inside automated pipelines
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A wrapper script runs `claude -p "Apply the codemod to src/legacy" --max-turns 6 > out.txt` and marks the CI step passed when out.txt contains the word "done". On some nights the run stops at its turn limit with the codemod half-applied, yet out.txt still has "done" in a progress line. How should the step decide whether the run succeeded?
opts: Require the last line of out.txt to be exactly "done" before passing.
Instruct Claude in the prompt to print FAILED when it could not finish.
Search out.txt for the words error, failed and incomplete as well.
Branch on the exit status of `claude -p`; it is non-zero on failure.
questions.explain: The exit status is a deterministic signal: Claude Code exits non-zero when the run fails, including when the turn limit is reached. A, B and C all keep judging success from model-written text, which is a different wording away from failing again. B also asks the model to report its own failure, the case where it may not.
bullets: The -p (--print) flag runs Claude Code non-interactively inside automated pipelines
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A dashboard needs, for every CI run of the PR reviewer, the session ID and what the run cost. The job calls `claude -p "Review this PR"` and the log holds only the review text. Which change gives a script those values in one machine-readable object?
opts: Ask in the prompt that the review ends with a line giving the session ID and the cost of the run.
Add `--output-format json` and read the fields from the object printed at the end of the run.
Add `--json-schema` with fields named `session_id` and `cost`, which Claude fills in itself.
Parse the plain-text log for lines that mention the session and the cost.
questions.explain: With `--output-format json` the run returns one object holding the result, the session ID and metadata such as `total_cost_usd`. A asks the model to state values it does not hold. C makes the model write the numbers, where a schema only shapes the answer it composes. D relies on text that the plain-text format never contains.
bullets: --output-format json and --json-schema enforce structured output in CI
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A review job runs `claude -p "$PROMPT" --output-format json --json-schema "$SCHEMA"` and a script then runs `jq -r '.structured_output.findings[].message'`. About 1 run in 150 fails in jq with `Cannot iterate over null`. In those runs the JSON object has a `result` text but no `structured_output` key. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The schema is too strict, so Claude Code rejects a few outputs and exits before it prints anything.
These PRs had no issues, and Claude Code leaves out the field when the findings list is empty.
Those runs ended without valid structured output, and the script never checks the field exists.
The `format` keyword in the schema is not enforced, so some runs returned free text instead.
questions.explain: When a run ends without valid structured output, for example because Claude declined the request, the response has no `structured_output` field, so the script must test for it first. A fits an invalid schema, which fails at start on every run and prints no object. B is wrong because an empty findings list is still valid output and appears in the field. D confuses `format`, which only annotates a value, with whether the field is present.
bullets: --output-format json and --json-schema enforce structured output in CI
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: The findings schema of a CI reviewer declares `fixed_by` as `{"type": "string", "format": "email"}` so the poster can mention the author. After a month, 3% of findings carry values such as `unknown` or `the author`, and the poster fails when it looks the author up. Claude Code raised no schema error. What is the most likely cause?
opts: `format` is treated as an annotation and not enforced, so strings that are not e-mail addresses pass.
The schema was applied to the top-level keys only, so nested fields such as this one were never checked.
These runs hit the turn limit, and output produced at that point skips schema validation.
`email` is not a valid value for `format`, so Claude Code dropped the constraint without a message.
questions.explain: Claude Code accepts `format`, such as `"format": "email"`, but treats it as an annotation and does not enforce it, so the poster must check the value itself. B and C invent limits on validation that the stem gives no sign of. D is refuted by the same behaviour: `email` is accepted, just not enforced.
bullets: --output-format json and --json-schema enforce structured output in CI
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: The CI reviewer keeps flagging generated files under `gen/` and the intentional raw SQL in `migrations/`, and developers dismiss about a third of its comments as noise. The team lead wants the review rules, what to skip and what counts as a defect, to guide CI runs and also developers' local sessions. Where should the rules go?
opts: In a personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on each developer's machine, loaded in all their sessions.
In the wiki page for contributors, with a link in the PR template.
In the `-p` prompt string, which is the only text Claude Code reads on a CI run.
In the repository's `CLAUDE.md`, which is committed and loaded in both places.
questions.explain: A project `CLAUDE.md` in the repository is checked out on the runner and read in local sessions (unless the run uses `--bare`), so one file serves both. A lives on each developer's machine, and the runner is a different one. B is documentation for people, which no Claude Code run loads. C is false: a CI run loads CLAUDE.md as well, and a long prompt string would leave local sessions out.
bullets: CLAUDE.md carries project context (testing standards, fixtures, review criteria) to CI-invoked Claude Code
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: An engineer put a rule in `CLAUDE.local.md` at the repository root: ignore TODO comments dated within the last 30 days. Her local `claude` sessions follow it. The CI reviewer, run with `claude -p` on a clean checkout of the same repository, flags every recent TODO. What is the most likely cause?
opts: `-p` runs do not load any CLAUDE.md files, so no project rules reach a CI run on a runner.
`CLAUDE.local.md` is personal and meant to be gitignored, so the clean checkout lacks it.
Rules about comments only take effect from a `CLAUDE.md` placed in the directory next to the code they cover.
`CLAUDE.local.md` is loaded only in interactive sessions, so `-p` runs skip it.
questions.explain: `CLAUDE.local.md` holds private preferences that the docs say to add to `.gitignore`, so it does not reach the runner; a rule CI must follow belongs in the committed `CLAUDE.md`. A is false, since `claude -p` discovers and loads CLAUDE.md as an interactive session does. C invents a placement rule. D is also false: the file loads alongside `CLAUDE.md` wherever it exists, and here it does not exist.
bullets: CLAUDE.md carries project context (testing standards, fixtures, review criteria) to CI-invoked Claude Code
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: The repository's CLAUDE.md has grown to 700 lines: the whole style guide, release history, an API reference, and four review rules that matter most (no request bodies in logs, no new `any` types, database calls only in `repo/`, reversible migrations). The CI reviewer applies those four rules in only about half of its runs. What is the most effective change?
opts: Move the CI job to a larger model, since the rules are already in the file.
Repeat the four rules in capital letters at the top and at the bottom of the file.
Cut the file down to the short, specific standards and criteria a CI run needs.
Copy the four rules into a second CLAUDE.md under `.github/`, so they load twice.
questions.explain: The file is read on every run, so a focused CLAUDE.md that holds only the standards and criteria keeps those rules from being buried. A assumes the model is the weak part when the rules are lost in volume. B adds emphasis to a file that is still long. D adds more text and a second place to keep in step.
bullets: CLAUDE.md carries project context (testing standards, fixtures, review criteria) to CI-invoked Claude Code
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A team reviews AI-written changes in a second step: the same `claude` session that wrote the code is asked, "Now review your changes." It approves almost everything, and human reviewers keep finding bugs that it passed. Which explanation fits best?
opts: The session still holds the reasoning behind the code, so it rarely questions it.
A session cannot read its own earlier edits, so it reviews an out-of-date copy of the files.
Reviewing needs a larger context window than writing, and the session has used most of its own.
A model tuned for writing code cannot be prompted into reviewing any code at all, even its own.
questions.explain: The generating session carries the assumptions behind its own decisions, which makes it a weaker reviewer than an independent instance that has not seen how the code was written. B is false, since a session sees its own edits. C blames space, when the reviewer fails in a short session too. D claims a limit that does not exist.
bullets: The session that wrote the code is a weaker reviewer of it than an independent review instance
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A pipeline makes two separate `claude -p` calls per PR. The reviewer call is given the diff plus the generator's closing summary of about 150 words: "edge cases covered: empty cart, expired coupon." In a test with 10 planted bugs, the reviewer found 7 when given only the diff and 3 when the summary was included. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The summary pushed part of the diff out of the reviewer's context window, so later hunks were skipped.
The reviewer obeyed the summary's wording as an instruction, so it stopped reviewing after the listed cases.
Two separate `claude -p` calls share one session by default, so the reviewer is not independent.
The summary states what the generator thinks is handled, which anchors the reviewer to its blind spots.
questions.explain: An independent review works because it does not inherit the author's assumptions; handing it the author's list of covered cases brings those assumptions back. A cannot hold for 150 words. B is not what happened, because the reviewer still reviewed, just toward the same gaps. C is false: each `claude -p` call starts a new session unless it is told to continue one.
bullets: The session that wrote the code is a weaker reviewer of it than an independent review instance
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: To cut pipeline time, an engineer proposes one call instead of two: `claude -p "Implement the ticket, then review your own diff and fix any problems"`. A trial on 20 tickets shows 35% less wall-clock time, and the combined run reports "no problems found" on 19 of them. The separate reviewer step used to block 6 of the same 20. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Adopt it, since it is faster for the same output, and add `--max-turns` to bound the run overall.
Reject it: the review needs an instance that did not write the code, so keep two calls.
Adopt it, and tell the merged run to be more critical when it reviews its own diff.
Reject it, and move the merged call to a larger model so it finds what the reviewer found.
questions.explain: The saving comes from dropping the independence that made the reviewer useful, as the 6 blocked tickets show. An independent instance reviewing the diff is what catches them. A trades quality for speed and a turn limit does not restore it. C asks for self-criticism inside the session that wrote the code. D assumes size, not perspective, was the gap.
bullets: The session that wrote the code is a weaker reviewer of it than an independent review instance
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A Jenkins stage that generates unit tests runs `claude "Write tests for src/billing/"` on a build agent. Every run is ended only by the 45-minute stage timeout, with no files written, and the agent has no terminal attached. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Run it with `-p`, so the prompt runs non-interactively and the process exits.
Raise the stage timeout to 90 minutes, to give Claude more time to finish the work.
Add `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, so that no approval prompt blocks the run.
Run the command under a pseudo-terminal, so the session can draw its screen.
questions.explain: Without `-p` an interactive session waits for input; `-p` runs the prompt non-interactively and exits when the response is complete. B waits longer on a process that never finishes. C removes approval prompts, but the session is still interactive and still waits for input when it has finished. D gives the session a screen to wait on.
bullets: Running Claude Code in CI with -p so that no interactive input hangs the job
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A cron entry on a shared server runs `claude "Summarise last week's merged PRs" >> weekly.md` every Monday at 06:00. The file `weekly.md` stays empty, and `ps` shows a `claude` process from each of the last four Mondays still running. What is the most effective change?
opts: Wrap the command in `nohup`, so it no longer depends on a terminal session.
Redirect stderr as well with `2>&1`, so that the failure message reaches `weekly.md`.
Move the entry to 02:00, when the server is less busy.
Add `-p` to the command, so each run prints its answer and exits.
questions.explain: Without `-p` each run opens an interactive session and waits for input, which is why old processes pile up and nothing is written. With `-p` the run prints its answer and exits. A detaches the same waiting session from a terminal. B would capture a message that no failure produced. C changes the time, not the waiting.
bullets: Running Claude Code in CI with -p so that no interactive input hangs the job
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A review script runs `claude -p "Review the diff in pr.diff" > review.txt`, then `claude --continue "Reduce the findings to the five most severe" > top5.txt`. The first command always finishes. The second sits until the job limit, and top5.txt is empty. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The follow-up exceeds the turn budget inherited from the first run, so it waits for a higher limit.
The first command's output file is still open, so the second command waits for it to be closed.
The second command has no `-p`, so it opens an interactive session that waits for input.
A session from a `-p` run is discarded when it exits, so `--continue` has nothing to load.
questions.explain: Every pipeline call needs `-p`, including a follow-up: `claude -p --continue` continues the earlier `-p` session non-interactively. A invents an inherited budget, and a run that hits its turn limit exits with an error rather than waiting. B is an ordinary shell concern that does not hold a process. D is wrong because `claude -p --continue` includes sessions created by `-p` runs.
bullets: Running Claude Code in CI with -p so that no interactive input hangs the job
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your bot posts review findings as inline PR comments, and its posting script needs each finding's file, line and text. Which schema passed to `--json-schema` lets the script work with no text parsing?
opts: An object with one required string field, `review`, that holds the complete text of the review.
A `findings` array of objects with required `file`, `line` (integer), `severity` and `message`.
An object with a `findings` array of strings, each one written in the form "path:line message" for parsing.
An object with a boolean `approved` and a string `reason` that explains the decision in full text.
