Run on the TypeScript web client, the reviewer classified the same 60 findings differently in 18 re-reviews, and it often rated rendering glitches as high. Which change is most effective?
opts: Add an example per level from the web client, such as a crash on submit for high and a misaligned label for low.
Replace the examples with a longer description of each level, so the definitions are no longer tied to one codebase.
Add a rule that web client findings are never rated above medium, since the client holds no sensitive data.
Pass each finding through a second reviewer that compares its level with the levels of similar findings.
questions.explain: The examples set what each level means, and none of them resembles client code, so the reviewer has to guess. Examples from the client fix that. B drops the concrete examples that the guide asks for. C classifies by location, and a script-injection flaw in the client would be capped at medium. D compares labels that come from the same unanchored judgment.
bullets: Defining each severity level with explicit criteria and concrete code examples for consistent classification
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: The severity section gives a code example for "high" (a SQL string built from user input) and for "medium" (an unchecked list index), and defines "low" as "everything else". Re-reviewing 40 pull requests twice, the reviewer assigned "medium" to 40% of the findings developers class as low, and the level of the same finding changed between runs about a quarter of the time. What explains this best?
opts: Two examples are too few; the reviewer needs about ten per level before it applies them evenly.
"Low" has no anchor of its own, so borderline findings drift to the nearest level that does.
The reviewer picks severity from how a finding is worded, so findings should follow a fixed template.
Three named levels cannot be applied consistently by a model, so a numeric scale is needed.
questions.explain: A level defined only as a leftover gives the model nothing to match, so ambiguous findings move to the levels that have examples. A invents a minimum count that the stem does not support. C blames wording when the missing piece is the low-level definition. D claims that named levels cannot work, which the well-anchored high level in the same prompt contradicts.
bullets: Defining each severity level with explicit criteria and concrete code examples for consistent classification
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A validator step labels each extraction discrepancy "error" (blocks the record) or "warning" (passes it with a note). In a trial, the same kind of discrepancy was labelled error in 26 of 60 runs and warning in the rest. Which definition of the two levels will classify most consistently?
opts: error: the discrepancy is important to the record. warning: the discrepancy is less important to the record. Decide using your overall view of the whole record.
error: any discrepancy in an amount field. warning: any discrepancy in every other field, whichever way the value differs.
error: value contradicts source, as with "Total 1,204.50" stored as 1204.05. warning: same meaning, as with "3 Mar 2026" stored as "2026-03-03".
error: the model is under 70% sure of the value. warning: the model is at least 70% sure of the value.
questions.explain: C defines both levels by what the discrepancy does and shows a real case for each. A restates the labels in other words. B decides by field, so a harmless format change in an amount would block the record while a wrong vendor id would only warn. D uses self-reported certainty, which says nothing about whether the value contradicts the source.
bullets: Defining each severity level with explicit criteria and concrete code examples for consistent classification
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: You rewrote the severity section with definitions and one code example per level, taken from 12 findings in last month's reviews. To check it, you rerun the reviewer on those 12 findings five times, and it labels them the same way every time. How should you evaluate whether the new section works?
opts: Accept the result, since identical labels over five runs show that the section classifies consistently.
Rerun the same 12 findings on another model, and keep the section if both models agree on every one.
Add the rest of last month's findings to the examples and rerun them, then compare the agreement.
Label a fresh set of findings not used as examples, then check the new levels against those labels.
questions.explain: The examples sit inside the prompt, so the 12 findings test memory and not classification. A fresh labelled set shows whether the criteria carry over to new code. A takes that memory as proof of consistency. B swaps in another model but keeps the same 12 findings. C feeds more findings into the examples, so no unseen test set is left.
bullets: Defining each severity level with explicit criteria and concrete code examples for consistent classification
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your CI pipeline asks Claude to summarise each failed test run for a chat channel in three labelled lines: Service, Likely cause, Owner team. The prompt describes the layout in a paragraph. In about 25% of runs the summary comes back as a bulleted list, a paragraph, or with the Owner line missing, and the channel bot drops any message it cannot parse. What is the most effective change?
opts: Add a few sample summaries in the exact layout, one per kind of failure.
Have the bot re-run the summary until one reply happens to match the layout.
Put the layout paragraph in capitals and repeat it again at the end of the prompt.
Ask Claude to review its own summary and fix the layout before it replies.
questions.explain: Samples show the layout instead of describing it, which is the most effective way to get consistent output when instructions alone vary. B spends extra calls and never changes why replies differ. C repeats an instruction that is already not enough. D asks the same model that varies to police its own output.
bullets: Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistent, usable output when instructions alone vary
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A code review bot must post findings in a four-field layout, and about 20% of findings used to break it. The team added three sample findings to the prompt, re-ran the three pull requests those samples were taken from, and every finding matched the layout. They want to ship. How should they judge whether the change fixed the inconsistency?
opts: Re-run the same three pull requests ten more times and check that each finding still matches.
Ask Claude whether each finding in the new output follows the required layout.
Run unseen recent pull requests and measure the share of findings that match.
Check that the sample findings are repeated word for word in the reviewer's output.
questions.explain: The three pull requests produced the samples, so matching on them shows little. Unseen pull requests show whether the layout holds in general, and a measured share can be compared with the old 20%. A repeats the same inputs. B uses the model's own opinion as the check. D tests copying, which is not what the team needs.
bullets: Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistent, usable output when instructions alone vary
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: You are adding sample findings to a CI review prompt that also contains a long block of review rules. Early tests show Claude sometimes treats a sample's wording as a rule to apply to the pull request itself. How should the samples be laid out in the prompt?
opts: Put them in the middle of the rules, so each sample sits next to the rule it illustrates.
Wrap them in example tags, separate from the rules, and make them relevant and varied.
Merge them into the rules text as sentences that begin with "for instance".
Put them last and label the whole prompt "examples only" so the rules are ignored.
questions.explain: Wrapping examples in their own tags lets Claude tell them from instructions, and relevant, varied examples avoid unintended patterns. A and C blur the boundary between rule and sample, which is how a sample gets read as a rule. D throws away the rules the reviewer still needs.
bullets: Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistent, usable output when instructions alone vary
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A CI reviewer reads the diff and the changed tests and must point out branches that no test exercises. It reliably flags a new function with no tests, but for one-line conditionals such as `if retries > limit: use_cache()` it reports an untested branch in about half of runs, with no pattern. Line coverage on those lines is already 100%, and the tests only ever run with retries below the limit. Which change is best?
opts: Examples of new functions with no tests, since those are the cases it already flags well.
Tell the reviewer to treat any line that holds a conditional as a possible untested branch.
Ask it to report its confidence for each finding and discard those below a fixed cut-off.
Add reasoned examples of covered lines that hide an untested branch and ones that do not.
questions.explain: The ambiguity is whether a covered line still hides an untested branch, and examples with reasons show how that call is made. A spends the examples on a case that already works. B flags every conditional and drowns the real gaps. C uses self-reported confidence, which is not evidence.
bullets: Examples show how ambiguous cases are handled (which tool, which coverage gap counts)
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A contract extractor must fill `signing_party`, and billing needs exactly one primary signer per contract. The full signature block is always in the input. In about 15% of contracts a company signs as buyer while a director also signs as guarantor, and the extractor returns one or the other with no consistency. The field description and schema were reviewed and are clear. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The signature block is cut off in long contracts, so the second signer is never seen.
The prompt shows no case with two signers, so each run picks one by chance.
The extractor needs a second pass that reads each document twice to find every signer.
The schema should allow a list, so that both signers can be recorded.
questions.explain: Nothing in the prompt shows how to settle the choice when two people sign, so it drifts between runs. Examples showing the decision and the reason fix that. A contradicts the stem, which says the full block is always present. C adds work while the missing guidance stays missing. D changes the data model although billing needs exactly one signer.
bullets: Examples show how ambiguous cases are handled (which tool, which coverage gap counts)
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A CI triage agent has two tools, `rerun_job` and `open_ticket`. For logs such as "timeout after fetching dependencies" it picks `rerun_job` in about 55% of cases and `open_ticket` in the rest, though the team's owners agree on the right tool for most of these. The tool descriptions were tuned last month and work for clear-cut failures. What is the best fix?
opts: A few ambiguous logs, each with the tool chosen and the reason it beat the other.
A keyword router in code that sends every log containing "timeout" to `rerun_job`.
Examples of clear-cut failures for each tool, so it sees many correct choices together.
A merged `handle_failure` tool that decides internally what to do with the log.
questions.explain: The missing piece is guidance on the borderline logs, and examples with reasons show how the choice is made. B turns one judgment into a text rule that misroutes real outages. C shows cases that already work. D hides the choice inside a tool and teaches nothing about it.
bullets: Examples show how ambiguous cases are handled (which tool, which coverage gap counts)
Write a few targeted examples for ambiguous cases that show why one action beat the alternatives
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: Your supplier-invoice extractor maps payment terms to a number of days. The prompt contains a table of eight phrasings, from "Net 30" to "Due on receipt", and it handles those well. A new supplier writes "payable within 45 days of receiving this invoice" and the extractor returns 30, the nearest row in the table. What would help most?
opts: Add the new supplier's phrasing as a ninth row in the table.
Add a similarity step that picks the closest table row and reports its score.
A few examples of varied wordings, each with the days and the reason.
Send every unfamiliar phrasing to a person before the invoice is accepted.
questions.explain: Examples that show how days follow from the wording let the model handle phrasings nobody listed. A fixes this one supplier and the next new wording fails again. B formalises the same wrong behaviour of snapping to a row. D adds manual work for a judgment the model can learn.
bullets: Examples let the model carry judgment over to new patterns instead of matching only listed cases
questions.principle: Let the model reason, and drive control flow from structured signals, not from parsing text or hard-coded sequences.

questions.q: The team added examples to a CI reviewer and known defect types are now caught consistently. Before rollout, an engineer wants evidence that the reviewer applies the same judgment to patterns the examples never showed. Which test gives that evidence?
opts: Re-run the pull requests that held the defects used in the examples and compare against last week.
Count how many of the example defect types appear in the reviewer's output.
Ask the reviewer to list other defect types it believes it could find.
Run it on real defects of a kind no example shows and count catches.
questions.explain: Only inputs outside the examples show whether judgment carries over rather than matching listed cases. A and B measure what the examples already cover. C relies on the model's claim about itself, not on results.
bullets: Examples let the model carry judgment over to new patterns instead of matching only listed cases
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: An extractor for purchase orders reached 97% accuracy on test documents after you added four examples, all taken from one big customer's template. In production, orders from other customers, whose totals sit at the top and whose line items are in a different order, are extracted correctly only 71% of the time. Which statement explains this?
opts: Few-shot examples help only with output format, not with the choice of which values to extract.
The four examples share one layout, so the model learned that template instead of the task.
The examples belong in the system prompt, where they apply to every document without exception.
Examples cost context, so the later part of each long order is no longer read.
questions.explain: When all examples look alike, the model picks up their shared layout as if it were part of the task, so other layouts fail. Varied examples fix that. A is untrue, since examples also teach what to extract. C changes where they sit, not what they show. D has no sign of truncation in the stem.
bullets: Examples let the model carry judgment over to new patterns instead of matching only listed cases
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Spot checks of a product-sheet extractor show that 9% of records carry a `warranty_months` value that appears nowhere in the source sheet; the typical value is 12. The field is already nullable and the prompt says to extract only what the sheet states. Which change most directly reduces these invented values?
opts: Examples of sheets without warranty text giving null, next to sheets that state one.
Examples drawn only from sheets that state a warranty, so it learns what a good record looks like.
A check that rejects any record whose warranty differs from the category's usual value.
A confidence score per field, with low-scoring values removed from the record.
questions.explain: Examples that show an absent field coming back as null teach the model that this is the correct answer, and sheets that state a value keep it extracting real ones. B shows only complete records, so absence is never demonstrated. C flags real unusual warranties and passes invented ones that match the usual value. D depends on self-reported confidence.
bullets: Examples reduce hallucination in extraction (informal measurements, varied document structures)
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A furniture-listing extractor fills `width_cm`, and the search page filters on that number. For phrases like "about two metres" it returns 200 correctly, but for "roughly shoebox-sized" it returns 33, and for "fits most hallways" it returns 90. Every such value is invented and lands items in the wrong search results. Telling the model "never estimate" cut the problem by only a few points. What is the best fix?
opts: Examples that convert each object comparison to a number using the object's typical size.
Run extraction twice and keep a width only when both runs return the same number.
Examples where measurable phrases give a number and object comparisons give null.
Make `width_cm` a free-text field so the original wording is kept as written.
questions.explain: The examples show where the line falls between a measurable phrase and an unquantified comparison, which the instruction alone could not teach. A demonstrates the invention it should stop. B can agree on the same invented number. D breaks the numeric filter that the search page depends on.
bullets: Examples reduce hallucination in extraction (informal measurements, varied document structures)
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A lease extractor returns records that all pass schema validation, yet a reviewer finds that 6% contain a `notice_period_days` that the lease text does not support: the lease states no period, or a different one. Running each lease twice and keeping only fields that agree removed little of this. Which approach should the team try next?
opts: Examples of complete leases in which every field, including the notice period, has a value.
Use a larger model tier for any lease that is longer than twenty pages of text.
Raise the number of runs per lease to five and take the majority value for each field.
Examples returning a value only with a supporting passage, else null.
questions.explain: Examples that return a value only when a passage supports it, and null otherwise, teach the model to stay empty when the text is silent. A shows only filled fields, so the model learns to always fill one. B and C add cost, while runs can agree on the same unsupported value.
bullets: Examples reduce hallucination in extraction (informal measurements, varied document structures)
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A CI bot must choose between blocking a merge and leaving a comment when a single integration test fails. In about 35% of ambiguous failures (one test, passed on the previous run) its choice changes between runs. You can write a small set of examples. Which design is best?
opts: A handful of past failures labelled block or comment, with no explanations.
A few borderline failures, each with the action chosen and why it beat the other.
One example per rule in the team's merge policy, written as a policy sentence each.
A single long example that walks through the decision process of the policy in prose.
questions.explain: Borderline cases with the reason for the choice show the trade-off the model must weigh. A gives answers without the reasoning, so the model copies surface features. C restates the policy and adds no borderline cases. D is one case in disguise and does not show the boundary.
bullets: Write a few targeted examples for ambiguous cases that show why one action beat the alternatives
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A CI reviewer's verdict on the same finding flips between runs about 12% of the time. Comparing 200 flipped findings shows three borderline patterns (a retry around a non-idempotent call, a broad exception catch that re-raises, a TODO that cites a ticket) behind 70% of the flips. The prompt has room for only a few examples. Where should they go?
opts: On those three patterns, each with the right verdict and the reason.
On the three most common finding types, with one clean example for each of them.
On ten findings the reviewer already gets right every time, to anchor the style.
On one example per review rule, so that every rule in the prompt is covered.
questions.explain: Examples should be spent where the model is actually uncertain, and the comparison of flips points at those patterns. B and C spend them on cases that already work. D spreads them thin over rules that mostly go right.
bullets: Write a few targeted examples for ambiguous cases that show why one action beat the alternatives
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A CI reviewer was given examples with reasons for ignoring hard-coded values. One example said: "Ignore this value, it is in the fixtures folder." Since then it has stopped reporting everything under `fixtures/`, including two real issues in code that builds a database URL there. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The reviewer took the folder named in the reason as the rule.
The reviewer memorised that single example file and compares each file with it.
Reasons in examples make the reviewer skip analysis, so they should be removed.
The example sits too close to the end of the prompt and has the largest weight.
questions.explain: A reason that points to a surface cue teaches the cue. A reason that names the property that decides, such as a placeholder value used only by tests, carries over to other files. B would not cover the whole folder. C is wrong because reasons are what make examples generalise. D invents a position effect that the stem gives no sign of.
bullets: Write a few targeted examples for ambiguous cases that show why one action beat the alternatives
Examples let the model carry judgment over to new patterns instead of matching only listed cases
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your CI comment bot files review findings by severity and accepts only the exact tokens high, medium or low. About 20% of findings arrive with other spellings such as Critical, sev-1 or HIGH!, so the bot drops them, and new spellings turn up every week. The prompt lists the allowed tokens in one sentence. What is the best change?
opts: Map every spelling the reviewer has produced so far to the three tokens, inside the bot.
Examples in which each finding uses a different spelling, so the model sees every variant.
Ask the reviewer to repeat the allowed tokens before each finding it writes.
Examples in the same layout where severity is always exactly high, medium or low.
questions.explain: Examples in the exact layout show the allowed tokens in use, which is what the one-sentence list did not achieve. A can never keep up with spellings that change weekly. B demonstrates the variation it should remove. C repeats the instruction that already fails.

Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistent, usable output when instructions alone vary
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Developers ignore the "suggested fix" line of a CI reviewer: in a sample of 100 findings, 61 say "consider refactoring this" or similar, and developers want a change they can apply without rewriting it. The other three fields look good, and the prompt says that fixes must be actionable. Which change should be tried first?
opts: Require every suggested fix to be at least 30 words long in the output.
Add examples whose fix field gives a concrete change, like the new line.
Add examples whose fix field names the idea, such as "use a context manager".
Remove the fix field and let developers decide how to resolve each issue.
questions.explain: Examples convey the level of detail wanted more clearly than a description, so showing concrete fixes in the layout closes the gap. A rewards length and gives vague text more words. C shows fixes at the same vague level the team wants to leave. D drops a field the team wants.
bullets: Use examples that show the exact review output layout: location, issue, severity, suggested fix
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A CI reviewer prompt asks for "file, finding, priority, remedy", while the three examples in it are written as "Location / Issue / Severity / Fix". Output labels now vary between runs: some use the instruction's names, some the examples' names, some a mix, and the comment bot expects one set. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Use one set of field names in both the instructions and every example.
Add a parsing step that maps each variant of the names to the expected ones.
Remove the examples so only the instruction's wording is left.
Add more examples until the examples' naming outweighs the instruction.

C loses the examples that make the layout consistent. D piles on more examples to fight a conflict that has a one-line fix.

questions.q: After you added examples to a CI reviewer, it flags nearly every JavaScript pull request for unsafe input handling and almost none in Python. The examples hold six genuine issues, all in JavaScript, and six acceptable cases, all in Python; each has a reason naming the unsafe or safe property. The model is simply stronger at finding input-handling problems in JavaScript.
Language differs along with the verdict, so the reviewer uses it as the cue.
The reasons in the examples make the reviewer skip analysis of the new code.

questions.q: After the team added acceptable-versus-problem examples, a CI reviewer's false positives for logging calls fell from 22 a week to 6. questions.q: You are writing one example for a CI reviewer that must separate a loop of database calls in a one-off migration script (acceptable) from the same loop on a web request path (a real issue). What should the example contain so the reviewer applies the idea to other scripts?

The code, the verdict, and a sentence naming the property, such as runs only once.
The code and the verdict, followed by the full text of the team's performance guideline.
The verdict and the file path only, without the code that is being judged.
questions.explain: The reason in terms of the deciding property transfers to scripts the examples never showed. A teaches a path rule. C buries the point in a long document. D leaves out the code the model has to read.

questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: An invoice extractor has three examples, all taken from the largest customers' invoices. A breakdown of errors by layout shows tables with the total in a column at 3%, running text at 4%, and invoices that give the total in a footnote at 31%. questions.q: A research assistant pulls the names and roles of executives from press releases (names in a quote block), annual reports (a table) and blog posts (names woven into prose). With a handful of slots for examples, which choice should work best?

questions.q: A required `invoice_number` comes back empty for 14% of invoices. Examples that keep the Invoice # label but vary how the number itself is formatted.

questions.q: A required `order_date` comes back empty on 11% of orders. Every affected order labels it in German or French (Bestelldatum, Date de commande), while English-labelled orders extract well. Translate every document into English before extraction runs.
Make `order_date` optional so those orders stop failing validation.
questions.explain: The failing orders differ in the label language, so examples in those languages show the model where the date sits. B varies notation, which is not what differs. C adds a lossy step for a problem the examples can handle. D hides the gap while the dates stay missing.
bullets: Use examples of varied formats to fix empty or null extraction of required fields
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Delivery notes arrive as text exported from a two-column PDF, where each label sits on one line and its value on the next. `delivery_date` is empty on 17% of them, though the dates are plainly present. The examples show "Date: 12 May" on a single line, and a prompt line saying that values may be on the next line was added last week and changed little. What is the best fix?
opts: Re-export the PDFs with a different tool so that labels and values share a line.
Add examples of the single-line layout with many more date notations.
Add examples in the flattened two-line layout, with the date on the value line.
Move the hint to the end of the prompt and repeat it in capitals.
questions.explain: Examples in the same layout as the failing inputs show where the value sits. A rebuilds the input side, which may not be possible for every sender. B varies notation, not layout. D repeats a hint that has already been tried.
bullets: Use examples of varied formats to fix empty or null extraction of required fields
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A receipt pipeline asks Claude to "respond with only a JSON object" and parses the reply with `json.loads`. Across 1,200 receipts, 31 replies failed to parse: some begin with "Here is the extracted data:" and others end with a note about an unreadable line. Which change most reliably removes these failures?
opts: Cut each reply down to the text between its first and last curly brace, and parse that part.
Define a strict tool whose `input_schema` is the receipt record, and read its input.
Repeat the instruction at the end of the prompt, and add two examples that show a bare JSON reply.
Re-send the request up to three times when a reply fails to parse, and keep the first one that parses.
questions.explain: A tool's input follows its schema, so the record arrives as structured data with no prose around it and nothing to parse. A hides the symptom, and it still breaks on a stray brace inside a note. C asks for compliance and cannot guarantee it. D pays for extra requests and still ends with a reply that happens to parse.
bullets: Tool use with JSON schemas is the most reliable route to schema-compliant output, with no JSON syntax errors

questions.q: An extraction prompt for purchase orders shows a 40-line example record and says every record must include `currency`. Across 5,000 documents, 90 records (1.8%) came back with no `currency` key, and the loader throws on each of them. The team wants the key present in every record, not just in most. Which configuration achieves that?
opts: Put the `currency` rule in capital letters at the very start of the system prompt, before everything else.
Send a second request for the 90 records that asks only for the missing key, then merge the answers.
Add a second example that shows `currency` beside the total, and also lower the temperature to zero.
Mark `currency` as required in a strict extraction tool's `input_schema`, and read the input.
questions.explain: Required fields in a strict tool schema are part of what the output is constrained to, so a record without the key cannot be returned. A and C make the omission less likely and cannot promise it. B repairs records after the loader has already failed and doubles the work on every miss.
bullets: Tool use with JSON schemas is the most reliable route to schema-compliant output, with no JSON syntax errors
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A CI job asks Claude for a review and sets the pull request's check status from the last line of the reply, which should read `VERDICT: PASS` or `VERDICT: FAIL`. In 2% of 2,000 runs the last line says things like "Verdict - pass" or "Overall: looks fine", and the status step errors. Which design is most reliable?
opts: Put the verdict and the comment in two fields of one strict tool; set the status from the verdict.
Make the status step case-insensitive and accept `pass`, `passed`, `ok` and `looks fine` as success.
Add a second request that reads the review text and answers PASS or FAIL for the status step to use.
Put three example last lines in the prompt, and tell the model to copy the format exactly as shown.
questions.explain: A schema with an enum for the verdict and a string for the comment makes both machine-readable and human-readable output arrive in fixed places. B chases wordings one at a time and fails on the next new phrase. C adds a model call to interpret text that did not need to be text. D is a request for compliance, which the 2% shows is not enough.
bullets: Tool use with JSON schemas is the most reliable route to schema-compliant output, with no JSON syntax errors
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A claims service passes three extraction tools, `extract_claim_form`, `extract_medical_bill` and `extract_police_report`, with `tool_choice` set to `any`. Each description is one sentence such as "Extracts data from the document." Every request now ends in a tool call, but a labelled sample of 800 shows 9% of medical bills processed by `extract_claim_form`, with plausible-looking fields. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: `any` falls back to the first tool in the list when a document could fit more than one schema.
These documents needed a forced tool instead, so `any` was the wrong mode for them.
Selection is left to the model, and descriptions that read alike give it little to go on.
Strict checking is off, so the model is free to send bill data to the wrong tool.
questions.explain: `any` guarantees that some tool is called and nothing about which one, so selection quality rests on the tool descriptions. A describes a fallback that does not exist. B would send every document through one schema, which is worse for mixed uploads. D confuses schema conformance with choosing the right tool: a bill fitted into the wrong schema can still be valid.
bullets: tool_choice auto may return text, any must call some tool, and a forced selection must call one named tool
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A CI step has two tools, `list_changed_files` and `report_review`, and uses `tool_choice: any` on a model that supports it. The system prompt says: "Before calling a tool, write a short paragraph explaining your reasoning; it will be posted on the pull request." Across 400 runs no paragraph was ever posted, although the tool calls and their inputs look correct. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The instruction comes after the tool descriptions, so the model treats it as optional.
The API starts the reply with a tool call under `any`, so no text can come before it.
A reply that contains a `tool_use` block has its text blocks discarded before it is returned.
Text is only allowed after the last tool of a run, and `list_changed_files` is called first.
questions.explain: With `any` or a forced tool the response begins with the tool call, so a paragraph written "before" it cannot exist; the reasoning has to travel in a field of the schema, or the mode has to be `auto`. A blames prompt order for a limit that sits in the API. C is false, since text and tool blocks can share a response under `auto`. D invents a rule about the last tool.
bullets: tool_choice auto may return text, any must call some tool, and a forced selection must call one named tool
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A shared extraction service exposes `extract_po` and `extract_invoice` to several inboxes. The purchase-order inbox receives only purchase orders, yet 3% of its documents go to `extract_invoice` because they mention payment terms. The other inboxes need both tools to stay available. On a model that supports forced tool use, what is the best configuration for the purchase-order inbox?
opts: Force `extract_po` with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_po"}` for that inbox.
Use `tool_choice: any` for that inbox, so the model has to call a tool and will pick the closest schema.
Keep `auto` and add a line to the system prompt saying that the inbox holds purchase orders.
Remove `extract_invoice` from the shared tool list so that every inbox uses `extract_po`.
questions.explain: When the type is known, naming the tool leaves the model nothing to choose. B still leaves the choice with the model, which is where the 3% comes from. C is a hint under `auto`, with no guarantee. D breaks the inboxes that do receive invoices.
bullets: tool_choice auto may return text, any must call some tool, and a forced selection must call one named tool
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: An invoice tool returns `vendor`, `total` and an array of `line_items`, and every response validates against its schema. A finance review of 600 invoices found 21 where the line items add up to a different amount than `total`, usually by a transposed digit. The team asks for a stricter schema. What is the most effective step?
opts: Add `minimum` and `maximum` bounds to `total` so that implausible totals are rejected.
Switch to a larger model, whose totals are less likely to be transposed.
Add a sentence to the tool description asking the model to check that the figures sum.
Compare the line-item sum with `total` in code, and send mismatches for review.
questions.explain: A schema checks the shape of a response, and a total that disagrees with its lines is still the right shape, so the relationship has to be checked in code. A bounds a single value and would pass a wrong total inside the range. B lowers the rate without checking anything. C asks the model to police itself.
bullets: Strict schemas remove syntax errors but not semantic errors such as line items that do not sum or values in the wrong field
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A purchase-order schema has two required string fields, `address_a` ("the first address") and `address_b` ("the second address"). Output validates every time, but a review of 500 multi-address orders found billing and shipping details swapped in 11%, because suppliers print them in different orders. Which change best addresses the cause?
opts: Switch strict checking on, so that each value stays in the field that the schema defines for it.
Reject any order in which the two addresses are identical, and send it back for a manual check.
Rename them `billing_address` and `shipping_address`, and describe how documents label each.
Add a `confidence` number to each address, and send low-confidence orders to a human for review.
questions.explain: The field names say nothing about meaning, so the model has no basis for assigning an address to either; names and descriptions that mirror the document labels give it one. A guarantees types, and a swapped address is still a string. B catches a case that is not the one described. D relies on the model's own confidence to find its mistakes.
bullets: Strict schemas remove syntax errors but not semantic errors such as line items that do not sum or values in the wrong field
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A team moved its contract extraction to a tool with a JSON schema and told management: "Schema validation passes on 100% of 4,000 documents, so extraction accuracy is now 100%." You are asked to review the claim. What is the most accurate response?
opts: Correct: a response that validates has every field filled from the right part of the document.
Validity covers form only; accuracy needs field-level comparison with labelled documents.
Partly right: add a check that the line items sum to the total, and call a pass accuracy.
Not credible: a model cannot reach 100% validity without a repair step after the response.
questions.explain: A schema constrains the form of the output and says nothing about whether a value is right, so accuracy must be measured against known answers. A treats form as truth. C catches one kind of error, and wrong values that still add up pass it. D doubts a result that tool schemas are designed to deliver.
bullets: Strict schemas remove syntax errors but not semantic errors such as line items that do not sum or values in the wrong field
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A vendor-invoice schema is being finalised. From 500 sampled documents, field presence is: `vendor_name` 100%, `total_amount` 100%, `due_date` 88%, `tax_id` 63% and `po_number` 41%. Downstream, only the vendor and the total are needed to post an invoice. Which design is best?
opts: Require `vendor_name` and `total_amount`, and make the other three optional or nullable.
Require all five, and tell the model to enter a placeholder when a value is missing.
Require the three fields present in more than half the documents, and make the other two optional.
Make every field optional, since the model will fill in whatever it finds.
questions.explain: A field belongs in `required` only if every document of this type has it; otherwise the schema pushes the model to supply something. B turns missing values into fake ones. C requires `due_date`, which is absent in 12% of documents, and `tax_id`, absent in 37%. D lets the two fields that posting depends on go missing.

questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A shipping-document schema defines `carrier` as an enum of the five carriers the company uses. After onboarding regional partners, 14% of documents name a carrier that is not listed, and the model assigns the nearest listed one, which corrupts the cost report. Which schema change fixes this and keeps reports groupable?
opts: Replace the enum with a free-text string so that any carrier name can be recorded.
Make `carrier` optional, so that unlisted carriers are left out of the record.
Add an `other` value to the enum and a `carrier_detail` string for the name.
Add the twenty partner carriers to the enum now, and repeat that whenever a partner joins.
questions.explain: `other` with a detail string keeps the known carriers as clean groups and records the rest without forcing a wrong match. A gives up grouping, since spelling variants become separate values. B drops the carrier for exactly the documents that are new. D can never be complete and lets errors reappear with each new partner.
bullets: Schema design: required versus optional fields, and enums with an other value plus a detail string
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A teammate reviewing your CI schema proposes adding an `other` value with a detail string to every enum. Two of them are `failure_type` (test, build, lint, timeout; new kinds appear every quarter) and `severity` (low, medium, high, critical; a policy scale that code uses to page the on-call engineer). How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Accept it for both, since an enum without an escape value fails on any input it does not list.
Reject it for both, since a detail string lets the model put anything into the field.
Accept it for `severity` only, since paging depends on it and a wrong value there costs more.
Accept it for `failure_type` only; `severity` is a closed scale that code maps to pages.
questions.explain: The pattern is for categories that will grow. A closed scale defined by policy has a fixed meaning in code, and an `other` there would be a value nothing can route. A applies the pattern where it adds a hole. B discards its benefit for the open field. C reverses the logic and makes the paging field the one that can escape its scale.
bullets: Schema design: required versus optional fields, and enums with an other value plus a detail string
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: An extraction service defines `record_invoice` and reads the result with `response.content[0].input`. In 400 requests, 140 raise an AttributeError, and the failing responses begin with a sentence such as "I'll extract the fields from this invoice." What is the best fix?
opts: Add "do not write any text before calling the tool" to the system prompt.
Look through the content blocks for the one of type `tool_use` and read its input.
Parse the first text block with `json.loads`, since the model repeats the fields in it.
Retry each failing request until the first block comes back as a tool call.
questions.explain: A response can hold a text block as well as the tool call, so the code should find the block by its type instead of by position. A asks for compliance on a point the code can handle on its own. C parses text that was never meant to hold the record. D spends requests to fit a response to a fragile assumption.

questions.q: An extraction tool is defined with `input_schema: {"type": "object"}` and a description that lists the wanted fields in prose. Across 1,000 documents the keys vary: `invoice_no`, `invoiceNumber` and `invoice_number` all appear, and the loader fails on 17% of the records. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The schema leaves the property names open, so nothing fixes the keys the model uses.
`tool_choice` is `auto`, so on some replies the model writes the record as text, with its own key names.
The field list belongs in the system prompt, because tool descriptions are read less closely.
Strict mode is off, and switching it on would map every spelling to the key the loader expects.

B is not what the stem shows, and under `auto` a text reply would not carry these keys either. C moves the list to another place where it is still prose. questions.q: Supplier contracts hold between 0 and 60 line items, each with `sku`, `quantity` and `unit_price`. You are defining the strict extraction tool, and the application will read the items from the `tool_use` response. Which design is best?

A single `line_items_json` string field, which the application parses.
A separate `add_line_item` tool, called once per line until the contract ends.
A `line_items` array whose items are objects with the three fields marked required.

B puts JSON inside a string, which brings back the syntax errors that the schema was there to remove. C needs a loop of calls that may stop early, with no record of what is missing.

About 7% of uploads are cover sheets or blank scans, and each is run through one of the extraction tools, producing records with invented-looking values. A line in the prompt tells the model to reply "not a document" for these, but no such reply ever appears. Which change fixes this?

Add a `flag_unprocessable` tool with a reason field, and keep `any`.
Repeat the "not a document" rule in bold in the system prompt, with two examples.

questions.q: Mixed claim uploads (accident forms, repair estimates, witness statements) arrive with no type label. On a labelled sample of 2,000, `tool_choice: any` (on a model that supports it) over three extraction tools picks the matching tool 99% of the time. A teammate proposes a separate classification request that picks the type first and then forces the matching tool "for certainty"; on the same sample the classifier is right 98.7% of the time. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Keep `any`: it already returns a structured result from the right tool, with no extra step.
Adopt it, since forcing a named tool is more reliable than letting the model choose between tools.
Adopt it, since `any` cannot be used when the documents carry no type label.
Keep `any`, but only if the model also reports a confidence score for the tool it chose.

The classifier would make the same kind of choice with slightly lower accuracy, and then add a call. B forgets that the forced tool is only as right as the classifier that names it. C reverses the purpose of `any`. D leans on self-reported confidence.

questions.q: A pipeline offers three extraction tools with `tool_choice: any`, so every request ends in a tool call. But in 1.5% of calls a numeric field such as `page_count` arrives as the string "12", and the loader throws. Which addition fixes this while keeping `any`?
opts: A sentence in the system prompt saying numeric fields must be numbers.
`strict: true` on the tool definitions.
A forced tool selection, which also fixes the types of that tool's fields.
A retry that re-sends the request whenever the loader throws.

questions.q: On a model that supports forced tool use, a claims pipeline forces `extract_claim_header` on its first request, then calls again with `auto` and two enrichment tools. The enrichment tools are being called with claim IDs that appear nowhere in the document, in nearly every run. The second request holds the original document and the enrichment tools. Which change fixes this?

Add a prompt rule saying that claim IDs must come from the document text.
Add the assistant's `tool_use` turn and a matching `tool_result` turn before the next request.
Use `any` on the second request, which carries over the arguments of the earlier tool call.

A would repeat the first step and still not give the model the result. B points the model at a document that holds no such ID. D describes a carry-over that does not exist.

Reject it: force the first request only, then use `auto` so lookups are optional.

A would stop the summary from ever being written. B forces a call in the second step even for leases that need no lookup. C has the same effect, since `any` also requires a tool call on each request.

questions.q: On a model that supports forced tool use, an ingestion service forces `extract_metadata` as its first call so that `title`, `author` and `date` exist before enrichment runs. In 5% of documents, scanned pages with no readable text, the metadata comes back with a plausible title and an author name that appear nowhere in the document. Which change best fixes this while keeping the extraction first?
opts: Make the three fields nullable, and describe null as nothing found in the document.
Switch to `auto`, so the model can reply that the page is unreadable instead of calling the tool.
Add "if the page is empty, say so before calling the tool" to the system prompt.
Skip the forced call for scanned pages, which an OCR step detects before the request.
questions.explain: A forced call cannot decline, so a schema that demands values makes the model supply some; allowing null lets it report absence and keeps the order of steps. B gives up the guarantee that extraction comes first. C asks for text before the tool call, which a forced call does not allow. D adds a detector for a case that the schema could simply express.

questions.q: A contract schema marks `termination_notice_days` as a required integer. In an audit of 300 contracts, 45 have no notice clause, yet all 45 records say 30 days, and a customer acted on one of them. Which change best prevents this?
opts: Add a few-shot example of a contract with no clause, where the correct value is shown as 0.
Allow null for the field, and describe null as the contract having no notice clause.
Lower the temperature, so that the model stops guessing a typical value for the field.
Send a second request that asks the model whether each extracted value appears in the contract.
questions.explain: A required field that the source may lack pushes the model to supply something, and 30 is simply a likely number. A nullable field gives it an honest answer. A teaches a sentinel that is also a real value, and 0 days is a legal notice period. C makes the guess more consistent, not more truthful. D adds a call that the schema change makes unnecessary.

questions.q: Receipts feeding a spending dashboard use `tip` as a required number, and the prompt says "use 0 when no tip appears". The dashboard shows average taxi tips of 0.4%. Spot checks show that many of those receipts have no tip line at all, because tips were paid in cash and are unknown, while others show a printed tip of 0. How should the design change?
opts: Keep the schema and add the receipts' tip line to the prompt as a separate note.
Make `tip` optional, and tell the model to leave it out whenever the value is zero.
Make `tip` nullable: null for no tip information, 0 for a printed zero.
Replace `tip` with a string field, so the model can write "none" or "unknown".
questions.explain: Two different facts, no information and a tip of zero, are being stored as the same number. A nullable field keeps them apart. A changes the prompt and keeps the collision. B drops real zeros and still cannot say "unknown". D loses the numeric type and brings back free-text variants.
bullets: Making fields optional or nullable when the source may lack the information, so the model does not invent values
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A review tool's schema requires `suggested_fix` (a string) for every finding, and developers apply suggested fixes automatically. In a month, 4% of the fixes for findings the model could not resolve were plausible but wrong patches, and two reached main. The team wants a fix only when one can be drawn from the code. Which design is best?
opts: Add a `fix_confidence` number, and apply only fixes above 0.9.
Add "only suggest a fix when you are sure" to the field description, and keep the field required.
Have a second model call review each suggested fix before it is applied.
Make `suggested_fix` nullable, with null for no fix, and apply only non-null fixes.

A relies on the model's own confidence. B asks the model to be careful and still requires a value. C adds a reviewer for a problem that the schema creates.

questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: An accounts-payable schema has `payment_status` with values `paid`, `unpaid` and `partial`. Some scanned invoices carry both a PAID stamp and a printed "Balance due: 410.00", and reviewers found the model splitting these between `paid` and `unpaid` almost at random, so 9% of 800 reviewed were misfiled. The three statuses cover every real case; the problem is evidence that conflicts. What is the best schema change?
opts: Add an `unclear` value, and route those records to a person.
Add an `other` value with a detail string, so the model can describe the conflict.
Allow null for the field, so that conflicting evidence can be reported as null.
Add a `confidence` field, and accept `paid` only when confidence is high.
questions.explain: An explicit value for ambiguity lets the model say so instead of guessing, and the record can be reviewed. B is for categories that are missing from the list, and the stem rules that out. C uses null, which means the information is absent, for a case where it is present and contradictory. D uses self-reported confidence to decide which guesses to trust.
bullets: Adding enum values such as unclear for ambiguous cases, and other plus a detail field for extensible categories
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A support-ticket schema has `product_area` as an enum that includes `other`, with a `product_area_detail` string. A quarter later, 19% of 6,000 tickets are `other`. In a sample of 300 of them, 40% of the details say "single sign-on", 25% say "data export" and the rest are scattered. How should you evaluate the schema and what should change?
opts: Leave it as it is: `other` with a detail is doing what it was designed to do.
Add enum values for the two recurring details, and keep `other` plus a detail for the rest.
Remove `other` and require the nearest listed area, so that the report totals stay complete.
Replace the enum with the detail strings, and group them with a clustering job each quarter.
questions.explain: The detail strings show that two categories have become common enough to deserve their own value, while the scattered tail still needs `other`. A ignores what the data shows. C hides new areas inside wrong ones. D throws away the stable categories for the 81% that fit them.
bullets: Adding enum values such as unclear for ambiguous cases, and other plus a detail field for extensible categories
Schema design: required versus optional fields, and enums with an other value plus a detail string
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: After a team added `unclear` to a failure-category enum, 41% of CI failures are labelled `unclear`; the labelled mistakes it was meant to cut had been 6%. The field description reads "use unclear if you are not fully certain". Logs for most of the `unclear` failures plainly show a timeout. What is the best fix?
opts: Remove `unclear` from the enum, which restores the earlier labelling of failures.
Cap `unclear` at 10% of failures per run, using an instruction in the prompt.
Define `unclear` as missing evidence, or evidence that points to several categories.
Let the model write the category as free text, then group the results in a later step.
questions.explain: The value exists but the description turns it into an escape from any doubt. Defining it by the state of the evidence restores its purpose. A returns to the 6% of confident wrong answers. B limits the count and does not say which failures qualify. D gives up the fixed categories.
bullets: Adding enum values such as unclear for ambiguous cases, and other plus a detail field for extensible categories
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: An invoice tool defines `total` as a number in a strict schema. Output always validates, but a reconciliation of 700 supplier invoices found 38 totals about a thousand times too small. The invoices come from many countries and print amounts as "1.234,50 €", "1,234.50" or "1 234,50", and the country is not reliably known. The prompt contains no formatting rules. What is the best fix?
opts: Change `total` to a string field, and convert the text to a number in the application code.
Add a `minimum` to `total` in the schema, so that implausibly small totals are rejected there.
Send each total that looks too small to a second request that checks it against the page.
Say in the prompt how separators work in each supplier format, and ask for a plain number.
questions.explain: The schema guarantees a number; it cannot know that the comma is a decimal point in the source. Rules in the prompt tell the model how to read each convention. A moves the same problem into code, where the string is just as ambiguous, because the locale is not known. B uses a numeric bound, which strict schemas do not support, and a bound would not tell the model how to read the amount. C patches the symptom and relies on guessing which totals look small.
bullets: Putting format normalization rules in the prompt alongside strict output schemas
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A review bot posts inline comments using the `file` field of a strict tool schema (a string). Comments fail to attach for 22% of findings: the field holds `./src/app.py`, `/repo/src/app.py` or `src/app.py` for the same file, and only the last form matches the diff. The checkout root varies per job in ways the bot cannot know in advance. What is the best fix?
opts: Tell the model to return repository-relative paths with no leading `./` or `/`.
Set `strict: true` on the tool so that the string follows the path format the diff uses.
Strip a fixed `/repo` prefix in the bot before it posts each comment.
Add a second pass that asks the model to check each path against the diff.
questions.explain: The schema only requires a string, so the convention has to be stated: one form, written where the model reads it. B misreads strict mode, which enforces the schema's types and nothing about path style. C handles only the checkout roots it was written for, and the others still fail. D adds a call for a rule that can be given up front.
bullets: Putting format normalization rules in the prompt alongside strict output schemas
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Invoices from UK, US and German suppliers print slash dates such as `03/04/2025`. The extraction tool returns `invoice_date` as a string, and the prompt says "convert dates to ISO 8601". Output is always valid, but 14% of dates in a sample of 500 have day and month reversed. Each request already includes the supplier's country code as metadata. What is the best change?
opts: Add `format: date` to the field, so that only dates the schema accepts are produced.
Compare each date with the upload date in code, and swap day and month when the date is in the future.
Tell the model which order each supplier country uses for slash dates, and to write ISO 8601.
Add a `date_order` enum that the model fills in per document, and apply it in code.
questions.explain: The date is ambiguous in the text itself, so the rule has to say how to resolve it, using evidence the request already carries. A checks that a date is well formed, and `04/03/2025` is well formed either way. B fixes only dates that land in the future. D asks the model to guess the order, which is the step that fails.
bullets: Putting format normalization rules in the prompt alongside strict output schemas
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your CI reviewer returns a JSON list of 10 to 25 findings per pull request. A validator checks each finding and, in about 6% of runs, rejects one or two, for example because the cited line lies outside the diff. The retry appends the line "Your previous output was invalid. Try again." to a conversation that already holds the diff and the earlier output, and only 30% of retries pass. What should the retry message contain instead?
opts: A reminder of the full schema, listing every field name, type and allowed value once more for the model.
The same line as before, but sent up to five times, because every attempt starts from a fresh sample.
The failing finding and the rule it broke, such as finding 7 citing line 412 when the diff ends at 188.
A request to explain why the output was invalid, followed by a corrected list of all of the findings.
questions.explain: The model can only repair what it is told about, and the validator knows which finding failed and why. A repeats a schema that the output already satisfied, since the failure is about a value. B sends no new information, so more attempts mostly repeat the same miss. D asks the model to work out the failure for itself, without the validator's findings.
bullets: Retry with error feedback: append the specific validation errors to the prompt so the model can correct itself
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A lease-extraction pipeline runs seven code checks on each output: dates in order, rent positive, deposit within three months of rent, and so on. The validator returns a single message, the first check that fails, and the pipeline appends it to the correction request, with a limit of three attempts. Leases can break up to six checks at once. 45% of such leases still fail after the third attempt, and the logs show a different check failing each time. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Run all seven checks, then append every failure to the same correction request.
Raise the limit to six attempts, so that every failing check gets a correction round of its own.
Order the checks by how often they fail, so that the likeliest error is corrected first.
Send each failing check as a separate request, then merge the corrected fields afterwards.
questions.explain: With every error in one request the model can fix all of them in a single pass. B costs up to six calls on the whole document and still corrects one problem per call. C changes the order but leaves one error per round. D splits the work across calls, so corrected fields can contradict each other, for example two dates.
bullets: Retry with error feedback: append the specific validation errors to the prompt so the model can correct itself
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your pipeline extracts names, dates and test results from lab reports. A code check flags results whose unit does not match the test type, in about 5% of reports. To correct them, the team asks the model "What did you get wrong?" and feeds its answer back with the report. For 4 in 10 corrected reports the answer names a different field from the one the check flagged, and the unit stays wrong. Which design is best?
opts: Ask the model to rate its confidence in each field, and retry only the fields it rates below 0.8 on the scale.
Give the explanation step to a larger model, because the current one is placing the mistake in the wrong field.
Ask for two separate explanations of the error, and keep the one that both of them point to as the cause.
Feed back the check's own result: the flagged field, the unit found and the units that are allowed.
questions.explain: The code already knows what failed, so its result is a more reliable correction signal than the model's account of its own mistake. A uses self-reported confidence, which is not evidence. B assumes a bigger model would be a better witness, which it need not be. C compares two self-explanations, and agreement between them is still the model's opinion.
bullets: Retry with error feedback: append the specific validation errors to the prompt so the model can correct itself
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: An insurer's pipeline extracts claim forms and requires policy_number. Format slips, such as a missing prefix, are fixed by one retry in 95% of cases. For 9% of forms the field stays wrong, and the logs show a different 10-digit number in each retried output. Those forms say only "see policy schedule", and the pipeline sends the model nothing but the claim form. What is the most likely reason retries cannot fix these forms?
opts: The correction messages are long, so the model overlooks the field in the retried prompt.
The number is nowhere in what the model receives, so each attempt can only guess a value.
Three attempts is too few for such a field, so the limit should be raised to ten attempts.
The model has not seen enough forms to learn how this insurer lays out its numbers.
questions.explain: A retry helps when the model has the information and mis-shapes it, which is why format slips are fixed. Here the value lives in a file the model never sees, and the changing numbers show guessing. A has no support in the logs, which show the field changing every time. C adds guesses to the same loop. D treats a missing input as a layout problem.
bullets: The limits of retry: it cannot help when the needed information is absent from the source, unlike format or structural errors
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A mortgage-document pipeline retries failed extractions with the specific errors appended. Across 40,000 packets the success rates are: first pass 88%, after one retry 96.5%, after two 97.2%, after three 97.3%. The packets still failing show the same error on every attempt, and each retry is a full call on a 60-page document. A manager asks whether to raise the limit from three to eight to reach the remaining 2.7%. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Lower the cap to one or two retries and send what remains to review, as later attempts add very little.
Raise it to eight, since the cost of a few extra calls is likely lower than the cost of a manual review.
Keep three, but run the last retry on a larger model so that it can resolve the hardest packets.
Remove retries and send all of the 12% of first-pass failures to review, which keeps the process predictable.
questions.explain: Most of the benefit comes from the first retry, and failures that repeat the same error across attempts are not the kind a retry repairs, so extra rounds add cost for little gain. B assumes more attempts will change those results. C expects a larger model to supply what is not in the input. D gives up the 8.5 points the first retry recovers.
bullets: The limits of retry: it cannot help when the needed information is absent from the source, unlike format or structural errors
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: The team rewrote the criteria for `optional-chaining-suggestion`. In the next two weeks its dismissal rate fell from 85% to 20%, and the number of findings raised with that pattern fell by 90%. A manager calls the rewrite a success. How should you evaluate the result?
opts: Accept it: the dismissal rate fell from 85% to 20%, which was the aim of the rewrite.
Roll back the rewrite, because a 90% fall in volume proves that the new criteria are broken.
Check a sample of code from before the rewrite, to see whether real issues are no longer raised.
Compare the dismissal rates of the other patterns, to see whether they moved along with this one.
questions.explain: A falling dismissal rate is only good if the findings that disappeared were the false ones, and only a sample of the code can show that. A reads the rate alone. B overreacts, since removing false positives would cut volume as well. D checks other patterns, which cannot show what this rewrite stopped raising.
bullets: Feedback loop design: a detected_pattern field shows which code constructs trigger findings, so dismissals can be analysed
Adding detected_pattern to structured findings to study false-positive patterns when developers dismiss them
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: About 38 in every 100 findings from your CI reviewer are dismissed by developers. Each finding carries file, line, severity, category (bug, security or style) and message. Dismissal rates look alike in every category and at every severity, and the team has no way to see what sort of code produces the unwanted ones. One review rule can fire on very different code. Which addition lets them find out most directly?
opts: A confidence score between 0 and 1 on every finding, so that low-scoring ones can be examined first.
A reviewer note on every dismissal, so that each developer explains in a line why it was dismissed.
A detected_pattern field naming the code construct that triggered each finding.
A rule_id field naming the review rule that fired, so that dismissals can be counted per rule.
questions.explain: Recording the construct on each finding lets dismissals be grouped by what triggered them. A is the model's own rating, and says nothing about constructs. B produces free text after the fact, one note at a time, with no common grouping. D counts per rule, but one rule fires on very different code, so the constructs stay hidden.
bullets: Feedback loop design: a detected_pattern field shows which code constructs trigger findings, so dismissals can be analysed
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Your CI reviewer emits detected_pattern from a fixed list of 25 names plus 'other' with a detail field. After six weeks, 34% of the 6,000 findings are labelled 'other', so the dismissal analysis says little about a third of the findings. What is the most effective next step?
opts: Remove 'other', so that every finding has to pick a listed pattern and the labels stay consistent.
Count the detail text under 'other', and add the most frequent constructs to the list.
Leave the list as it is, since a large 'other' group shows that the reviewer raises unusual code.
Replace the list with free-text labels, so that no finding is ever forced into 'other'.
questions.explain: The detail values show which constructs the list is missing, so promoting the frequent ones makes the next analysis cover them. A forces findings into the wrong patterns and corrupts the counts. C accepts a third of the data as unanalysable. D brings back labels that vary from finding to finding.
bullets: Feedback loop design: a detected_pattern field shows which code constructs trigger findings, so dismissals can be analysed
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A team moves its purchase-order extractor to a strict tool schema. JSON parse failures fall from 3% to zero, so an engineer proposes deleting the validation and retry layer. That layer also checks that line totals add up to the order total and that quantity and unit price are not swapped. A sample of 500 orders contains 14 whose total does not add up. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Keep the semantic checks and retries: a schema removes syntax failures, not wrong values.
Delete the layer, since zero parse failures show that the extracted values are now correct.
Delete the layer, and audit a sample of 50 orders by hand each night to find bad totals.
Replace it with a stricter schema that requires each order's total to equal the sum of its lines.
questions.explain: The schema guarantees valid structure and types, but a total that does not add up is a valid number in the wrong place. B treats a syntax result as proof of correctness. C finds bad totals a day late and by hand, though a check can find them on every order. D asks the schema to express arithmetic across fields, which it cannot.
bullets: Semantic validation errors (values do not add up, wrong field) differ from schema syntax errors, which tool use removes
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A freight pipeline extracts ship_date and delivery_date from bills of lading. Both are required ISO date strings, and every output passes the schema. In 3% of documents the model puts the delivery date into ship_date and the booking date into delivery_date, so deliveries appear to happen before shipping. Which check catches this?
opts: Add a date format and a date pattern to both fields, so only real calendar dates are accepted.
Mark both fields as required and forbid extra properties, so that a shifted value cannot appear.
A code check that rejects a delivery_date earlier than ship_date and returns the error to the model.
A line in the prompt asking the model to confirm that each date is in the right field before it answers.
questions.explain: Wrong-field placement is a semantic error, and a rule that compares the two fields can detect it, then feed the specific error to a retry. A and B tighten syntax, which every swapped output already satisfies. D asks the model to catch its own slip, which is the behaviour that failed.
bullets: Semantic validation errors (values do not add up, wrong field) differ from schema syntax errors, which tool use removes
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: Your CI reviewer returns findings through a strict tool schema where `line` is an integer. Parsing has not failed in two months, yet developers report that on large diffs about one finding in five points 10 to 40 lines away from the code it describes. All the numbers are valid integers inside the file's length, and the API does not enforce `minimum` or `maximum` on that field. What is the best fix?
opts: Add a minimum and a maximum to `line`, so that the number must fall inside the file's length.
Add a code_snippet field, verify it against the cited line in code, and send mismatches back.
Tell the model in the prompt to count lines carefully before it writes each number in a finding.
Move to a model with a bigger context window, since long diffs are not being read reliably.
questions.explain: The numbers are valid and wrong, a semantic error that a check against the file can find and turn into a specific message for a retry. A would not exclude them, since the stem says they are already inside the file. C asks for care without any means to tell when it failed. D assumes a reading limit that the evidence does not show.
bullets: Semantic validation errors (values do not add up, wrong field) differ from schema syntax errors, which tool use removes
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: An invoice pipeline retries a failed extraction by sending the invoice again plus the validator's message, for example "due_date is earlier than issue_date". The flagged field is fixed in 90% of retries, but 12% of retried outputs now hold a wrong value in a field that was right the first time, usually in the line items. Which change most directly removes the new errors?
