opts: Include the earlier extraction in the follow-up, so that the model edits it, not restarts.
Add 'change only the flagged field' to the retry prompt, and leave everything else exactly as it is.
Run the retry at temperature 0, so that unchanged fields come back identical every time.
Run two retries and keep each field's value only where both retries gave the same answer.
questions.explain: With the earlier output in front of it, the model can correct the one field and keep the rest. B gives an instruction with nothing to preserve, since the request carries no earlier values. C lowers randomness but a fresh extraction can still differ. D doubles the calls and still starts each retry from nothing.
bullets: Follow-up requests that carry the original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation errors
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: To save tokens on 90-page contracts, a retry sends the model only its failed JSON and the check message "effective_date is after expiry_date". The new output passes the check every time, but an audit against the PDFs finds that 35% of the retried dates differ from the contract. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The message gives the rule but no example of a correct date, so the model picks one at random.
A correction needs two rounds to settle on the right values, and only one round was allowed.
With no contract in the request, the model rearranged values until the check passed.
The message names the wrong field, so the model edits a date that was correct.
questions.explain: The model has nothing to read the true dates from, so it can only satisfy the rule. A and B would not make passing outputs wrong at this rate: an example date is no evidence about this contract, and a second round would have the same inputs. D contradicts the stem, where the message names both dates involved.
bullets: Follow-up requests that carry the original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation errors
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A validator finds that 2 of your CI reviewer's 19 findings cite files the pull request does not touch. You now build the follow-up request for self-correction, and the model has to be able to see what the pull request actually changed. Which contents should it carry?
opts: The two bad findings and the validator's messages, since the other 17 findings are already correct.
The diff and an instruction to produce all of the findings again, noting that some were invalid.
The diff and the validator's messages, because the earlier findings could anchor the model on its mistakes.
The diff, the full 19-finding output and the validator's messages for the two failures.
questions.explain: The model needs the source to check against, its earlier output to correct, and the specific errors. A leaves out the diff, so there is nothing to check file names against. B omits the output and the errors, so the 17 good findings may change. C omits the output, so the model must rebuild all 19 findings with no sign of which two were wrong.
bullets: Follow-up requests that carry the original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation errors
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Your invoice pipeline extracts stated_total as printed and calculated_total from the lines, and on a mismatch it retries with the specific discrepancy appended. After the change 70% of retried pairs agree, yet an audit against the PDFs finds that in most of those the retry rewrote stated_total to equal the sum of the lines, while the document prints a different figure. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Retry again with the size of the discrepancy in the message, so that a specific error leads to a correct total.
Lock stated_total in the schema, so that on a retry the model can only change calculated_total.
Add a second extraction pass with a different prompt, and keep the total on which both passes agree.
Stop retrying a flagged pair, keep both figures as printed, set a discrepancy flag and send it to review.
questions.explain: The invoice itself contradicts its lines, so no retry can produce a right answer, and one that makes the figures agree has altered the transcription. A repeats the loop that caused the rewrite. B relies on a schema locking feature that does not exist. C compares two passes that can both be pulled toward the sum of the lines.
bullets: Self-correction flows: calculated_total beside stated_total, and conflict_detected booleans for inconsistent sources
Telling when a retry will fail (information only in a document not provided) from when it will work (format, structure)
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Last week 1,000 customs-form extractions failed validation. By error: 560 have dates written as "31.12.2025" where ISO is required, 240 put the gross weight into the net_weight field, and 200 have an empty exporter_license_no because the licence is on a separate permit that was not part of the submission. You must decide what each group gets. What is the best policy?
opts: Retry all three groups with the errors appended, up to three attempts each, then review what still fails.
Retry the date and weight groups with their errors, and mark the licence group null with a flag.
Retry only the date group, because weight mix-ups are meaning errors that a retry cannot correct.
Retry the weight and licence groups with their errors, and convert the dates with a pattern in code.
questions.explain: Format and structural errors are the kind a retry corrects, while the licence number cannot be produced from documents that do not contain it. A spends three attempts per form on the 200 that cannot succeed. C treats a wrong-field error as beyond repair, though the model has the weight. D retries the one group that cannot be fixed.
bullets: Telling when a retry will fail (information only in a document not provided) from when it will work (format, structure)
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A pipeline converts PDFs to text and sends the text to the model. 7% of mortgage packets fail the check that signature_date must be present, and every retry with the error appended fails the same way. A reviewer opens a failed packet and finds the signature page is page 14. The converter's log for those packets shows "pages processed: 10". What is the most effective fix?
opts: Raise the converter's page limit so the signature page is sent, then re-run those packets.
Add worked examples of signature blocks to the prompt, so the model finds them more reliably.
Raise the retry limit from three to six for the packets that still fail the signature check.
Make signature_date nullable, so that these packets pass the check without a date.
questions.explain: The date is in the document but not in what the model is given, so no retry can find it, and the converter has to supply it. B would help a model that can see a signature block, and this one cannot. C repeats a loop that has failed identically. D hides a fixable data loss instead of correcting it.
bullets: Telling when a retry will fail (information only in a document not provided) from when it will work (format, structure)
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: After six weeks the dashboard groups 2,100 dismissed findings by detected_pattern. `optional-chaining-suggestion` accounts for 41% of all dismissals and is dismissed 85% of the times it is raised. `sql-string-concat` was raised 190 times and dismissed 4% of the time. The team has time for one change this sprint. What is the best use of the data?
opts: Hide every finding that falls below a given confidence score, until overall dismissals drop under 20%.
Ask developers to leave a reason on each dismissal, then read the reasons next quarter.
Hide both patterns until the reviewer is retrained, since each ranks near the top of the list.
Rewrite the criteria for the optional-chaining pattern with skip examples, then measure it again.
questions.explain: The data points at one pattern that developers reject nearly every time, so it is the one to fix, and a re-measure shows whether the change worked. A applies a self-reported score to all patterns, including the accurate ones. B delays any action and gathers text, when the pattern counts already show where the problem is. C also hides sql-string-concat, which developers act on 96% of the time.
bullets: Adding detected_pattern to structured findings to study false-positive patterns when developers dismiss them
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: The weekly report ranks detected_pattern values by dismissal rate: `rare-regex-backtracking` 5 of 6 dismissed (83%), `unchecked-array-index` 280 of 400 (70%), and `hardcoded-credential` 3 of 90 (3%). The team has time to retune the criteria for one pattern this sprint. Which should it choose?
opts: `rare-regex-backtracking`, since it has the highest dismissal rate of the three patterns.
`hardcoded-credential`, since a pattern that few people act on needs the most careful review.
All three patterns, because a dismissal rate is only useful when each pattern is retuned together.
`unchecked-array-index`, since 400 findings back its rate and it wastes the most reviews.
questions.explain: A pattern with 400 findings and 70% dismissed is a reliable signal and the largest cost to developers. A rests on six findings, too few to say anything. B has it backwards, since 3% dismissed means developers act on it. C spreads one sprint over patterns that do not all need work.
bullets: Adding detected_pattern to structured findings to study false-positive patterns when developers dismiss them
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: The pattern analysis shows `missing-error-handling` dismissed 62% of 480 times, and the team plans to rewrite its criteria to cut that. A lead notes that about 90% of those dismissals came from two services during a release freeze, and that elsewhere the pattern is dismissed 20% of the time. How should you evaluate the plan?
opts: Proceed, since a 62% dismissal rate is above any acceptable level whatever the source of the dismissals.
Hold it, and sample the freeze-period dismissals to see whether they were false positives or deferrals.
Proceed, but only for the two services, since they produce most of the dismissals.
Hold it, drop the freeze-period dismissals from the data, and treat the 20% rate as the true one.
questions.explain: A dismissal is a signal, not proof of a false positive, so the freeze-period dismissals need checking before they drive a rewrite. A takes every dismissal as an error. C keeps the unverified assumption and narrows the scope. D discards data on a guess, and the 20% may itself include deferrals.
bullets: Adding detected_pattern to structured findings to study false-positive patterns when developers dismiss them
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Rate confirmations list base freight, a fuel surcharge and accessorial lines, and print a total at the bottom. Your pipeline stores the printed total. A quarterly audit found that 2.4% of confirmations print a total that differs from the sum of their lines, and carriers were overpaid. Which schema change best lets the pipeline catch this?
opts: Replace the printed total with the model's own sum, since the lines are what the carrier is owed.
Add a total_confidence field, and send low-confidence totals to review.
Extract calculated_total from the lines next to stated_total, and flag every pair that differs.
Make total required and non-null, so that the model returns a number for every confirmation.
questions.explain: Holding both figures makes a disagreement visible, whichever figure is wrong. A drops the printed total, so the document's own error is never flagged. B uses the model's self-rating, which does not detect arithmetic. D forces a value to appear but does not check it.
bullets: Self-correction flows: calculated_total beside stated_total, and conflict_detected booleans for inconsistent sources
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Permit applications state the applicant's date of birth in the form header and again in an attached ID scan, and about 3% show two different dates. The pipeline asks for one date_of_birth, and the model silently takes the header's. Eligibility depends on age, wrong approvals have occurred, and reviewers need to see both values to decide. A null date skips the age rule, and no queue routes nulls to a person. What is the best change?
opts: Extract both dates, set conflict_detected when they differ, and route those cases to review.
Take the later of the two dates, since a correction is usually entered after the original.
Take the ID scan's date, since an official document outranks a form field.
Return null for date_of_birth whenever the two differ, and let the eligibility check reject nulls.
questions.explain: The flag turns an inconsistent source into a visible case, with both values kept for the reviewer. B and C choose a value by a rule nobody has agreed, so a wrong date still enters the record silently. D loses both values and gives the reviewer no reason for the rejection.
bullets: Self-correction flows: calculated_total beside stated_total, and conflict_detected booleans for inconsistent sources
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your pipeline extracts calculated_total and stated_total from supplier invoices and flags any pair that differs. Since launch, 18% of invoices are flagged, and reviewers find that most flagged invoices are correct. The prompt describes calculated_total as "the total of the invoice", and the flagged pairs typically differ by the tax amount. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Lower the review priority of flagged invoices, since most of them turn out to be correct.
Define calculated_total as the line items plus the tax lines shown, and compare with a small tolerance.
Drop calculated_total and trust the stated total, since the printed figure is what the supplier will be paid.
Add a tax_total field and ask the model to say which of the two totals it trusts more.
questions.explain: The two fields measure different things, so differences are produced by the definitions and not by errors in the invoices. A leaves the noise in place and risks hiding the real mismatches. C removes the check that the design exists for. D relies on a self-reported preference instead of comparing like with like.
bullets: Self-correction flows: calculated_total beside stated_total, and conflict_detected booleans for inconsistent sources
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A team extracting meter readings from utility bills wants a way to flag bad extractions. One proposal is a self-reported `confidence` from 0 to 1 on each field. The other is to extract a computed usage (current reading minus previous reading) next to the usage printed on the bill, and flag bills where they differ. A pilot of 300 bills holds 11 known extraction errors. How should you evaluate the two designs?
opts: Prefer confidence: it covers every field, while the usage comparison covers only one figure read.
Prefer confidence, once it has been calibrated against the 11 known errors in the pilot sample.
Use both, and flag a bill only when the two designs agree that it is wrong.
Prefer the comparison: it tests a figure against the bill, and confidence is only an opinion.
questions.explain: A disagreement between a computed and a printed figure is evidence from the document, while a self-reported score is not. A values breadth of coverage over whether the signal means anything. B still rests on the model's opinion of itself, however it is calibrated. C flags only the bills where both signals fire, so errors caught by one alone go through.
bullets: Self-correction flows: calculated_total beside stated_total, and conflict_detected booleans for inconsistent sources
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your nightly job asks Claude to draft unit tests for 1,200 modules through the Message Batches API, submitted at 01:00. For three weeks the batch ended between 01:40 and 02:10, and a release engineer wants the runbook to promise testers a finished suite by 03:00 every night. On one Friday the batch was still running at 20:00, and running the whole job synchronously takes about three hours. How should you evaluate the promise?
opts: Keep it: three weeks of timings show the usual duration, and the Friday run is one outlier to investigate later.
Drop it: the API sets no latency guarantee, only a 24-hour limit, so later steps must cope with a late suite.
Keep it, and cancel any batch still running at 03:00 so that the work can be rerun with synchronous calls.
Drop it, and promise 12 hours instead, since half of the 24-hour limit leaves room for a slow night.
questions.explain: The service sets an upper bound of 24 hours and no latency guarantee, so a fixed delivery time cannot be promised from observed timings. A treats a typical time as a guarantee, and the Friday run shows how far it can stray. C starts a three-hour synchronous run at 03:00, so the suite would still miss the promise. D swaps one unsupported number for another.
bullets: Message Batches API facts: half the cost, up to a 24-hour window, no guaranteed latency
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A batch of 40,000 scanned-form extractions was submitted at 21:00. A day later it shows as ended: 36,500 results are succeeded, none are errored, and 3,500 carry the result type expired. The forms behind the expired results look ordinary, and a synchronous test of ten of them extracts cleanly. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Those forms exceeded the context limit, so the service stopped them before they ran.
The forms were malformed, and the service marked them expired after checking them.
Their ids repeated, so the service dropped the second copy of each.
Processing ran out of time before those requests reached the model.
questions.explain: An expired result means the batch reached its expiration before that request was sent to the model, so the request never ran at all. A and B describe input problems, which would show up as errored results and would also fail in the synchronous test. C invents a duplicate-dropping behaviour.
bullets: Message Batches API facts: half the cost, up to a 24-hour window, no guaranteed latency
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: An insurer's intake service must have claim fields extracted within 3 hours of a document arriving, because adjusters begin from them. It makes one synchronous call per document today. A proposal moves it to the Message Batches API, noting that most batches finish within an hour and cost half as much. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Adopt it with hourly submission, since a batch that finishes in an hour fits inside a 3-hour limit.
Adopt it, and move the deadline in the service agreement to 24 hours to match the batch limit.
Keep it synchronous: batches carry no latency guarantee, so a 3-hour deadline cannot be promised.
Adopt it with submission every 30 minutes, so that no document waits long for a batch to start.
questions.explain: The deadline is a business requirement, and an API with no latency guarantee and a 24-hour limit cannot promise it. A and D count the typical hour (or the wait to submit) and ignore that processing can take far longer. B changes the requirement instead of meeting it.
bullets: Message Batches API facts: half the cost, up to a 24-hour window, no guaranteed latency
Matching the API approach (synchronous or batch) to the workflow's latency requirement
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A release pipeline holds each production deploy until Claude has summarised the breaking changes since the last release. Deploys happen about 12 times a day, each must have the summary before it goes out, and none may wait more than 10 minutes for it. In your own tests, batches of these summaries took 25 to 60 minutes. A teammate proposes the Message Batches API for the saving. What is the best response?
opts: Keep the stage synchronous: a deploy that waits on the result cannot absorb a batch's open turnaround.
Move it to batches and submit the summary when the release's first commit lands, so it is ready by deploy time.
Move it to batches with a 10-minute timeout, then fall back to a synchronous call.
Move it to batches with a 24-hour timeout, and ship when the summary lands.
questions.explain: A stage that blocks a deploy needs an answer on demand, and batches give no latency guarantee. B hopes that an early start finishes in time and cannot cover commits that land later. C would fall back on most deploys, since the tests took 25 to 60 minutes against a 10-minute limit, so it pays twice and still waits. D drops the requirement that the deploy waits for the summary.
bullets: Batch suits non-blocking, latency-tolerant work and does not suit blocking workflows
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A document service runs three Claude workloads: (1) extraction shown to a user in the upload form within seconds so the user can confirm it, (2) a nightly reconciliation report that finance reads some time the next afternoon, and (3) re-extraction of 90,000 stored forms after a schema change, needed by the end of next week. Cost is the concern. Which workloads should move to the Message Batches API?
opts: Only workload 2, as the others have a user or a deadline attached.
Workloads 2 and 3, with workload 1 left synchronous.
Workloads 1 and 2, since both run every day and so save the most over time.
All three, with the upload form showing a pending state until a batch ends.
questions.explain: The report and the re-extraction can both wait, so both suit batches; the upload form has a person waiting for an answer in seconds. A leaves out the re-extraction, whose deadline is a week away. C picks the workload with a user waiting. D turns an instant confirmation into an open-ended wait.
bullets: Batch suits non-blocking, latency-tolerant work and does not suit blocking workflows
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A nightly Message Batch drafts tests for 1,200 modules and normally ends within the hour. After the release train was changed to start its 06:00 build only once the batch has ended, builds began at 14:00 and at 21:00 on two nights. Running the generation synchronously would take about nine hours. The team wants the build to stop waiting on the batch. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Poll the batch every minute, so that the build starts as soon as the last result lands.
Split the modules across 12 batches submitted at 01:00, so that each of them ends sooner.
Move generation to synchronous calls started at 01:00, so the suite is ready before the build.
Build at 06:00 with the last finished batch's tests, and add new ones when they land.
questions.explain: The batch suits work that nobody waits on, and the change turned it into a gate. Taking the gate away restores that. A speeds up noticing the end, not the end itself. B does not change the 24-hour limit or promise that smaller batches finish sooner. C needs about nine hours, so it cannot finish before 06:00.
bullets: Batch suits non-blocking, latency-tolerant work and does not suit blocking workflows
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline has Claude call a `lookup_vendor` tool to fill an `approved` field for each of 30,000 invoices. To save cost, the team ran a pilot of 200 as a Message Batch with the tool defined in every request. All 200 results are succeeded, but each has stop_reason "tool_use" and no `approved` value. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Batch requests cannot carry tool definitions at all, so the call was malformed from the start.
The `lookup_vendor` schema lacks a required field, so Claude cannot finish the call it began.
No step inside a batch request runs the tool and returns its result for Claude to continue.
The custom_id values were not attached to the tool calls, so the results were never matched.
questions.explain: A request in a batch is processed on its own, so a client-side tool call cannot be executed and answered inside it. The result ends at the tool request, which is why the field is empty. A is false, since the tool definition was accepted. B would give a schema problem, not a clean tool_use result. D confuses matching results with running tools.
bullets: A batch request cannot run a tool mid-request and return the result to the model
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A nightly job must produce 6,000 unit tests. For each, Claude writes the test, a `run_tests` tool executes it, and when it fails Claude reads the output and revises the test before it is accepted. Nobody looks at the result until morning. Which design fits?
opts: Run the loop on the synchronous API overnight, with your code executing `run_tests` between turns.
Submit the loop as a Message Batch with `run_tests` defined, so that Claude runs it between its own turns.
Submit a Message Batch and tell Claude to mentally run each test and fix it before it answers.
Submit a Message Batch with extended thinking on, so that Claude checks every test before it answers.
questions.explain: The loop needs a tool executed and its output returned to the model, which a batch request cannot do for a client-side tool, so the loopbelongs on the synchronous API even if it runs overnight. B expects the batch to run the tool. C and D ask the model to imagine a result that only a real test run can give.
bullets: A batch request cannot run a tool mid-request and return the result to the model
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Three nightly CI jobs are candidates for the Message Batches API: (1) labelling 50,000 failure logs, with each log's text supplied in its prompt, (2) an agent that investigates each failing test by calling `git_blame` and `read_file` and following what they return, and (3) summarising each day's commit messages, also supplied in the prompt. Which jobs can be submitted as batches without redesign?
opts: Jobs 1, 2 and 3, as the API runs the tool calls inside a batch.
Jobs 1 and 3, whose requests are answered in a single turn.
Job 2 only, as it does the most work per request and so saves the most.
Job 1 only, as it has by far the most requests.
questions.explain: Requests answered in one turn from supplied text fit a batch. Job 2 depends on tool results coming back to the model mid-request, which a batch cannot do. A is false: the API does not run client-side tools such as git_blame and read_file inside a batch.C picks the one job that cannot work. D leaves out job 3, which has the same shape as job 1.
bullets: A batch request cannot run a tool mid-request and return the result to the model
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A team submits 9,000 contract extractions as one batch, using each file's storage path as its custom_id. Six hours later the batch ends: 2,200 results are errored with an invalid request message, and 6,800 succeeded. The failures include `legal/2024/Acme Corp v2.pdf`, while the successes include `legal-2024-acme_v1`. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The failed documents exceed the context limit, so the service rejected their requests.
Requests with long paths exceed a size limit that applies to the batch as a whole.
Claude declined to read contracts from that folder, so the service marked them as errors.
Those ids hold characters that the field does not allow.
questions.explain: The id field accepts only letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, up to 64 characters, and the failed ids break that rule while the successful ones keep it. A would affect documents by length, not by how their ids are written. B invents a size rule tied to path length. C describes a refusal, which would not be reported as an invalid request.
bullets: custom_id correlates each batch request with its result
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A CI team runs per-file review requests as a Message Batch of 3,000. Their client code pairs the i-th result line with the i-th request in its list and sets no custom_id. Across 20 test batches the pairing came out right every time, so a reviewer asks you to approve the code for production. How should you evaluate it?
opts: Approve it: 20 matching batches are strong evidence that the order will hold in production.
Approve it, with a count check that rejects any batch whose result total differs from its request total.
Reject it: results can come back in any order, so each request needs an id and matching should use it.
Reject it, and sort the results by completion time before pairing so that the order is restored.
questions.explain: The documentation says results can arrive in any order and may not match the submission order, so matching has to use the id carried by each request. A reads a small sample as a guarantee. B checks the count, which stays right when the results are paired wrongly. D swaps one unreliable order for another.
bullets: custom_id correlates each batch request with its result
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Contracts are re-uploaded with corrections while their extraction is still waiting in a batch. Each document keeps its ID and gains a revision number on every upload. Last week a result for revision 3 arrived after revision 4 had been stored, and it overwrote the newer fields in 41 records. A separate loader writes results and sees only the result lines. How should the requests be identified to prevent this?
opts: Build each custom_id from document ID and revision, and have the loader skip stale results.
Keep the latest-finished result for each document ID, because the newest result is the best.
Cancel every pending batch whenever a document is re-uploaded, and resubmit the whole set.
Ask Claude to repeat the revision number in each extraction, and have the loader compare it.
questions.explain: The id travels with the request and comes back with its result, so putting the revision in it lets the loader decide without extra lookups. B uses finishing order, which is exactly what failed. C throws away the work of every other document. D leans on generated text for something the id field exists to carry.
bullets: custom_id correlates each batch request with its result
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: One code-review prompt serves two triggers: a pull request being opened, where merging is blocked until the review posts, and a weekly sweep of 2,000 older files. Merges happen at any hour across three time zones. Cost is up, and the team wants the Message Batches API wherever it fits. Which design is best?
opts: Send all reviews as batches, and show the pull request check as pending until its result arrives.
Send pull request reviews synchronously and the weekly sweep as a batch.
Send reviews synchronously by day and as batches by night, as nobody is waiting overnight.
Send every review synchronously, and cut cost by shortening the prompt.
questions.explain: The trigger decides whether someone is blocked, so it decides the API. A makes merges wait for an open-ended result. C assumes nobody waits at night, but merges happen at any hour. D gives up the saving on work that can wait.
bullets: Matching the API approach (synchronous or batch) to the workflow's latency requirement
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A nightly job extracts fields from about 15,000 partner documents received during the day and loads them into a warehouse that analysts query the next afternoon, and they accept data a day old. It runs as 15,000 synchronous calls with retries, and its spend is the team's largest line. Nobody looks at individual results before the load, and a delay of a day is acceptable. What is the most effective change?
opts: Run more calls in parallel so that the job ends earlier and fewer retries are needed overall.
Move the job to a smaller model, since the documents are fairly simple to read.
Add a check after each call and retry the failed documents one by one.
Submit them as a Message Batch, since no one needs a single result before morning.
questions.explain: The job is latency-tolerant and fully synchronous, so batching halves its cost without anyone noticing. A finishes sooner, which nobody asked for. B changes the model without an evidence that quality would hold. C adds more calls to a job that is already paid for at full price.
bullets: Matching the API approach (synchronous or batch) to the workflow's latency requirement
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A `/review-all` command lets a developer ask Claude to review all 6,000 files of a service before opening a pull request. Developers abandon the command after about ten minutes of waiting, and these reviews are most of the team's Claude spend. A teammate says the volume makes it a natural fit for the Message Batches API. What is the best response?
opts: Agree, and email each developer the results when the batch ends.
Agree, and cut the work into 60 batches of 100 files so that each ends sooner.
Keep it synchronous, with reviews in parallel, since a person is waiting.
Agree, and add a progress bar that polls the batch until its results arrive.
questions.explain: What matters is whether someone is waiting, not how large the job is. These developers expect output inside minutes, which a batch cannot promise. A and D accept an open wait that has already led to abandoned runs. B does not shorten the 24-hour limit.
bullets: Matching the API approach (synchronous or batch) to the workflow's latency requirement
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Partner documents arrive around the clock, and each must have its extracted fields available within 54 hours of arrival. Processing a Message Batch can take up to 24 hours. The pipeline submits a batch every hour, producing hundreds of small batches, and the team wants to submit as rarely as the deadline allows. Which schedule is the least frequent that still guarantees the deadline?
opts: Every 24 hours.
Every 12 hours, twice a day.
Every 36 hours, a day and a half.
Every 48 hours, every other day.
questions.explain: The worst case is the wait for the next submission plus up to 24 hours of processing. Every 24 hours gives 48 hours, inside 54. B also meets the deadline but submits more often than needed. C gives 60 hours and D gives 72, both past 54.
bullets: Working out how often to submit batches so that the SLA holds given the 24-hour processing window
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A pipeline sends each merged change's test suggestions through a Message Batch submitted once a day at 02:00. The promise to developers is suggestions within 40 hours of the merge. A month of data shows 11% of changes missed it, nearly all merged within a few hours after 02:00 on days when the batch ran for most of its window. Splitting the daily batch into ten smaller ones submitted together did not help. Which change fixes the schedule?
opts: Keep submitting once a day, but move the submission to 14:00 when fewer merges are waiting.
Submit every 12 hours, and treat the 24-hour limit as the processing time.
Submit every 36 hours, so that each batch is larger and slow days become rare.
Keep the daily batch, and request faster processing for changes merged just after 02:00.
questions.explain: A change merged just after a submission waits almost a full interval, then up to 24 hours more. With a daily schedule that is nearly 48 hours, past 40, and a 12-hour interval brings it to 36. A moves the cutoff without shortening the interval. C lengthens the interval and so the wait. D relies on a priority option that the API does not offer.
bullets: Working out how often to submit batches so that the SLA holds given the 24-hour processing window
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A service promises extracted fields within 26 hours of a document's arrival. An engineer plans one batch every 24 hours, arguing that batches usually finish in under an hour, so the worst case is 24 hours of waiting plus about one hour, which is 25. How should you evaluate the plan?
opts: Accept it: its worst case of 25 hours sits comfortably inside the 26-hour promise made.
Accept it, and resubmit anything that expires in the next day's batch of requests.
Reject it: budget 24 hours for processing, so submit every 2 hours or sooner.
Reject it: with 24 hours budgeted for processing, submitting every 12 hours is enough.
questions.explain: A guarantee has to use the upper bound of 24 hours for processing, not the usual time. That leaves 2 hours of waiting inside a 26-hour promise. A uses the typical hour. B resubmits expired work into a batch that is another day away. D budgets 24 hours correctly, but 12 plus 24 is 36, past 26.
bullets: Working out how often to submit batches so that the SLA holds given the 24-hour processing window
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: In a nightly batch of 1,800 per-file reviews, 35 requests errored because their source files exceed the context limit. The fix is to split each of those files into four parts, review each part as its own request, and merge the findings per file. How should the resubmitted requests be identified?
opts: Reuse the original custom_id on all four parts, since the findings belong to that file.
Give the parts new random ids, and keep the mapping in memory until the batch ends.
Number the parts 1 to 140 in order, and pair them with files by position.
Build each id from the original plus the part number, so results map to file and part.
questions.explain: An id that carries the file and the part lets the results be merged per file and traced to what was resubmitted. A is wrong because each custom_id must be unique, so four requests with one id are not allowed. B loses the link if the process restarts. C pairs by position, and results do not come back in submission order.
bullets: After failures, resubmit only the failed documents by custom_id, with the fix the failure calls for
custom_id correlates each batch request with its result
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A 20,000-document extraction batch ends with 19,500 succeeded, 400 expired, 80 errored with internal server errors, and 20 errored because the documents exceed the context limit; all 20 are scans of more than 300 pages. What is the most efficient recovery?
opts: Resubmit the 480 expired and server-error ids as is, and chunk the 20 scans.
Resubmit all 500 ids unchanged, and repeat until the error count reaches zero.
Resubmit the 20,000 documents in a new batch, so one set of results covers everything.
Run the 500 ids on the synchronous API, which returns faster than a second batch.
questions.explain: Expired and server-error requests did not fail because of their input, so they can go again as they are, while the oversized scans fail the same way until they are changed. B resubmits the 20 scans unchanged, and they fail again. C repeats 19,500 successes. D gives up the saving and still sends the 20 scans unchanged.
bullets: After failures, resubmit only the failed documents by custom_id, with the fix the failure calls for
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: An extraction service receives about 20,000 documents a day. Roughly 5% are flagged urgent and a clerk needs their fields within a few minutes; the rest are read by analysts the following afternoon. Spend is high and everything now runs synchronously. Which routing is best?
opts: Send everything as a batch, and place the urgent documents first within each batch.
Send urgent documents as small batches submitted every minute, and the rest as one daily batch.
Keep everything synchronous, and batch only the documents that arrive overnight.
Send urgent documents synchronously and the rest as a Message Batch.
questions.explain: The flag marks who is waiting: urgent documents need an answer in minutes, which a batch cannot promise, while the rest tolerate a day. A assumes order inside a batch changes when results come back, and there is no such guarantee. B submits often, but each small batch can still take up to 24 hours. C batches by arrival time, which says nothing about who is waiting.
bullets: Matching the API approach (synchronous or batch) to the workflow's latency requirement
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Before a 60,000-form extraction batch, the team tuned the prompt on 25 clean, typed forms until it got 100% valid output. The batch finished with 71% of results usable, and the failures cluster on faxed, rotated and handwritten forms, which are 30% of the volume. Which earlier step would have been most effective?
opts: Tuning on a sample with faxed, rotated and handwritten forms in real proportions.
Tuning on many more clean typed forms, since a larger sample gives a more reliable success rate.
Submitting the full batch first, and fixing the prompt from whichever results come back wrong.
Tuning only on the faxed forms, since those are the hardest to read.
questions.explain: A sample only predicts first-pass success if it looks like the volume, including the hard cases. B adds more of the easy case. C turns the whole run into the test, and every wrong result is a resubmission. D tunes on one slice and may break the typed forms that already worked.
bullets: Refine the prompt on a sample set before processing a large volume in a batch
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A team is tuning the prompt for a 3,000-request test-generation batch. Each round submits the whole batch, waits about five hours for the results, and then edits the prompt; after five rounds the prompt is still changing. How should the tuning be done instead?
opts: Submit several prompt variants as separate full batches in the same round, and compare them.
Poll the batch status more often, so that each round starts as soon as the results land.
Iterate on a sample with synchronous calls, then submit the full batch once.
Cut each round to a batch of 300 requests, so that every round finishes much sooner.
questions.explain: A sample run through the synchronous API returns in seconds, so many prompt edits fit in an afternoon and the large batch is submitted once. A multiplies the work by the number of variants. B saves minutes from a five-hour wait. D keeps the wait, since a smaller batch carries no latency guarantee either.
bullets: Refine the prompt on a sample set before processing a large volume in a batch
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A team tuned its prompt on 120 invoices drawn from one supplier until all outputs were valid against the schema, then ran 40,000 invoices from 300 suppliers as one batch. Spot checks found the invoice total in the wrong field in 14% of records, mostly on layouts the sample never contained. How should the prompt have been refined before the batch?
opts: On more invoices from the same supplier, until two rounds in a row look clean.
On a sample spanning the layouts, scored against hand-checked values for each field.
On the first 5,000 invoices submitted as a batch, using the errors to adjust the prompt.
On the same 120 invoices, run twice, keeping the prompt if both runs give identical output.
questions.explain: Refinement raises first-pass success only if the sample resembles the volume and is scored on correct values. A and D keep the single-supplier sample, so unseen layouts stay unseen, and D measures steadiness, not accuracy. C makes a large batch the test, with hours of waiting per round.
bullets: Refine the prompt on a sample set before processing a large volume in a batch
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your invoice extraction pipeline sends each document to Claude, then adds a second turn in the same conversation on every invoice: "Re-read the invoice and confirm every field." The confirmation succeeds on 99% of invoices. A human audit of 300 invoices still finds 8% of fields wrong, and in 41 of the 46 wrong cases the confirmation text repeats the same column mapping that caused the error, such as a net amount read as the gross amount. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The second turn builds on a reading that is still in the conversation, so it tends to confirm that reading.
The confirmation turn is skipped unless the first answer parses against the schema, so some answers are never rechecked.
The conversation is long by the second turn, so the invoice text has been dropped before the model re-reads it.
The request covers every field, so the model spreads its attention too thin to notice single mistakes.
questions.explain: The model that made the first reading is still holding the reasoning behind it, so asking it to confirm mostly repeats the same interpretation; the repeated column mapping shows this. B conflicts with the stem, where the turn runs on every invoice. C would produce random misses, not one mapping repeated, and the invoice is still in the conversation. D predicts scattered misses too, where the audit found the same mistake again and again.
bullets: A model keeps its reasoning context from generation, so it is less likely to question its own decisions in the same session
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: In your CI environment, Claude Code implements a `bulk_discount()` function and, in the same session, writes its unit tests. All 14 tests pass, including five edge cases such as the maximum quantity, and line coverage is 96%. A week later, orders with quantity 0 receive a negative total. Review finds that the faulty arithmetic sits on a line the tests do run, but never with that input. The ticket did not mention zero quantities. What explains the gap most directly?
opts: Coverage of 96% is too low, and the untested 4% of lines held the zero-quantity logic.
Tests written after the code are dropped when the session ends, so the final run used an older test file.
The tests came from the same reasoning as the function, so they share its view of valid input.
The session ran short of context while writing tests, so it stopped before it reached the odd inputs.
questions.explain: The session that wrote the function also chose which inputs were worth testing, so the tests inherit the same blind spot and pass. A is ruled out because the faulty line is covered. B invents a behaviour, and the tests did run. D conflicts with the stem, where the session finished and covered five edge cases.
bullets: A model keeps its reasoning context from generation, so it is less likely to question its own decisions in the same session
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: After extracting contract terms, your pipeline asks the same Claude conversation to justify each ambiguous field, for example why a notice period is 60 days when two clauses disagree. The justifications read as coherent for 97% of fields, yet an audit finds 12% of those fields wrong. How should you evaluate the justification step as a quality control?
opts: Keep it, and audit a 5% sample, since a coherent explanation is good evidence that the field is right.
Replace it with a second instance that reads only the document, and review the fields where they disagree.
Require longer justifications that quote the clause text, so a wrong field becomes harder to explain convincingly.
Move the justification into a structured output field, so the explanation is checked against the schema.
questions.explain: An explanation produced by the session that chose the value is built from the same reasoning, so it sounds convincing whether or not the value is right; an instance that reads the document afresh is a real second view. A treats fluency as proof. C stays in the same session, and a quoted clause can be misread just as confidently. D checks that the explanation has the right shape, not that it is true.
bullets: A model keeps its reasoning context from generation, so it is less likely to question its own decisions in the same session
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your CI job has one Claude session generate a patch and then review it. On a set of 20 seeded defects, the review caught 5. Enabling extended thinking with a large budget for the review step raised that to 6. A fresh instance given only the diff and the repository caught 13. What should you do next?
opts: Raise the thinking budget again, since the move from 5 to 6 shows that deeper reasoning helps.
Add a checklist of 30 common defect types to the review prompt of the generating session.
Move the review to a larger model but keep it inside the generating session.
Make the review a separate instance that has not seen how the patch was produced.
questions.explain: The big gain came from taking the generator's reasoning out of the reviewer, which more thinking in the same session cannot do. A chases a one-defect improvement. B adds instructions to a session that still believes its own choices. C changes the model, not the shared context that produced the blind spot.
bullets: Independent review instances without the generator's reasoning beat self-review instructions or extended thinking
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your CI finder pass returns about 40 candidate findings per PR, and a labelled sample shows only a quarter are real. You add a verification stage. Which design best follows a verification pass with reported confidence and calibrated routing?
opts: Ask the finder to attach a confidence to each finding, and drop the lowest 60% on that score alone, unseen.
Pass each candidate and its code to a separate checker that reports confidence, and route by measured bands.
Repeat the finder three times and post whatever two of the repeats both report, with a note on each.
Post all 40 with a label saying they are unverified, and let developers decide which ones deserve a close read.
questions.explain: A separate pass checks each candidate against the code, and routing on its confidence is sound once bands are measured against labelled outcomes. A trusts the finder's own score and drops findings unseen. C repeats the same finder, whose repeated mistakes agree with each other. D moves the filtering to developers, which is the cost that the stage should remove.
bullets: Running verification passes where the model reports confidence beside each finding, to route review in a calibrated way
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: To improve review quality without extra calls, a team appends this to the generating session: "Forget how you wrote this and review it as a skeptical outsider." On 20 seeded defects the session caught 4, while a fresh instance given only the diff caught 12. Which explanation fits best?
opts: The instruction cannot remove the reasoning from the conversation, so the code is still read through it.
A skeptical persona makes the model reject correct code, so many of its flags were false alarms.
Review instructions apply only to the first turn of a session, so the appended request was ignored.
The fresh instance had a larger context window than the session, which is why it reached more of the defects.
questions.explain: The reasoning that produced the code is still sitting in the session, and a request to ignore it does not remove it. B is contradicted by the stem, which counts defects caught. C invents a rule about first turns. D has nothing in the stem behind it, and window size was not shown to matter.
bullets: Independent review instances without the generator's reasoning beat self-review instructions or extended thinking
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A legal-tech pipeline sends each 90-page contract with its amendments to Claude in one call and asks for every obligation and key date. Obligations from the first 20 pages come back detailed, those after page 60 are thin, and across repeated runs the notice period is 30 days in one and 60 in another. The base contract says 30 and an amendment on page 81 says 60. What is the most effective redesign?
opts: Run the single call three times and keep only the values on which all three runs agree.
Put the amendments first in the prompt, so the later pages are read with more care.
Extract section by section in separate passes, then run one pass that reconciles terms across sections.
Move to a model with a bigger context window, so that the entire contract fits and is read in a single call.
questions.explain: Local extraction gives each section full attention, and a separate pass looks at what only shows up across sections, such as an amendment that overrides a clause. A drops the notice period whenever runs differ, so the conflict is hidden and not resolved. B reorders the prompt and the single pass still thins out. D adds room, but the thin coverage comes from one pass doing too much.
bullets: Large reviews split into per-file local passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Your CI reviews a 28-file pull request in a single pass. Run to run on the same commit, the findings cluster in different places: one run comments heavily on files 1 to 9, the next on files 14 to 22. The prompt already defines four severity levels with examples, the diff is fed in the same order every time, 4-file PRs give stable findings, context use is 6% of the window, and every run ends with `stop_reason: "end_turn"`. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The prompt lacks guidance on which files matter, so each run decides for itself which to examine closely.
Each run reads the files in a different order, so a fixed file order would make the findings identical.
The output limit is reached at a different point in each run, so the later files are cut off.
One pass over 28 files spreads attention unevenly, and where the depth lands changes from run to run.
questions.explain: When one pass covers many files, depth falls where attention thins, and which files get it varies, which per-file passes would remove by giving every file the same focus. A is weakened by the prompt's severity definitions, which speak to importance. B is ruled out because the order is fixed. C is ruled out by `end_turn`, which is not a truncated response.
bullets: Large reviews split into per-file local passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your team reviews pull requests with one Claude pass. The median PR is 3 files and 90% are under 8 files, but a few migration PRs touch 40 to 120 files and cannot be split by their authors. A pilot found review quality unchanged up to about 15 files and falling sharply beyond 30, where late files get one-line comments. A proposal would run per-file passes plus an integration pass on every PR. How should you evaluate it?
opts: Adopt it for every PR, so that all authors get the same review process.
Adopt it only for PRs above about 30 files, and keep the single pass for smaller ones.
Reject it: splitting removes context that a single pass keeps, and a larger window fixes the migrations.
Reject it, and require migration authors to split their work so that no review exceeds eight files.
questions.explain: The weakness shows only on large changes, so the extra passes belong there and nowhere else, since each one is another call. A pays for passes on PRs that have no dilution problem. C offers a bigger window for a problem that is about focus. D asks for what the stem says authors cannot do.
bullets: Large reviews split into per-file local passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: In a Claude Code session, Claude has just implemented a retry wrapper from `SPEC.md`. You want an independent review before opening the pull request. Which setup gives the most independent check?
opts: Fork the current conversation into a subagent and ask it to review, so it can see the files and the discussion.
Start a read-only reviewer subagent and pass it the implementation plan and a note on the trade-offs Claude chose.
Start a reviewer subagent and point it at the changed files and `SPEC.md`.
Ask the current session to re-read the changed files from disk and review them against `SPEC.md`.
questions.explain: A non-fork subagent has no conversation history, only the prompt string plus project CLAUDE.md, so pointing it at the code and the spec gives it what it needs to check and nothing of the author's reasoning. A copies the conversation, so the reasoning comes along. B puts the author's plan and trade-offs into the prompt, and read-only tools do not undo that. D keeps everything the session already believes.
bullets: Using a second independent Claude instance to review generated code without the generator's reasoning context
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: You add a second Claude instance to review invoice extractions. The extractor produces a JSON record plus about 200 words of notes on how it resolved each unclear field. The reviewer will run on every invoice and should catch misread values. Which input should it receive?
opts: The source invoice and the extracted JSON, but not the extractor's notes.
The source invoice, the JSON and the notes, so that it can check the extractor's reasoning.
The extracted JSON and the notes, so it can judge consistency without rereading the invoice.
The source invoice, the JSON and a one-line list of the fields the extractor found unclear.
questions.explain: The reviewer needs the source to check against and the record to check, and nothing that tells it how the extractor came to its values. B and D pass along the extractor's reasoning or doubts, which points the reviewer toward the same spots. C removes the source, so it cannot find a misread value at all.
bullets: Using a second independent Claude instance to review generated code without the generator's reasoning context
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: To review 2,000 extracted invoice records, a single reviewer conversation works through them in order. Its detection of planted errors is 85% in the first 50 records and 55% after the 400th. Its early comments show it accepted a day-first date reading for one supplier, and it has applied that reading since. Context use is under 30%. What is the most effective change?
opts: Remind the reviewer every 100 records to re-check its date assumptions against the source documents.
Summarise the conversation every 200 records so that it stays short and keeps its earlier conclusions.
Switch the reviewer to a model with more context room, so that nothing in the conversation is dropped.
Make each record its own reviewer call, given only the source document and the record.
questions.explain: The long conversation turns the reviewer's earlier judgments into context it then defers to, so independence erodes with every record; a fresh call per record starts without them. A asks the same drifting session to police itself. B keeps the earlier conclusions in the summary. C is unneeded, since context use is under 30%.
bullets: Using a second independent Claude instance to review generated code without the generator's reasoning context
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A PR changes `normalize_date()` in `dates.py` so that it returns `None` for malformed input instead of raising. Your pipeline runs a per-file pass on each of the 3 changed files and an integration pass over the same 3 files. All pass cleanly. Two days after the merge, six unchanged modules that call `normalize_date()` crash on `None`. How should the pipeline change?
opts: Name the six callers in the per-file prompt, so that each pass checks them for crashes.
Let the integration pass search the repository for callers of the changed functions and check them.
Run a per-file pass on every file in the repository whenever a function's return value changes.
Tell the per-file pass to flag every changed return value, so that the integration pass gets a warning.
questions.explain: Following a changed function's data to the code that uses it is the integration pass's job, and here the affected files are outside the diff, so that pass needs to look beyond it. A cannot work, since nobody knows the callers beforehand. C pays for hundreds of per-file passes where a targeted search would do. D produces a flag, and the pass receiving it still cannot see the callers.
bullets: Splitting multi-file reviews into per-file passes for local issues plus integration passes for cross-file data flow
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: To save time, your pipeline runs one reviewer per file in parallel, and each posts its own inline comments. On a 12-file change, `cache.py` is told to make `get_user` asynchronous, while `api.py` is told to keep `get_user` synchronous because `api.py` calls it that way. Developers lose time deciding who is right. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Have each pass read the other files' diffs before it comments, so each can see what it conflicts with.
Run the per-file passes one after another, each told to avoid contradicting the earlier ones.
Hold the per-file findings back, and let an integration pass reconcile them before any are posted.
Add a rule to every per-file prompt: do not suggest changing the signature of a function.
questions.explain: Each per-file pass sees one file, so conflicts between them are expected, and the cross-file pass is the place to settle them before a developer sees them. A loads every diff into every pass and brings back the dilution that per-file passes avoid. B gives up the parallelism and still relies on each pass remembering earlier comments. D silences valid findings about signatures.
bullets: Splitting multi-file reviews into per-file passes for local issues plus integration passes for cross-file data flow
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A nightly job extracts supplier invoices, one document per call. A separate Claude instance then validates each record against its own document, and all 2,000 records from last night validate. Finance still reports invoice number `INV-4471` under two different suppliers, and "Acme Ltd" and "ACME Limited" counted as two vendors. Which gap in the review design best explains this?
opts: No pass looks across records, and these problems exist only between documents.
The validation pass is not an independent instance, so it confirms whatever the extractor produced.
The batch is too large for one validation call, so records beyond the first few hundred were never checked.
The validation pass reads each document in too much detail, so it overlooks problems between records.
questions.explain: Checking each record against its own source is the local pass, and it passed; duplicates and name variants appear only when records are compared, which needs a pass over all of them. B conflicts with the stem, where a separate instance validates. C conflicts with it too, since all 2,000 records were validated. D treats detail as the cause, when no local look could find a problem that spans documents.
bullets: Splitting multi-file reviews into per-file passes for local issues plus integration passes for cross-file data flow
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your integration pass receives the diff plus the per-file findings, and its prompt says "Review this whole change thoroughly". It re-reports local issues the per-file passes already judged, and in 9 of 40 PRs it calls a line a bug that a per-file pass had cleared with a stated reason. Its cross-file findings are few. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Remove the per-file findings from its input, so that it forms its own view without being influenced.
Raise its thinking budget, so that it resolves disagreements with the per-file passes by reasoning.
Tell it to prefer the per-file verdict whenever the two disagree, and drop its own.
Scope its prompt to cross-file data flow and interface mismatches, using local verdicts as input.
questions.explain: The integration pass exists for what a single file cannot show; when it is told to redo everything, it competes with the passes that have already given each file full attention, and contradicts them. A removes the context it should build on. B keeps it doing the wrong job with more effort. C settles the contradiction by discarding the pass's own output, so the cross-file findings could go too.
bullets: Splitting multi-file reviews into per-file passes for local issues plus integration passes for cross-file data flow
Large reviews split into per-file local passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A verification pass in your extraction pipeline reports a confidence from 0 to 1 beside each extracted field, and fields at 0.90 or above skip human review. The team labelled 400 fields by hand. Fields at 0.90 or above were correct 99% of the time for amounts and 86% for dates, and skipping review requires at least 97% accuracy. What should you change?
opts: Raise the cutoff for all fields to 0.97, since the cutoff should equal the accuracy you require.
Keep the cutoff, and add a line to the prompt asking the model to be more careful with dates.
Set a cutoff for each field type from the labelled results, and keep dates in review until 97%.
Keep the cutoff, since the accuracy across both field types is above 90% and close enough.
questions.explain: A confidence value is only useful once it is measured against outcomes, and the labels show it means different things for different field types, so routing needs per-type cutoffs set from measured accuracy. A confuses a confidence value with an accuracy rate. B hopes a prompt changes the numbers. D accepts a result below the stated requirement.
bullets: Running verification passes where the model reports confidence beside each finding, to route review in a calibrated way
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A verification pass gives each CI review finding a confidence, and findings at 0.80 or above are posted automatically. For three months about 40% of findings cleared the cutoff and developers accepted 90% of them. After a model update, 85% of findings clear it and developers accept only 68%. The prompt did not change, and a hand-labelled sample confirms that the posted findings are less often correct. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The new model's stated confidence no longer lines up with outcomes, so the old cutoff has lost its meaning.
Developers have become stricter reviewers, so acceptance fell while the findings stayed as accurate as before.
The new model finds more real issues, so a larger share of its findings legitimately clears the cutoff.
Confidence values are rounded to two places, so many findings tie at 0.80 and pass the cutoff.
questions.explain: The share above the cutoff jumped while accuracy fell, which means the numbers the model reports mean something different now; the cutoff has to be re-measured against labelled outcomes after a change like this. B is ruled out by the labelled sample. C conflicts with the lower accuracy. D invents a rounding effect that would not appear only after an update.
bullets: Running verification passes where the model reports confidence beside each finding, to route review in a calibrated way
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your verification pass attaches a confidence to each finding. Over 1,000 hand-labelled findings: the 0.9 to 1.0 band had 600 findings with 540 correct; the 0.7 to 0.9 band had 300 with 180 correct; below 0.7 there were 100 with 20 correct. Policy: post automatically only a band whose measured precision is at least 85%, send every other finding to a reviewer, and discard none. Which routing meets the policy?
opts: Post automatically at 0.7 and above, and send findings below 0.7 to a reviewer.
Post every finding automatically, and let developers dismiss the wrong ones.
Post at 0.9 and above, discard findings below 0.7, and send the middle band to a reviewer.
Post at 0.9 and above, and send every finding below 0.9 to a reviewer.
questions.explain: Only the top band measures 90%, above the 85% bar, and the policy sends everything else to a person. A would post a mix of bands at 80% precision (720 of 900). B posts at 74%. C breaks the rule that none are discarded.
bullets: Running verification passes where the model reports confidence beside each finding, to route review in a calibrated way
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your extraction call returns each field with a self-reported confidence. 96% of fields report 0.9 or higher, yet a labelled audit finds only 62% of those fields correct, so the confidence cannot route anything: no cutoff on it reaches the required 97% accuracy. A separate instance given only the document and the extracted record produces a wide spread of confidences, and 91% of its 0.9-and-above fields are correct. Which design should you adopt?
opts: Keep the extractor's confidence, and raise the cutoff to 0.99 until the audit accuracy reaches 91%.
Add a verification pass by a separate instance, and route on its confidence once labels back it.
Ask the extractor to rate its confidence on a 1 to 10 scale, which spreads the values more.
Average the extractor's and the verifier's confidence, and route on the average.
questions.explain: A verifier that has not seen the extractor's reasoning is less swayed by it, and its confidence is worth routing on once labelled data shows it separates right from wrong. A keeps a number that is high for nearly everything. C changes the scale of a score that carries no signal. D blends the useful score with the useless one.
bullets: Running verification passes where the model reports confidence beside each finding, to route review in a calibrated way
Independent review instances without the generator's reasoning beat self-review instructions or extended thinking
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A market research agent condenses each round's findings into a short summary before starting the next round. The raw round 1 tool results contain "operating margin 14.2% in fiscal 2025" and "warranty reserves up 31% year on year". After four rounds the report says margins are healthy and warranty costs are rising, although its prompt asks for a figure with every claim. Neither number appears in the agent's notes, and token usage never passed 40% of the window. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The oldest tool results were cut off by the context limit before the report was written up.
The report prompt's concise style led the model to swap numbers for more general wording.
Summaries turned the exact figures into vague wording, which later rounds inherited.
The search tool returned snippets in round 1 that left out the figures from its pages.
questions.explain: Condensing round after round keeps the gist and drops the exact values, so nothing later could quote them. A is ruled out by the usage figure. B fails because the prompt asks for figures, and a model cannot quote what it was not given. D contradicts the raw results, which hold both numbers.
bullets: Progressive summarization turns numbers, percentages, dates and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A support team compresses long chats into a running summary and must decide whether it is safe to ship. Chats average 45 turns, and the amounts, dates and deadlines customers state come back in the agent's later replies. Which evaluation is most informative?
opts: Take the amounts, dates and deadlines from sampled transcripts and check each survives in the summary.
Have a reviewer model rate each summary for readability and tone, and ship when the average is high enough.
Measure how much shorter each summary is than its chat, and ship once summaries are small enough.
Ask the agent at the end of each chat whether it remembers the key details, and count the confident answers.
questions.explain: The risk is lost specifics, so the check has to compare those specifics before and after. B grades style, which a summary can have while losing every figure. C measures size, not content. D relies on the agent's own sense of what it remembers.
bullets: Progressive summarization turns numbers, percentages, dates and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A contract extraction job handles 120-page agreements by summarising each 20-page chunk and then extracting payment terms from the six summaries. The summary prompt already tells the model to keep every amount and notice period exactly. On 20% of contracts, amounts and notice periods still come back as "standard" or "several weeks". Which change to the pipeline fixes this?
opts: Make each chunk summary twice as long, and extract from the longer summaries as before.
Add a check that rejects any extraction containing words such as standard or several.
Summarise the six summaries into one, so all payment terms sit together in a single text.
Extract the payment fields from each chunk directly, and merge the records afterwards.
questions.explain: Values must be read from the source text, not from a condensed version of it. A still extracts from summaries, which keep the gist and lose exact values. B only catches the symptom and has no source to retry from. C summarises a second time and loses more.
bullets: Progressive summarization turns numbers, percentages, dates and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A synthesis step receives 10 subagent reports of about 6,000 tokens each (60,000 in total) in a fixed order and leaves out findings from reports 4 to 7 in about 60% of runs. Engineers disagree on whether the cause is where the reports sit or something about those subagents' content. Which test separates the two explanations?
opts: Compare the length of reports 4 to 7 with the others, since short reports are the easiest to overlook.
Shuffle the report order across runs and see if omissions follow the position or the reports.
Add a sentence telling the model to cover every report, and see whether the omission rate falls.
Ask the model why it left out each finding, and read its explanations for a common cause.
questions.explain: Changing only the order, with the content fixed, shows whether omissions track position. A is a correlation with a possible third cause. C tests a remedy, and a drop would not say why the findings were missed. D relies on explanations the model builds after the fact.
bullets: Models handle the start and end of long inputs reliably but may omit findings from the middle
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A support agent's prompt holds 45 policy articles (about 90,000 tokens) in arbitrary order.
