Rules from the first and last few articles are applied reliably, but rules from the middle of the set are missed in about 40% of the tickets that need them. For each ticket type, the 8 highest-priority articles are known. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Switch to a bigger-window model, so the set fits with plenty of room to spare.
Add an instruction at the start of the prompt saying that every article deserves the same careful reading.
Include the full set twice, so that most rules also appear in a stronger position once.
Open with a short summary of the key rules, and put the highest-priority articles at the start and end.
questions.explain: Content at the edges of a long input is used more reliably, so the rules that matter most should sit there, with a short summary first. A adds room but not attention. B asks for evenness the model does not deliver. C doubles the length, which makes the problem worse.
bullets: Models handle the start and end of long inputs reliably but may omit findings from the middle
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A clause-review agent is given 14 contracts (about 70,000 tokens) in one prompt, built fresh from the files, and asked to list every termination clause. It lists most clauses from the first three and last three contracts but only 2 of the 9 clauses in contracts 6 to 9. The response ended with `stop_reason` "end_turn" after 700 of the 4,096 output tokens allowed, and all contracts use the same file format. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Material in the middle of a long input gets less reliable attention than the start and end.
The report reached its output limit, which cut it off before the later clauses could be written.
The model cannot parse the middle contracts, so it reads them as blank pages.
An earlier summarising step removed those clauses, so they never reached the review prompt.
questions.explain: The input held every contract and the response finished normally with room to spare, which points to position. B contradicts the end_turn stop and the unused output budget. C is unlikely when the format matches the contracts that were read well. D fails because the prompt is built fresh from the files.
bullets: Models handle the start and end of long inputs reliably but may omit findings from the middle
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A billing agent calls `get_account_history` for each customer question. Each call returns 24 months of transactions, about 7,000 tokens, while most questions concern the latest invoice. The system prompt is 600 tokens and replies average 150. After five lookups, replies start missing details from the customer's first message, and each request is about 35,000 tokens larger than at the start. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The system prompt has grown too long for the model to keep the first message in clear view.
Tool results pile up in the history, and most of their tokens bear little on the question.
The model's own replies are long enough to push the customer's first message out of its view.
The API keeps no record of earlier messages, so the first message was never seen again.
questions.explain: Five lookups add about 35,000 tokens, most of it history the question does not need, and the model attends less well as the input grows. A and C are ruled out by the 600 and 150 token figures. D contradicts the growing request size, which shows earlier content is being sent.
bullets: Tool results pile up in context and use tokens out of proportion to their relevance
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A support agent's tool results fill most of its context in long chats, and it uses six tools. The team wants to know which tool to trim first. Which measurement best answers that?
opts: The average latency of each tool call, since slow tools tend to return the largest results.
The number of calls to each tool per chat, since the most called tool adds the most tokens.
Each tool's share of context tokens, set against how many of its fields the replies used.
The agent's own estimate of which tool results it found least useful, collected after each chat.
questions.explain: Trimming pays where many tokens are carried for few used fields, so both numbers are needed. A guesses size from speed. B ignores how large each result is, so a cheap tool called often can outrank a costly one. D depends on the agent's self-report.
bullets: Tool results pile up in context and use tokens out of proportion to their relevance
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A research agent runs for hundreds of turns with six tools. The tool definitions total 2,000 tokens, but early search results that are no longer needed now take over 150,000 tokens of the history. Which approach targets this source of context pressure?
opts: Context editing, which removes old `tool_result` blocks from the conversation history.
Reduce the number of tools from six to three, so the definitions take less of the window.
Summarise the tool definitions into shorter text, so they take less space in each request.
A higher `max_tokens` value, so the model has more room to write after the history has grown.
questions.explain: The weight is in old results, and context editing removes exactly those; it is a beta feature, so check its availability for your platform. B and C shrink tool definitions, which here are only 2,000 tokens. D changes the output limit and leaves the history as large as it was.
bullets: Tool results pile up in context and use tokens out of proportion to their relevance
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A chat service sends only the last six messages with each request. In chats longer than 25 turns, 30% of replies ask for an order number the customer gave in turn 2 or contradict a refund promise the agent made in turn 5. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Raise the window to the last twelve messages, so that most of the early details stay in view.
Instruct the model in its system prompt to keep hold of every number and promise given in the chat.
Ask customers to restate their order number whenever the agent needs to look something up again.
Send the complete conversation history with every request, as the model sees only what it holds.
questions.explain: The model has no memory outside the request, so coherence over 25 turns needs the whole exchange sent. A still drops everything older than twelve messages. B asks the model to remember what it is never shown. C pushes the repair onto the customer.
bullets: Each API request must carry the complete conversation history for the exchange to stay coherent
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A script wraps the Messages API for a coding assistant. For each follow-up it sends the new instruction plus the assistant's latest code block, about 3,000 tokens in all. During a long review the assistant keeps reverting decisions made earlier in the chat, such as agreed `snake_case` naming and a banned library. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The decisions belong in a rules file such as CLAUDE.md, which the script never loads.
Earlier exchanges are absent from each request, so the model cannot see those decisions.
The latest code block is long enough that the model skips the instruction in the new message.
The context window was exceeded, so the model dropped the oldest part of each request.
questions.explain: Each request is all the model has, and the script leaves the earlier turns out. A would help for lasting conventions, but these were agreed in this chat and the model never sees that chat. C is unlikely when the instruction is present in a short request. D cannot apply to requests of about 3,000 tokens.
bullets: Each API request must carry the complete conversation history for the exchange to stay coherent
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: To save tokens, a support harness sends each request with only the customer's messages and the current tool results, leaving out the agent's own earlier replies. Customers report that the agent offers the same goodwill voucher twice and contradicts a deadline it gave earlier. Each request carries the right customer's messages, and tool results are short and correct. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The voucher tool treats a repeated call as a new request, so a second voucher is issued.
A longer system prompt is needed, listing in advance which offers the agent is allowed to make.
The agent cannot see its own earlier commitments, as they are left out of each request.
The tool results are long enough that the model overlooks the earlier voucher record inside them.
questions.explain: The conversation is only as complete as what is sent, and the agent's own turns hold its promises. A blames a tool the evidence does not implicate. B treats the symptom with static text that cannot know what was offered. D contradicts the statement that the results are short.
bullets: Each API request must carry the complete conversation history for the exchange to stay coherent
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A support harness writes a case-facts block (order number, refund 86.40, ticket status) as the first message of the conversation. At turn 30 the conversation is compacted into a summary using a prompt that asks for exact figures. Afterwards the agent asks for the order number again and quotes a refund of "about 90". The block was correct before compaction. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The block sat inside the summarised history, so it was condensed along with everything else.
The summary was too short, and a longer summary would have kept the exact refund amount intact.
The block should have been stored in the tool results, which compaction leaves untouched.
The model stops reading the first message of a conversation once a summary has been created.
questions.explain: A block that lives inside the summarised history is summarised with it, so it belongs in every prompt outside that history. B fails because summaries of any length are lossy, and the prompt already asked for exact figures. C assumes tool results are exempt from summarising, which nothing in the stem supports, and facts kept in the history stay exposed. D has no support either.
bullets: Keeping transactional facts in a persistent case-facts block in each prompt, outside the summarized history
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: In a returns agent, the model rewrites the case-facts block after each turn from its memory of the chat. Amounts must match the order system exactly, yet 4% of recorded refund amounts are transposed or rounded (148.20 stored as 184.20), although each amount appears exactly in a structured `get_order` result. Which fix best removes the errors?
opts: Add a second model call that proofreads the block against the conversation after each update.
Move the block-writing step to a larger model, which copies figures from earlier turns more accurately.
Have the harness copy the amount, date and status fields from each tool result into the block in code.
Tell the model to copy figures exactly and to check each digit twice before it writes the block.
questions.explain: The values already exist as structured fields, so code can carry them across without any chance of a transposition. A and B still depend on a model reproducing digits, which may be right most of the time. D is an instruction, and instructions give only probable compliance.
bullets: Keeping transactional facts in a persistent case-facts block in each prompt, outside the summarized history
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: You are designing the persistent block that a returns agent receives in every prompt, outside the summarised history. Which content belongs in it?
opts: The agent's reasoning for each decision, so later turns can follow why it acted as it did.
Order numbers, amounts, dates and statuses confirmed by tools, kept as short labelled fields.
The full lookup result for each order, so the agent need not fetch the record again.
A paragraph on the customer's mood and the tone of earlier replies, so the agent stays consistent.
questions.explain: The block is for exact transactional facts, which are the first thing a summary blurs. A is reasoning, which grows quickly and is not a fact to preserve. C copies the verbose record, which defeats the purpose of a compact block. D holds soft content that a summary can carry.
bullets: Keeping transactional facts in a persistent case-facts block in each prompt, outside the summarized history
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A team stores structured issue records (order ID, amount, status) in a separate layer for chats in which customers raise three or more problems. They must decide whether it fixes cross-issue mix-ups before rollout. Which evaluation is most convincing?
opts: Check that every stored record validates against its JSON schema in a sample of multi-issue chats.
Replay only single-issue chats with the layer on, because they are the cleanest to score.
Compare the final conversation summary with the stored records and confirm both mention each issue.
Replay multi-issue chats and check each reply's figures against the matching issue's record.
questions.explain: Mix-ups show when a figure from one issue is used for another, so replies must be checked against the matching record. A shows that records are well formed, not that they are correct or used correctly. B leaves out the chats where the failure occurs. C compares two artefacts and never checks a reply.
bullets: Keeping structured issue data in a separate context layer for sessions that raise several issues
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A market-brief agent researches three competitors in one session, alternating between them, and keeps its notes as one running log. Figures sit in tables that are copied forward from turn to turn, and the brief compares the three side by side. In 9% of briefs a figure such as a headcount or contract value is credited to the wrong competitor, although the citations are intact. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Keep a structured record per competitor (metric, value, date) in a layer outside the log.
Ask the agent to name the competitor in every sentence of the log, so that each figure carries its owner.
Research each competitor in its own session, and merge the three finished briefs by hand afterwards.
Reorder the log so each competitor's notes form one block, and tell the model to read block by block.
questions.explain: Separate structured records stop figures from different entities blending. B does not reach the figures, which live in tables rather than sentences. D relies on the model keeping a long log straight, which is the thing that is failing. C gives up the side-by-side comparison the brief needs and adds manual work.
bullets: Keeping structured issue data in a separate context layer for sessions that raise several issues
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: An extraction agent processes 12 supplier invoices of about 8 pages each, one at a time, in one session that must stay under 60,000 tokens while the 12 invoices take about 110,000. By invoice 10 it sometimes attaches line items from invoice 3 to the wrong invoice number. Which design keeps the figures straight?
opts: Keep prose notes on each invoice in the running chat, and summarise them every few invoices.
Track only a running total across the invoices, which is the figure the final report needs.
Keep a record per invoice (number, total, status, items) outside the chat, sent each time.
Send all 12 invoices in full with each request, so every line item is in view at once.
questions.explain: A compact record per invoice carries what later steps need without the pages. A keeps the same prose and loses precision when it is summarised. B drops the per-invoice detail the mix-up is about. D exceeds the stated budget.
bullets: Keeping structured issue data in a separate context layer for sessions that raise several issues
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A lookup tool returns a 6,000-character JSON record per order. An engineer proposes cutting each result to its first 2,000 characters before it enters the context. Tests show that `refund_eligible` and `delivered_on`, which the agent needs, appear after character 3,500 in about a third of records. What is the best approach?
opts: Cut to the first 3,500 characters instead, because that covers the two fields in most of the records.
Keep the proposed cut, and tell the agent to ask for the rest when a field seems to be missing.
Summarise each record with a model call before it enters the context, and keep only that summary text.
Keep named fields only (`refund_eligible`, `delivered_on`, status, total) and drop the rest.
questions.explain: Trimming should keep what the decision needs by field, whatever its position. A still loses the fields in records where they come later and keeps unneeded text. B leaves the agent to notice a gap it cannot see. C adds a lossy model step where a fixed selection would do.
bullets: Trimming verbose tool outputs to the relevant fields before they accumulate in context
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A coding agent runs its test suite through a wrapper that returns all output: 4,000 lines, about 40 of which describe failing tests, interleaved with passing lines in run order. Four such runs fill much of the context. How should the wrapper change what it returns?
opts: Return the last 200 lines, since failures and the summary line are usually printed near the end.
Return the failing test names with their error lines, plus the pass and fail counts.
Return the first 200 lines, and let the agent re-run the suite with a filter if it needs more.
Have the agent summarise the output in its next message, and then ignore the original lines.
questions.explain: The agent acts on failures, so those and the counts are what to keep. A and C keep a slice by position, and with interleaved output most failures fall outside it. D leaves the full output in context, where it still uses the tokens.
bullets: Trimming verbose tool outputs to the relevant fields before they accumulate in context
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: After trimming `get_order` results to five fields, context use dropped by about 85%. Fifteen different other fields have each turned out to matter in 0.1% to 1% of cases, and the agent cannot see them. Which design keeps the saving and handles those cases?
opts: Keep the five-field default, and add an optional parameter for requesting named extra fields.
Restore all 40 fields on every lookup, since a missing field is worse than extra tokens.
Add the fifteen occasionally needed fields to the default set returned by every lookup.
Add a second tool returning the full record, and tell the agent to call it after every lookup.
questions.explain: The default stays small and the agent can ask for the rarely needed field when a case calls for it. B gives back the whole cost. C does the same, to a smaller degree, for fields most cases do not use. D reloads the full record on every lookup, which cancels the trimming.
bullets: Trimming verbose tool outputs to the relevant fields before they accumulate in context
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A reconciliation step receives 40 extracted invoice records (about 30,000 tokens) and must flag mismatches against purchase orders, including payments split across two invoices. An earlier step has already listed the 8 records with a suspected mismatch. The step flags the first and last records reliably but misses about half the mismatches in records 15 to 25. How should you arrange the input?
opts: Shorten the field names in the records, so each record takes fewer tokens.
Send the records in four batches of ten, and merge the flagged results afterwards.
Open with the 8 suspected mismatches, then the records under a header per invoice.
Add a line before the records saying that records in the middle deserve some extra attention.
questions.explain: A summary of key findings up front, with the detail under clear headers, offsets the weak middle of a long input. A trims tokens but leaves the same positions. B cannot catch payments split across invoices that land in different batches. D asks for an attention the model does not reliably give.
bullets: Putting a key-findings summary first and organizing detail under explicit section headers to offset position effects
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: An assistant for human agents receives a customer's case file (about 45,000 tokens of tickets, order notes and chat logs) plus the agent's question: was the customer promised a refund? Which prompt layout works best?
opts: The question first, then the instructions, then the file in creation order with no headers.
The instructions and question first, then the file under headers, and a key-findings summary at the end.
The first half of the file, then the question, then the second half, so the question is not buried.
A key-findings summary first, then the file under headers by record type, then the question last.
questions.explain: Long material goes near the top with its key findings first and organised under headers, and the question closes the prompt. A and B put the question ahead of the data, and A has no structure. B also puts the summary after 45,000 tokens of detail. C splits the file around the question.
bullets: Putting a key-findings summary first and organizing detail under explicit section headers to offset position effects
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A coordinator joins five subagent outputs into one block, each starting with only the word "Findings" and giving no record of its subagent or source locations. In 12% of reports a claim is credited to the wrong source, although every cited source is real. What is the most effective change?
opts: Ask the synthesis agent to double-check each attribution once it has written the report.
Require each output to carry its subagent, topic and sources as labelled sections.
Reduce the number of subagents to three, so that there are fewer outputs to keep apart.
Order the five outputs alphabetically by topic, so that related claims are kept together.
questions.explain: Source locations carried in each output, and labelled sections, let the synthesis tie each claim to its origin. A asks the model to check a distinction it could not see in the first place. C reduces volume and keeps outputs unlabelled. D changes the order and leaves the outputs indistinguishable.
bullets: Requiring subagents to return metadata (dates, source locations, method) in structured outputs for accurate synthesis
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A coordinator combines a billing subagent's "refund: pending" with a shipping subagent's "return: received" and tells a customer that the refund is still pending. It had been paid three days earlier. The billing subagent had read a ledger snapshot that refreshes weekly. What should change?
opts: Require every status in a subagent's output to carry its as-of time and its source system.
Have the coordinator prefer the shipping subagent's status whenever the two statuses seem to disagree.
Add a line to the coordinator's prompt telling it to treat any pending status with caution.
Have the billing subagent repeat its lookup once whenever the result is a pending status.
questions.explain: With as-of time and source attached, the coordinator can see that the status is old and weigh it. B picks a winner by rule and is wrong when billing is right. C is vague advice with nothing to act on. D rereads the same weekly snapshot and returns the same answer.
bullets: Requiring subagents to return metadata (dates, source locations, method) in structured outputs for accurate synthesis
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: You are specifying the structured output of a web research subagent whose findings feed a synthesis agent that must reconcile claims from different sources. Which set of fields supports accurate synthesis?
opts: The claim, a confidence score the subagent gives itself, and a line describing its search strategy.
The claim, the full text of the page it came from, and the subagent's reasoning for choosing it.
The claim, the source URL and a relevance score, leaving dates and method for synthesis to find later.
The claim, its value, the source URL with section, the data date, and how the figure was measured.
questions.explain: Synthesis can compare claims only when each carries where it came from, when it applies and how it was obtained. A relies on self-reported confidence and a strategy line that says little about the figure. B brings back the volume a structured output is meant to remove. C leaves out the metadata that cannot be recovered afterwards.
bullets: Requiring subagents to return metadata (dates, source locations, method) in structured outputs for accurate synthesis
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Two analysis subagents inspect a repository for dead code, and both branches matter to the release. One reports that `parse_legacy` has no callers, the other reports three callers, and each finding is only a function name and a verdict. The main agent, which has no repository access of its own, deletes the function and the release build fails. It later emerges that one subagent searched `main` with grep and the other `release/4` through the compiler's call graph. What should change?
opts: Run both subagents on the same single branch, so that their verdicts agree with each other.
Require each finding to name the branch searched and the method used.
Have the main agent re-run both searches itself whenever the two verdicts differ.
Add a third subagent that casts the deciding vote whenever two verdicts conflict.
questions.explain: The verdicts were both right for what each searched, and the main agent could not see that. Branch and method in each finding let it reconcile them, and the main agent receives only the subagent's final message. A removes the release branch from the analysis. C is impossible without repository access. D adds a vote and still cannot tell which scope each result covered.
bullets: Requiring subagents to return metadata (dates, source locations, method) in structured outputs for accurate synthesis
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: An exploration subagent maps where a deprecated API is used, across 90 files and 140 call sites, and returns the full text of every file it opened, about 35,000 tokens. The main agent has roughly 12,000 tokens of room left, needs each location for its refactor plan, and begins dropping files from it. What is the most effective change?
opts: Have the subagent return a prose summary of each file in place of the file text.
Have the main agent read the returned text in two halves, and plan the whole refactor in two steps.
Have the subagent return a list of file path, line, symbol and relevance score per use.
Ask the subagent to return the same file text with the most important files placed first.
questions.explain: The main agent needs where and how each use occurs, not the file contents. A still returns about 90 summaries in prose, which stay long and may not give exact lines. B splits the plan, so no step sees all the uses. D keeps the volume and just reorders it.
bullets: Having upstream agents return structured data instead of verbose content when downstream agents have small budgets
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: Six research subagents each return 12 structured findings (fact, citation, and a relevance score each subagent assigns by its own judgement), about 3,000 tokens per subagent. The synthesis agent can take in 8,000 tokens. Cutting the combined input at 8,000 tokens drops three subagents entirely. What is the best way to fit the budget?
opts: Cap each subagent at about 1,300 tokens, returning its top-priority findings with citations.
Ask each subagent for a 250-word narrative of its findings in place of the structured items.
Cut the combined input at 8,000 tokens, but shuffle the subagent order each run to spread the loss.
Send the findings in two requests and have the synthesis agent write two reports to be merged.
questions.explain: Each subagent knows its own material, so a capped, prioritised, structured list sized to its share keeps every source represented with citations. B drops the citations and structure that make checking possible. C still throws away whole subagents, just different ones each time. D splits the synthesis and leaves it without a view of all the findings.
bullets: Having upstream agents return structured data instead of verbose content when downstream agents have small budgets
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: You changed research subagents from returning narrative reasoning to returning key facts, citations and relevance scores, because the downstream synthesis budget is small. How should you check that the change did not lose information the reports need?
opts: Compare the token counts of old and new outputs, and accept the change if the new ones are under budget.
Ask the synthesis agent to rate its confidence in each report, and compare the averages before and after.
Read a sample of the new outputs and confirm that they look complete and are easy to read.
Run the same questions under both formats and compare the reports against facts known from the sources.
questions.explain: The outcome that matters is report quality against known facts, measured under both formats. A shows only that the output fits. B uses the agent's self-reported confidence, which is not evidence of accuracy. C checks how the outputs look, and a tidy output can still lack a needed fact.
bullets: Having upstream agents return structured data instead of verbose content when downstream agents have small budgets
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your support agent can refund up to 150 pounds, replace damaged goods and move delivery slots. A manager reviews a day of conversations and asks which one the agent should have handed to a human. Which conversation is it?
opts: A customer returning five items from two orders, all inside the return window, who wants a single refund for both.
A customer whose parcel arrived five days late, who is annoyed and wants the shipping fee back, as the policy allows.
A customer wanting a refund on a laptop bought 11 months ago, outside a 30-day window only a supervisor can waive.
A customer whose replacement request needs three lookups across two systems before the photo can be matched to the order.
questions.explain: The laptop request is a policy exception that only a supervisor can grant, so it belongs with a human. A is intricate but sits fully inside the policy. B comes from an annoyed customer, yet the policy allows the fix. D takes several tool calls and is still within what the agent is allowed to do.
bullets: Escalation triggers: the customer asks for a human, a policy exception or gap, or no meaningful progress (complexity alone is not a trigger)
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: During a ledger outage, a customer's 48 pound refund has failed nine times in 12 minutes: `process_refund` returns "ledger temporarily unavailable" each time, and the agent retries with the same arguments while apologising. The status page says repairs may take hours, no other tool can pay a refund, and store credit needs a supervisor's approval. Which change to the agent's behaviour is most effective?
opts: Escalate to a human with the details and the attempts so far, once repeated tries bring no change.
Retry on a longer schedule, say once a minute, until the ledger answers, and keep the customer posted meanwhile.
Offer store credit for the same amount, since the credit tool still works and the value reaches the customer now.
Tell the customer that the refund cannot be made and ask them to come back once the outage has been fixed.
questions.explain: Nine identical failures with no way forward are a lack of meaningful progress, so the case goes to a person who can decide what to do. B keeps trying a path the status page says is down for hours. C grants a remedy the agent is not allowed to give. D ends the conversation with nobody owning the refund.
bullets: Escalation triggers: the customer asks for a human, a policy exception or gap, or no meaningful progress (complexity alone is not a trigger)
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A customer disputes a billing error. `get_customer` on her name returns three accounts. She says she has no order number to hand and cannot read mail at the address she used. She has refused every identifier the agent has asked for, including the last four digits of her card. Eight turns later the conversation is no closer to one account. What should the agent do?
opts: Take the account whose postcode she remembers best, then ask her to confirm the amount of the disputed charge.
Keep asking for other identifiers one at a time until she gives one that narrows the three accounts.
Hand the case to a human, listing the three candidate accounts and the identifiers already asked for.
End the chat politely and point her to the website, where she can open a ticket and attach documents.
questions.explain: Eight turns with no narrowing is the no-meaningful-progress trigger, so the case needs a person who can verify her another way, and the summary saves them repeating the questions. A is still a heuristic pick, with a weak check on top. B repeats an approach she has refused eight times. D sends her away with nobody owning the dispute.
bullets: Escalation triggers: the customer asks for a human, a policy exception or gap, or no meaningful progress (complexity alone is not a trigger)
Several customer matches call for asking for more identifiers, not for picking one by a heuristic
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A product lead notes that 12 intents, such as address changes and delivery-slot moves, are fixed by the agent in 95% of attempts. She proposes that on these intents the agent always tries the fix first and hands over only after the customer has asked for a person twice. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opts: Adopt it: a 95% success rate means trying first leaves most customers better off, whatever they asked for.
Adopt it, but only for customers whose earlier conversations rated the agent positively.
Reject it, and send all 12 intents straight to a human, since the agent should not touch them alone.
Adopt it for customers who have not asked for a person, and hand over at once when one has asked.
questions.explain: Offering a fix suits straightforward issues when the customer has only shown frustration, but a customer who explicitly asks for a person is owed the handover at once. A overrides stated requests because the odds look good. B filters on past ratings, which says nothing about what this customer asked for. C throws away a 95% fix rate the customers who did not ask for a person would benefit from.
bullets: Escalate at once when the customer explicitly demands a person, but offer to resolve when the issue is straightforward and only frustration was shown
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A quarterly review compares two kinds of chat. In 400 chats the customer vented but did not ask for a person; the agent acknowledged the frustration and offered a fix, and 83% ended without a handover. In 150 chats the customer wrote something like "transfer me" or "get me an agent". Within those 150, the 66 where the agent tried a fix first scored 1.8 out of 5 on satisfaction, against 3.9 for the 84 handed over at once, with the same mix of intents. What do these results most strongly indicate?
opts: Fix attempts need better scripts, because the customers in the second group reacted badly to the wording.
A request for a person should be honoured at once, while venting without one is where a fix is offered.
Both kinds of chat should begin with an offered fix, as the first group shows that offers work for most customers.
The low scores come from harder cases, so they say nothing about how the agent responded to the request.
questions.explain: The same intent mix with a gap of 1.8 against 3.9 points at the response itself: a fix attempt after an explicit request hurts, while an offer after venting works. A blames wording that no result in the stem examines. C ignores that the offers worked in the group that never asked for a person. D is ruled out by the stem, which gives the two sets the same intent mix.
bullets: Escalate at once when the customer explicitly demands a person, but offer to resolve when the issue is straightforward and only frustration was shown
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: An agent's prompt says to hand over at once when a customer explicitly asks for a person, and otherwise to try to resolve the issue. Four customers write in. For which message should the agent hand over immediately, without attempting a fix?
opts: "Third email about this refund and nobody has answered. This is ridiculous."
"Forget the order number. Put me through to an agent now."
"Does a human handle refunds over 500 pounds, or does this bot do it?"
"I have tried this chat three times today and it keeps asking the same question."
questions.explain: Only B is an explicit request for a person. A shows frustration but asks for nothing, so the agent acknowledges it and offers a fix. C asks a question about how refunds work, which the agent can answer. D describes a failing conversation, and the fix is a better answer, not a handover.
bullets: Escalate at once when the customer explicitly demands a person, but offer to resolve when the issue is straightforward and only frustration was shown
Honour an explicit request for a human straight away, without trying to investigate first
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: Your agent escalates when a sentiment score falls below -0.4. QA reviewed 60 cases in which a human was needed, such as exceptions to the returns window, but the agent settled or refused them on its own. In 52 of the 60 the sentiment score was above 0 and the customer was courteous. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Sentiment measures mood, and a polite customer can still ask for what only a human may approve.
The threshold of -0.4 is set too low, so raising it to 0 would also catch the courteous customers.
The sentiment model learned from general text and should be retrained on this company's tickets.
Courteous customers write short messages, and the classifier scores short messages as neutral.
questions.explain: Whether a case needs a person depends on the request, not on how the customer feels, so a mood score misses polite exception requests. B would send every mildly negative chat to humans while the courteous exceptions still pass through. C improves how well mood is measured but not what it tells you. D invents a classifier quirk the stem does not mention.
bullets: Sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable stand-ins for how complex a case really is
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Each agent reply carries a `confidence` field from 1 to 10, and the team plans to escalate below 6. A labelled set of 800 past conversations exists, in which reviewers marked those that needed a human. Before launch, an engineer is asked how to find out whether the score is a usable escalation signal. Which analysis is most informative?
opts: Replay each conversation several times and check that the agent gives the same score on every run.
Ask the agent to explain each score in a sentence, and have reviewers read a sample of the explanations.
Plot how the scores are distributed, and accept the signal if they spread across the whole range of 1 to 10.
Compare the scores with the reviewers' labels, counting cases needing a human that scored 6 or more.
questions.explain: The question is whether the score tracks the need for a person, so it must be set against the reviewers' labels. A tests consistency, and a score can be steady and still wrong. B checks that the explanation reads well, not that the score is right. C shows a spread but not whether the spread follows case difficulty.
bullets: Sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable stand-ins for how complex a case really is
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A customer writes warmly: "Thanks for the help so far! Could you also waive the early-termination fee? I have only had the plan for two months." Sentiment scores +0.8, and the agent rates its own confidence at 9 out of 10. The policy says that early-termination fees are waived only by the retention team. What is the sound basis for the agent's next step?
opts: The positive sentiment: a happy customer will take a polite refusal well, so the agent can decline.
The 9 out of 10 confidence: the agent feels sure, so it should go ahead and grant the waiver.
The policy reserves fee waivers for the retention team, so the agent hands it over.
The two-month tenure: a new customer is a churn risk, so the agent should pass the case on.
questions.explain: The deciding fact is that the policy reserves this exception for another team. A and B both lean on a signal, mood or the agent's own rating, that says nothing about whether the agent may decide. D picks a different proxy, and tenure does not make a request outside policy any more or less so.
bullets: Sentiment and self-reported confidence are unreliable stand-ins for how complex a case really is
Escalation triggers: the customer asks for a human, a policy exception or gap, or no meaningful progress (complexity alone is not a trigger)
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: Customers who write in from a shared household landline are looked up by phone number. `get_customer` often returns two or three records, and the agent takes the one whose first name matches the name given in the chat. In a sample of 500 chats, 17 showed another household member's order details to the caller. Which change is most effective?
opts: Match on first name and the most recent order date together, which narrows the choice to a single record more often.
Ask for an email address or order number whenever more than one record comes back, and look up again.
Show only the order status, not its contents, whenever more than one record matches the phone number.
Have the tool return only the record with the highest relevance score, so the agent never sees the others.
questions.explain: Names typed into a chat are unverified, so the choice needs a detail that tells the records apart, which the customer can supply. A is a heuristic with one more field. C still serves the call from a record picked by guess. D hides the ambiguity inside the tool, so nobody can see the other records exist.
bullets: Several customer matches call for asking for more identifiers, not for picking one by a heuristic
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A research coordinator asks a web-search subagent about "Halden Group's 2025 emissions". The search returns two organisations with that name: a Norwegian shipping firm and a UK care-home chain. The subagent takes the first result and writes a confident section. In 4 of 30 test runs it was the wrong company, and the requester never named a sector. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Return both candidates with details such as country and sector, so the requester can be asked which is meant.
Choose the organisation with the higher search rank, and state the choice and its rank in the report for readers to check.
Research both companies in full and merge the emissions figures into one section that cites both sets of sources.
Choose the organisation that appears in more of the retrieved sources, as that is probably the one the requester meant.
questions.explain: Two real candidates and no deciding fact in the request mean the subagent returns both, with enough detail to tell them apart, to the coordinator, which asks the requester. B keeps the guess and only labels it. C blends two unrelated companies into figures that describe neither. D swaps the first-result heuristic for a popularity one.
bullets: Several customer matches call for asking for more identifiers, not for picking one by a heuristic
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: An extraction pipeline reads the sender's name from forwarded complaint emails and links each to a customer record. When two records share a name, it takes the one whose text is closest to the email. About 3% of cases are filed under the wrong customer, nearly all with names that two records share. Most emails quote an order number in the body. What change is most effective?
opts: Pick the record with the most orders in the last 90 days, since an active customer is more likely to be right.
Link only when the similarity is above 0.95, so that near-ties between two records are rarer.
Run a second pass in which the model chooses between the two records using its own judgment.
When two records match, leave the link empty, read the order number, and queue for review if absent.
questions.explain: When names cannot separate two records, a further identifier has to, and if none is found the case waits for a person instead of being guessed. A swaps one heuristic for another. B does nothing for identical names, which tie at any threshold. C asks the model to guess again with no new fact.
bullets: Several customer matches call for asking for more identifiers, not for picking one by a heuristic
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: Your support agent's prompt says to "escalate complex or sensitive cases". In a review of 300 conversations it escalated 41% of water-damage warranty claims, which the policy lets it settle when the indicator strip is intact, yet it settled warranty-transfer requests that need a supervisor's approval. What change is most effective?
opts: Add a classifier model in front of the agent that predicts which warranty claims need a human to see.
Move to a larger model, which will judge better which warranty claims are complex or sensitive.
Replace the vague wording with explicit criteria and examples of escalate and settle cases.
Repeat the rule in capitals, and add that the agent should escalate only when it is truly necessary.
questions.explain: The agent draws the line in the wrong place in both directions, which points to unclear criteria, and examples that show the boundary fix that most directly. A adds a component before the simple prompt change has been tried. B assumes a bigger model would guess your company's boundary correctly. D adds emphasis, with no new information about where the boundary lies.
bullets: Put explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples in the system prompt, showing when to escalate and when to resolve
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: You are writing the examples for the escalation section of a system prompt. The agent handles refunds, damaged goods and subscription changes, and its worst errors fall on the boundary: requests that look alike but differ in whether the policy covers them. Which set of examples is best?
opts: Six cases that escalate, each for a different reason, so that the agent learns every trigger.
Four look-alike pairs, one covered by policy and one not, each with a one-line reason.
Ten resolved cases of every common type, so that the agent learns what normal handling looks like.
Three cases of angry customers who were escalated, quoting the exact words each customer used.
questions.explain: Pairs that differ only in the deciding fact teach the boundary where the errors occur, and the reason names the rule. A shows only one side, so nothing teaches the agent when to settle. C shows only handling, with no case that crosses the line. D teaches that anger is the trigger, which is not an escalation criterion.
bullets: Put explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples in the system prompt, showing when to escalate and when to resolve
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: After you added six escalation criteria to the prompt, escalations fell from 38% to 31%. QA still finds that in 15% of chats the agent sends refunds below the 150 pound limit to humans "to be safe". The prompt lists the six escalation triggers with one example of each, and nothing else about escalation. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The prompt shows only when to escalate, with no cases to settle, so in-limit refunds still look risky.
Six criteria are more than the agent can apply, so the list should be cut to the three most common triggers.
The limit should be repeated at the top of the prompt, since the agent may overlook it among the criteria.
The agent's confidence in refunds is low, so a confidence threshold would filter out the needless escalations.
questions.explain: The examples all point one way, so the agent has no picture of a case it should settle itself and plays safe. Adding settle examples next to the triggers corrects that. B removes triggers that are working. C assumes the limit is overlooked, which the stem does not suggest. D uses the agent's own rating as the filter, which does not track whether a case needs a human.
bullets: Put explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples in the system prompt, showing when to escalate and when to resolve
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Human agents complain that handovers arrive with little context. A team lead proposes that, when a customer explicitly asks for a person, the agent first runs `get_customer` and `lookup_order` to write a briefing, and then hands over. This adds about 40 seconds. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Adopt it: a better briefing shortens the human's handling time, so the customer is helped sooner overall.
Adopt it, but tell the customer in advance that the briefing will take about 40 seconds.
Reject it: hand over at once with what the conversation holds, and let the human look up the rest.
Adopt it only for customers who have already given an order number, since those lookups tend to succeed.
questions.explain: The customer asked for a person, and every second of investigation first goes against that request; the human can do the lookups with the issue as stated in hand. A trades the customer's wish for the team's convenience. B only announces the delay. D narrows the proposal without changing what it does to a customer who asked for a person.
bullets: Honour an explicit request for a human straight away, without trying to investigate first
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A customer's name returns two accounts. The agent has twice asked for an email address or order number. The customer now writes: "No more questions. Get me a person." What should the agent do?
opts: Ask once more, explaining that the details are needed so that the human can find the right account.
Take the account with the latest order, escalate with it, and mention that the match was a guess.
Say it can still fix the problem if the customer gives one detail, and escalate if they decline.
Escalate now with the issue as stated, noting that two accounts match and neither is confirmed.
questions.explain: The customer has made an explicit request, so the handover happens now, and the open ambiguity travels with it. A and C keep working on the case after the request, only phrased as a favour. B settles the ambiguity by guessing, so the human may start from the wrong account.
bullets: Honour an explicit request for a human straight away, without trying to investigate first
Instruct the agent to ask for extra identifiers when a tool returns several matches, not to choose by heuristics
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: The cancellation prompt says: "Try to keep the customer with a 20% discount offer before any handover." In 130 chats where the customer had written "connect me to an agent", the agent made the offer first, 61% of those customers repeated the request at least once, and satisfaction averaged 2.0 out of 5. How should the prompt change?
opts: Shorten the offer and put it in the same message as the handover notice, so that the customer sees both together.
Hand over at once when the customer asks for a person, and keep the offer for those who have not asked.
Make the offer only once per customer, and hand over if the customer then repeats the request.
Raise the discount to 30% for customers who ask for a person, as a better offer is more likely to hold them.
questions.explain: An explicit request outranks the retention step, which belongs with customers who have only voiced doubt. A still puts an offer in front of the handover. C delays the handover by one more offer. D tries to buy the customer out of the request.
bullets: Honour an explicit request for a human straight away, without trying to investigate first
Escalate at once when the customer explicitly demands a person, but offer to resolve when the issue is straightforward and only frustration was shown
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A customer was charged twice for the same 34.50 pound order and writes: "This is ridiculous. I am sick of this company." The agent can reverse duplicate charges up to 100 pounds with `reverse_charge`, and the customer has not asked for a person. What should the agent do?
opts: Acknowledge the frustration briefly, reverse the duplicate charge and confirm that it is done.
Hand the conversation to a human, because a customer this upset is at risk of leaving.
Explain first how the duplicate happened, to show that the company's process is sound, then reverse it.
Reverse the charge and add a voucher for 20% of the order to show how seriously the company takes it.
questions.explain: The issue is inside the agent's reach, so it acknowledges the feeling and fixes the problem; a handover stays available if the customer asks. B treats mood as a reason to escalate. C puts a defence of the company ahead of the fix. D invents a goodwill policy the business never set.
bullets: Acknowledge frustration and offer a fix within the agent's reach; escalate only if the customer repeats the preference
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: You are writing the prompt rule for customers who say they would prefer a person but have made no request for one, for example "honestly I'd rather talk to someone". In current logs, an agent that hands over on the first such remark gives up on 29% of cases it could have fixed in one tool call. Which rule fits best?
opts: Hand over on the first remark of this kind, since the customer has said what they want.
Offer a fix up to three times, and hand over only if the customer asks a fourth time.
Offer a fix once, and keep offering for as long as the customer's tone becomes less negative.
Acknowledge the frustration and offer a fix once; hand over if the preference is repeated.
questions.explain: A first remark of preference with a fix within reach earns one offer, and a repeat shows the customer means it. A gives up fixable cases. B and C make the customer ask again and again, or wait for their mood to change, before a request is honoured.
bullets: Acknowledge frustration and offer a fix within the agent's reach; escalate only if the customer repeats the preference
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A frustrated customer wants a refund on a blender bought 140 days ago and says the company "never listens". The returns window is 30 days, and the policy says exceptions to the window are decided by a supervisor. What should the agent do?
opts: Acknowledge the frustration, explain the 30-day window and decline, so the customer has a clear answer.
Acknowledge the frustration and offer store credit worth half the price as a goodwill gesture.
Acknowledge the frustration, say the request needs a supervisor's decision, and escalate with a case summary.
Acknowledge the frustration and offer troubleshooting for the blender before anything is decided on the refund.
questions.explain: Acknowledging the feeling is right, but this request is an exception that only a supervisor may decide, so it goes up with a summary. A makes the supervisor's decision for them. B invents a remedy outside policy. D offers a fix for a problem the customer did not raise.
bullets: Acknowledge frustration and offer a fix within the agent's reach; escalate only if the customer repeats the preference
Escalation triggers: the customer asks for a human, a policy exception or gap, or no meaningful progress (complexity alone is not a trigger)
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: The returns policy covers sending back a whole bundle unopened, and sending back a single unopened item from a bundle. It says nothing about bundles that have been partly used. In a pilot the agent approved 52% of requests to return a partly used bundle and refused 48%, with no pattern by price, customer or tone, and QA judged about half the rulings wrong. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Sampling randomness: at a lower temperature the agent would give the same ruling on similar requests.
The policy is silent on these requests, so the agent improvises rulings that differ per chat.
The agent weighs the customer's tone, so calmer customers get refusals and anxious ones get approvals.
The policy search returns the unopened-bundle clause first, so the agent applies it to used bundles.
questions.explain: Requests the policy does not address leave the agent to decide for itself, and that gives the inconsistent rulings seen; such requests should go to a person who owns the policy. A would at best make the improvisation consistent. C is ruled out by the stem, which finds no pattern by tone. D would produce steady approvals, not an even split.
bullets: Escalate when policy is ambiguous or silent on the specific request
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: The subscription policy covers cancelling and refunding a month. A customer on parental leave asks to pause for three months and keep her price. The policy says nothing about pausing, and no tool exists for it, though the agent can cancel and resubscribe. What should the agent do?
opts: Escalate to a human with the request, noting that the policy does not address pausing.
Cancel now and resubscribe in three months, treating a pause as a cancellation with a return.
Decline, because the policy only describes cancelling and refunding, so a pause is not on offer.
Offer 50% off for the three months, which gives her most of the benefit of a pause.
questions.explain: A request the policy neither allows nor forbids is a gap that a person must settle. B stretches cancel and resubscribe into something the policy never promised, including her price. C turns silence into a refusal. D invents a discount.
bullets: Escalate when policy is ambiguous or silent on the specific request
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: After you added "escalate when the policy does not address the request", escalations rose from 12% to 37%. In a sample of 100 escalations, 70 were for requests that the policy does cover, in sections near its end. The policy runs to 9,000 characters, and the log shows that the string `get_policy` returns to the agent is 2,000 characters long. What is the root cause?
opts: The criterion is too broad, so the agent should escalate only when it also reports low confidence.
The agent treats unfamiliar wording as a gap, so the criterion needs examples of true gaps.
A model cannot recognise a policy gap by reading the policy, so the criterion should be dropped.
The tool gives the agent only part of the policy, so covered requests look unaddressed.
questions.explain: A gap can be judged only against the whole policy, and the agent sees under a quarter of it, so covered requests look like gaps. A adds an unreliable signal to a criterion that is working as written. B would be worth doing if the agent saw the full text, but the evidence points at the truncated result. C drops a criterion the guide recommends.
bullets: Escalate when policy is ambiguous or silent on the specific request
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Customers who write from a shared company mailbox are looked up with `search_orders(email)`, which can return up to eight orders. The agent's prompt says to "pick the most plausible order", and 6% of refunds go to the wrong order. The orders belong to different employees and are private to each, and the customer is available in the chat to reply. Which rewrite of the instruction is best?
opts: List all the returned orders to the customer and ask which is theirs, then act on that choice.
Pick the most plausible order, tell the customer which one was chosen, and ask them to confirm.
If several orders come back, ask for the order number or the item and delivery date, then act.
Use only the most recent order from the shared mailbox, since it is the one most likely to be open.
questions.explain: With several matches the agent asks for a detail that tells the orders apart and acts only when one fits. A reads every order on the mailbox out to whoever is in the chat, including other people's. B keeps the guess and asks the customer to approve it. D swaps the guess for a simpler rule.
bullets: Instruct the agent to ask for extra identifiers when a tool returns several matches, not to choose by heuristics
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Two records for "Priya Raman" differ in email address and order history but share name and postal address. The agent's prompt tells it to ask for additional identifiers when several records match, and in 41% of these cases it asks for "your full name and address", then asks again, and the customer abandons the chat. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The identifiers it asks for are ones both records share, so the answer cannot narrow the match.
It asks too early, and should first try to infer the right record from the customer's earlier messages.
Asking for any identifier feels like an interrogation, so these cases should go to a human at once.
The tool should return only the most recent record, so the agent has no need to ask the customer.
questions.explain: Asking is right, but the identifiers must be ones that differ between the records, such as email or recent order details; name and address cannot separate these two. B goes back to guessing. C escalates a case that one good question can resolve. D hides the second record and brings back the original mistake.
bullets: Instruct the agent to ask for extra identifiers when a tool returns several matches, not to choose by heuristics
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A developer works in Claude Code with an MCP tool `find_service`. For "billing" it returns three services: billing-api, billing-worker and billing-ui. In about 1 of 4 sessions the agent edits the first one, often the wrong one. You are adding one line to CLAUDE.md. Which line is best?
opts: When a lookup returns several candidates, guess the one that seems closest to the task and say which.
When a lookup returns several candidates, list them and ask which one is meant before editing anything.
When a lookup returns several candidates, edit all of them and then remove the changes that were not needed.
When a lookup returns several candidates, deny edits to all of them until a hook approves the target.
questions.explain: Several equal matches and an interactive developer make a short question the cheapest way to get the right target. A is still a guess, only announced. C makes unwanted edits and relies on cleaning up afterwards. D builds a hook for a case where asking one question settles it.
bullets: Instruct the agent to ask for extra identifiers when a tool returns several matches, not to choose by heuristics
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A patent-search subagent queried one index with an 800-term boolean string, with the terms joined by OR. The index refused it, and the subagent returned: failure type `query_too_complex`, the query it sent, the 12 hits it had gathered from the first 60 terms, and a note that the same index accepts at most 100 terms per query. The coordinator must pick its next step. Which is the best one?
opts: Re-run the same query on the same index in case the refusal was temporary, then use the 12 hits if it fails again.
Give up on this index, drop the 12 hits because they came from an incomplete query, and rely on the other subagents.
Send a new subagent the same 800-term query with a longer timeout, so that the index has time to process it.
Split the query into groups of at most 100 terms, run each on the same index, and merge with the 12 hits.
questions.explain: The failure type and the stated limit show that the cause is the shape of the query, so a modified query on the same source is the intelligent recovery, and the partial hits stay useful. A repeats an attempt that cannot work. B discards usable results and a reachable source. C changes the timeout, which is not what was refused.
bullets: Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator recover intelligently
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A support coordinator runs a billing subagent and a shipping subagent for a customer asking "why was I charged twice and where is my parcel?". The billing subagent reports failure type `ledger_timeout`, the account it queried, and no results. The shipping subagent returns a full tracking history. What should the coordinator do?
opts: Answer the parcel part now, say the charge check is open, and retry the ledger for that account.
Hold the whole reply until billing succeeds, so the customer receives one complete answer.
Tell the customer both parts are unavailable, and offer to hand the case to a person right away.
Treat the missing billing result as proof that no duplicate charge exists, and answer on that basis.
questions.explain: The context says what failed and for which account, so the coordinator can use the part that worked and make a targeted retry for the rest. B and C let one failed subagent block or misreport work that succeeded. D reads a failure as a finding.
bullets: Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator recover intelligently
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: An extraction coordinator sends 40-page contracts to a reader subagent. For one contract the subagent returns fields from pages 1 to 37, plus a failure record: pages 38 to 40, failure type `no_text_layer`, tried: text extraction twice. The coordinator currently marks the contract failed and re-queues all 40 pages. How should recovery work instead?
opts: Raise the retry count for text extraction on this contract, since two attempts did not settle it.
Keep the 37 pages' fields and send only pages 38 to 40 to a path that can read scanned images.
Store the 37 pages' fields as the final record and mark the contract complete to avoid more cost.
Re-queue all 40 pages to a second reader subagent, to check that the first one read pages 1 to 37 correctly.
questions.explain: The record gives a failure type, the scope of the failure and the work already done, so the coordinator can redo only the missing part by a different route. A repeats an approach that the failure type says cannot work. C hides a gap in the record. D repeats finished work.
bullets: Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator recover intelligently
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A coordinator sent two subagents to check a regulator's enforcement database and a court-records site for a named company. Subagent 1 returns status `ok`, 0 matches, and the three queries it ran. Subagent 2 returns status `failed`, failure type `access_denied`, 0 matches. How should the coordinator treat them?
opts: Both as unknown, because neither produced a match to cite in the report.
Subagent 1 as a finding of none, and subagent 2 as a source still to cover another way.
Both as findings of absence, since either way the company has no matches in the sources checked.
Subagent 2 as a finding of absence, and subagent 1 as unreliable until it repeats its three queries.
questions.explain: A query that ran and found nothing is a real result, while a source that refused access has told the coordinator nothing about the company. A and C erase the difference between those two. D reverses it.
bullets: Access failures that need a retry decision differ from valid empty results (a successful query with no matches)
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A support coordinator looks up warranty cover through a subagent. For customers whose products are outside every warranty programme, the subagent returns an empty list with status `ok`. The coordinator's own retry code fires whenever a subagent returns an empty list, so it then spends three more subagent calls on a different search. These extra calls appear in 30% of conversations and never change the answer. What is the most effective change?
opts: Raise the subagent's timeout so that slow lookups finish before the coordinator's retry code runs.
Have the subagent return a confidence value, which the coordinator uses to skip the extra search.
Fire the coordinator's retry on `status: failed`, and treat an empty `ok` list as the answer.
Cap the coordinator at one extra subagent call per conversation, whatever the status says.
questions.explain: An `ok` status with an empty list is a complete answer for an uncovered product, so retries belong to failures only. A targets slowness, but the lookups here finished with status `ok`. B adds a self-reported number to a distinction the status already makes. D lowers the waste but still retries real answers and still allows one retry on a failure.
bullets: Access failures that need a retry decision differ from valid empty results (a successful query with no matches)
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A research subagent reports two problems to the coordinator. Problem 1: the news archive timed out after 30 seconds on a broad query. Problem 2: the licensed journal service answered `access_denied` for a subscription the team does not hold. Which retry decision for the coordinator is best?
opts: Retry problem 1 with a narrower query, and use another source for problem 2.
Retry both with the same query, because the coordinator cannot know which failures will clear.
Retry problem 2 with a longer timeout, and treat problem 1 as a gap because it already failed once.
Treat both as gaps and stop, because the subagent already used its attempts on them.
questions.explain: A timeout may clear with a changed attempt, while a denied subscription will not clear by repeating it, so the failure types point to different decisions. B ignores the types. C swaps them. D stops although problem 1 has an obvious modified attempt left.
bullets: Access failures that need a retry decision differ from valid empty results (a successful query with no matches)
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A literature-review coordinator receives `{"status": "search unavailable"}` from a subagent whenever any of its three databases fails, and in 27% of runs the final report drops that topic entirely. A sample of the failures shows that 40% were paywall or `access_denied` errors, which fail the same way on every retry, and the rest were timeouts. Which change is most effective?
opts: Add an instruction telling the coordinator to retry any topic whose status is `search unavailable`.
Switch the subagent to a larger model, which will better judge what went wrong before replying.
Raise the subagent's timeouts so that fewer databases fail in the first place.
Return the failure type, the database and query tried, and any results already gathered.
questions.explain: With context, the coordinator can retry the timeouts, switch database for the paywalls, and keep results already found. A retries all of them blindly, and the 40% never clear. B gives a model more to guess about without the facts. C reduces how often timeouts occur but leaves every remaining failure opaque.
bullets: A generic status such as 'search unavailable' hides context the coordinator needs
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A support coordinator gets `Order system error` from the order subagent, which has already retried each call three times with backoff before returning it. The coordinator escalates every such case to a human, 41% of tickets, and the escalation policy matches what the support team wrote. A sample shows 60% of the cases were a deploy window that ended minutes later, and 40% were permanent (cancelled orders, missing permissions). What is the root cause of the over-escalation?
opts: The coordinator's escalation policy is stricter than it should be for order problems.
The message cannot tell the coordinator a deploy window that clears from a failure that does not.
The order service deploys too often, and its schedule should be moved to quieter hours.
The order subagent should retry for several minutes before reporting, so the message is never needed.
questions.explain: One message covers transient and permanent failures, so escalating every case is the only safe choice for the coordinator. A contradicts the stem, since the policy matches the support team's. C addresses frequency while the missing signal stays. D keeps the customer waiting for the 40% that never clear and still returns an opaque message.
bullets: A generic status such as 'search unavailable' hides context the coordinator needs
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A trace-review team notes that the final report often says "market-size data unavailable" with no cause. They propose that the subagent keep the generic message but write the details to its log file, which engineers can open. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Accept it: the details are kept, and engineers can find the cause when they review the run.
Reject it: the live recovery decision needs the details in what comes back, not in a log.
Accept it, provided the log also records the time of each failure for later analysis.
Reject it, and rerun the subagent in case a later final message shows the cause.
questions.explain: The coordinator decides whether to retry, switch source or report a gap while the run is live, from what the subagent returns, so the details belong in that message.
