A and C help later review but not that decision. D reruns the subagent in the hope of a different message, when the details could simply be returned.
bullets: A generic status such as 'search unavailable' hides context the coordinator needs
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: An invoice pipeline's page reader catches every exception and returns a blank record for that page so the batch continues. Month-end reconciliation finds 5% of invoices with a blank total, and each had gone through with status `done`. Which change addresses the cause?
opts: Add a nightly job that scans for blank totals and re-queues those invoices for the reader.
Ask the downstream agent to ignore invoices whose total is blank when it prepares the monthly figures.
Return a failure record with the type, page and partial fields, and mark the invoice as incomplete.
Have the reader retry each page five times before it returns a blank record.
questions.explain: The blank record converts a failure into a success, so nothing downstream can know a page was lost. Reporting the failure with its context fixes that at the source. A repairs some losses after the fact and leaves the status misleading. B hides the loss from the figures. D delays the same blank result for pages that never succeed.
bullets: Silently turning errors into empty successes, and ending a whole workflow on one failure, are both anti-patterns
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A coordinator runs five source-specific subagents in parallel, each about 90% done after 20 minutes. The patent subagent hits a licence error. The coordinator cancels the other four and ends the run with no report. This happens in 22% of runs. What is the best design?
opts: Retry the patent subagent from the start before cancelling the others, to see if the error clears.
Wait for the other four to finish, then stop the run, because one missing source makes any report incomplete.
Cancel the others as now, but store their partial work for a manual restart later.
Let the four finish, record the patent failure with its cause, and build the report with that gap marked.
questions.explain: One source failing is a coverage problem, not a reason to discard finished work from four others. A retries a licence error that repeating will not fix. B and C still produce no report for the reader. D delivers a report that is usable and honest about what is missing.
bullets: Silently turning errors into empty successes, and ending a whole workflow on one failure, are both anti-patterns
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: In a code review for your research agent, a colleague adds a wrapper around every subagent call: `try: return run() except Exception: return []`. They say the report stays clean because failures no longer interrupt the run. How should you evaluate it?
opts: Accept it: the coordinator can still run its checks on the lists it receives from each subagent.
Accept it, if the wrapper writes the exception to a log so that engineers can find the failures later.
Reject it, and instead stop the whole run on the first exception so no failure goes unnoticed.
Reject it: a failed call becomes an empty success, so the report may claim there is nothing to find.
questions.explain: An empty list is how a source with no matches looks, so the wrapper hides failures from everything that reads the result. A assumes the checks can see a difference the wrapper removed. B records it where the coordinator cannot use it. C swaps one anti-pattern for the other by ending everything on a single failure.
bullets: Silently turning errors into empty successes, and ending a whole workflow on one failure, are both anti-patterns
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: You are writing the output format for a web-search subagent in a multi-agent research system, so that the coordinator can recover on its own when a search fails. Which failure record should the subagent return?
opts: `failure_type`, `source`, `query_attempted`, `partial_results`, and `alternatives` to try.
`failure_type`, `source`, `query_attempted`, and `alternatives`, with partial results left in the log.
`failure_type`, `source`, `query_attempted`, `partial_results`, and a `confidence` between 0 and 1.
`status: "failed"`, `source`, `query_attempted`, `partial_results`, and `alternatives`.
questions.explain: These fields cover what failed, what was tried, what survives, and where to go next, which are the decisions the coordinator must make. B leaves the surviving results out of what comes back. C swaps the alternatives for a self-reported number that suggests no next step. D has only a generic status, so the coordinator cannot tell a timeout from a denied subscription.
bullets: Return structured error context: failure type, what was attempted, partial results, possible alternatives
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A support subagent checks eight order IDs against a shipping API. After 6 succeed it hits a throttle and returns `{"failure_type": "throttled", "query": "order 7"}`. The coordinator re-runs all eight IDs, which costs extra API calls and re-triggers the throttle in 15% of runs. What is the missing piece?
opts: The six lookups that succeeded, so that the coordinator re-runs only the order IDs left.
A longer delay, which the subagent should wait before it returns the failure to the coordinator.
A confidence score for the six lookups, so the coordinator can decide whether to trust them.
A field naming the model that ran the subagent, so the coordinator can retry with another.
questions.explain: The record shows what failed but not what was done, so the coordinator cannot avoid repeating finished work. B moves the same limit later without saving anything. C and D add information that does not change which IDs remain.
bullets: Return structured error context: failure type, what was attempted, partial results, possible alternatives
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A research system has three layers: a search subagent, the coordinator, and a synthesis subagent. The search subagent returns failure type `paywall`, the query, and 3 partial results. The coordinator passes the synthesis agent only "search partly failed" plus the results. The final report states 3-source findings as complete. Where was the context lost?
opts: In the search subagent, whose failure record was missing a field for the number of sources.
In the synthesis subagent, which should have inferred the gap from the shortage of results.
In the report format, which needs a longer summary section to fit every failure in.
In the coordinator, which summarised the record and did not pass the fields on.
questions.explain: The search subagent supplied everything; the coordinator compressed it into a phrase, so the next layer could not tell what was missing. A is contradicted by the record in the stem. B asks the agent to guess from absence. C treats it as a space problem while the fields were never passed on.
bullets: Return structured error context: failure type, what was attempted, partial results, possible alternatives
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A coordinator is compiling a prior-art brief from six source subagents. Four report `status: ok` with 0 results after three phrasings each, one reports `ok` with 3 results, and one reports `failed` with failure type `timeout`. The brief must state which sources found nothing. What should the coordinator do next?
opts: Re-run all six with broader queries, since an empty result might hide a hit.
Retry only the timed-out source, narrowed, and report the four empty `ok` sources as searched, no hits.
Report the timed-out source as having no hits too, since five of six sources agree there is little to find.
Hold the brief and escalate to a person until every source returns at least one result.
questions.explain: The four empty results are complete answers, and only the timeout is a failure with a sensible modified retry. A repeats searches that succeeded. C turns an unsearched source into a finding. D treats a valid empty result as a fault and blocks the brief for no reason.
bullets: Report access failures and valid empty results differently so the coordinator can decide appropriately
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A contract-review coordinator asks a subagent to find indemnity clauses in 30 contracts. It reports 0 clauses for 4 contracts, all with `status: ok`. A reviewer opens them and finds two are scanned images, whose text extraction returned an empty string, and that the other two have no indemnity clause. What is the best change?
opts: Add a rule that any contract with 0 clauses is sent to a person, whatever the cause.
Have the subagent run extraction a second time for contracts with 0 clauses, then report the result.
Report an unreadable document as a failure with its type; keep `ok` and 0 for readable ones.
Give the subagent a larger context window, which will let it read more of each contract.
questions.explain: The subagent has to say whether it could read the document, since 0 clauses is only a finding when the text was read. A hands people the contracts that really have none and does not name the cause. B repeats an extraction that gives the same empty string. D addresses length when the contract had no text.
bullets: Report access failures and valid empty results differently so the coordinator can decide appropriately
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Before release you must show that your research system tells a source that was unreachable from a source with no matches. How should you evaluate it?
opts: Compare the length of reports from a run with all sources up against a run with one source down.
Ask the coordinator at the end of each run how confident it is that no sources were missed.
Time out one source, seed another with no matches, and check the report words them apart.
Run the system on 200 live topics and check that none finishes with an unhandled exception.
questions.explain: Injecting both conditions deliberately checks the distinction directly, with known ground truth. A depends on report length, which can change for other reasons. B uses the agent's own confidence. D shows that nothing crashed, which a system that swallows failures would also pass.
bullets: Report access failures and valid empty results differently so the coordinator can decide appropriately
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A journal-search subagent is assigned to peer-reviewed sources, and the coordinator tracks which source types are covered. Its journal API times out after backoff retries and one try on the publisher's mirror. It can also reach a general web search tool. What should it do?
opts: Switch to the web search and return its results as if they came from journals, so coverage is complete.
Return the failure with the attempts made and the partial results, for the coordinator to act on.
Keep retrying the journal API until it answers, since the coordinator is waiting for journal results.
Return an empty result set with status `ok`, because no peer-reviewed article was found.
questions.explain: The subagent has done its local recovery for this source, and which other source type to use is a coverage decision that belongs to the coordinator, so the failure goes up with what is needed to decide. A changes the source type and hides it. C has no end and blocks the coordinator. D reports a failure as no matches.
bullets: Subagents recover locally from transient failures and propagate only what they cannot resolve, with attempts and partial results
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A search subagent makes three attempts in all at each failed request, spacing the attempts as the API's documentation advises, then reports the failure type and the three attempts to the coordinator. The coordinator re-runs the failed subagent call up to three times. Against a rate-limited API, logs show nine identical requests for each outage, and the API blocks the key for an hour in 12% of outages. What is the root cause?
opts: The coordinator's retry count is too high for the allowance the API gives one key.
The subagent's three attempts are more than the API tolerates in a single outage.
The API is shared with other teams, so the block comes from their traffic and not from this system.
The coordinator repeats the same call blindly although the report shows it was exhausted.
questions.explain: The subagent's attempts are the local recovery, and its report says they were used up. The coordinator should act on that, with a changed query or another source, and not repeat the call. A and B adjust numbers inside a pattern that multiplies. C blames outside traffic although the log shows nine identical requests from this system.
bullets: Subagents recover locally from transient failures and propagate only what they cannot resolve, with attempts and partial results
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A news subagent runs ten queries, retries two failures with backoff and gives up on a third after a refused connection, writing each attempt in its tool calls. The coordinator's next step is wrong each time: it re-queries the same host, because the only thing it received was "1 query failed". What should change?
opts: The subagent's final message should state the failed query, the host, what it tried, and the results so far.
The coordinator should read the subagent's tool calls to see what was attempted before it chooses the next step.
The subagent should write its attempts to a shared file that the coordinator is told to open.
The subagent should stop after the first failure and let the coordinator decide whether to retry.
questions.explain: The coordinator receives the subagent's final message, and its tool calls stay inside the subagent, so whatever must inform the next step has to be in that message. B assumes tool calls are returned to the parent, but only the final message is. C adds a channel for something one message can carry. D drops local recovery for failures that backoff would clear.
bullets: Subagents recover locally from transient failures and propagate only what they cannot resolve, with attempts and partial results
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A synthesis agent builds a report on seven topics. Sources for topic 5 were unavailable (the licensed database was denied and the archive timed out), and the other six are well covered by 3 to 5 sources each. Which output is best?
opts: Leave topic 5 out, so that every section of the report is supported and the report reads consistently.
Write topic 5 from the model's background knowledge, marked with a footnote that no source was found.
Include topic 5 with a coverage note: no findings, sources unavailable, and the failures behind it.
Place a single line at the start of the report saying that coverage may be incomplete for some topics.
questions.explain: The reader should see which part is supported and which is a gap, with the reason. A removes the gap from view. B fills it with content that has no source behind it. D warns generally and does not say which topic or why.
bullets: Structure synthesis output with coverage annotations: well-supported findings versus gaps from unavailable sources
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: Reviewers of a research report say every section reads equally confident. Run logs show sections 2 and 6 rest on one source each because the other sources timed out, while the rest cite four or more. Which change to the synthesis output fixes this?
opts: Add a coverage field to each finding: how many sources support it and which were unavailable.
Have the synthesis agent give each finding a confidence percentage, based on how sure it feels.
Remove findings supported by a single source, so that every statement in the report is well supported.
Move the failed-source list to a final appendix, which readers can consult if they want to.
questions.explain: The annotation travels with each finding, so a reader sees which findings are thin and why. B uses a self-reported number that does not reflect the sources. C removes true information instead of labelling it. D separates the gaps from the findings they affect.
bullets: Structure synthesis output with coverage annotations: well-supported findings versus gaps from unavailable sources
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: A synthesis agent ends its brief on seven topics with the line "All 7 topics covered". Topics 3 and 6 rest on partial subagent results because the archive and a licensed database failed, and each carries `status: partial` in the data the agent received. A reader finds the gaps a month later. Which closing line is best?
opts: State how many topics were covered and an average coverage percentage across all seven.
List the topics that rest on full results, and email the two partial topics to the author separately.
Say all 7 topics are covered, since each topic's `status: partial` is already shown in its section.
Name the 5 fully supported topics, mark topics 3 and 6 as partial, and give each failed source.
questions.explain: The closing line must separate supported topics from gaps and give the reason, because readers act on it first. A averages the gap away. B moves the warning out of the brief. C keeps the headline claim and leaves the gap to a field that the closing line contradicts.
bullets: Structure synthesis output with coverage annotations: well-supported findings versus gaps from unavailable sources
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A developer spends four hours in one Claude Code session mapping a billing service. In the first hour the agent named `LedgerReconciler` and `RetryPolicyV2` and said tax is computed in `InvoiceBuilder`. By hour four, after 300 turns, it says "a repository class typically handles this" and places tax calculation in a different module. `/context` shows 78% used, mostly file reads and command output. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The repository index went stale as files changed, so searches now return generic matches.
Hours of tool output bury the earlier findings, so answers drift toward generic patterns.
`CLAUDE.md` stopped loading after the first hour, so the class names are no longer visible.
The model's sampling temperature rises as a session grows, which makes its answers vary more.
questions.explain: Accuracy and recall fall as the accumulated context grows, so specifics found early give way to generic wording and contradictions. A invents an index; Claude Code searches the files directly. C is wrong because the project-root CLAUDE.md is re-injected from disk after compaction. D describes a setting that does not change during a session.
bullets: Context degradation in long sessions: inconsistent answers and generic 'typical patterns' instead of specific classes found earlier
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: In a long session an agent says unit tests for `payments/` live under `tests/unit/`, while a colleague insists they sit in `payments/tests/`. The engineer suspects the search tooling. The session is at hour six with about 60% of the context in use. Which check best separates a tooling fault from context degradation?
opts: Ask the same question again in this same session and see whether the answer changes at all.
Ask the agent to rate its confidence in the answer on a scale of 1 to 10, then compare.
Ask the same question in a fresh session on the same checkout and compare the answers.
Run the agent's search command by hand and check that it returns results at all.
questions.explain: A fresh session has the same tools and the same files but none of the accumulated history, so a specific, correct answer there points to the long context. A repeats the question inside the same context, which proves little. B uses self-reported confidence, which is not evidence. D shows the command runs, not whether the agent still uses its results well.
bullets: Context degradation in long sessions: inconsistent answers and generic 'typical patterns' instead of specific classes found earlier
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A research team runs a 1M-token model and argues that context degradation cannot affect them: their agent sessions peak at 40% of the window. Yet in 25-turn runs over 40 sources, the agent now says "industry sources generally agree" where it earlier named six analyst reports. How should the team read this?
opts: Quality holds steady until the window is nearly full, so the search tool must be at fault.
The effect appears only after compaction, so switching compaction off will restore the specifics.
A window this large removes the effect, so the source list must be confusing the agent.
Accuracy and recall can fall as content builds up, well below the limit, so curate context.
questions.explain: The docs tie degradation to growing token count, not to hitting the limit, so curating what stays in context matters at 40% too. A assumes a cliff at the limit and blames a tool without evidence. B ties the effect to compaction, but the run never compacted. C treats a larger window as a cure; it only changes where the limit sits.
bullets: Context degradation in long sessions: inconsistent answers and generic 'typical patterns' instead of specific classes found earlier
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: An agent is finding every authentication call site in a 600-file monorepo and expects the session to run for hours. The developer wants the confirmed sites to survive context turnover. Which approach is most effective?
opts: Have the agent append each confirmed site (file, symbol, status) to a notes file as it goes.
Ask the agent for one full summary of all confirmed sites once the exploration has finished.
Record the confirmed sites in `CLAUDE.md`, so that every later session starts with them.
Keep the sites in the conversation and rely on the model's large context window to hold all of them.
questions.explain: A file written as findings appear is on disk, so compaction does not affect it, and a new session can read it. B writes everything at the end, after the earlier findings may already have been summarised away. C puts task findings in a file meant for standing rules, which every later task would then load. D leaves the findings inside the context that degrades.
bullets: Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A research agent keeps `notes/findings.md` and has 85 correct entries by turn 60. In a final check, it states a market figure that contradicts entry 31. The tool log shows the agent called Read on the notes file at turn 1, when it was empty, and wrote to it at turns 12, 19 and 33 only. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The notes were kept in Markdown rather than JSON, so the agent was unable to use the entries.
The agent wrote the file but never read it back, so the entries did not reach its context.
Files written during a session are lost from disk when the context is later compacted away.
An 85-entry file is too large for the Read tool to return in one call, so it was cut off.
questions.explain: A scratchpad helps only when its contents are brought back into context; here the only Read happened when the file was empty. A blames the format, although Markdown notes are fine. C is wrong because files on disk are not part of the conversation and stay put. D invents a limit that 85 short entries would not reach.
bullets: Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: After three hours mapping a legacy order system, a developer wants the agent's scratchpad to be useful to a colleague who picks up tomorrow. Which kind of entry is most useful?
opts: The full text of each file the agent read, so nothing is lost between sessions.
A running prose guess about the overall design, updated whenever the agent changes its mind.
Confirmed facts with file paths and symbol names, plus a list of questions still open.
A log of every command the agent ran, in order, with its raw output.
questions.explain: Specific, checkable facts with locations, plus open questions, give a reader what the agent would otherwise have to rediscover. A copies the files back into context, which defeats the purpose. B keeps the vague, generic wording that degradation produces. D records activity instead of conclusions and would fill context again.
bullets: Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A developer asks the main agent which of 14 nightly load-test runs regressed. Each run prints about 6,000 lines of timing tables. After reading all of them in the main conversation, the agent forgets the 5% regression threshold agreed earlier and flags runs the team had already accepted. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Run `/clear` before the comparison starts, then paste the agreed threshold back in afterwards.
Limit each read to the first 200 lines of a run so that less text enters the context window.
Move to a model with a bigger window, and carry on reading every run in the main chat.
Delegate the comparison to a subagent that returns the regressed runs and their deltas.
questions.explain: The timing tables stay in the subagent's context, and only the short result returns, so the threshold stays in view. A throws away the session along with the noise. B drops lines that may hold the regression. C keeps the bulk in the main context, only moving the limit.
bullets: Subagents isolate verbose exploration output while the main agent keeps high-level understanding
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A team is moving a 1,200-file legacy application to a new framework. The lead wants the main agent to keep the overall picture and make design decisions throughout a two-day effort. Which structure fits best?
opts: The main agent keeps a module map and decisions; a subagent per module returns a short summary.
The main agent reads each module in turn and runs `/clear` between modules to keep the context small.
One subagent explores the whole application and returns everything it found for the main agent to use.
The main agent reads all modules itself, and subagents are used only to make the edits afterwards.
questions.explain: The module reads stay in subagent contexts, and the main agent holds the map, decisions and summaries. B clears the map with each module. C returns an application-sized report into the main context and loses the isolation. D leaves the verbose reading where it does the most harm.
bullets: Subagents isolate verbose exploration output while the main agent keeps high-level understanding
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: A research coordinator spawns subagents that each read about 200,000 tokens of company filings. After the first subagent finishes, the coordinator's own context has grown by 28,000 tokens, and after four the coordinator is losing track of the overall plan. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Subagent contexts are merged into the coordinator's when a subagent finishes.
The subagents should have run in parallel, because sequential runs keep results longer in context.
The coordinator should have read the filings itself so that nothing gets compressed.
Each subagent's final message was long, and only that message enters the coordinator's context.
questions.explain: Isolation holds only if what comes back is short: the final message is the one thing the coordinator receives, so a long report brings the bulk back in. A is false; contexts stay separate. B changes timing, not size. C would put all the filings in the coordinator's context, which is worse.
bullets: Subagents isolate verbose exploration output while the main agent keeps high-level understanding
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A research run with a coordinator and six subagents crashed at about 70% completion when a host restarted. On restart the coordinator spawned all six again, and the run repeated about two hours of work. Which design best avoids this next time?
opts: Each subagent exports state to a known path; the coordinator reloads a manifest on resume.
Ask the coordinator to remember which subagents finished, and trust that memory after the restart.
Raise the host's timeout so that long runs are less likely to be interrupted by a restart.
Save only the final report, since the earlier steps can be regenerated from it later.
questions.explain: State exported to known locations and indexed by a manifest survives the process, so the coordinator can skip finished work. B relies on memory that died with the process. C reduces how often crashes occur, but does not help once one happens. D keeps nothing until the end, so a mid-run crash has nothing to restore.
bullets: Crash recovery needs structured state: each agent exports state to a known place and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A coordinator resumes an extraction run from `manifest.json`, which lists all 12 chunks as `done`. The merged output is missing the results of 3 chunks. The file's modification time is 10 minutes before the crash, yet all 12 `done` entries were added within the first second of the run. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The subagents wrote output that was too large for the coordinator to merge into one file.
The manifest was updated before each chunk's state was exported, so `done` meant nothing.
The coordinator should have reloaded its own conversation instead of reading a manifest file.
A larger context window was needed to hold all twelve chunk results at once during merging.
questions.explain: Entries written in the first second cannot reflect finished work; a manifest should change only after the matching state export is safely written. A has no support in the log. C offers an unrelated mechanism that would not know about chunk files. D treats a bookkeeping error as a capacity problem.
bullets: Crash recovery needs structured state: each agent exports state to a known place and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A team designs what each research agent should export so that a replacement agent can continue after a crash. Which export is best?
opts: The agent's complete transcript, which a replacement can read through from the start.
A structured list of finished items with their findings and sources, but no list of pending ones.
Structured entries of finished items, with sources, and the identifiers still pending.
The agent's own estimate of how complete the work is, shown as a percentage of the total.
questions.explain: Structured state lets a replacement skip finished items, reuse findings with their sources and pick up the pending ones. A brings back the bulk and the noise. B records what is done but gives a replacement no way to know what remains. D is a self-report that says nothing about which items remain.
bullets: Crash recovery needs structured state: each agent exports state to a known place and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A developer has the main agent trace refund flow dependencies in an 80-file service. Tracing in the main conversation has already consumed 40% of the context, and three more questions about the same service are queued. How should the next question be delegated?
opts: Spawn a subagent told to explore the service and report anything that seems relevant to it.
Spawn one subagent per file, so that each of the 80 files is read separately in isolation.
Finish tracing in the main conversation first, then spawn a subagent to summarise what it found.
Spawn a subagent with the exact question and the answer shape wanted, e.g. callers per module.
questions.explain: A subagent starts without the conversation or the files already read, so it needs a precise question and an answer shape. A is vague and invites a sprawling report. B creates 80 contexts and loses the connections between files. C summarises after the verbose reading has already filled the main context.
bullets: Spawning subagents for specific questions while the main agent keeps coordinating
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A coordinator asks a subagent to "find all test files" in a large repository. The subagent returns 2,100 paths, about 18,000 tokens, and the coordinator's context jumps. The coordinator only needs to know which directories hold tests and how many files each framework has. What is the best change?
opts: Ask for counts grouped by directory and framework, with the full path list saved to a file.
Ask the subagent to return only the first 100 paths it finds, and ignore the remaining ones.
Do the search in the main conversation and pipe the output through `head` to cut it short.
Spawn a second subagent to condense the first subagent's list before it reaches the coordinator.
questions.explain: The request should shape the answer to what the coordinator will use, and the full list stays available on disk. B returns an arbitrary slice that may miss whole directories. C puts the search back in the main context. D adds a second agent to fix a problem that a better request avoids.
bullets: Spawning subagents for specific questions while the main agent keeps coordinating
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: A developer wants a subagent to help understand an invoice extraction pipeline in which totals sometimes differ by a cent between ingest and export. Which delegation request is best?
opts: Review the whole extraction package, read every module in it, and report anything that looks wrong or surprising.
Trace where `invoice_total` is rounded between ingest and export; return file and line for each step.
Build a deep understanding of the pipeline so that you can answer later questions about it.
Read every module under `extract/` and return their contents with your comments added.
questions.explain: A specific question with a defined return gives a short answer the main agent can use. A is open-ended and returns a broad report. C asks for understanding that stays in the subagent, because it does not carry over to later questions. D copies the verbose material back into the main context.
bullets: Spawning subagents for specific questions while the main agent keeps coordinating
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A team wants its codebase-exploration agent to counter context degradation. Which instruction, added to the task prompt, best sets up the behaviour?
opts: Every 20 turns, write a summary of everything you know into the chat so that it stays visible to you.
Keep what you learn in mind throughout, and tell me if you feel unsure about any earlier detail.
Append each finding to `.scratch/findings.md` as path, symbol, fact; read it before new questions.
Write all findings to a single notes file once the whole exploration is finished, then read it.
questions.explain: Writing as findings appear and reading before each new question puts verified specifics back in front of the model. A keeps the summaries inside the conversation that degrades. B relies on the model's recall, which is the thing that fails. D writes too late: earlier findings may already be lost.
bullets: Having agents keep scratchpad files and consult them for later questions
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A research agent's scratchpad has grown to 4,000 lines over a week of work. Reading it in full at the start of each question now uses about 25,000 tokens, and answers have started to blur again. What is the best change?
opts: Keep a one-line index plus per-topic files, and read the index and only the topics needed.
Stop re-reading the scratchpad and rely on the agent's memory of what it contains instead.
Have a larger model rewrite the scratchpad into a shorter summary at the end of each night.
Delete entries once the file passes 4,000 lines, starting from the oldest, to keep it short.
questions.explain: An index lets the agent find relevant entries while detail stays out of context until needed. B abandons the mechanism that counters degradation. C risks summaries that lose specifics, and the model size does not matter. D discards findings by age instead of relevance.
bullets: Having agents keep scratchpad files and consult them for later questions
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: An exploration session is auto-compacted at turn 90. The agent keeps a scratchpad, last updated at the end of the previous phase. Afterwards it re-reads the scratchpad but still cannot name about 40 call sites that it found earlier in the current phase, though it recalls everything from before. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Compaction deletes files that were written less than an hour before it ran, as a safety measure.
The scratchpad format could not hold call sites, so the agent skipped recording them as it worked.
Compaction summarises only the most recent turns and keeps the older turns word for word in the context.
Findings were written only at phase end, so the current phase's findings lived in the conversation.
questions.explain: What was only in the conversation was compressed; what was on disk is still intact, which matches the pattern. A has no basis, since compaction does not touch files. B does not fit an agent that recalls everything that was recorded. C has it backwards: compaction summarises older conversation.
bullets: Having agents keep scratchpad files and consult them for later questions
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A research coordinator finishes phase one, which found 30 candidate sources, and now spawns eight subagents to read the chosen sources in depth. How should it start the phase-two subagents?
opts: Tell them to continue from phase one, since the earlier work is part of the shared context here.
Put a short phase-one summary (ranked sources, reasons, exclusions, open questions) in each prompt.
Give each subagent the raw phase-one transcript so that it has absolutely everything to work from.
Let each subagent rediscover the sources itself, to avoid carrying forward any earlier mistakes made.
questions.explain: A new subagent has only its prompt, so a compact summary of what phase one decided must be put there. A assumes an inheritance that does not exist. C brings back the full bulk the phase split was meant to avoid. D repeats phase one eight times.
bullets: Summarizing one exploration phase and injecting the summary into the next phase's subagents
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A code-audit coordinator injects a complete 600-word phase-one summary listing the 40 modules flagged as risky. Phase-two reviewers flag 14 further modules that phase one examined and rejected, and about a third of the reviewers' time goes to them. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Phase-two subagents inherited an outdated copy of the phase-one conversation from the coordinator.
The summary was cut off by a prompt length limit, so the rejections at its end never arrived.
The summary recorded what was found but not what was ruled out, so reviewers re-derived it.
The reviewers were given too much context, which made them check more modules than needed.
questions.explain: A summary that lists the 40 flagged modules but not the rejected ones gives the next phase no reason to skip them. A is wrong because new subagents inherit nothing. B invents a truncation; the summary reached the prompts and simply lacked the rejections. D mistakes the cause: the context given was incomplete, not excessive.
bullets: Summarizing one exploration phase and injecting the summary into the next phase's subagents
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: A coordinator is about to launch eight phase-two subagents. One engineer proposes injecting the full 25,000-token phase-one transcript into each "so nothing is lost"; another proposes a 1,500-token summary. How should you evaluate the proposals?
opts: Use the summary of decisions and evidence, with a pointer to the files that hold the detail.
Use the full transcript, because any summary will drop something that a subagent turns out to need.
Use neither, so the subagents work independently and avoid anchoring on what phase one decided.
Use a summary with conclusions only, because sources would use up context for no real gain.
questions.explain: A summary that carries decisions and evidence, plus pointers to detail, gives each subagent what it needs and spends little of its context. B puts the noise and 200,000 tokens of repeated bulk into the eight prompts. C wastes the phase-one work without any reason to need independence. D leaves out the evidence the next phase must check.
bullets: Summarizing one exploration phase and injecting the summary into the next phase's subagents
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: After a crash, a coordinator reloads its manifest, which lists three agents as `done` and two as `incomplete` with the paths of their state files. How should it resume?
opts: Respawn all five agents, and tell them that some of their work may already have been done today.
Ask the model to infer from the earlier final report which of the agents had finished.
Reload only the last report written, and respawn those agents that the report did not mention.
Skip the three done agents; respawn the two with their state file contents in the prompts.
questions.explain: The manifest says what to skip, and the exported state gives the respawned agents their starting point. A repeats finished work and leaves the agents to guess. B replaces recorded status with inference. C depends on a report that a crash may have prevented from being written.
bullets: Designing crash recovery with manifests that the coordinator loads and injects into agent prompts
questions.principle: Code guarantees, prompts only persuade: when a rule must always hold, enforce it in code (hooks, gates), not instructions.

questions.q: A resumed extraction run repeats 140 documents that were already processed. The coordinator's log shows it parsed a manifest with 140 `done` entries, then spawned six extractor agents with the prompt "process batch 3 of 5". What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The manifest was too long to be parsed, so the coordinator ignored it when it spawned them.
The coordinator read the manifest but did not put its contents into the extractors' prompts.
Extractors always restart from the first document of a batch after a crash has occurred.
The extractors' context was already full, which made them drop the earlier documents of a batch.
questions.explain: Fresh agents know only their prompt, so a manifest the coordinator read but did not pass on cannot change what they do. A contradicts the log, which shows it was parsed. C describes behaviour nothing in the setup mandates. D cannot apply to newly spawned agents with empty contexts.
bullets: Designing crash recovery with manifests that the coordinator loads and injects into agent prompts
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A refactoring run over 30 modules crashed while one agent was editing module 17. The manifest marks 1 to 16 `done` and 17 `in_progress`, and module 17's files on disk are partly changed. What is the best way to resume module 17?
opts: Treat module 17 as finished, since its files on disk already show some of the changes made.
Run `git checkout .` and restart all 30 modules from the beginning, to be certain of the result.
Mark it incomplete, inject its saved state, and tell the new agent to re-check the disk.
Skip module 17 and continue, then ask the model whether anything was left undone afterwards.
questions.explain: The saved state shows what was intended and the disk shows what happened, so the new agent must be told about both. A assumes a half-edited module is complete. B discards sixteen finished modules. D leaves a possibly broken module for the model to guess about.
bullets: Designing crash recovery with manifests that the coordinator loads and injects into agent prompts
questions.principle: Keep facts, sources and failures intact as they move through the system; never let them vanish silently.

questions.q: After three hours exploring authentication code, a developer's context is at 70%. The findings exist only in the conversation, and nothing has been written to disk. Next the agent will write a migration plan for the auth module. What is the best step before starting the plan?
opts: Run `/compact` with instructions to keep the auth module's paths, call sites and open questions.
Run `/clear` so that the planning starts with an empty context and no leftover detail at all.
Wait for auto-compaction, which keeps whatever the model finds most important at that moment.
Run `/compact` with no instructions, so that the default summary covers the whole session evenly.
questions.explain: A focused `/compact` lets you choose what the summary keeps, instead of what the automatic pass guesses. B is destructive here: findings never written to disk would be erased. C leaves the choice to the model, and may happen at a bad moment. D spreads the summary over everything, including the verbose output.
bullets: Using /compact to cut context use when exploration has filled it with verbose discovery output
questions.principle: Nothing is inherited or inferred: state context, criteria and examples explicitly.

questions.q: A repository has `.claude/rules/billing.md` with `paths:` frontmatter for `billing/**`, requiring amounts in cents. During a long session the agent follows it while editing billing files. After `/compact`, it edits a billing file that it had read before the compaction and writes decimal amounts, though the rule file is unchanged. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: `/compact` removes every rule file from the session, including the root-level ones loaded at start.
The rule loaded into the conversation when billing files were read, so the summary absorbed it.
The rule file is re-injected from disk after compaction, so the agent chose to ignore it.
The rule is too long, so compaction cut it down to its first few lines when it re-injected.
questions.explain: Path-scoped rules load into message history when a matching file is touched, so compaction summarises them with the rest. A is wrong: unscoped rules and the root CLAUDE.md are re-injected. C is wrong because the docs say the rule is summarised away with the rest of the history, not re-injected. D confuses this with the size cap on skill bodies. The docs' own fix: drop `paths:` or move the rule to the root CLAUDE.md.
bullets: Using /compact to cut context use when exploration has filled it with verbose discovery output
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: An agent must answer questions about one 4 MB generated schema file. Each read of the file fills the context, automatic compaction summarises it, and the next read fills the context again. After a few attempts Claude Code stops compacting and reports an error. What is the best fix?
opts: Run `/compact` by hand each time the error appears, and repeat until the read completes.
Move to a model with a bigger window, hoping the entire file then fits in a single read.
Run `/clear` and repeat the same full read in the fresh session, now that the context is empty.
Have a subagent search the file, or read targeted ranges, and return only what is needed.
questions.explain: The file is the problem, so keep it out of the main context and bring back only the relevant parts. A repeats the loop that already failed. B moves the limit, but 4 MB of text remains a large read. C returns to the same full read that fills the context again.
bullets: Using /compact to cut context use when exploration has filled it with verbose discovery output
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Your QA team checked 2,000 supplier documents by hand and scored the extractor at about 97% overall. Since launch, the customs team has complained that nearly every customs declaration it receives has a wrong tariff code. Customs declarations are 3% of volume, the tariff-code field appears on all ten document types, and the other nine types are each at about 97% or better. Which explanation best fits the mismatch?
opts: The audit sample was too small to be trusted, so its 97% figure is mostly noise.
The tariff-code field is read badly by the model, whatever type of document it appears in.
Overall accuracy is dominated by the common types, so one weak type barely moves it.
The customs team is comparing declarations against a stricter standard than the audit used.
questions.explain: A figure averaged over all documents is mostly the large types, so a weak 3% slice can fail most of its documents while the total stays at 97%. A is not supported, since 2,000 documents give a stable overall figure, just not a per-type one. B contradicts the stem, because the other nine types are fine. D blames a reviewer for a complaint the audit design could not have shown.
bullets: An overall accuracy figure such as 97% can hide weak results on particular document types or fields
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: A support agent reads incoming emails and fills a form with order number, product, return reason and refund amount. The weekly dashboard shows 97% overall accuracy and has been flat for two months, yet the refunds team keeps correcting the refund amount by hand. Which change to the reporting best lets the team see where the pipeline is weak?
opts: Report accuracy per field and email type, with the number of checked items beside each cell.
Raise the target on the existing dashboard figure from 97% to 99% and alert when it is missed.
Add the average confidence score for the week beside the accuracy figure on the dashboard.
Double the weekly audit sample so that the overall figure moves less from week to week.
questions.explain: The overall figure averages fields that behave differently, so only a per-field view with counts shows the refund amount problem. B asks for a tighter version of the same number. C adds a score that is not measured against outcomes. D steadies the average without splitting it.
bullets: An overall accuracy figure such as 97% can hide weak results on particular document types or fields
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: An invoice extractor reads 12 fields per invoice. A hand check of 500 invoices shows each individual field is correct about 97% of the time. The finance system, however, rejects roughly 3 in 10 posted records because some value is wrong, and the team suspects the finance system's validation. What does the evidence point to?
opts: Per-field accuracy understates record-level errors, since one wrong field among twelve spoils a record.
The finance system is over-strict, because 97% accuracy should produce rejections in about 3% of records.
The invoice sample was drawn from easy documents, so the real field accuracy must be far below 97%.
Rejections come from the confidence threshold, because lowering it would admit fewer wrong fields.
questions.explain: A record is only usable when all its fields are right, so a 97% per-field rate leaves a large share of records with at least one error; the metric must also be reported per record. B mistakes a per-field rate for a per-record rate. C assumes a bias the stem does not show. D reverses the effect of a threshold, which would send more fields to people, not fewer wrong ones to the finance system.
bullets: An overall accuracy figure such as 97% can hide weak results on particular document types or fields
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Fields below 0.85 confidence go to a review queue, and the rest are posted automatically. To judge the pipeline, the team reports the correction rate from the queue: reviewers changed 6% of items. A manager concludes that the pipeline is about 94% accurate overall. What is the main flaw in this estimate?
opts: It tells you nothing about the auto-posted fields, whose error rate has never been checked.
Six percent of the queue is too small a share of all fields to give a usable estimate.
Reviewers disagree with each other, so their corrections give an unreliable measure of accuracy.
A correction rate counts only changed values, so it cannot be turned into an accuracy figure at all.
questions.explain: The queue holds only the low-confidence items, so the quality of what posts without a person has never been observed; it has to be sampled directly. B comments on the size of the figure and C on the reviewers, but even a perfect queue measurement would say nothing about the auto-posted fields. D is wrong because corrections do give the queue's own accuracy; the trouble is which items they cover.
bullets: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions measures their error rate and reveals new error patterns
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your extraction pipeline auto-posts any field above 0.90 confidence. Three weeks ago a new supplier started sending invoices with the tax shown in a footnote, and the model now reads the wrong number at 0.95 confidence. Nothing in the review queue shows it, and a customer found it. Which sampling design would most likely have caught it early?
opts: Sample only fields in the 0.90 to 0.92 band, since a pattern shows first where confidence is weakest.
Sample the queue items that reviewers corrected most often, and extend the review to similar fields.
Sample the fields that validators flagged, because any new pattern must trip a validator first.
Draw weekly at random within each type from the posted band, plus a small plain random share.
questions.explain: A recurring random draw from the posted band, spread over types with a plain random share for what no stratum anticipated, can show a pattern that confidence and validators miss. A looks only at a thin edge of the band and the stem's error sits at 0.95. C assumes validators cover every new error. B examines the queue, where this error never appeared.
bullets: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions measures their error rate and reveals new error patterns
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A research assistant extracts figures from reports and posts those above 0.9 confidence. Each week a reviewer picks the 20 posted figures that look odd and checks them. Last month 30% of the picks were wrong, and leadership proposed pausing the assistant. The reviewer says the picks are the interesting ones, not typical ones. How should the measurement change?
opts: Keep the hand-picked checks as the error measure, since they surface the most informative failures.
Sample at random within each report type, and keep the hand-picked list only as a lead.
Raise the weekly pick from 20 to 100 so that the error rate stops swinging so much.
Check only the 20 posted figures with the highest confidence, because those are the ones nobody would review.
questions.explain: Hand-picked items are biased towards errors, so the 30% describes the picks, not the posted stream; a random draw gives an error rate you can report, and the picks stay useful for finding causes. A keeps the biased figure. C scales the same bias. D chooses by confidence rather than at random, so it still does not describe the stream.
bullets: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions measures their error rate and reveals new error patterns
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your extractor gives each 12-field invoice a single document confidence. Invoices under 0.9 go to reviewers, who take 6 minutes each because they re-key all twelve fields. Labelled data show that on a typical flagged invoice only one or two fields are wrong, and the rest are right over 99% of the time. What design change best cuts review effort without removing coverage?
opts: Give every field its own confidence, and show reviewers only fields under their threshold.
Lower the document threshold from 0.9 to 0.8 so that fewer invoices reach the reviewers at all.
Ask the model to list the fields it is unsure of, and trust that list as the review set each day.
Train reviewers to skim each flagged invoice and only re-key the fields that look wrong to them.
questions.explain: Field-level scores, with a threshold measured on labelled data for each field, send people to the fields that need them. B cuts volume but lets more wrong fields through unmeasured. C replaces a calibrated score with an uncalibrated list. D leaves the decision to the reviewer's eye, which is slow and varies by person.
bullets: Field-level confidence scores, calibrated on labelled validation sets, decide where review attention goes
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: You are building the labelled validation set that will calibrate review thresholds for a pipeline that handles 8 document types. The pilot customer sent 300 clean, typed invoices, which are the easiest to label. In production, 40% of volume is scanned forms and 15% is handwritten notes. What should the validation set look like?
opts: The 300 pilot invoices, because clean labels give the most accurate threshold.
A labelled sample from production documents of all eight types, scans and handwriting too.
The 300 pilot invoices plus several hundred more invoices from the same pilot customer.
Documents labelled by the model itself, because they can cover far more types at no extra cost.
questions.explain: Thresholds only mean something on documents like those they will be applied to, so the set must be drawn from the production mix, all eight types included. A calibrates on an easy slice and applies the result to scans and handwriting. C adds volume but no variety, so the easy slice still stands in for everything. D uses model labels as the ground truth they are meant to be checked against.
bullets: Field-level confidence scores, calibrated on labelled validation sets, decide where review attention goes
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A labelled set shows how fields behave by confidence band. 0.95 and above: 22% of fields, 0.4% wrong. 0.90 to 0.95: 24% of fields, 2.0% wrong. 0.80 to 0.90: 25%, 6.0% wrong. 0.70 to 0.80: 17%, 9.0% wrong. The rest fall below 0.70. Policy allows at most 1.5% wrong among all auto-posted fields taken together, and wants as much posted automatically as that allows. Which threshold do you set?
opts: 0.90: fields above it are 1.2% wrong together, which fits though one band alone does not.
0.95, because the 0.90 to 0.95 band alone is 2.0% wrong, which is above the limit.
0.80, since it posts 71% of fields and is the highest volume that stays near the limit.
0.70, because the extra volume is worth a few more errors that reviewers can clean up later.
questions.explain: The limit covers all auto-posted fields together, so the bands are combined: the top two give (22% x 0.4% + 24% x 2.0%) / 46% = 1.2% wrong while posting 46% of fields. B judges one band alone against a limit that covers the whole posted set, and gives up volume. C adds the 6.0% band and reaches about 2.9% together. D reaches about 4.1% and leaves the errors in posted data.
bullets: Field-level confidence scores, calibrated on labelled validation sets, decide where review attention goes
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: Before auto-posting high-confidence extractions, the team tabulates labelled results. Policy: automate a type-and-field combination only if accuracy is at least 98% on at least 200 labelled items. Invoices: total 99.1% (n=420), due date 98.6% (n=420), line items 93.0% (n=420). Receipts: total 98.9% (n=35). Credit notes: total 98.0% (n=210). Which set may be automated?
opts: Invoice total and due date, and receipt total, because every one of them is above 98%.
Invoice total, due date and line items, because invoices average above 98% over their three fields.
Invoice total and due date only, because the credit note result is exactly on the limit.
Invoice total, due date and credit note total, since each meets both rules.
questions.explain: Each combination is judged on its own accuracy and its own sample size: invoice total, invoice due date and credit note total pass both tests. A includes receipt total, whose 35 items are too few. B lets the strong fields carry the line items at 93%. C wrongly drops the credit note, which sits exactly at 98.0% and meets the rule.
bullets: Accuracy must be checked by document type and field segment before high-confidence extractions are automated
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: The pipeline has been validated on English invoices, with 97.8% accuracy in every segment. The company now receives German and Spanish invoices at 30% of volume, and the plan is to put them straight into the existing auto-post rule because the layouts look the same. What should happen first?
opts: Run them through the existing rule and treat the first month's complaints as the test.
Translate each invoice to English first, since validation then transfers directly.
Auto-post them with the English thresholds at once, and double the weekly sampling for a month.
Keep them in full review while each language and field is measured on a labelled sample.
questions.explain: Accuracy for one segment does not carry over to another, so the new languages need their own labelled measurement before automation. A treats customers as the test. B adds a translation step that creates new errors and still has not been measured. C posts unmeasured values from day one, and sampling finds the problem only after wrong values have been posted.
bullets: Accuracy must be checked by document type and field segment before high-confidence extractions are automated
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: Six months after launch, policy requires every stratum to stay under 2% errors among auto-posted fields, and the dashboard shows 1.4% overall. The weekly stratified sample of 60 faxed documents, which are 4% of auto-posted volume, has shown 6% to 8% errors in each of the last four weeks, while every other stratum stays under 1.5%. What is the best response?
opts: Do nothing, since the overall figure meets the limit and faxes are a small share of volume.
Return faxed documents to full review until fixed, and keep sampling the other strata.
Raise the confidence threshold for all documents so that fewer faxed extractions pass.
Stop auto-posting entirely until the whole pipeline has been revalidated on fresh labels.
questions.explain: The policy applies to each stratum, and four weekly samples of 60 all above it make the fax result a pattern, not noise, so pull that segment back to review and leave the healthy ones running. A lets a known bad segment through because it is small. C penalises every segment, and a global threshold was never shown to fix faxes. D stops work that the sample shows is healthy.
bullets: Accuracy must be checked by document type and field segment before high-confidence extractions are automated
An overall accuracy figure such as 97% can hide weak results on particular document types or fields
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: You sample 50 auto-posted extractions at random from each of five document types and review them. Errors found: invoices 1, receipts 0, purchase orders 3, credit notes 2, bills of lading 6. Auto-posted volume is invoices 70%, receipts 15%, purchase orders 8%, credit notes 5%, bills of lading 2%. How should you report the error rate for the auto-posted stream as a whole?
opts: Pool all 250 reviewed items and divide the 12 errors by 250, giving one overall rate.
Take the simple average of the five stratum error rates and report it as the stream rate.
Report the worst stratum, bills of lading, as the error rate for the whole stream.
Weight each stratum's rate by its volume share, and publish the five rates too.
questions.explain: Strata were sampled equally but contribute unequally to the stream, so each stratum's rate is weighted by its volume share; the per-stratum rates stay visible so a weak one is not hidden. A and B treat the five strata as equal in size, which overweights the rare types. C is the right figure for that stratum and the wrong one for the stream.
bullets: Setting up stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for ongoing error measurement
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: Your weekly plan reviews 10 random auto-posted extractions from each of eight strata. After a month no errors were found in any stratum, and a manager says the auto-post error rate is zero. The target is under 3% errors in each stratum. How should the plan change?
opts: Keep the 10-per-stratum plan, because zero errors in every stratum already shows the target is met.
Raise each stratum to about 100 items a week, so that a clean result can rule out rates above 3%.
Merge the eight strata into one pool of 80 items, which gives a single more reliable figure.
Drop the eight strata and review the 80 items that have the highest model confidence.
questions.explain: Ten clean items fit a stratum with 10% errors about one time in three (0.9 to the power 10 is 0.35), so they cannot show the 3% target is met; about 100 items make a clean result unlikely if the rate were 3% or more. A takes a thin sample as proof. C gives one number for eight strata, so a weak stratum is hidden and each stratum's target is still untested. D swaps random draws for a biased pick.
bullets: Setting up stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for ongoing error measurement
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A support agent auto-resolves refund cases using extracted order data. The QA team ran a thorough stratified review of 600 auto-resolved cases at launch, found 1.2% errors, and stopped sampling. Two months later a new product line doubled the share of bundle orders, and complaints about bundle refunds are rising. What should have been in the plan from the start?
opts: A one-off sample at a larger size, since the launch result would then have held for longer.
A rule to re-run the launch sample only when complaints exceed a set number per week.
A recurring random sample per stratum, with the strata revised as the order mix shifts.
A switch to full review of every auto-resolved case for the first six months of operation.
questions.explain: The input mix shifts after launch, so measurement has to continue and the strata must follow the mix. A cannot see a change that has not happened yet. B waits for customers to find the problem. D removes the automation benefit for six months and still stops afterwards.
bullets: Setting up stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for ongoing error measurement
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A prompt change lifted overall extraction accuracy on the support team's labelled set from 95.4% to 97.1%, and the team wants to cut human review on the strength of it. The per-segment table shows typed emails up from 96% to 99% (92% of volume), but forwarded screenshots down from 88% to 75% (8% of volume). What should you do?
opts: Cut review for everything, because the overall figure improved and the screenshot slice is small.
Cut review for typed emails only, keep screenshots in full review, and investigate the drop.
Keep the old prompt for screenshots and the new one for typed emails, without further testing.
Cut review for everything but ask the model to be careful with screenshots in the new prompt.
questions.explain: The overall gain came entirely from the dominant segment while a segment fell sharply, so review can reduce only where the segment-level result supports it. A trades a 13-point drop for a better average. C routes between prompts with no measurement of the combined set-up. D hopes a prompt line fixes a regression that has not been diagnosed.
bullets: Analysing accuracy by document type and field before human review is reduced
An overall accuracy figure such as 97% can hide weak results on particular document types or fields
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: The accuracy analysis by document type shows invoices at 98.0%, purchase orders at 97.5% and credit notes at 97.2%, all above the 97% bar, so the team prepares to cut review for all three. Reviewers report that corrections to the tax amount happen in every document type. What does the analysis miss?
opts: The type-level split is correct, so the corrections must come from reviewers who are too strict.
Averaging within each type can hide a field that is weak in all of them, so split by field.
The three types are too close to each other, so the analysis needs a fourth type to be meaningful.
Accuracy should be measured on corrections made by reviewers, not on a labelled set.
questions.explain: A weak field spread across every type can be diluted by the strong fields of each type, so accuracy has to be broken down by type and by field before review is reduced. A dismisses the corrections without checking. C adds a type but not the field view. D swaps the labelled ground truth for a count that only covers queued items.
bullets: Analysing accuracy by document type and field before human review is reduced
questions.principle: Fix the root cause the evidence points to, and do not blame a component that is working.

questions.q: Reviewers cannot keep up: the queue grows by 300 items a day. A report on the last month's reviewed items shows that for supplier-A invoices the reviewers changed under 1% of the extracted values, while for handwritten notes they changed 35%. The team wants a defensible way to shrink the queue. What is the best step?
opts: Raise the global confidence threshold so fewer items enter the queue, whatever their type.
Drop the oldest items from the queue so that reviewers are always working on the freshest cases.
Take supplier-A invoices out of review once a labelled sample confirms them, and keep sampling.
Ask reviewers to skim each item and approve it quickly unless something looks clearly wrong.
questions.explain: The correction rates are a lead, and a labelled sample confirms them for the segment before its review is reduced; sampling then keeps watching it. A shrinks the queue by dropping the checks of every type, including the 35% one. B drops items by age, not by risk. D lowers the quality of every review.
bullets: Analysing accuracy by document type and field before human review is reduced
Routing low-confidence or ambiguous/contradictory extractions to people, spending limited reviewer capacity wisely
questions.principle: Take the smallest change that fixes the problem first; do not add infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried.

questions.q: You are designing the extraction tool schema for invoices, and review must be routed per field. Which output design supports calibrating thresholds with labelled data and routing per field?
opts: One confidence number for the whole invoice, plus the list of field names the model finds hard.
Each field returned with a free-text note on how sure the model is of its value.
Each field returned with a yes-or-no flag saying whether a person should check it.
Each field returned as an object holding its value and its own confidence score.
questions.explain: Calibration compares each field's reported confidence with labelled outcomes, so every field needs its own value and score in a structured form. A offers only a document score and a list the model chooses. B hides the signal in text that code cannot threshold or compare with labelled outcomes. C gives a decision the model has already made, so there is no score to calibrate a threshold on.
bullets: Having the model output field-level confidence, then calibrating review thresholds on labelled validation sets
questions.principle: Match the feature to the workload, and know what actually exists and what it does.

questions.q: Thresholds were set from a 300-document labelled set that gave 98% accuracy above 0.88 confidence; the prompt was refined over several rounds, each checked against that same set. In production, a stratified sample of the auto-posted band finds 93% accuracy, with no model update and no change in document mix. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The labelled set overlapped the documents used to tune the prompt, so calibration looked too good.
Reviewers who produced the production labels are stricter than those who produced the validation labels.
Confidence scores drift slowly over time, so a drop after a few weeks is unavoidable in any system.
The threshold of 0.88 is too coarse, and a threshold of 0.885 would restore the 98%.
questions.explain: A validation set that the prompt was tuned on gives optimistic numbers, so the threshold looked safer than it was. B invents a labelling difference the stem does not mention. C asserts drift with no change to explain it. D treats five-thousandths of a point as the cause of a five-point gap.
bullets: Having the model output field-level confidence, then calibrating review thresholds on labelled validation sets
questions.principle: Verify independently; self-review and self-reported confidence are not evidence.

questions.q: A support agent extracts a refund form from emails and reports a confidence per field. The labelled set has 600 fields. In the 0.5 to 0.7 band there are only 12 fields, and 11 are correct. A teammate proposes auto-posting that band, citing 92% accuracy. What is the right call?
opts: Auto-post the band, since 92% is above the 90% policy bar.
Auto-post the band, but ask the model to explain each value before it is posted.
Auto-post the band only for the fields that reviewers rate as easy, and review the rest.
Keep the band in review and label more fields there before trusting it.
questions.explain: Twelve labelled fields are too few to say what accuracy the band really has, so the threshold for it cannot be calibrated yet and the band stays with people while labels accumulate. A treats a thin estimate as measured. B adds a self-explanation that is not evidence. C relies on reviewers' impressions instead of labelled data.
bullets: Having the model output field-level confidence, then calibrating review thresholds on labelled validation sets
questions.principle: Escalate on customer requests, policy gaps and lack of progress, not on sentiment or a confidence score.

questions.q: Each day 1,500 fields fall below the review threshold, but reviewers can handle 400. Labelled data show that errors in the amount, tax and bank-account fields cost far more to fix after posting than errors in notes or reference fields. How should the queue be ordered?
opts: First in, first out, so that no item waits longer than another.
By lowest confidence overall, whatever the field, until the 400 are used.
By likelihood of error and cost of an error, with high-impact fields first.
At random each day, so that every field type gets reviewed equally often over time.
questions.explain: With room for 400 of 1,500, attention should go where a wrong value is both likely and expensive; calibrated confidence gives the likelihood and the field type gives the cost.
